cards.q: List the domains that make up the scope of modern anaesthesiology practice according to Miller.
cards.a:
Five domains of care, which together place anaesthesia at the centre of perioperative medicine.
- **Preoperative evaluation** and management of comorbid disease
- **Intraprocedural care**
- **Postoperative care**, including acute pain management
- **Critical care, resuscitation and retrieval**
- **Chronic pain** management
cards.e: Because of this breadth, Miller frames anaesthesia as central to perioperative medicine and to the wider health system. It therefore affects global health and the burden of disease, not only what happens in the operating room. Examiners like candidates to list all five rather than stopping at "the OR plus ICU".

cards.q: Which forces does Miller identify as reshaping anaesthesia practice in the 21st century?
cards.a:
Internal and external pressures acting together:
- **Changing patient populations** (older, more comorbid, obese, opioid-exposed)
- **Changing locations of care** (NORA, ambulatory centres, offices, the home)
- **Workforce shortages** and changing workforce composition
- **Escalating costs** and the move to value-based payment
- **Safety and quality** expectations
- **External disruptions**: conflict, climate change, COVID-19
- **Research** pressures and the explosion of **data**
cards.e: These forces affect training, how practices are organised and the safety of care. The chapter's message is that anaesthetists should lead the response, including in health policy and resource allocation, instead of only reacting to it.

cards.q: How large is the global surgical volume and what has driven the rise in demand for anaesthesia services?
cards.a:
More than **300 million** people had surgery worldwide in **2012**, and volume has risen since then.
- There was only a small dip in **2021** due to COVID-19
- Global moves towards universal access to safe surgery will push volumes higher
- **Interventional procedures** (radiology, pulmonology, gastroenterology, cardiology) have greatly increased requests for anaesthesia
cards.e: In high-income countries growth is driven mainly by ageing and better management of chronic disease. In low- and middle-income countries it is driven by better maternal and child health and by control of infectious disease. Oxford Handbook notes that postoperative mortality worldwide within 48 h fell from about 1% before the 1970s to about 0.12% since the 1990s, but remains 2–3 times higher in developing countries.

cards.q: What demographic projections about ageing does Miller cite, and why do they matter to anaesthetists?
cards.a:
The **WHO** projects that people **over 60** will make up nearly **one quarter** of the global population by **2050**. In the US, people aged 65 or older (Medicare-eligible) will exceed **78 million by 2030**.
- The effect will be greatest in **high-income countries** because of better preventive care and chronic disease management
- More patients at both **extremes of age** (including newborns, whose outcomes are improving) now receive surgery
cards.e: Older patients have less physiological reserve and organ function, so the whole perioperative pathway has to be managed carefully. The cost of caring for an ageing population is a challenge for every nation and a reason anaesthetists should take part in health policy.

cards.q: Why are mild cognitive impairment and dementia important in older surgical patients?
cards.a:
They are associated with **postoperative delirium**, **prolonged hospital stay**, **institutionalisation**, **higher readmission rates** and **mortality**.
- Care is increasingly delivered by **multidisciplinary teams** that include anaesthetists
- The anaesthetist may be the **first to identify** comorbid disease, which makes appropriate **referral** an important part of the role
cards.e: Oxford Handbook gives delirium after hip fracture surgery as about 1 in 2, and postoperative cognitive dysfunction in patients over 60 as about 1 in 4 at one week. Screening cognition preoperatively lets you set expectations and plan delirium prevention.

cards.q: Give Miller's obesity statistics and explain why obesity is a challenge for anaesthesia.
cards.a:
Obesity is now a **global epidemic**.
- **2016**: worldwide, overweight affected **39%** of adults and **18%** of children and adolescents
- **US**: obesity prevalence rose from **30.5% to 41.9%** between 2017 and 2020
- At every age it brings a higher **burden of disease and injury**, more contact with health services, and harder delivery of safe surgical and anaesthetic care
cards.e: The detailed anaesthetic management of obesity is covered in Miller Ch 54. Lippincott notes that morbidly obese patients with OSA often have persistent hypoxia, which can lead to pulmonary hypertension, and that they have more cardiac disease and compression neuropathies.

cards.q: Summarise the opioid epidemic data in Miller Ch 1 and the anaesthetist's role in addressing it.
cards.a:
The epidemic began with **liberal prescribing** for acute and chronic pain (including postoperative pain). It was made worse by **diversion** of prescribed drugs and a move to **non-prescribed opioids**.
- WHO: about **27 million** people had opioid use disorder worldwide in **2015**
- US **2017**: more than **191 million** opioid prescriptions (**58.7 per 100 persons**), with marked regional variation
- Up to **2.7 million** Americans have opioid use disorder
- **2016**: opioids involved in **42,249** overdose deaths, **66.4%** of all drug overdose deaths
cards.e: As experts in opioid pharmacology, anaesthetists and pain specialists are expected to help solve the crisis, mainly through **multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia** and responsible discharge prescribing. US HHS strategy includes better access to treatment and recovery, wider distribution of overdose-reversal drugs, better public health data and research on pain and addiction.

cards.q: Besides age, obesity and opioid use, which other patient factors does Miller list as changing the anaesthetic population?
cards.a:
Growing numbers of patients with:
- **Diabetes mellitus**
- **Immune compromise**
- **Food insecurity and malnutrition**, which can profoundly affect perioperative outcome
cards.e: Malnutrition is easy to miss in high-income settings. It is one reason ERAS pathways include preadmission nutritional support. Miller's point is that the anaesthetic population is becoming more heterogeneous and needs individualised care.

cards.q: Why has anaesthesia care moved outside the operating room, and what safety obligation follows?
cards.a:
Drivers of the move:
- Traditional OR care is **costly**, and its services may be **unnecessarily complex** for simple procedures
- Rapid growth in **ambulatory** surgery (in the US despite curbs on reimbursement)
- Rise of **minimally invasive** and interventional procedures by cardiologists, radiologists, endoscopists and pain physicians
Obligation: the **same standards** as the OR suite must be available. Accrediting agencies require provision for **extended admission and escalation of care** if clinically needed.
cards.e: Remote sites often lack the usual help for complex patients and crises. Anaesthetists are responsible for making sure monitoring, equipment, drugs and backup match OR practice. NORA is covered in Ch 69.

cards.q: How has the home become a setting for perioperative care, and what problems does this create?
cards.a:
Several trends move care into the home:
- Patients in high-income countries are no longer admitted **before the day of surgery**
- Preoperative assessment uses clinics and increasingly **telemedicine**
- Many procedures are **same-day**, and within **ERAS** protocols even post-inpatient recovery continues at home
- The US CMS **Acute Hospital at Home** waiver paid for hospital-level care at home during the public health emergency
- Remote monitoring can **passively collect** respiratory and circulatory data before and after surgery
Problem: early discharge can create **clinical and social burdens for families**, especially those caring for older relatives.
cards.e: Miller therefore says anaesthetists must help decide the **most appropriate setting** for a procedure, the plan for post-procedure oversight and the management of **transitions of care**.

cards.q: What is the anaesthesia department's role when sedation for colonoscopy is given by non-anaesthesiologists?
cards.a:
Colon cancer screening has caused an **exponential rise** in colonoscopy referrals. Sedation providers vary internationally.
- The anaesthesia service should have **input into credentialling** non-anaesthesia sedation providers, so that their education and training are adequate
- US and international guidelines accept that non-anaesthesiologist physicians and nurse practitioners give endoscopy sedation, including **propofol-based** deep sedation and general anaesthesia
- For any **high-risk patient**, an anaesthesiologist **should take part** in the care
cards.e: Anaesthetists commonly coordinate or medically direct these services, particularly for older patients with multiple comorbidities. The trap is to think the department has no responsibility for sedation it does not personally give.

cards.q: Why is there a global shortage of anaesthesia providers?
cards.a:
Several pressures act together:
- New graduates **not keeping pace** with **retirements**
- **Work-hour restrictions** and more attention to **work–life balance**, which affect recruitment and retention
- **Rising demand** across the continuum of care
- **Subspecialisation**: separate subspecialty call pools (cardiac, transplant, paediatric, critical care, pain, palliative care) need more staff
- **COVID-19** made shortages worse, partly through **burnout**, and they persisted after admissions fell
cards.e: In the US the number of residency positions is limited by federal funding caps. Workforce supply is an equity issue as well, because shortages fall hardest on rural and underserved populations (see Ch 2).

cards.q: How have countries and organisations responded to anaesthesia workforce shortages?
cards.a:
Main responses:
- Most **OECD** countries have **increased medical school admissions**. In the US no extra pre- or postgraduate education funds came with this
- The **AAMC** proposed reviewing the cap on federally funded positions, **better use of technology** and **more team-based care**
- Expansion of **non-physician providers**: in the US, physician and non-physician anaesthesia provider numbers are **approaching parity**, and nurse anaesthetists and anaesthesia assistants are growing faster
cards.e: Team-based care raises scope-of-practice questions for non-physician providers. It is nevertheless already common worldwide. Ch 2 describes how training and supervision of these cadres vary between countries.

cards.q: What did the ASA's 2017 statement on the anaesthesia care team set out?
cards.a:
A vision of **physician-led** anaesthesia care teams. Anaesthesiologists have particular responsibility for:
- **Governance, planning and oversight** of anaesthesia care
- **Advanced airway management**
- **Resuscitation**
cards.e: Similar team models are established or emerging elsewhere. In Ch 2, Miller notes that supervision models range from autonomous nurse anaesthetists to direct physician supervision, and that quality varies with training.

cards.q: What does Miller say about gender and diversity in the anaesthesia workforce?
cards.a:
Diversity supports **safe, high-quality care, better outcomes and innovation**.
- Women now make up **over 50%** of medical students in many countries, but US anaesthesiology residencies historically recruited fewer women (**37%**)
- Women in academic departments have faced problems with **promotion and salary equity**, and few have historically become professors, chairs or society leaders, although numbers are rising
- Crises such as **COVID-19** tend to add to the carer responsibilities of women
- Schemes such as **Athena SWAN** support recruitment and advancement, and inclusion programmes for diverse racial, ethnic, gender and sexual identities should be actively supported
cards.e: Examiners may ask why diversity is a safety issue. Miller links it directly to patient care quality and innovation, not only to fairness.

cards.q: What proportion of GDP is spent on health care, and what did the Institute of Medicine recommend?
cards.a:
Health care consumes about **8% of GDP** on average and nearly **18% in the US**, yet higher spending has **not produced better outcomes**.
- The Institute of Medicine called for competition to be built around the **value** of services rather than their **volume**
- Anaesthetists should understand the **costs** of the care they give and work with surgeons and health-system leaders to promote **value-based care**
cards.e: Drug and technology costs are major contributors to anaesthesia costs and need collaborative solutions. Ch 3 develops the payment models that follow from this.

cards.q: Compare fee-for-service with pay-for-performance and value-based payment models.
cards.a:
**Fee-for-service** pays for **inputs** (volume of services). **Pay-for-performance/value-based** models reward care that follows evidence and improves measured performance while costs stay the same or fall.
Measures rewarded can be:
- **Process**, e.g. timely perioperative antibiotics
- **Output**, e.g. meeting targets for urgent surgery
- **Outcome**, e.g. fewer central line–associated bloodstream infections
cards.e: FFS dominates where there is no universal coverage, especially the US. Be ready to classify a given quality measure as process, output or outcome. Oxford Handbook gives the timing standard for prophylactic antibiotics as within 60 min before incision, a classic process measure.

cards.q: Name US pay-for-performance programmes and explain why their effect on outcomes has been limited.
cards.a:
Examples: the CMS **Premier Hospital Quality Incentive Demonstration** (2003–2009) and the national **Hospital Value-Based Purchasing** programme adopted after the Affordable Care Act (2011).
Reasons for limited effect:
- **Complex reporting** systems
- **Small** financial incentives or penalties
- **Delayed** payments
- **High cost** of implementing the programmes for practices
cards.e: The pilots did show that clinicians can understand costs and change practice in response to evidence. Other countries moving to P4P have had variable success. The lesson is that incentives must be meaningful and timely to change behaviour.

cards.q: What are "never events", and how do payers use them?
cards.a:
Serious, largely preventable harms that should never occur, for example:
- **Wrong-side surgery**
- **Retained foreign object**
- **Mismatched blood transfusion**
Payers increasingly **refuse to pay** for avoidable complications and never events.
cards.e: Because anaesthesia spans the whole perioperative continuum, anaesthetists can influence many of these practices (e.g. checklist use, transfusion checks). Miller adds that more research is needed to show which practices really improve outcomes.

cards.q: What is a bundled payment, and how does the Perioperative Surgical Home relate to it?
cards.a:
A **single payment** for an **entire episode of care**, covering hospital and physician services for a defined period, designed to make all providers coordinate.
- Included in the US Affordable Care Act reforms, but not widely implemented
- The CMS **Bundled Payments for Care Improvement** programme tested this for surgical episodes such as **total joint arthroplasty**
- The ASA promoted the **Perioperative Surgical Home** as an **anaesthesiologist-led** model that coordinates team care, reduces cost and length of stay, and improves quality
cards.e: Under bundling, complications and readmissions come out of a fixed sum, so every provider has a financial reason to prevent them. Ch 3 describes the PSH in detail.

cards.q: Describe how incident reporting has contributed to anaesthesia safety, and name current reporting systems.
cards.a:
Incident reporting began in the US **over 50 years ago**. For anaesthesia it has shown a fall in anaesthesia-related mortality to **less than 1 per million population**.
- **Anesthesia Incident Reporting System (AIRS)** run by the Anesthesia Quality Institute
- **Wake Up Safe** run by the Society for Pediatric Anesthesia
cards.e: Note that the figure is per million **population**, not per anaesthetic. Oxford Handbook gives the risk of death related to anaesthesia as about **1:100,000** for ASA 1–2 patients, rising 5–10 times in ASA 3–4 or emergency patients. Do not mix up these denominators.

cards.q: Which human-factors and communication strategies has anaesthesia used to improve safety?
cards.a:
Strategies:
- **Simulation training** to improve **situational awareness** and **team functioning**
- **Checklists**, **time outs**, and structured communication at **transitions of care**
- Attention to **professionalism** and collegial work
- A **psychologically safe** environment where staff **speak up** (e.g. before a wrong-side procedure) and address **bullying and sexual harassment**
cards.e: Anaesthetists were pivotal in developing, implementing and evaluating the **WHO Surgical Safety Checklist**. Oxford Handbook adds that steep hierarchies stop staff raising concerns, and that briefings and debriefings combined with the checklist build a safety culture.

cards.q: What is the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, and what are its three phases?
cards.a:
A **19-item** checklist from the WHO **Safe Surgery Saves Lives** challenge. It was tested in eight centres in high- and low/middle-income countries and **reduced complications and mortality**.
- **Sign In** (before induction): identity, procedure, site, consent, machine and drug check, allergy, airway and blood-loss risk, monitoring available
- **Time Out** (before incision): team introductions, final confirmation, antibiotics, anticipated critical events
- **Sign Out** (before leaving theatre): counts, specimen labelling, postoperative concerns
cards.e: Miller credits anaesthesiologists as pivotal in its development. Oxford stresses it is meant to change team culture, not to be a tick-box exercise, and that it may be adapted locally; in low-income settings a pulse oximeter is the minimum monitoring standard.

cards.q: What distinguishes quality improvement from patient safety in Miller's framing?
cards.a: **Safety** focuses on preventing **error and harm**. **Quality improvement** is a continuous process that improves **outcomes and patient experience** by **measuring** care and making **systematic changes** to fix shortfalls.
cards.e: Anaesthesia was one of the first specialties to focus on patient safety. Miller argues the next step is to keep safety central while building quality measurement and improvement (see Ch 5).

cards.q: How is anaesthesia quality measured in the US, and how has the definition of quality widened?
cards.a:
The **Anesthesia Quality Institute** set up the **National Anesthesia Clinical Outcomes Registry (NACOR)** to collect quality data systematically for local and national improvement.
Quality now also covers:
- Outcomes **beyond the immediate perioperative period**, which matter to patients and families
- **Patient-centred care** and **patient satisfaction** as outcome measures
cards.e: Registries such as NACOR allow benchmarking between practices. Anaesthetists are expected to keep leading the safety and quality agenda because of their history, training and central position in the perioperative team.

cards.q: Which external disruptions have affected anaesthesia practice, and how has the specialty responded?
cards.a:
**Conflict** (both international and domestic), the **COVID-19 pandemic** and **climate change**.
Responses:
- Taking clinical skills into **new environments**
- New ways to **protect patients and staff** from harm
- Better **crisis management** through simulation and interdisciplinary training
- Recognising the effect on **physician well-being**: burnout and mental health problems
- Taking responsibility for the **climate impact** of clinical decisions
cards.e: Miller links well-being directly to quality and safety. Without addressing burnout, the specialty loses providers it needs to deliver care (Ch 6).

cards.q: What concerns does Miller raise about the funding of anaesthesia research?
cards.a:
US biomedical and health services research funding **more than doubled between 1994 and 2012**, but government funding growth has **not kept pace with inflation**.
Risks of shifting to private funding:
- Focus on **financial** rather than patient and societal benefit
- Less **early-stage** research, more device development and clinical trials
- Research effort is poorly **mapped** onto the **global burden of disease**
- Neglect of **health services research**
cards.e: Anaesthesiology fares poorly in NIH funding compared with other disciplines, and COVID-19 made this worse. Specialty-specific funding is therefore increasingly important, particularly for early-career investigators.

cards.q: Why are specialty-specific research foundations important? Give an example with figures.
cards.a:
They fund **early-career investigators** and help them win larger federal grants.
- The **Foundation for Anesthesia Education and Research (FAER)** has awarded more than **$35 million** since **1986**
- Each **$1** of FAER funding has been followed by about **$17** in federal funding
- The **International Anesthesia Research Society** and other national bodies run similar programmes
cards.e: Remember the $17-per-$1 leverage figure. Miller warns that the US must address these funding limits if it is to stay competitive, as governments elsewhere are funding basic and translational research.

cards.q: What practical forces reduce the amount and quality of anaesthesia research?
cards.a:
Several pressures:
- **Throughput pressure**: hospitals want more cases at lower cost, leaving less room for trials
- Academic anaesthetists spend more time on **hands-on clinical care**
- **High costs** of labour, infrastructure and compliance make US drug trials expensive
- A **reduced pipeline** of new anaesthetic drugs and few incentives to develop them while existing drugs remain profitable
cards.e: Together these explain why new anaesthetic drugs are rare. The response Miller describes is collaborative, multicentre research rather than isolated single-centre work.

cards.q: Why are anaesthesia trials increasingly run by large multicentre networks, and what other collaborative trends are there?
cards.a:
**Single-centre studies** are too slow and too small: they cannot enrol enough patients to settle important questions.
- Research teams now include **biostatisticians, health informaticians and health economists**
- Partnerships between **basic, clinical and implementation scientists** speed translation into practice
- Collaborative trials worked with unprecedented success during **COVID-19** (severe COVID pneumonia treatments, surgical safety studies)
- Anaesthetists are increasingly involved in **implementation science**
cards.e: Large pragmatic trials need many patients because important perioperative outcomes are rare. Database research also needs collaboration between institutions, clinicians and data experts.

cards.q: How does Miller propose that registries and biobanks lead to perioperative precision medicine?
cards.a:
By pairing **large, high-resolution patient registries** with **routine biobanking** of perioperative patients.
- This allows **phenotyping** of perioperative conditions
- **Proteomic, genomic, lipidomic and metabolomic** analysis with advanced biostatistics and computing
- Uses: **risk prediction**, phenotyping of pre-existing disease, predicting **drug responsiveness**, decision support and cost-effectiveness
cards.e: Other fields have already combined clinical data with molecular analysis; Miller says perioperative medicine urgently needs to do the same. Funding remains the main barrier.

cards.q: What threats to research integrity does Miller describe?
cards.a:
Anaesthesiology has had **high-profile research misconduct**: **fabrication**, **falsification** and **misleading reporting**.
- This has damaged the specialty's reputation and in some cases **put patients at risk**
- Strict **peer review** is needed to ensure reliable data and to limit **conflicts of interest**
- Clinicians also find it harder to identify **reliable, evidence-based** information despite easy access to large volumes of material
cards.e: Miller also argues that physicians must lead the generation of evidence for the specialty, while welcoming research by other professions that provide anaesthesia care.

cards.q: What sources of health care data are now available for anaesthesia research and quality work?
cards.a:
Data sources:
- **EHRs** integrating data from surgical equipment, anaesthesia delivery systems and physiological monitors
- **Billing** systems, **government and insurance** databases, **disease registries**, **public health** reporting
- Shared **research databases** and **biobanks** (including genetic databanks)
- **Metadata** from electronic resources and social media
cards.e: These data need management and analytic methods often beyond the practising clinician (Ch 87). They support research, guideline development and comparison of safety and quality between settings and regions.

cards.q: What are the limitations of database research compared with randomised trials?
cards.a:
Database research may seem a cheap alternative to RCTs, but it suffers from:
- **Missing data**
- **Misclassification**
- **Biased attainment** of data
- **Inability to link** datasets, or **inaccurate linkage**
- **Lack of verification**
cards.e: For this reason Miller expects **pragmatic, flexible RCTs** to stay relevant. In exams, link these problems to bias and confounding: a large sample does not fix a systematic error.

cards.q: What future trends does Miller predict for the location and personalisation of anaesthesia care?
cards.a:
Trends:
- Care continues to move into **preoperative clinics**, **intervention suites**, **extended PACUs** and **patients' homes**
- **Integrated EMRs**, large registries and **predictive analytics** support evidence-based, cost-effective care by multidisciplinary teams
- **Precision medicine** using omic data for risk prediction and drug response
- More patients at **extremes of age** gaining access to care, so care must be more **individualised**
cards.e: Miller also stresses the patient's role in **shared decision-making** and end-of-life choices (Ch 7) and the need for anaesthetists to engage in **health policy** on resource distribution.

cards.q: In what other ways, beyond the OR, does Miller see anaesthetists contributing to health systems?
cards.a:
Contributions:
- **Leading or providing intensive care**: in many countries ICU is run by anaesthesia departments, and intensivist training comes from joint anaesthesia–ICU colleges and societies
- **Crisis leadership** (e.g. during the COVID-19 pandemic)
- **Health policy** and resource allocation
- **Education** of the next generation and **research**
- Leadership roles in departments, health systems and politics
cards.e: Miller attributes the specialty's advances to anaesthetists' commitment to leadership, teaching and research. The concluding message is that 21st-century disruptions create leadership opportunities for the next generation.

cards.q: Your department is asked to start a sedation service for endoscopy and interventional radiology in a building with no operating theatres. Using Miller's principles, what must be in place before you agree?
cards.a:
Plan the service to OR standards:
- **Monitoring, equipment and drugs** equivalent to OR standards, including airway and resuscitation equipment
- Trained staff and appropriate **patient selection**, with anaesthetist-led care for high-risk patients
- A defined pathway to **escalate care** (transfer to OR, PACU or ICU, or extended admission) if the patient deteriorates
- Use of the **WHO checklist**/time out and team briefing adapted to the procedure
- **Quality and safety data** collection and incident reporting for the new service
cards.e: Miller stresses that remote sites often lack the usual support for crises, so the anaesthetist is responsible for making sure OR standards are available there. Oxford Handbook notes that the checklist should be adapted to local practice without being made too simple. Ch 69 covers NORA in detail.

cards.q: A hospital manager wants to cut anaesthesia costs by reducing staffing. How would you frame the discussion using value-based care?
cards.a:
Argue from **value** (outcomes and safety relative to cost) rather than cost alone:
- Bring **quality and safety data** (registry, incident reports, complication rates)
- Show how anaesthesia-led pathways (ERAS, perioperative medicine, PSH) reduce **complications, length of stay, readmissions** and total episode cost
- Point out that under **bundled payments** and non-payment for avoidable complications, harm caused by understaffing costs the hospital money
- Highlight **workforce shortages** and burnout, which make further cuts unsafe and threaten retention
cards.e: Miller notes that value-based payment requires documentation of quality, safety and equity, which anaesthesia departments are well placed to provide. Cost-cutting that increases complications is false economy under episode-based payment.

cards.q: The gastroenterology department plans to run its own propofol sedation lists for screening colonoscopies using nurse sedationists. They ask whether anaesthesia needs to be involved. How do you respond?
cards.a:
Support access, but insist on governance:
- Accept that guidelines allow **non-anaesthesiologist** providers, including propofol-based sedation
- Ask for **anaesthesia input into credentialling**: training, airway and resuscitation skills, competency assessment
- Agree **patient selection criteria**: older or **high-risk patients with multiple comorbidities** should have an **anaesthesiologist** involved
- Agree escalation, monitoring standards and audit
cards.e: Colon cancer screening has caused an exponential rise in colonoscopy demand, so anaesthesia cannot staff every list. Miller's position is shared responsibility: anaesthesia sets the standards and looks after the high-risk patients.

cards.q: An 84-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment who lives with her elderly husband is booked for day-case surgery under general anaesthesia. Her daughter worries about how they will cope at home. How do you plan her care?
cards.a:
Treat this as a **transition-of-care** problem as well as an anaesthetic one:
- Assess **cognition and frailty**, and recognise her higher risk of **postoperative delirium**, prolonged stay, readmission and institutionalisation
- Decide the **appropriate setting**: day-case only if home support is adequate, otherwise plan an overnight or extended stay
- Use techniques that reduce delirium risk and opioid use (regional or multimodal analgesia)
- Arrange **post-procedure oversight**: clear written instructions to family, telephone follow-up, possibly **remote monitoring**
- Communicate with her **primary care provider** and refer onwards for comorbidities found
cards.e: Miller warns that shorter hospital stays can create clinical and social problems for families caring for older relatives, and says anaesthetists must help choose the setting and manage transitions. The anaesthetist is often the first to identify cognitive impairment.

cards.q: During a time out, the circulating nurse notices the consent form says left knee but the surgeon has prepped the right knee. She hesitates to speak because the surgeon is senior and impatient. As the anaesthetist, what do you do, and what does this show about safety culture?
cards.a:
**Stop the procedure** and support the nurse:
- Invite her to state her concern and confirm site against consent, marking, imaging and the patient record
- Do not proceed until the discrepancy is resolved
- Afterwards, debrief the team and report through the **incident reporting** system
Principles shown: **psychological safety**, the duty to **speak up**, flat hierarchy at the checklist, and professional behaviour.
cards.e: Miller describes creating environments where staff voice safety worries (e.g. a wrong-side procedure about to start) and address inappropriate behaviour. Wrong-side surgery is a never event. Oxford Handbook notes that steep hierarchies stop team members raising concerns even when patients are at risk.

cards.q: A registrar presents a retrospective analysis of 200,000 anaesthetic records from a national database showing that one anaesthetic technique is associated with lower mortality. They propose changing departmental policy immediately. How do you critique this?
cards.a:
Acknowledge the value of the data, then examine the weaknesses:
- **Missing data** and **misclassification** of exposure or outcome
- **Biased attainment** (which patients get which technique: confounding by indication)
- **Linkage errors** between datasets and **lack of verification** of coded data
- Association does not show causation; large numbers do not remove systematic bias
Recommendation: treat this as **hypothesis-generating**. Look for supporting evidence and consider a **pragmatic multicentre RCT** before changing practice.
cards.e: Miller lists exactly these limitations of database research and expects flexible pragmatic RCTs to remain relevant. Multicentre networks exist because single centres cannot recruit enough patients for rare outcomes.

cards.q: A 45-year-old man taking long-term high-dose oral opioids for chronic back pain is scheduled for a laminectomy. The surgeon plans to discharge him with a large opioid supply. How does the population-level opioid epidemic influence your plan?
cards.a:
Plan **opioid-sparing, multimodal** care and responsible prescribing:
- Continue his baseline opioid and plan analgesia with **multimodal** adjuncts and regional techniques where suitable
- Involve the **acute or chronic pain service** before and after surgery
- Agree a **limited, defined discharge prescription** with a tapering plan and a named prescriber, to reduce **diversion**
- Screen for **opioid use disorder** and ensure access to overdose reversal and follow-up
cards.e: Miller attributes the epidemic partly to liberal postoperative prescribing and diversion, and says anaesthetists, as opioid pharmacology experts, must help resolve it, largely through improved multimodal pain management. Ch 3 notes that perioperative pain teams reduce opioid need and length of stay in chronic pain patients.

cards.q: How many people lack access to safe anaesthesia and surgical care, and what share of the global disease burden is surgical?
cards.a:
More than **5 billion** of the world's roughly 7 billion people lack access to safe, affordable anaesthesia and surgical care. A similar large proportion lack basic **oxygen therapy**.
- Surgical disease accounts for about **30%** of the global disease burden
- Less than **1%** of development assistance for health supports anaesthesia and surgical care
cards.e: This mismatch between burden and funding is one of the most striking in global health. Miller calls lack of access to safe anaesthesia and surgery one of the most neglected crises in global health.

cards.q: How does mortality from surgical conditions compare with HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria?
cards.a: Surgical conditions cause about **16.9 million** deaths a year, **more than four times** the combined total for TB (**1.21 million**), HIV/AIDS (**1.03 million**) and malaria (**0.72 million**).
cards.e: The burden falls mainly on LMICs. Yet surgery receives a tiny fraction of the funding these infectious diseases attract; in US global health funding (FY2022, $12.2 billion), HIV alone received about $5.5 billion.

cards.q: What is the economic cost of untreated surgical disease in LMICs?
cards.a:
Without scale-up:
- Surgical conditions could cut annual **GDP growth by about 2%** in LMICs by 2030, compared with **1.3%** estimated for malaria, which successfully attracted investment
- Cumulative productivity losses of more than **US$12 trillion** (LCOGS: **$12.3 trillion**) between **2015 and 2030**
cards.e: Economic framing was key to mobilising funding for malaria, and global surgery advocates use the same argument. Surgery is presented as an investment that promotes economic growth.

cards.q: State the World Bank income classification thresholds (GNI per capita) used in Miller.
cards.a:
For 2022–2023:
- **Low income**: less than **$1085**
- **Lower-middle income**: **$1086–4255**
- **Upper-middle income**: **$4256–13,205**
- **High income**: more than **$13,205**
cards.e: Disease burden is reported by World Bank income group or, increasingly, by socio-demographic index. The global health community no longer uses terms such as "third world", "developed" or "developing".

cards.q: Why does Miller use the term "global health equity" rather than "global health", and how is it defined?
cards.a:
**Global health equity** is a multidisciplinary field of study, research, practice and advocacy **rooted in social justice**. It seeks ways to make health and its determinants more equitable **wherever people live**, with emphasis on populations at greatest risk.
Reasons for the change:
- "Global health" is often misread as **outreach** or mission trips abroad
- Its predecessors carry a **negative legacy**: "tropical medicine" protected **colonisers**; "international health" meant projects in poor countries led by rich ones
- Global health programmes often show **power imbalances** favouring wealthier participants and do not raise up local priorities
cards.e: Global health equity is **not** the same as international aid or transfer of technology from HICs to LMICs. It combines strategies aimed at whole populations (e.g. injury prevention) with those aimed at individuals (clinical care), and needs international cooperation.

cards.q: Define "global surgery" (2014) and explain its relevance to anaesthesia.
cards.a:
An area of study, research, practice and advocacy that prioritises **better health outcomes and health equity** for all people worldwide with surgical conditions.
- Includes **all surgical specialties**, obstetrics and gynaecology, **anaesthesia**, perioperative care, aspects of emergency medicine, rehabilitation, palliative care, nursing and allied health
- Covers **underserved populations in all countries**, with emphasis on those affected by **conflict, displacement and disaster**
- Emphasises **supraterritorial and transnational** determinants and solutions
cards.e: The shortened definition does not mention anaesthesia directly, but "global surgery" has become the rallying point for anaesthesia equity work. Miller says if surgery is the "neglected stepchild" of global health, anaesthesia is the "forgotten relative".

cards.q: What are the social determinants of health, and what are the five domains?
cards.a:
Non-medical factors in homes, schools, communities and workplaces that shape most of health. They sit **downstream** of **structural determinants** (governance, economic and social conditions).
Five domains:
- **Economic stability**
- **Education access and quality**
- **Health care access and quality**
- **Neighbourhood and built environment**
- **Social and community context**
cards.e: No country outspends the US on health care, yet it is not in the top 25 for life expectancy, showing that most health is not determined by health care. Rudolf Virchow argued in the 19th century that medicine must enter political and social life.

cards.q: Give examples of how economic stability and the built environment affect health.
cards.a:
Economic stability:
- About **1 in 10** Americans (around 37 million) live in poverty; **1.2 billion** people worldwide live in **extreme poverty** (less than **$1.90/day**)
- Poverty is linked to obesity, asthma, diabetes, maternal mortality and heart disease; COVID-19 may have set back poverty reduction by up to 10 years
Built environment:
- Life expectancy about **85 years in Japan** vs about **54 in the Central African Republic**, and differences of **more than 20 years** between neighbourhoods of the same city
- **Two million Americans** lack running water or sanitation; the **Flint, Michigan** lead contamination resulted from poor governance and systemic racism
cards.e: Other built-environment factors are food deserts, mould and poor ventilation (asthma, CO and lead poisoning), and crime, which causes chronic stress and sedentary behaviour. Trauma outcomes are worse by socioeconomic status even in HICs.

cards.q: How do education and social and community context influence health?
cards.a:
Education:
- Higher education leads to better-paid, safer jobs, better housing and the ability to reflect on one's own well-being
- **85%** of the world's population is literate, but some communities have literacy **below 30%**, which limits **health literacy**
Social and community context:
- Workplace conditions, **incarceration**, civic participation and community cohesion
- **Structural conflict** and **unconscious bias**
- Harmful traditional practices, e.g. **female genital mutilation**, causing pain and obstetric complications
cards.e: Positive relationships at home and work can buffer negative effects. Health care access and quality is different from access to emergency services: reliance on the ED is linked to worse cancer, cardiac and stroke outcomes.

cards.q: What is a DALY, and what is the socio-demographic index (SDI)?
cards.a:
**DALY** (disability-adjusted life year) = **YLL** (years of life lost to premature death) + **YLD** (years lived with disability). One DALY is one lost year of healthy life. It was developed for the **GBD 1990** study and is used to guide resource allocation.
**SDI** is a composite of three predictors of health:
- **Income per capita**
- Average **educational attainment** (population over 15 years)
- **Total fertility rate**
It runs from 0 (lowest income and education, highest fertility) to 1.
cards.e: Leading causes of DALYs are now reported by World Bank income level or by SDI quintile. In low-SDI countries diarrhoea/LRI, neonatal disorders and NTDs/malaria still lead, whereas globally cardiovascular disease now ranks first.

cards.q: Compare the three main attempts to estimate the global burden of surgical disease.
cards.a:
Three estimates:
- **DCP2 (2006)**: educated guess by **18 surgeons** in an online survey; **11%** of burden. Widely quoted but probably a large **underestimate**
- **DCP3 (2015)**: modelled scaling-up of essential surgery in LMICs; **1.4 million deaths** and **77.2 million DALYs** preventable each year
- **LCOGS (2015)**: surveyed **173** clinicians and public health workers; **28–32%** of GBD needs a surgeon, so **30%** is surgically treatable, about **17 million deaths** a year
cards.e: Of preventable surgical deaths, **77%** stem from **injuries**, **14%** from **maternal–neonatal conditions** and **9%** from **digestive diseases**. Unintentional injury is the largest single contributor to DALYs worldwide.

cards.q: Why is the surgical disease burden hard to measure, and what alternative metrics have been proposed?
cards.a:
Difficulties:
- **Complex methodology** (e.g. IHME/GBD studies)
- **Defining surgical disease**: the same tumour may be treated surgically in one patient and with chemotherapy in another
- **Disability weighting** and attributing **DALYs averted** to specific procedures
Proposed alternatives: **disease prevalence**, **treatment backlogs** for non-fatal conditions, harm from **delays in care**, **social and economic benefit**, and **value of a statistical life** instead of cost per DALY averted.
cards.e: Better data drive advocacy and resource allocation, and Miller sees this as a key role for academic anaesthesia. The epidemiological transition (longer lives, more NCDs and road traffic injuries) will raise the surgical burden in LMICs.

cards.q: Summarise the global burden of pain.
cards.a:
Pain is among the commonest reasons to seek care and among the **top five causes of DALYs**.
- **Four of the ten leading causes of YLD** are painful: low back pain, neck pain, musculoskeletal pain, migraine
- **10–25%** of the world's population have recurring or chronic pain
- More than **80% of refugees** have chronic somatic pain after trauma
- These figures exclude cancer, injury and postoperative pain
cards.e: Uncontrolled pain harms health and productivity, including higher risk of myocardial infarction and chronification. Anaesthesia providers often have the most experience with analgesics and so play an expanded role, especially in resource-constrained settings.

cards.q: Define serious health-related suffering (SHS) and give the key statistics from the 2017 Lancet Commission on pain relief and palliative care.
cards.a:
**SHS** is suffering from illness or injury that compromises physical, social or emotional function and **cannot be relieved without medical intervention**.
- About **half of all deaths** worldwide involve SHS
- More than **80%** of people dying with SHS are in **LMICs**
- About **2.5 million children** die with SHS each year; **98%** are in LMICs, and over **90%** of these deaths could be avoided
cards.e: Top conditions associated with SHS include **HIV, malignancy and injury**. HIV is not usually a pain condition anaesthetists manage, but it is a useful rallying point for wider analgesic access. Diabetes, sickle cell disease and leprosy are also major sources of pain in many countries.

cards.q: What is known about the global burden of critical illness and oxygen access?
cards.a:
Data are limited, but:
- LMICs have a **higher burden**, higher mortality from recoverable illness and **younger** patients
- As much as **90%** of the population in many countries may have no access to **oxygen**
- In sub-Saharan African studies, **hypoxaemia** prevalence was **4–12%** with mortality **50–80%**; in one study only **6%** of those needing invasive ventilation received it
- Survey of over 200 hospitals in 12 African countries: fewer than **50%** had uninterrupted oxygen and fewer than **25%** had a **concentrator**
cards.e: Oxygen is on the WHO Essential Medicines List. Much critical illness (sepsis, trauma, obstetric emergencies, respiratory failure) can be averted with cheap, low-tech measures: oxygen, fluids, monitors and antibiotics.

cards.q: What did the COVID-19 pandemic reveal about global critical care inequity?
cards.a:
It exposed **oxygen insecurity** and ICU disparities in every country:
- Over **600 million** infected and over **6 million** deaths in two years
- Over **half a million** COVID patients in LMICs needed oxygen **daily**, excluding non-COVID hypoxaemic patients (children with pneumonia, malaria, HIV)
- **Critical care beds per 100,000** are more than **20 times** higher in HICs than LMICs
- **ARDS mortality** is about **70% higher** in many LMICs
cards.e: Even within HICs, critical care access and outcomes varied by social determinants, which the pandemic made visible. Miller sees investment in oxygen ecosystems after the pandemic as a major opportunity for health equity.

cards.q: Give the key maternal health disparities described in Miller Ch 2.
cards.a:
Of about **300,000** maternal deaths a year, **99%** are in low-resource settings (**66%** in sub-Saharan Africa), and most are preventable with basic surgical, anaesthetic and perioperative care.
- About **75%** are due to **haemorrhage** (mostly postpartum), **infection**, **pre-eclampsia/eclampsia**, delivery complications and **unsafe abortion**
- **ASOS**: maternal mortality after caesarean section in sub-Saharan Africa was **50 times** that of HICs
- In the US, **non-Hispanic Black women** are **3–4 times** more likely to die of pregnancy-related causes, and up to **12 times** in some cities
cards.e: Barriers for women include poverty, distance, lack of information, poor-quality services and cultural practices. Structural racism is increasingly recognised as a driver of disparities in HICs; reducing it needs quality improvement from preconception to postpartum.

cards.q: How many people lack access to surgery when access is defined more completely, and where is access worst?
cards.a:
Counting only the **distribution of operating theatres**, more than **2 billion** people lack access. Adding **timeliness, capacity, safety and affordability**, nearly **5 billion** do.
- In **sub-Saharan Africa** and **South Asia**, more than **95%** of people lack access
- In North America and Europe more than **95%** generally have access
- **1.7 billion children** lack surgical care (Global Initiative for Children's Surgery)
- About **143 million** additional procedures are needed each year
cards.e: Universal access to essential surgery (injury, obstetric complications, abdominal emergencies, cataract, congenital anomalies) would prevent about **1.5 million deaths** a year, **6–7%** of preventable deaths in LMICs. Injury causes nearly 5 million deaths a year, mostly in LMICs.

cards.q: State the LCOGS figures on surgical volume and its distribution.
cards.a:
Of about **313 million** procedures a year, just **6%** take place in the **poorest countries**, which hold more than a **third** of the global population.
- In low- and lower-middle-income countries, **9 of 10** people cannot access basic surgery
- **143 million** additional procedures are needed each year in LMICs
- Low operative volume is linked to **high case-fatality** from common treatable conditions
- The largest unmet need is in **South Asia** and in central, eastern and western **sub-Saharan Africa**
cards.e: Miller elsewhere cites an older estimate of **234 million** major procedures with only **3%** in LMICs housing 30% of the population. The message is the same: volume is concentrated where need is lowest. The LCOGS target is at least **5000 procedures per 100,000** by 2030.

cards.q: How has anaesthesia safety changed over time in high-income countries, and what monitoring gaps remain globally?
cards.a:
Perioperative safety has improved more than **10-fold** in half a century, mainly in HICs. In the US, anaesthesia-related mortality is now below **1:13,000** (even lower in healthy patients), down from about **1:1560** around 1950.
Gaps:
- About **32 million** people a year receive anaesthesia **without adequate monitoring**
- More than **77,000** operating rooms (**19%**) lack **pulse oximetry**, over **70%** in some regions
cards.e: Pulse oximetry is the minimum monitoring standard in the WHO checklist for low-income settings. Oxford Handbook gives anaesthesia-related death for ASA 1–2 patients in HICs as about 1:100,000, showing how wide the gap is.

cards.q: What perioperative mortality rates are reported from low-income countries, and what did ASOS show?
cards.a:
Reported POMRs from LICs vary widely: **0.2–6%** overall, about **10%** for **emergency** surgery and **20%** for **typhoid intestinal perforation**.
**ASOS** (247 hospitals, 25 African countries, adult inpatient surgery): **30-day in-hospital mortality 2.1%**, **twice the global average**, despite patients being **younger** with **lower ASA** status.
cards.e: Methods differ between studies, so comparisons need care. ASOS suggests that the excess deaths come from failure to rescue after complications rather than from sicker patients.

cards.q: Give examples of anaesthesia-related mortality reported from African countries and the causes identified.
cards.a:
Reported in the **1:100s**:
- Malawi **1:504**, Zimbabwe **1:482**, Nigeria **1:387** (caesarean section), Togo **1:133 to 1:250**
- Togo, 24-hour outcomes: **30 deaths in 1464 cases**, **22 avoidable**, **11** due to avoidable anaesthetic complications
- Another Togo survey: fewer than half of 26 facilities had **pulse oximetry**, **none** had capnography
- South Africa: **2.35%** of maternal deaths anaesthesia-related, **93%** avoidable; a common cause was **spinal anaesthesia** by providers unable to manage the airway or convert to GA
cards.e: Other common avoidable causes are **inadequate staffing**, **inadequate monitoring** and **drug overdose**. Most of these deaths are preventable with basic equipment and training.

cards.q: What did a meta-analysis show about anaesthesia-related maternal mortality in LMICs?
cards.a:
Risk of death from anaesthesia in obstetric procedures was **1.2 per 1000** in LMICs, vs **3.8 per million** in the US.
- Higher with **general anaesthesia** and with **non-physician** providers
- Anaesthesia caused **2.8%** of maternal deaths and **13.8%** of deaths during or after **caesarean section** in LMICs
- Compared with the US, mortality was about **900-fold** higher for **general** anaesthesia and **300-fold** higher for **neuraxial**
cards.e: The much higher GA figure reflects airway management without adequate equipment, skills or monitoring. Oxford Handbook gives UK maternal death attributable to anaesthesia as less than 1 in 300,000 maternities.

cards.q: Why must perioperative mortality in LICs be interpreted cautiously as a measure of surgical disease mortality?
cards.a:
Because many patients **never reach surgery**.
- In a HIC (more than 95% access), the risk of dying from a **ruptured viscus** is about the same as the risk of dying from surgery for it
- In a LIC, perioperative mortality for a ruptured viscus may be **10%**, but most patients with the condition **never get to hospital**, so true mortality from the disease is much higher
cards.e: A low hospital POMR can hide very poor population outcomes. Access metrics are needed alongside perioperative mortality.

cards.q: What disparities in surgical outcome exist within the same health system, including in HICs?
cards.a:
Disparities linked to:
- **Urban vs rural** and **public vs private** care
- **Race**, even within the same hospital: obstetric, oncological and trauma outcomes, perioperative **analgesia** and **anxiolysis**
- **English language proficiency**, associated with length of stay and readmission
cards.e: Miller says these findings should prompt investment in social and structural determinants of health and commitments to eliminate **racism and implicit bias**.

cards.q: What are the figures for catastrophic health expenditure from surgery?
cards.a:
Each year:
- About **33 million** people face catastrophic **out-of-pocket** expenditure paying for surgery and anaesthesia
- A further **48 million** face catastrophe from **non-medical costs** (transport, lodging, food)
- About **a quarter** of people who have surgery suffer financial catastrophe
- **3.7 billion** people (nearly half the world) are **at risk** if they need surgery, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and South/Southeast Asia
cards.e: Affordability affects analgesia and transfusion too: in South America a month of opioids for chronic pain can cost **200%** of annual income, and in India (GNI per capita about **$1670**) a unit of blood may cost up to **$247** despite a legal limit of **$25**. WHO and World Bank prioritise **financial risk protection** as part of universal health coverage.

cards.q: Outline the key milestones that brought surgery and anaesthesia onto the global health agenda.
cards.a:
Timeline:
- **1980**: WHO Director-General **Halfdan Mahler**, "Surgery and Health for All", called lack of surgical access a serious social inequity
- **2004**: WHO **Emergency and Essential Surgical Care** programme; **2005**: WHO **GIEESC**
- **2006**: **DCP2** surgery chapter; **2007**: the Burden of Surgical Disease Working Group (which became **ASAP**) and the Bellagio Essential Surgery Group
- **2008**: **Safe Surgery Saves Lives** and the **WHO Surgical Safety Checklist**; surgery called the "neglected stepchild" of global health
- **2014**: **Amsterdam Declaration** on Essential Surgical Care
- **2015**: **WHA resolution 68.15**, **DCP3** and the **Lancet Commission on Global Surgery**
cards.e: World Bank President Jim Kim echoed Mahler in 2015, calling surgery an indivisible, indispensable part of health care. The pain agenda was added by the 2017 Lancet Commission on pain relief and palliative care.

cards.q: What is WHA resolution 68.15 and what are its five focus areas?
cards.a:
Passed **unanimously** at the **68th World Health Assembly (2015)** to strengthen **emergency and essential surgical and anaesthesia care** as a component of **universal health coverage**.
Five focus areas:
- **Workforce**
- **Essential medicines**
- **Information management**
- **Service delivery**
- **Advocacy**
cards.e: Linking surgery to universal health coverage gave it a place in priority-setting from which it had been missing, e.g. in the Millennium Development Goals. The SDGs do not name surgery, but their NCD, injury, workforce and UHC targets depend on it.

cards.q: List the four key messages of the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery (LCOGS).
cards.a:
Key messages:
- **5 billion** people lack access to safe, affordable surgical and anaesthesia care; **143 million** additional procedures needed yearly
- **33 million** catastrophic expenditures from paying for surgery, plus **48 million** from non-medical costs
- Surgical investment in LMICs **is affordable, saves lives and boosts economic growth**; scaling at the rate of the best-performing LMICs would let **two-thirds** of countries reach **5000 procedures per 100,000** by **2030**, avoiding losses of **$12.3 trillion**
- Surgery is an **indivisible, indispensable** part of health care; UHC and the SDGs cannot be achieved without it
cards.e: LCOGS also gave a framework for **national surgical, obstetric and anaesthesia plans (NSOAPs)**, which can become rallying points for national advocacy.

cards.q: Summarise the key messages of Disease Control Priorities 3rd edition (DCP3) on essential surgery.
cards.a:
Key messages:
- Essential surgery would avert about **1.5 million deaths** a year, **6–7%** of avertable deaths in LMICs
- Essential procedures are among the **most cost-effective** health interventions
- **First-level hospitals** deliver **28 of 44** essential procedures, and **23 of these 28** are emergencies, so such hospitals must be **widely geographically available**
- **Task-sharing** is safe and effective while workforces are built
- The **WHO checklist** and similar measures improve safety
- **Universal coverage of essential surgery** should be funded early; full coverage at first-level hospitals would cost just over **$3 billion** a year with a **benefit–cost ratio better than 10:1**
cards.e: The emphasis on emergency procedures at first-level hospitals is why geographical access (the second delay) matters so much.

cards.q: What two misperceptions delayed recognition of surgery and anaesthesia as global public health priorities?
cards.a:
Two misperceptions:
- The burdens of surgical disease and pain were **vastly underestimated** in **scope and scale**
- Surgery and anaesthesia were wrongly assumed to be **too expensive and technology-dependent** to deliver safely and cost-effectively in resource-constrained settings
cards.e: Both came from a historical data void in LMICs. Services such as **Aravind Eye Hospitals**, **Indus Hospital** and the **Narayana Hrudayalaya** heart hospital show that safe, affordable, cost-effective surgery is feasible in these settings.

cards.q: How are WHO cost-effectiveness thresholds defined?
cards.a:
GDP-based thresholds (WHO Commission on Macroeconomics and Health, WHO-CHOICE):
- Cost per DALY averted **less than average per capita income**: **very cost-effective**
- Less than **three times** per capita income: **cost-effective**
- More than three times: **not cost-effective**
cards.e: Several methods of setting thresholds exist, each with pros and cons. This GDP-based one is the most commonly cited.

cards.q: Give data showing that surgery is cost-effective compared with other public health interventions.
cards.a:
Costs per DALY averted:
- **Emergency obstetric care, Bangladesh 2003**: less than **$11/DALY**, three times more cost-effective than **measles vaccine**
- Essential surgery at first-level hospitals: many at **$10–100/DALY**
- Compare **immunisations $13–26**, **bed nets $6–22**, **HIV treatment about $500**
- **Paediatric OR in Uganda**: **$6.39/DALY**, about **$398 per life saved**, running cost about **$41,000/year**, net economic benefit over **$5 million/year**
cards.e: At the 2012 **Copenhagen Consensus**, economists including four Nobel laureates ranked **expanding surgical capacity ($3 billion/year)** as the top priority for spending $75 billion on global welfare. Surgery is as cost-effective as vaccination.

cards.q: Why has political prioritisation of global surgery and anaesthesia lagged?
cards.a:
Contributing factors:
- **Lack of burden data** and misperceptions about safety and cost
- A **fragmented** global surgery community lacking **consensus and leadership**, poor **political strategy** (e.g. missing the MDGs)
- Because surgical disease and pain are **not pandemic**, they fail to spur donor action the way HIV or Ebola did
- They are **not disease-specific** and hard to **market** (cleft lip is easy to show; trauma, hernia and caesarean section are not)
cards.e: Successful national prioritisation needs sustained advocacy, effective framing, robust country-level data and regional and international partners. Surgery can no longer be treated as a **vertical** (disease-specific) programme; it is part of UHC.

cards.q: What are Shiffman's four challenges facing global health networks?
cards.a:
Four challenges:
- **Problem definition**: building internal consensus on the problem and its solutions
- **Positioning**: portraying the issue so that external audiences act
- **Coalition-building**: alliances with actors **outside the health sector** (HIC providers too often dominate)
- **Governance**: institutions that enable collective action
cards.e: All four apply to global anaesthesia and surgery. Organisations such as the WFSA, the G4 Alliance, GICS and LCOGS are attempts to tackle them.

cards.q: What funding and advocacy strategies does Miller recommend for global surgery and anaesthesia?
cards.a:
Strategies:
- Find **new funding streams**: global donors, national budgets, private sector, innovative models, as the HIV/vaccine initiatives did (**PEPFAR, Gavi, the Global Fund**)
- **Public–private partnerships** and patient-level **financial risk protection**
- Use the post-COVID focus on **oxygen, critical care, monitors and workforce** to strengthen health systems
- Align messages with **LCOGS, Global Health 2035, WHA 68.15 and the SDGs**, emphasising UHC
- Academic institutions: coordinated **research**, a global advocacy voice, harmonised **education**, and support for global health careers
cards.e: Advocacy needs partnership with non-physician anaesthesia cadres, who give a large share of anaesthesia in LICs.

cards.q: Give examples of the severity of anaesthesia workforce shortages in LMICs and HICs.
cards.a:
LMIC examples:
- **Central African Republic**: **2** physician anaesthesiologists and **3** NPAPs for nearly **5 million** people
- **Ethiopia**: just over **100** physician anaesthesiologists for over **100 million**
- **Uganda**: **84%** of 64 hospitals had no physician anaesthesiologist, **8%** no trained anaesthesia provider
- **East Africa** referral hospitals: only **7%** of providers reported adequate staffing
HIC example: **36%** of rural US hospitals reported delay or cancellation of surgery due to lack of anaesthesia providers
cards.e: In Uganda, lack of staff correlated most closely with emergency obstetric mortality. In HICs, trauma mortality worsens from just five miles away from an urban trauma centre.

cards.q: What is the recommended surgical, anaesthetic and obstetric (SAO) workforce density, and what evidence supports it?
cards.a:
LCOGS target: **20 SAO specialists per 100,000** by **2030**, with **5–10 anaesthesia providers per 100,000**.
- SAO density correlates with **life expectancy**
- From 0 to 20 per 100,000, **maternal mortality fell 13.1%** for every **10-unit** rise in density
- Gains continue above 20, but smaller beyond **30–40**
cards.e: The optimal number is unknown and depends on local needs. Current density is about **0.7 per 100,000** in LICs vs **56.9** in HICs.

cards.q: Describe the global distribution of the physician anaesthesia workforce.
cards.a:
Key figures:
- Africa: about **0.6** physician anaesthesiologists per 100,000, vs about **21** in Europe and **16** in the US
- **23** African countries have fewer than **0.5** per 100,000
- **64** countries report total anaesthesia provider density below **5 per 100,000**; including NPAPs, **70** countries are still below 5 and **12** African countries below 1
- **14-fold** difference in physician workforce density between HICs and LICs
- **12%** of the SAO workforce serves about a **third** of the world; LICs and LMICs have **48%** of the population but **20%** of the workforce
cards.e: In many LICs, non-physician providers give most anaesthesia care, so any workforce plan must include them.

cards.q: Why does the anaesthesia workforce crisis persist in LMICs?
cards.a:
Contributing factors:
- Limited **training infrastructure** and **cost of training**
- Low **professional status** and lack of **career advancement**, especially for NPAPs
- Perceived limited job opportunities compared with other fields
- **Inefficient hiring**, **burnout**
- **Internal brain drain** (urban private practice) and **external brain drain** (emigration)
- No consensus on practice models and polarised views on **who should give anaesthesia**
cards.e: **Task-sharing** is a prominent but controversial part of workforce expansion. Long-term solutions need **locally led** national plans for advocacy, implementation and evaluation, supported by international partners.

cards.q: How variable is non-physician anaesthesia training in sub-Saharan Africa, and what is needed to scale the workforce safely?
cards.a:
Formal NPAP programmes last **3 to 72 months**, with different entry requirements, **no standardised curricula or assessments**, and different scopes of practice. Africa alone has more than **30** distinct training pathways.
Needs:
- Shared frameworks for **training, competency assessment** and **practice models** that fit local resources
- Quality initiatives (**education programmes, credentialling bodies, licensing exams**), which matter as much as numbers
cards.e: Too much heterogeneity and lack of consensus is itself a barrier to scaling the global workforce. Task-sharing with NPAPs will likely be central in most of these countries.

cards.q: What is the "three delays" framework?
cards.a:
Taken from maternal health, it describes barriers to timely safe care:
- **First delay: seeking care**, due to financial, cultural, educational and other patient factors, including **fear of anaesthesia** or of poor surgical outcome
- **Second delay: reaching care**, due to distance, roads and transport costs
- **Third delay: receiving care** at the facility, due to lack of staff, equipment, drugs, blood and utilities
cards.e: Infrastructure work often concentrates on facilities (the third delay), but measures to reduce the second delay, such as **prehospital systems**, are cost-effective and undervalued.

cards.q: Give data on the second and third delays.
cards.a:
Second delay:
- DCP3: about **4.7 million** deaths a year in LMICs from surgical conditions could be addressed by **prehospital and emergency** care
- In Uganda fewer than **25%** live within **2 hours** of a surgical facility; about **2 billion** people worldwide lack access because of this delay
Third delay (800 first-level facilities in LICs):
- Able to do **caesarean section 64%**, **laparotomy 58%**, **open fracture repair 40%**
- Reliable **electricity 31%**, **running water 22%**, **oxygen 24%**
cards.e: Without reliable utilities, monitors, ventilators, anaesthesia machines and autoclaves often do not work even when present. Most capacity assessment tools have focused on surgery, with little ability to assess anaesthesia or analgesia capacity.

cards.q: Give examples of basic anaesthesia equipment shortages in LMIC facilities.
cards.a:
Survey findings:
- **Zambia**: **35%** of 28 district hospitals had no **laryngoscope**
- **Nigeria**: **53%** of facilities could not provide **general anaesthesia**
- **DRC**: **40%** of hospitals lacked **suction**
- **Guatemala**: only **17%** had **capnography**
- **Uganda** (2014): **paediatric airway** equipment **22%**, adult airway equipment **41%**, **pulse oximeter 28%**
- **East Africa** referral hospitals: only **4%** of providers reported a full set of ECG, oximetry, BP, capnography, thermometer, stethoscope, difficult airway cart, suction, recovery room and ICU
cards.e: Poor access to indicator strips, maintenance, power and distilled water also means low compliance with 2016 WHO/PAHO standards for cleaning and sterilisation. The WHO checklist requires pulse oximetry and a machine check, which many facilities cannot yet meet.

cards.q: What did the ASOS-2 trial test and what did it show?
cards.a:
A cluster-randomised trial of **five low-tech interventions** to reduce postoperative mortality in Africa:
- Admit patients to **higher-care wards**
- **More frequent** nursing observations
- Place patients **in view of the nursing station**
- Allow **family to stay** on the ward
- Put **postoperative surveillance guides** at the bedside
Result: it did not meet enrolment or show a mortality difference. Of **160** intervention hospitals, only **59%** could implement **two or more** of the interventions.
cards.e: The lesson is that even very simple interventions are limited by staffing and infrastructure. This supports ASOS's suggestion that excess deaths come from failure to detect and rescue postoperative deterioration.

cards.q: What problems are associated with donated medical equipment in LMICs?
cards.a:
Common problems:
- Donations made **without understanding local needs** or communicating with recipients
- No **technical support** or access to **consumables**
- Donors unaware of **WHO guidelines on medical device donation**
- **Purchase price** is only about **20%** of lifetime cost
- Up to **30%** of donated equipment never or only briefly works, ending in "equipment graveyards"
cards.e: Example: donated modern anaesthesia machines that need reliable power, piped gases, biomedical support, CO2 absorbent and circuits. Without these they are of little use, which is why drawover systems remain important.

cards.q: Which anaesthetic drugs are on the WHO Essential Medicines List, and what are the notable additions and deletions?
cards.a:
Key anaesthesia items:
- Inhalational: **halothane, isoflurane, nitrous oxide**, **sevoflurane (added 2023)**, **oxygen**
- IV: **ketamine**, **propofol (or thiopental)**
- Local: **bupivacaine, lidocaine, lidocaine with epinephrine**; **ephedrine** (complementary list, for spinal hypotension at delivery)
- Neuromuscular: **atracurium, suxamethonium, vecuronium, neostigmine**, pyridostigmine (complementary)
- Premedication and sedation: **atropine, midazolam, morphine**
- **Deletions**: **ether (2005)** and **pethidine (2003)**
cards.e: Despite the list existing for over 40 years, shortages persist. In Uganda only **2%** of surgical facilities had all 12 surveyed anaesthetic drugs and **19%** had half; in the DRC only **33%** had bupivacaine, **21%** thiopental and **16%** halothane. About **1 in 10** medical products in LMICs are substandard or falsified.

cards.q: Why does a facility survey showing no rocuronium, sevoflurane or propofol not necessarily mean anaesthesia cannot be given safely?
cards.a:
Because **suxamethonium, halothane, isoflurane or thiopental** may be available and are acceptable alternatives.
- There is only an **evolving consensus** on global standards for anaesthesia equipment and drugs
- Different assessment tools collect different data and may **over- or underestimate** capacity
cards.e: WFSA, GICS and others are developing anaesthesia-specific tools (e.g. the WFSA Anaesthesia Facility Assessment Tool) to assess capacity consistently. Harmonising these tools helps planning.

cards.q: What are the key transfusion challenges in LMICs, with figures?
cards.a:
LCOGS recommends at least **15 blood donations per 1000 people per year**. LICs collect **4.6** vs **32.1** in HICs.
- **71** countries get most blood from **family or paid donors**
- **50%** of countries cannot **separate components**
- **23.5%** of countries screen less than 100% for at least one of **HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis**
- Most LMICs cannot meet need from **voluntary non-remunerated donors** alone, as WHO advocates
cards.e: Miller suggests rethinking well-meant but context-limited policies such as **VNRD-only** mandates, requirements for **on-site pathologists** and **mandatory replacement units**. Global advocacy for safe blood dates back to WHA28.72 (1975).

cards.q: How unequal is global opioid consumption?
cards.a:
About **5–5.5 billion** people have limited or no access to opioid analgesia.
- **Six HICs** account for **80%** of global opioid consumption
- Countries with **17%** of the population (Canada, US, Western Europe, Australia, New Zealand) use **92%**
- Consumption in **Africa and South Asia** has fallen in recent decades
- Morphine-equivalent per patient in need: e.g. Canada about **68,000 mg** (over 3000% of need met) vs **Nigeria 0.8 mg (0.2%)** and **Haiti 5.3 mg (0.8%)**
cards.e: Countries with lower GDP or human development index have less opioid access. Inequitable analgesia also exists within HICs, including the US.

cards.q: Classify the barriers to analgesic access listed in Miller (Box 2.4).
cards.a:
Four groups:
- **Knowledge and attitudes**: limited provider training, poor health literacy, **opiophobia** (fear of addiction, diversion, side effects), cultural beliefs, little data on need, pain hard to "put a face to"
- **Regulation and policy**: **prohibitionist bias**, costly implementation, onerous rules on who prescribes and for what dose, duration and indication, **fear of prosecution**
- **Economics**: poverty, high analgesic prices, cost of enforcing regulations, little financial protection
- **Health systems**: supply chains (import, procurement, storage, distribution), few analgesic options, few trained providers or facilities, weak government capacity
cards.e: The risk of addiction from appropriate use is greatly exaggerated, especially for acute, cancer and end-of-life pain. Excessive regulation confuses tolerance with dependence and users with addicts.

cards.q: Why are opioids often unaffordable in LMICs?
cards.a:
Prices relative to income are much higher:
- In **Argentina and Mexico**, a month of opioid for cancer pain cost more than **200%** of average **monthly** income
- In **Rwanda**, injectable morphine cost **six times** the lowest price in the International Drug Price Indicator Guide
Drivers: **import costs, taxes, licensing fees, storage, sales restrictions** and limited public financing.
cards.e: Many of these costs come from international regulation and misconceptions about addiction, so policy reform is as important as subsidy.

cards.q: What is the 1961 UN Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, and how has it restricted analgesic access?
cards.a:
The main international drug control treaty. Its preamble says medical use of narcotics is **indispensable** for pain relief. It controls **opium, cannabis and coca**, requires governments to report **estimates of medical need** and keep records, restricts trade, and created the **International Narcotics Control Board (INCB)**.
How it restricts access:
- Poor countries lack resources to make **accurate estimates**, so they get **inadequate supply**
- Example (2017): **Chad** (14.5 million people) estimated 341 g fentanyl and 249 g morphine vs **Canada** (36.3 million) 150,000 g fentanyl and 4,750,000 g morphine
- By approving such underestimates, the INCB effectively **prevents legal access**
- It hinders emergency scale-up in disasters, e.g. the **2010 Haiti earthquake**
cards.e: Earlier milestones were the 1909 Shanghai International Opium Convention and the 1912 Hague Opium Convention. Each country must designate an enforcement office, e.g. the DEA in the US.

cards.q: Give examples of national drug policies that have restricted opioid access, and of reforms that improved it.
cards.a:
Restrictive:
- **India**'s 1985 **NDPS Act**, with extreme penalties (including death), led to a more than **90%** fall in medical morphine use
- **Armenia**: only **oncologists** with approval of several providers may prescribe outpatient opioids
- **Ukraine**: providers had to travel to patients' homes to give outpatient opioids
- **Jordan**: maximum prescription **10 days** for cancer pain, **3 days** otherwise
Successful reforms:
- **Vietnam and India**: grassroots and civil society work reduced opiophobia and licensing barriers, increasing access **without more diversion**
- **Uganda**: Hospice Africa Uganda persuaded the Ministry to import morphine powder (**1993**) and give oral morphine free to cancer and HIV patients; in **2004** **nurses and clinical officers** with palliative training could prescribe
cards.e: The Ugandan model is being adopted in Rwanda, Nigeria, Kenya, Swaziland and Malawi. Addiction treatment (methadone, buprenorphine) only reached the WHO EML in **2006**; morphine was on the first EML in **1977** and the WHO pain ladder appeared in **1986**.

cards.q: Why is ketamine important globally, and what threatened its availability?
cards.a:
Ketamine is **cheap, accessible and safe**, and is critical for anaesthesia and analgesia in LMICs.
- Because of domestic ketamine abuse, **China** repeatedly lobbied the **INCB** to make ketamine **Schedule I** worldwide
- This would have removed nearly universal ketamine access in LMICs and worsened the global pain crisis
- The attempts were recognised as **violating international regulatory policy**
cards.e: The episode shows how drug control aimed at illicit use can harm medical access in poor countries. Miller argues that rethinking international analgesic policy, including the Single Convention, is essential.

cards.q: What is the global status of tramadol, and why is it a concern?
cards.a:
Tramadol is **not controlled by international regulations**, so it is widely available, for analgesia and for abuse.
- Abuse is widespread in HICs (e.g. Canada) and many countries in **Africa and the Middle East**
- In **Cameroon** it has been found in **groundwater** from human excretion
- It is **not an adequate substitute** for opioids and is **not** on the WHO Essential Medicines List
cards.e: It is cheap and common in resource-limited perioperative care, so users must understand its side effects, abuse potential and inferiority to opioids in many situations.

cards.q: Outline the history of anaesthesia outside the US and the founding of the WFSA.
cards.a:
Key points:
- Pre-modern analgesia: **Aztecs and Maya** used herbal drinks and local numbing agents; Mesopotamian and Egyptian texts describe **belladonna, cannabis, mandragora**; Phoenicians used opium poppy
- After **Morton's 1846** ether demonstration, ether was used in **1847** in Canada, Mexico, South Africa, Norway, Romania, India and Australia
- In some countries modern anaesthesia began with **war** (Paraguay 1864–70, Vietnam)
- The **WFSA** was founded in **1956** with **26** founding members
