cards.e: Landmarks include the **Epstein–Macintosh–Oxford (EMO)** ether vaporiser, halogenated volatiles, cocaine local anaesthesia and spinal anaesthesia. Some LICs **still use ether** over 170 years on.

cards.q: Describe the main training pathways for physician anaesthesiologists worldwide.
cards.a:
Main patterns:
- **Specialist residency** of **3–5 years** after medical school (sometimes after an internship), sometimes with a research year or thesis
- Qualification by **master's degree** (e.g. Uganda), **certification exam** (e.g. Canada, Mexico, European regional exam), or **Ministry of Health licence** without exam (Colombia)
- **Apprenticeship model** (graduated supervision) vs **competency-based** training (e.g. Canada, Romania; growing in the US and India)
- Shorter **alternative pathways**: Diploma in Anaesthesia (India, Pakistan, South Africa for GPs), Vietnam "first/second specialist", **6-month** Indian programme for rural emergency obstetric anaesthesia, Mexican rural programmes, **GP anaesthetists** (Canada, Australia)
cards.e: Specialists usually have a broad scope (preoperative optimisation, intraoperative care, recovery, often critical care and pain) and practise independently. GP anaesthetists mainly work in rural areas and often limit themselves to healthier patients and routine cases.

cards.q: Describe the training and practice of US Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetists (CRNAs).
cards.a:
Training up to **42 months** after working as an **intensive care nurse**, with at least **465 hours** of classroom teaching, at least **600 clinical cases** and **2000 clinical hours**, moving towards a **Doctor of Nursing Practice**.
- Broad scope: preoperative evaluation, induction, maintenance, emergence and immediate postoperative care
- More often practise in **rural** areas
- **19 US states** have opted out of the physician supervision requirement; elsewhere they work under indirect supervision
cards.e: Worldwide, nurse anaesthetist training usually lasts **1–4 years**, and supervision ranges from full autonomy to indirect physician supervision.

cards.q: Compare non-nurse, non-physician anaesthesia providers and anaesthesia technicians in different countries.
cards.a:
Non-nurse, non-physician providers:
- **Clinical or anaesthetic officers** in many African countries, often about **2 years** of training, frequently the **primary independent** providers
- **BSc Anaesthesia** in Uganda (two years of medical school then anaesthetic training)
- **Anaesthetic Scientific Officers** in Papua New Guinea
- **Certified Anesthesiologist Assistants** (US): full care under direct or indirect physician supervision
- **Anaesthesia Assistants** (Canada): MAC and procedures including some intubation, but **not** the primary provider
Technicians (do not give anaesthesia): US anaesthesia technicians, UK **Operating Department Practitioners**, Indian **OT Technologists**
cards.e: Unlike nurse anaesthetists, whose scope reliably covers induction to emergence, the scope of non-nurse providers varies widely. What providers do in practice can differ from what they are licensed to do, which complicates workforce planning.

cards.q: Describe the range of anaesthesia practice models worldwide.
cards.a:
Main models:
- **Physician-only** but using other physicians (GPs, diploma holders) to extend services: Canada, Australia, India, Pakistan, South Africa
- **Predominantly specialist** with trainees providing much service and technicians or assistants as essential team members: UK, Norway
- **Nurse anaesthetists** with **indirect physician supervision** (Norway, Vietnam, parts of the US) or **independently** (other parts of the US)
- **NPAPs giving most anaesthesia** where shortages are worst: Fiji, Paraguay (under **surgeon** supervision), many African countries
cards.e: The Latin American confederation **CLASA** holds that anaesthesia is a **strictly medical act** to be given only by anaesthesiologists. In South Korea, CRNAs have practised for over 50 years but their legal status has been questioned.

cards.q: What are the common global and regional challenges in delivering anaesthesia care?
cards.a:
Recurring themes:
- **Maldistribution**: e.g. **70%** of anaesthesiologists within 300 miles of Mexico City work in the city; over half of **1169** rural US counties had **no** anaesthesia provider; about a third of US children live more than **50 miles** from a paediatric anaesthesiologist
- **Salary** pressures and **dual practice**, causing emigration (Africa and South Asia to the Middle East and Europe; Romania to western Europe)
- Inconsistent access to **drugs and equipment** (fentanyl, amiodarone, gas analysers, defibrillators, oxygen, electricity)
- **Inconsistent training and certification** standards
cards.e: Short-term contracts and financial incentives are common but unstable ways to staff rural areas. The WHO checklist and **WHO-WFSA international safe anaesthesia practice standards** set minimum standards, but adoption is not universal.

cards.q: Compare anaesthesia practice environments in public LMIC systems, wealthy public systems and private systems.
cards.a:
Three types:
- **LMIC public systems**: few providers, scarce resources, financially insecure patients who often must **buy their own supplies** (e.g. family sent to buy volatile agent, propofol, suxamethonium and paracetamol). Highest risk to safety
- **Wealthy public systems** (e.g. Norway): little inequity, nearly everything needed for safe care, reliably good outcomes
- **Private systems**: timely, high-quality care, but may bankrupt some families and cannot be offered to everyone; include **charitable and religious** providers serving the neediest
cards.e: Health spending ranges from about **$11,000** per person per year in the US to about **$20** in Madagascar. Almost every country could benefit from better access to anaesthesia, including the US.

cards.q: Which four factors determine safe anaesthesia practice anywhere, and why is "copy-and-paste" practice risky?
cards.a:
**Personnel, equipment, medications and patients**. Disruption of any one limits safe practice, whether in an LMIC, a rural HIC, a pandemic surge, or a military or humanitarian field hospital.
- Evidence-based HIC practices sometimes have **unintended harmful effects** in LMICs
- Transplanting HIC frameworks unchanged may not improve outcomes
cards.e: Understanding the **local context** is essential before treating patients or trying to change practice. COVID-19 showed that no setting is immune to resource limits, so all providers should develop skills for working with limited resources.

cards.q: What personnel issues should a visiting anaesthetist expect in resource-constrained settings?
cards.a:
Typical issues:
- Many providers have **limited training** and work **in isolation** without supervision
- Many are skilled within a narrow range but use a **"recipe" anaesthetic** that may not adapt to complex cases
- **Perioperative care** is underdeveloped; preoperative optimisation and postoperative nursing may be absent
- **PACU** may be an unstaffed corridor; patients must be **more fully recovered** before leaving theatre
- Postoperative ventilation may fall to the **anaesthetist or family members**, sometimes doing manual ventilation
cards.e: Assess the knowledge and experience of the local provider first. There are always opportunities for **two-way learning**.

cards.q: What are the requirements of an inhalational anaesthesia system, and how does a drawover system meet them?
cards.a:
Any system must deliver **accurate volatile concentrations**, avoid **CO2 rebreathing**, allow **IPPV** and provide **oxygen-enriched** gas.
Drawover components:
- A **low-resistance**, temperature-compensated or buffered vaporiser calibrated to the agent (EMO, OMV, DDV)
- A **self-inflating bag or bellows**, preceded by a **one-way valve** so flow is unidirectional
- A **non-rebreathing valve** at the patient end
Advantages: **no compressed gas or electricity**, runs on **room air**, **cannot deliver a hypoxic mixture**.
cards.e: Ambient air is the "drawing" gas. Vaporisers stay accurate with **intermittent** flow but lose accuracy with continuous flow. Systems that can use several volatile agents are the most versatile.

cards.q: How do you increase FiO2 in a drawover system?
cards.a:
Add oxygen at the **vaporiser inlet** with a **reservoir**.
- Without a reservoir, FiO2 cannot exceed about **0.3** whatever the oxygen flow
- With **1 m of 22 mm corrugated tubing** (about **415 mL**) as reservoir at normal adult minute ventilation: **1 L/min** O2 gives FiO2 about **0.3**, and **4 L/min** gives about **0.6**
cards.e: Oxygen can come from a cylinder or a concentrator. Lippincott shows how to estimate cylinder duration: an E-cylinder at 1000 psig is about half full (about 330 L) and lasts about 3 hours at 2 L/min, which matters when cylinders are the backup supply.

cards.q: How should drawover anaesthesia be adapted for children?
cards.a:
Convert to a **semi-continuous flow** to overcome dead space at the non-rebreathing valve: squeeze the bellows or self-inflating bag to drive oxygen-enriched gas through the vaporiser into an **Ayre's T-piece** (squeeze and release about **12 times per minute** with a bag).
Ventilation guide by weight:
- **Under 5 kg**: assisted ventilation throughout
- **5–10 kg**: spontaneous for short cases, assisted for longer ones
- **Over 10 kg**: spontaneous for most operations unless paralysis or a long procedure is needed
cards.e: Both valves must be used to keep flow unidirectional because it is still a low-pressure system. This method keeps vaporiser output more accurate than fully continuous flow via a Farman entrainer or direct oxygen to the vaporiser.

cards.q: What are all-in-one drawover anaesthesia machines and why are they suitable for resource-limited settings?
cards.a:
Machines such as the **Universal Anaesthesia Machine (Gradian Health)** and the **Glostavent (Diamedica)**, based on drawover principles (not plenum machines).
- Cheaper and easier to maintain than modern workstations
- Work **without power** and **without pressurised oxygen**; oxygen can come from a cylinder or **integrated concentrator**
- An **uninterruptible power supply** runs monitors and ventilators during power cuts
- Manufacturers invest in **local training and service support**
cards.e: Whatever set-up is used, a **power-failure and oxygen-failure plan** is essential and will differ by setting.

cards.q: How do oxygen concentrators work, and what are their limitations?
cards.a:
**Pressure swing adsorption** with **zeolite** removes nitrogen from air, giving **90–96%** oxygen (about **85%** at high flows).
Limitations:
- Most deliver no more than **10 L/min**
- Output pressure is well below **3.4 bar (50 psi)**, so they **cannot drive** most ventilators without a built-in turbine or compressor
- Performance falls in **heat and humidity**: only **2 of 8** models gave more than **82%** oxygen at **35°C**
- Many do not meet WHO guidelines; output purity varies with poor maintenance
cards.e: Higher flows can be obtained by combining concentrators. Use a portable oxygen analyser to check output; **ultrasonic** analysers need no consumables or calibration. Common faults (dirty filters, low voltage, heat) can often be fixed by non-engineers.

cards.q: How can monitoring be achieved when electronic monitors are scarce?
cards.a:
Rely more on **clinical signs**: pulse volume, chest movement, pupil size, compliance of bellows or bag.
- Monitors should have a working **internal battery**
- **Pulse oximetry** is invaluable but not universal; cheap devices may be inaccurate and may perform worse in **dark skin**
- **Capnography and ECG** are often unavailable
- A **precordial stethoscope** (ordinary stethoscope with suction or oxygen tubing extension) gives beat-to-beat heart rate, breathing, airway patency and tube position, and may detect **hypovolaemia** (quieter heart tones) before alarms
cards.e: These clinical skills reflect the WHO-WFSA standards, which set pulse oximetry as a minimum where possible. A drop in precordial heart sounds is an early, cheap warning sign.

cards.q: How should a difficult airway be managed with very limited equipment?
cards.a:
Prioritise oxygenation and safety:
- Keep **spontaneous breathing** and oxygenation until the airway is secured
- Consider **face mask**, **regional anaesthesia** or **ketamine** instead of complex airway management
- An **awake look** with direct laryngoscopy helps planning
- Consider **tracheostomy under local anaesthesia** when surgical skill exceeds airway resources
- Useful skills: **retrograde** and **blind nasal** intubation, airway **topicalisation** (transtracheal lidocaine, gargled or sprayed lidocaine with epinephrine)
- Confirm the tube without capnography by **condensation**, bag movement, **auscultation**, or rarely an oesophageal bulb
cards.e: Often only a **Macintosh 3** blade is available; bougies and supraglottic devices are rare. An improvised introducer can be made from wire inside a suction catheter with the tip covered. Lippincott notes that laryngospasm usually responds to positive pressure with 100% oxygen, with small-dose suxamethonium (0.25 mg/kg) if it persists.

cards.q: Describe the technique of blind nasal intubation.
cards.a:
Steps:
- Advance the tube along the **floor of the nose** during **inspiration**, listening to breath sounds through the tube
- If it enters the **oesophagus**: **extend** the neck
- If it catches on the **anterior larynx**: **flex** the neck
- **Lift the jaw** to stop the tube hitting the epiglottis
- **Rotate** the tube or slightly **inflate the cuff** to help it enter the trachea
cards.e: Miller compares it to the Patil guide technique. It is valuable where fibreoptic and video laryngoscopes are absent and spontaneous breathing must be preserved.

cards.q: How is regional anaesthesia practised in resource-limited settings?
cards.a:
Practice notes:
- **Spinal** is universally taught and used for more cases than in HICs (e.g. appendicectomy); usual drug **hyperbaric 0.5% bupivacaine**; a **21 G hypodermic needle** can act as introducer for blunt spinal needles
- Not all providers can manage **spinal hypotension**; teach **uterine wedge** and reverse Trendelenburg positioning; dilute **0.5 mg epinephrine in 500 mL 5% dextrose** to treat hypotension carefully when vasopressors are scarce
- **Epidurals** are rare (skills, equipment, preservative-free drugs, pumps, postoperative staffing); elastomeric pumps can replace infusion pumps
- **Caudals** via a **22 G cannula** in children
- **Landmark** blocks: ankle, digital, axillary, penile, wrist, fascia iliaca, femoral, rectus sheath, field blocks for hernia
cards.e: Fatal **LA toxicity** during penile blocks for circumcision still occurs due to dosing errors. Where **lipid emulsion** is limited, prefer **distal, low-volume, shorter-acting** blocks. Spinal looks simple, but patient selection matters when pressors and fluids are scarce.

cards.q: What improvised vascular access techniques does Miller describe?
cards.a:
Techniques:
- **Scalp veins** in critically ill infants
- Rapid **right internal jugular** or **intraperitoneal** cannula in a child dying of hypovolaemic shock (e.g. cholera) while seeking a definitive line
- **Intraosseous** access with an **18 G or 16 G** needle (or butterfly) in an infant **tibia**: twist through the cortex until a sudden give, and an entire anaesthetic can be run through it
cards.e: Cannulas may be of poor quality, with the needle protruding beyond the cannula tip. Without infusion pumps, providers must calculate rates by **drop factor**, knowing that giving sets vary.

cards.q: Why is halothane widely used in LICs, and what are its key pharmacological features?
cards.a:
It is the **cheapest** volatile (Uganda, 250 mL: halothane about **$21**, isoflurane about **$39**, sevoflurane about **$250**), so it dominates in rural and non-teaching hospitals.
- **Potent**: MAC **0.8%**; sweet smelling, good for inhalational induction
- **Blood:gas coefficient 2.4**: slow onset and offset, which can help when intubating a difficult airway under halothane alone
- **Myocardial depressant** and **arrhythmogenic**, especially with high end-tidal CO2
- Reduce the inspired concentration quickly once IV access is established
cards.e: Ether use has fallen sharply since 2013 and it is off the EML. Nitrous oxide is often unavailable or expensive, and medical air can cost **4–5 times** more than oxygen, so cases are often done on 100% oxygen.

cards.q: Why is ketamine so widely used in LMICs, and what cautions apply?
cards.a:
Like an "intravenous ether": **sympathomimetic**, **preserves airway reflexes**, **strong analgesic**; it causes **salivation**.
Uses: induction in **hypovolaemic or septic shock**, **TIVA** (e.g. laparotomy), postoperative **infusion** (IV or SC) when opioids are scarce; S-ketamine as an adjunct to regional anaesthesia.
Cautions:
- Can cause **cardiac arrest** in maximally sympathetically stimulated patients
- Possible **oxytocic** effect: caution as sole anaesthetic in pregnant patients for non-obstetric surgery
- **Apnoea in neonates** even while they move in response to surgery
- Prolonged waking and **hallucinations**, as benzodiazepines (usually diazepam) may not be given
cards.e: A **5-day ketamine course** to train mid-level non-anaesthesia providers for emergency anaesthesia in rural Africa has been highly **controversial**. Propofol is widespread and thiopentone common outside HICs.

cards.q: What are the features of perioperative analgesia in resource-limited settings?
cards.a:
Key features:
- **Morphine** is the most available opioid but still hard to get; oral morphine is available where palliative care is developed (e.g. Uganda)
- **Pethidine** is common but **not on the WHO EML** and not recommended for routine postoperative pain (variable efficacy, side effects)
- Opioids are rarely given beyond **48 h** because of opiophobia and supply
- **Intramuscular** dosing is common; a **subcutaneous cannula** (often over the deltoid) for opioids avoids repeated injections and can stay **48–72 h**
- **Paracetamol** and **NSAIDs** (IM diclofenac) are widely available; **tramadol** is common but inferior
cards.e: The main teaching challenge is the concept of **multimodal analgesia**, which is usually possible, including regional techniques, even with limited drugs. PCA is generally unavailable.

cards.q: What are the practical issues with neuromuscular blockers in resource-limited settings?
cards.a:
Key issues:
- **Suxamethonium** is universally available and may be the **safest** relaxant when there is no ventilator or reversal
- It rarely causes malignant hyperthermia but can cause **masseter spasm**, especially in children with neuromuscular disorders
- **Suxamethonium and atracurium lose potency with heat**; cold storage is difficult
- For abdominal closure, a **small dose of suxamethonium** at the end with hand ventilation helps close the peritoneum and rectus and allows faster offset of the volatile
cards.e: Availability of non-depolarising drugs varies, so providers must be ready to use agents they rarely use in HICs.

cards.q: How is transfusion handled where blood services are limited?
cards.a:
Providers may need to:
- Do **ABO typing** (e.g. **EldonCard**) and **cross-matching** themselves
- Use **whole blood** more than components (refrigeration reduces platelet and clotting factor activity)
- Rely on **directed donation** from relatives and **mandatory exchange** (someone must donate before units are released)
- Use **normovolaemic haemodilution** or improvised **intraoperative cell salvage** (cup, gauze filter, anticoagulant, 60 mL syringe)
cards.e: There are no absolute transfusion thresholds, which creates dilemmas, e.g. whether to proceed with a hernia repair at Hb 8 or 7 with no blood available. None of these improvisations replaces a proper transfusion service.

cards.q: How do patient characteristics differ in many LMIC settings, and how does this affect anaesthetic planning?
cards.a:
Differences:
- More than **50%** of the population is **under 18**; fewer comorbidities and less polypharmacy
- **Late presentation** with advanced disease (impassable roads, insecurity, traditional healers or bone-setters, poverty)
- Common **anaemia, malnutrition, low-grade malaria, helminths**, which may need treatment before major surgery
- Families provide much inpatient care, so they want **short stays**; patients mobilise early but may not follow instructions
- Few affordable investigations, so decisions rest on **clinical judgement**
cards.e: Providers must be skilled with **trauma, obstetric and paediatric** patients and with context-specific optimisation of common conditions such as hypertension and diabetes (e.g. finding temperature-stable, non-counterfeit drugs).

cards.q: What are the CUGH global health competency domains?
cards.a:
The **Consortium of Universities for Global Health** lists **11 domains**, each with **4 levels** (level I for all providers with any link to global health, up to level IV for lifelong engagement):
- Global burden of disease; globalisation of health and health care; social and environmental determinants; capacity strengthening; collaboration, partnering and communication; ethics; professional practice; health equity and social justice; programme management; sociocultural and political awareness; strategic analysis
cards.e: Miller says basic global health competencies (access, affordability, disease burden, determinants of health, ethics, equity) are relevant to **all** anaesthesia providers and should be part of training. Those pursuing global health careers may add epidemiology, health policy, health economics, anthropology, ethics and implementation science.

cards.q: What non-clinical pitfalls and ethical problems commonly arise in short-term global health work?
cards.a:
Common pitfalls:
- Interventions that do not fit the **context** (e.g. inappropriate equipment donations)
- **No follow-up plan**
- Failure to **engage local stakeholders**
- Overemphasis on **short-term** solutions
- **Draining local resources**
Ethical problems: appropriate **scope of practice**, fair distribution of local and external resources, and poor understanding of **local social and cultural norms**.
cards.e: In a survey of Ugandan surgical and anaesthesia trainees, **75%** said visiting groups improved their training, but **40%** said they had a neutral or negative effect on patient care, only **15%** felt their research matched local priorities, and **31%** were uncomfortable with the ethics of visitors' clinical decisions.

cards.q: What structured training opportunities exist for anaesthetists interested in global health?
cards.a:
Options:
- **UK**: 6-month to 1-year global health placements with a formal curriculum and clinical, research and educational parts, assessed by **RCoA** standards (clinical evaluations, case-based discussions)
- Formal **global health tracks** in residency, **global anaesthesia fellowships**, and equity training built into core curricula
cards.e: Most opportunities are still short-term electives without structured competency training. Miller says institutions offering global health experiences have a duty to prepare trainees formally.

cards.q: Which priority actions does Miller list for the global anaesthesia community?
cards.a:
Six priorities:
- **Develop infrastructure** and **expand the workforce**
- **Improve data** to drive policy and practice
- Provide **financial risk protection** for surgical patients
- Improve **referral and prehospital** systems
- Ensure **essential medicines** (including opioids and oxygen)
cards.e: Miller says the global anaesthesia community lags behind other disciplines and must quickly invest in research, implementation and policy, and financing. Action must be prompt and balanced with, but not overshadowed by, research agendas. Anaesthetists work across disciplines and can lead joint advocacy.

cards.q: You are joining a short-term volunteer surgical mission to a district hospital with intermittent electricity and no piped oxygen. What anaesthetic preparation and techniques would you prioritise?
cards.a:
Before travel:
- Learn the **local context**: staff, drugs, equipment and existing practice; work through local leaders
- Revise **drawover** anaesthesia and ketamine, spinal and landmark regional techniques
Equipment and oxygen:
- Confirm an **oxygen source**: concentrator plus **cylinder backup**, reservoir tubing for drawover; calculate cylinder duration
- Battery-backed **pulse oximeter**, precordial stethoscope, foot or bulb suction
- A **power-failure and oxygen-failure plan**
Practice:
- Ensure patients are **fully recovered** before leaving theatre, as PACU care may be minimal
- Plan **follow-up** and **teach local providers** so capacity remains after you leave
cards.e: Miller warns against context-inappropriate interventions, lack of follow-up and draining local resources. Much LIC anaesthetic mortality is avoidable with basic monitoring, oxygen and trained staff. Lippincott: an E-cylinder at 1000 psig holds about 330 L and lasts about 3 h at 2 L/min.

cards.q: A ministry of health asks how to measure progress in surgical access. Which indicators from this chapter would you recommend?
cards.a:
Use LCOGS-style system indicators:
- **Access**: proportion of the population within **2 hours** of a facility able to do caesarean section, laparotomy and open fracture repair
- **Workforce**: **SAO density** (target **20 per 100,000**; anaesthesia **5–10 per 100,000**)
- **Surgical volume**: procedures per 100,000 (target at least **5000 by 2030**)
- **Perioperative mortality rate**
- **Financial risk protection**: catastrophic expenditure from surgery
- **Blood supply**: donations per 1000 (minimum **15**)
cards.e: Miller lists improved data to drive policy as a core priority. These indicators can be built into a **national surgical, obstetric and anaesthesia plan (NSOAP)**. POMR must be read alongside access, because many patients never reach surgery.

cards.q: A 24-year-old woman at term arrives at a rural African district hospital with severe antepartum haemorrhage. The only anaesthesia provider is a nurse with one year of training, 250 mL of compatible blood is available, there is no capnography and no paediatrician. What anaesthetic approach would you consider, and how do you decide?
cards.a:
There is no single right answer; choose what this team can do most safely:
- **Options**: local infiltration alone; intermittent IV **ketamine** with nasal oxygen; or **RSI** with ketamine, suxamethonium and halothane
- **Spinal is relatively unsafe** with active haemorrhage and hypovolaemia, especially without vasopressors
- **Ketamine** keeps blood pressure and airway reflexes; beware cardiac arrest in a maximally stressed patient
- GA without capnography or skilled airway support carries the highest LMIC risk (maternal anaesthetic mortality about **900-fold** higher than US for GA)
- Resuscitate with available fluids and blood; call any available help; prepare for neonatal resuscitation yourself
cards.e: Miller uses this scenario to show that "standard of care" depends on local resources and skills. Learn local resources, listen to local providers, be humble, and above all focus on patient safety. In South Africa many avoidable anaesthetic maternal deaths followed spinals by staff unable to manage the airway or convert to GA.

cards.q: A 6-month-old (7 kg) needs a 90-minute inguinal hernia repair at a hospital where your only anaesthesia equipment is an EMO-type drawover vaporiser, an Oxford inflating bellows and an oxygen concentrator. How do you set up and conduct the anaesthetic?
cards.a:
Set-up:
- Add oxygen from the concentrator at the vaporiser inlet with a **reservoir tube**
- Convert to semi-continuous flow: drive gas with the **bellows** into an **Ayre's T-piece**, using both valves for unidirectional flow
Conduct:
- At **5–10 kg**, spontaneous breathing is acceptable for short cases, but for 90 min plan **assisted ventilation**
- Monitor clinically (pulse oximeter if available, **precordial stethoscope**, bag movement)
- Consider a **caudal** (22 G cannula, bupivacaine) for analgesia, with careful dosing
- Recover fully in theatre before handing over
cards.e: Continuous flow through the bellows and T-piece overcomes dead space at the non-rebreathing valve while keeping the vaporiser accurate. Miller's weight guide: under 5 kg assisted, 5–10 kg spontaneous for short and assisted for long, over 10 kg spontaneous for most.

cards.q: A 30-year-old man with neck trauma and trismus needs an urgent laparotomy at a hospital with one Macintosh 3 blade, no bougie, no supraglottic airway and no capnography. How do you plan airway management?
cards.a:
Plan to **keep spontaneous breathing**:
- Do an **awake look** with direct laryngoscopy after **topicalisation** (gargled or sprayed lidocaine, transtracheal lidocaine)
- Consider **blind nasal intubation** during inspiration, adjusting neck flexion or extension and lifting the jaw
- Consider an improvised **introducer** (wire inside a suction catheter, tip covered)
- If intubation looks unsafe, discuss **tracheostomy under local anaesthesia** with the surgeon before induction
- Confirm the tube by **condensation**, bag movement and **auscultation**
- Have suction (foot pump) ready; avoid apnoeic induction unless the airway is secured
cards.e: In resource-poor settings it is often safer to keep oxygenation and spontaneous breathing, or to use regional or ketamine techniques, than to attempt complex airway management. Surgical skill may exceed what the anaesthetic equipment allows.

cards.q: During a spinal for caesarean section in a rural hospital, the patient's blood pressure drops to 70/40 mmHg. There is no phenylephrine or ephedrine and only one bag of crystalloid. What do you do?
cards.a:
Immediate actions:
- **Left uterine displacement** (improvised wedge) and leg elevation; give the crystalloid
- Prepare a dilute epinephrine infusion: **0.5 mg in 500 mL 5% dextrose** (about 1 microgram/mL), titrated **cautiously**
- Give oxygen; monitor pulse, consciousness and fetal condition
- Be ready to manage a **high block**, airway problems and conversion to GA
Afterwards: review **patient selection** for spinal when vasopressors are unavailable, and ask for pressors to be stocked (ephedrine is on the EML complementary list for this use).
cards.e: Miller notes that all providers are taught spinals but not all are taught to manage spinal hypotension and complications. In South Africa many avoidable anaesthetic maternal deaths followed spinals by providers who could not manage the airway.

cards.q: A hospital in a low-income country is offered a donated modern anaesthesia workstation by a high-income hospital. The local biomedical engineer asks your opinion. What do you advise?
cards.a:
Assess **fitness for context** before accepting:
- Does it need **mains power**, **pressurised oxygen and air**, CO2 absorbent, proprietary circuits, filters or sensors that are unavailable locally?
- Is there **technical support**, training and a supply of **consumables** and spare parts?
- Budget for **lifetime cost**: purchase is only about **20%**
- Check against **WHO medical device donation guidelines**
- Consider alternatives: a **drawover** or **all-in-one** machine (UAM, Glostavent) that works without power or piped gas, with local service support
cards.e: Up to 30% of donated equipment never or only briefly works and ends up in equipment graveyards. Many donations happen without communication about local needs.

cards.q: A district hospital has three oxygen concentrators supplying a busy paediatric ward during a pneumonia outbreak. Nurses split each outlet to several children, and some remain hypoxaemic. How do you troubleshoot oxygen delivery?
cards.a:
Systematic approach:
- **Check purity** with a portable (preferably **ultrasonic**) oxygen analyser; purity falls at high flow and in **heat**
- Check **flow** to each child: compare split circuits by putting tubing ends in **cups of water**; splitting often gives too little flow
- Look for common faults: **dirty filters**, **low voltage**, compressor or valve failure, high room temperature
- **Combine** concentrators for higher-flow patients; remember most give at most **10 L/min** and cannot drive ventilators
- Add **cylinders** as backup and use **oxygen-conservation** methods; prioritise the most hypoxaemic children
cards.e: Up to 90% of people in some countries lack reliable oxygen, and hypoxaemic patients in sub-Saharan Africa have 50–80% mortality. Not all concentrators work in hot climates (2 of 8 tested gave more than 82% at 35°C).

cards.q: You are asked to help a ministry of health in a low-income country improve access to morphine for postoperative and cancer pain. Uptake is very low despite morphine being on the national EML. What barriers do you expect, and what strategies would you propose?
cards.a:
Expected barriers:
- **Opiophobia** among providers, patients and policymakers; little prescriber training
- **Restrictive regulation** (limits on prescribers, duration, indications) and **fear of prosecution**
- **Underestimated INCB national estimates** under the Single Convention, giving too little supply
- **Cost**, import taxes and supply chain problems
Strategies:
- Better **needs estimates** and reporting to the INCB
- **Education** for providers and the public; reduce licensing barriers
- Allow trained **nurses and clinical officers** to prescribe, as in **Uganda**
- **Local production** of low-cost **oral morphine** (Hospice Africa Uganda model)
- Use **multimodal** analgesia and regional techniques alongside
cards.e: Vietnam and India reduced barriers through grassroots and civil-society work and increased access **without more diversion**. India's 1985 NDPS Act shows the opposite: harsh penalties cut medical morphine use by more than 90%.

cards.q: Define perioperative medicine as described by Miller and state its goal.
cards.a:
An evolving model of care that **coordinates perioperative management across the continuum**, from the first **contemplation of surgery** through to **recovery**.
- Goal: improve care by **aligning patient goals and expectations with clinical objectives**, and improve clinical management and decision-making
- It needs **coordination and shared decision-making** among many providers inside and beyond the hospital
cards.e: It has been shown to improve outcomes and quality and often to reduce length of stay and cost. The hallmark of any successful model is **collaboration among all providers**, not ownership by one specialty.

cards.q: Is perioperative medicine "owned" by anaesthesiology? Explain Miller's position.
cards.a:
No. It is **not a specialty-specific** model of care.
- Anaesthetists are **well positioned** to lead because they understand the interaction of patient, anaesthetic and surgical factors
- Success needs collaboration with **surgeons, hospitalists, medical specialists, nurses** and primary care
- The specific model depends on the department's interest and commitment, existing relationships in the health system, and patient needs
cards.e: A common trap is to describe perioperative medicine as "anaesthetists running everything". Miller stresses defining roles and building new collaborations to optimise transitions along the continuum.

cards.q: Why has the scope of anaesthesia practice expanded beyond intraoperative care?
cards.a:
Several factors:
- New anaesthetic techniques, monitoring and evidence-based management have made anaesthesia **safer**
- **Minimally invasive** surgery and interventional procedures moved care into **non-OR settings**
- Patients **previously considered unfit** for surgery now undergo complex procedures
- **Subspecialty training** (critical care, pain, transplant, cardiac and others) gives broader skills
- **Rising costs** and **payment reform** push systems towards coordinated, value-based care
cards.e: As a result, OR anaesthesia and intraoperative care **no longer dominate** most practices. Each practice must respond to the needs of its patient population and to surgeons' expectations.

cards.q: How have anaesthetists changed preoperative assessment to improve outcomes and reduce cost?
cards.a:
By using **evidence-based protocols** that standardise preoperative management and **cut low-value testing**.
- A formal preoperative visit is **not required for most healthy patients**
- Many patients have a **telephone consultation**, often by a nurse practitioner, instead of a visit, laboratory tests and imaging
- A comprehensive evaluation and **optimisation** is reserved for patients with significant comorbidity
cards.e: Oxford Handbook (NICE-based) says a test should be done only if its result will improve information, treatment or outcome, and that routine tests do not benefit low-risk patients. Lippincott adds that a thorough history and examination is more useful than routine PFTs in planning anaesthesia for lung disease.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 3 · Oxford Handbook Ch 1 · Lippincott Ch 21

cards.q: For complex patients, how should preoperative assessment and optimisation be organised?
cards.a:
As an integral part of the perioperative continuum, led by the anaesthetist:
- **Targeted investigations** where they change management (e.g. **echocardiogram**, focused **pulmonary function** tests)
- Interpretation together with the physician who knows the patient and will resume care
- **Formal specialist consultation** (cardiology, nephrology, respiratory) for only **a select few**
- Referral for **prehabilitation** when comorbidity will affect recovery from major surgery
cards.e: The anaesthetist is often best placed to define optimisation because they understand how chronic disease interacts with anaesthesia and surgery. Lippincott notes that the indications for cardiac investigation are the same as outside surgery: coronary intervention before surgery is rarely justified unless it lowers the combined risk.

cards.q: What is prehabilitation and when is it indicated?
cards.a:
**Preoperative conditioning** to improve a patient's clinical status before major surgery.
- Indicated for patients with **significant underlying conditions** expected to affect the **postoperative course and recovery**
- It is part of the anaesthetist's expanded preoperative role in perioperative medicine
cards.e: Exercise capacity is an objective target. Oxford Handbook notes that fitness is the only major prognostic variable not routinely recorded, and that an anaerobic threshold below **11 mL O2/kg/min** on CPET predicts higher mortality after major surgery. A 6-minute walk over 563 m suggests AT above 11.

cards.q: How is functional capacity expressed in METs, and what threshold predicts perioperative risk?
cards.a:
**1 MET** = oxygen consumption of **3.5 mL O2/kg/min** (resting).
- About 1 MET: dressing or eating
- About 2 METs: walking downstairs, cooking
- About 4 METs: gardening
- About 5 METs: climbing one to two flights of stairs
Inability to reach **4 METs** is associated with more perioperative cardiopulmonary complications.
cards.e: Lippincott and Oxford both use the 4-MET threshold (e.g. climbing a flight of stairs). Functional capacity guides whether further cardiac testing or prehabilitation is worthwhile.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 3 · Lippincott Ch 21 · Oxford Handbook Ch 2

cards.q: Which intraoperative system initiatives does Miller describe as improving safety and efficiency?
cards.a:
Initiatives:
- **Checklists**, which improve OR patient safety
- The routine **briefing/time out** before surgery, which reduces **wrong-site surgery** and improves communication
- **Debriefings** at the end of a case: confirm the procedure done, clarify postoperative expectations, account for all supplies and materials
- The NHS **"Productive Operating Theatre"** programme
cards.e: These measures reduced complications and in some cases costs. Oxford Handbook lists briefing items (team roles, list order, equipment, concerns) and debriefing items (what went well, what to improve), and says combining them with the WHO checklist builds safety culture.

cards.q: What did the NHS "Productive Operating Theatre" programme achieve?
cards.a:
A programme including **briefings and debriefings** to improve productivity and outcomes. Results:
- **Fewer errors** and smoother transition out of the OR
- **Higher OR utilisation**
- **Shorter turnaround times**
- **Less waste** and significant **financial savings**
cards.e: The NHS extended the approach to wards ("The Productive Ward"). Miller's point is that anaesthetists must take part in such system initiatives to achieve sustained gains.

cards.q: Why is the postoperative period a priority for anaesthetists if intraoperative safety is already high?
cards.a:
Intraoperative complications have fallen dramatically, but **postoperative complication rates remain high**.
- Anaesthetic choices have effects **beyond the immediate recovery period**, including after discharge
- Example: post-extubation **stridor or dysphagia** can last days and impair airway protection, particularly during **sleep**, possibly contributing to pneumonia that appears after discharge
- **Pneumonia** and **surgical site infection** top the list of health care–associated infections, and both are influenced by intraoperative care
cards.e: The Academy of Medicine (formerly the Institute of Medicine) acknowledged anaesthesia's safety gains. The next frontier is understanding how anaesthetic management contributes to later adverse outcomes and changing practice to prevent them.

cards.q: Give three examples of intraoperative management affecting longer-term outcome.
cards.a:
Miller's examples:
- **Fluid and vasopressor management** affects postoperative **metabolic status and renal function**
- **Intraoperative glucose control** affects **wound healing**
- **Anaesthetic management** influences **postoperative cognitive dysfunction** in adults and children
cards.e: Other complications Miller links partly to intraoperative care include aspiration, renal failure, pressure ulcers, ventilator-associated pneumonia and central line infections. These lengthen stay and increase rehabilitation needs, so they also drive cost.

cards.q: How can remote monitoring extend the anaesthetist's role after surgery?
cards.a:
Monitoring vital signs and respiratory and cardiovascular variables **in hospital or at home** allows the anaesthetist to:
- Optimise **opioid-sparing** pain management
- Detect and manage **postoperative delirium**
- Identify **late sequelae** of surgery and anaesthesia
- Prevent **unrecognised complications** during recovery
cards.e: This is part of moving responsibility past the PACU. Ch 1 adds that home monitoring can also gather information before surgery in high-risk patients.

cards.q: What anaesthesia-related problems does the surgeon's operative note usually miss at discharge, and how should they be handled?
cards.a:
The operative note rarely covers:
- **Airway concerns** or risk of airway obstruction
- Sequelae of **anaesthetic agents, opioids, muscle relaxants** or **regional blocks**
Handling: the anaesthetist can address postoperative anaesthesia-related problems and coordinate handover to the **primary care provider**, often by **phone or teleconference**, sometimes by a formal **postoperative clinic visit**.
cards.e: Patients get discharge instructions when they are often unable to understand or retain them. Even "simple" procedures have under-recognised postoperative issues, so coordinated follow-up benefits nearly all patients, many of whom are unsure which clinician is in charge of their care.

cards.q: Why does compartmentalisation of perioperative care threaten coordination, and what is the remedy?
cards.a:
Preoperative assessment is often done in a **separate clinic** at a different time, with **electronic communication only** and no direct contact with the intraoperative anaesthetist. Postoperative care is given by **yet other providers** (PACU, pain, ICU).
- Risk: **fragmented care** and loss of a coordinated plan
- Remedy: **direct communication and collaboration** among all anaesthesia providers and others, evidence-based **clinical pathways**, and **co-management agreements** for complex groups
cards.e: Miller is explicit that the **EHR cannot replace direct communication** between providers when managing complex problems. Subspecialisation brings expertise but can also fragment care.

cards.q: What are co-management agreements and when are they used?
cards.a:
Formal agreements with other specialists (e.g. hospitalists, geriatricians) that **define roles and responsibilities** across the perioperative continuum.
- Used for **geriatric patients** and those with **complex comorbidities**
- In PSH models they have produced **fewer cancellations, fewer complications, shorter stays and fewer readmissions**
cards.e: The key benefit is clarity: everyone knows who manages which problem at each stage. Ambiguous responsibility at handovers is a common source of harm.

cards.q: Describe Miller's example of an integrated, anaesthesia-led perioperative pathway for a patient with chronic severe pain undergoing complex surgery.
cards.a:
Care stays within the anaesthesia department throughout:
- **Preoperative evaluation programme**: extensive assessment and optimisation
- **Intraoperative anaesthetist** who has communicated with the patient and knows the preoperative issues
- Seamless handover to a **critical care anaesthetist** in ICU (ventilation, haemodynamics, fluids)
- **Pain service** working with the intensivist
- A department member manages **transition** to another facility or home and communicates with the **primary care provider**
cards.e: The model uses many anaesthetists with different expertise, each committed to one coordinated plan. Miller notes that the biggest barrier is often the department's own members, who must agree that coordination matters.

cards.q: What is the most prominent barrier to an anaesthesia department taking a larger perioperative role, and how is it overcome?
cards.a:
The **department's own members**. There must be **consensus** that a coordinated strategy is important.
- Make clear that perioperative care is a **shared, comprehensive** commitment of a diverse group, not extra work for a few
- Ensure subspecialists have **protected support** so clinical service and other departmental duties are not compromised
- Acquire **operational, clinical and financial data** and the analytical capacity to interpret it
cards.e: Departments also need new clinical and management skills. Lack of data and analytics is a practical barrier, especially for small practices.

cards.q: Why has there been consolidation of US anaesthesia practices, and what advantages does it bring?
cards.a:
New perioperative models need **operational, clinical and financial data** and **analytical expertise**, which small practices struggle to provide.
- Large regional or national groups can analyse practice and **document the value** of anaesthesia services clinically and financially
- Some groups became **multispecialty** or recruited **hospitalists** to broaden clinical skills
- They are better placed to **negotiate** with hospitals, especially over the **share of bundled payments**
cards.e: Every practice, whatever its size, still has to find a way to develop this data capability. The examinable link is that payment reform rewards those who can measure and prove value.

cards.q: Explain why fee-for-service is criticised and list the US alternative payment models Miller describes.
cards.a:
**FFS** is associated with **overuse** of some services, **higher costs** and **poor coordination**.
Alternatives under the **MACRA (2015)** legislation:
- **Alternative Payment Models (APMs)**, including **bundled payments** and incentive payments for reducing cost, with penalties when costs stay high
- The **Quality Payment Program**, including the **Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS)**
- **Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs)**: systems take clinical and financial responsibility for a **population**
cards.e: These models **shift financial risk to providers**. Anaesthetists who reduce the cost of a surgical episode can benefit through bundled payments, shared savings and ACO participation. Know which metrics a practice will be paid or penalised on.

cards.q: How are payers responding to the costs of complications and readmissions, and why does it matter for anaesthesia?
cards.a:
Government and private payers are **reducing payment** for costs related to complications and **denying payment for readmissions**.
- Some of these complications relate to **anaesthetic management**
- Anaesthetists must identify perioperative risks and change management to improve outcomes and **reduce costs**
cards.e: Costs come from the procedure, complications, post-discharge care and readmissions. This turns complication prevention into a financial priority for the department as well as a clinical one.

cards.q: What evidence does Miller give for the value of anaesthesia subspecialists in perioperative care?
cards.a:
Examples:
- **Transplant anaesthetists** in patient selection, optimisation and transitions: many patients now **bypass ICU** and have **shorter stays**
- Similar benefits in **cardiac, paediatric and neurosurgical** care
- **Pain medicine** teams using multimodal analgesia (especially in chronic pain patients): **less opioid**, sometimes **shorter stay** and better **satisfaction**
- **Critical care** physicians: fewer complications of **mechanical ventilation**, earlier **sepsis** diagnosis and treatment, better **renal** management
cards.e: The common factor is collaboration with surgeons and the wider team; subspecialty skill alone is not enough.

cards.q: What are the key elements of any successful model of perioperative management?
cards.a:
Three elements:
- **Understanding the specific patient population** included (e.g. a particular procedure)
- **Sufficient clinical and financial information** to evaluate management and its implications
- **Coordination and collaboration** among all participating providers
cards.e: Models have drawn on the **hospitalist** model for inpatients and the **medical home** model for chronic disease. No single model fits every population or setting.

cards.q: What is the Patient-Centred Medical Home (PCMH), and what lessons does it offer perioperative care?
cards.a:
A model where a **primary care physician** gives comprehensive, coordinated care to a **population**, mainly to **reduce ED visits and admissions**. It uses nurses, respiratory therapists and physiotherapists to manage asthma, COPD, heart failure and diabetes. Payment combines **FFS plus a coordination payment**.
Lessons:
- Preoperative assessment must be comprehensive enough to manage **chronic conditions**, not defer them
- Underlying disease must shape the **procedure and postoperative plan** (e.g. diabetic neuropathy limiting rehabilitation)
- Others can deliver much of the care, but **one physician** must coordinate, with data on costs and outcomes
cards.e: The PCMH improved care for some chronic diseases, but financial success was inconsistent and it sometimes **increased admissions**. The responsible perioperative physician may be the anaesthetist, surgeon or hospitalist, with a good handoff to primary care later.

cards.q: Describe the surgical hospitalist model, including its strengths and unresolved issues.
cards.a:
Hospitalists (internists, paediatricians or interested surgeons) manage the **medical care of surgical inpatients**, sometimes attached to a service or surgeon.
Strengths:
- Better **timeliness of interventions** and **patient and staff satisfaction**
- Frees surgeons to concentrate on the operation
Unresolved issues:
- Limited evidence on **length of stay and readmissions**
- The **relationship with the anaesthetist** in the immediate postoperative period is **not standardised**
cards.e: The hospitalist must understand procedure-specific physiology (e.g. **cerebral autoregulation** after neurovascular surgery). Whether care passes from anaesthetist to hospitalist or to an intensivist, roles must be clearly defined.

cards.q: What is ERAS, and which elements does it typically contain?
cards.a:
**Enhanced Recovery After Surgery**: evidence-based, multidisciplinary pathways covering the whole perioperative period to improve outcomes and efficiency.
Typical elements:
- **Preadmission**: nutrition, smoking cessation, alcohol control, medical optimisation, patient information
- **Preoperative**: selective bowel preparation, **carbohydrate drinks**, no prolonged fasting
- **Intraoperative**: minimally invasive surgery, **opioid-sparing** and regional anaesthesia, **balanced fluids**, **temperature control**, **PONV prophylaxis**, fewer drains and tubes
- **Postoperative**: early removal of tubes, stopping IV fluids, **early oral intake** and **mobilisation**, **multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia**, post-discharge follow-up
cards.e: In Miller's ERAS figure, "no NPO" means clear fluids and carbohydrate drinks until **2 h** before anaesthesia. Oxford Handbook explains why this is safe: clear fluids empty with a half-life of 10–20 min and are cleared within about 2 h.

cards.q: What outcome improvements have ERAS protocols produced, and in which procedures?
cards.a:
Successful protocols include **colorectal** (laparoscopic and open), **breast**, **urological**, **living liver donor** and **elective craniotomy**.
- **Length of stay** reduced by up to about **30%**
- **Postoperative complications** reduced by up to about **50%**
- Better pain control with **less opioid**
cards.e: The most successful programmes include **all** providers involved in the patient's course. ERAS is a value-based approach because it improves outcomes and lowers cost together.

cards.q: Why must ERAS protocols be audited and revised after implementation? Give Miller's example.
cards.a:
Implementation can produce **unexpected harm**, so clinical, financial and resource data should be **reviewed regularly** and the protocol changed.
- Example: a **colorectal** ERAS protocol showed **more acute kidney injury**
- Patients at risk had **longer operations** and **diverticulitis**
- Response: introduce **goal-directed fluid therapy** during and after surgery, with follow-up to assess the change
cards.e: Restrictive fluids are a typical ERAS element, so an AKI signal is plausible. Miller also urges that future protocols include **outcomes that matter most to patients**.

cards.q: What is the Perioperative Surgical Home (PSH) and what are its ASA-defined goals?
cards.a:
An ASA-developed, patient-centred model that manages the patient from **scheduling of surgery** through the whole perioperative period and back to the **primary care provider**, using evidence-based pathways to improve outcomes and **reduce total cost**, including home care and skilled nursing.
Goals:
- **Identify** the patient and proposed plan
- **Facilitate communication** among surgeons, anaesthetists and others
- Thorough **preoperative assessment** and care plan, including comorbidity management
- Develop and use **evidence-based protocols** throughout
- **Manage care across the continuum**
- **Measure and publicly report** outcomes and performance
cards.e: There is no single prescribed PSH model; the lead may be the anaesthetist or the surgeon. Reported results include better care, lower cost, shorter stay, fewer readmissions and good patient and provider satisfaction.

cards.q: Compare the Perioperative Surgical Home with ERAS and with the PCMH.
cards.a:
**ERAS** reengineers care for a **focused procedure** using evidence-based protocol elements around surgery.
**PSH** is **broader and more comprehensive**: it covers from the decision to operate to return home, includes comorbidity management, care coordination and **public reporting**, and needs more **leadership and institutional commitment**.
**PCMH** manages **chronic disease in outpatients** over the long term; the PSH applies similar coordination ideas to the **surgical episode**.
cards.e: All three aim to align goals of patients, providers, hospitals and payers. A common exam trap is to call the PSH "ERAS with another name": it is a system-wide care model that can contain ERAS pathways.

cards.q: What does implementation of a PSH require, and where has it been most successful?
cards.a:
Requirements:
- A designated **physician leader/champion** with training in **process improvement**
- Support from **surgeons and hospital administrators**
- Coordination across **inpatient and outpatient** settings, sometimes several health systems
Most comprehensive success: **closed, integrated systems** such as the **Veterans Administration** and **Kaiser**.
cards.e: It is harder when rehabilitation, skilled nursing or home care providers are outside the system. Whether the model can extend to broader populations is still unknown.

cards.q: What new competencies does Miller say anaesthetists need to practise perioperative medicine?
cards.a:
New competencies:
- Management of **medical comorbidities** beyond the immediate perioperative period
- **Health economics**: costs, outcomes, quality, safety and **payment models** and their metrics
- **Biomedical informatics and data science** to use EHR and big data
- **Process improvement** and leadership skills for roles such as perioperative medical director or chief quality officer
cards.e: Payers are testing alternative payment models that reward documented value, and many transfer financial risk to providers. Anaesthetists who understand these models can show the value of their services.

cards.q: What role does Miller see for artificial intelligence in perioperative care, and what are its limits?
cards.a:
AI can analyse **complex data across the continuum** (preoperative, intraoperative, surgical, postoperative) to:
- Improve **diagnostic and therapeutic decisions**
- Identify interventions whose **risk outweighs benefit** for an individual patient
- Support **value-based** care by improving quality and safety and lowering cost
Limit: AI **will not and should not replace** the relationship between the anaesthetist, the patient and the team. It is **another source of information** that supports clinical judgement.
cards.e: Miller describes AI as exciting, somewhat intimidating and potentially transformative. It depends on large EHR-based databases, which is one reason informatics skills are now needed.

cards.q: What is perioperative precision medicine, and what currently limits its use?
cards.a:
Individualising care using **genetic variants, phenotype, molecular derangements** and other variables, e.g. **genetic prediction of analgesic response** and prediction of complication risk.
Limits:
- Use in routine practice has been **limited** so far
- More **pharmacogenetic studies** of common perioperative drugs are needed
- It depends on **large databases, machine learning and AI** to support, not replace, clinical judgement
cards.e: Progress needs collaboration between perioperative clinicians and the developers of diagnostic tools. Ch 1 links this to biobanking and registry building.

cards.q: What leadership roles have anaesthetists taken in health systems, and why are they suited to them?
cards.a:
Roles: **perioperative medical director**, **chief quality officer** and other administrative positions in perioperative care and broader health-system management.
Why suited:
- Knowledge of **OR management** and the complexity and high cost of the perioperative environment
- Experience leading **safety and quality** improvement
- Understanding of patients' surgical and medical needs across the continuum
cards.e: These positions let anaesthetists put perioperative medicine models into practice, affecting patient satisfaction, quality, safety and value.

cards.q: Your hospital wants to launch an ERAS pathway for colorectal surgery. What is the anaesthetist's role in setting it up?
cards.a:
Co-lead a **multidisciplinary** team (surgery, nursing, dietetics, physiotherapy, pharmacy, management) and own the anaesthetic elements:
- **Preoperative**: patient education, smoking and alcohol advice, nutrition, medical optimisation, **carbohydrate loading** with clear fluids until 2 h before anaesthesia
- **Intraoperative**: opioid-sparing and regional techniques, **PONV prophylaxis**, **balanced/goal-directed fluids**, **temperature control**
- **Postoperative**: multimodal analgesia, early IV fluid stop, early feeding and mobilisation
- **Audit**: length of stay, complications (including **AKI**), readmissions, compliance and patient-reported outcomes; revise the protocol when signals appear
cards.e: Miller cites ERAS as reducing stay by up to 30% and complications by up to 50%, and gives the colorectal AKI example to show why ongoing audit is essential. Oxford Handbook supports the 2-hour clear-fluid rule.

cards.q: A frail 82-year-old woman with diabetes, CKD and heart failure is referred for elective major abdominal surgery. How would a perioperative medicine approach differ from a standard pre-anaesthetic check?
cards.a:
It starts earlier and looks wider:
- **Shared decision-making** about whether surgery matches her goals and expectations
- Structured **risk assessment** including functional capacity (METs; CPET if available) and cognition
- **Optimisation and prehabilitation** of comorbidities, with targeted tests (e.g. echo) and selective specialist input
- **Co-management agreement** with a hospitalist or geriatrician defining roles
- A named **coordinating physician**, and planning for ICU/HDU need, rehabilitation and **handover to primary care**
cards.e: The aim is to align the patient's goals and expectations with the clinical plan. Miller's PCMH lessons apply: chronic disease must be managed as part of the surgical episode, not deferred. Oxford notes that an anaerobic threshold below 11 mL/kg/min on CPET predicts higher mortality.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 3 · Oxford Handbook Ch 1 · Oxford Handbook Ch 2

cards.q: Three months after a colorectal ERAS pathway is introduced, audit shows a rise in postoperative acute kidney injury, mostly in long operations for diverticulitis. What do you do?
cards.a:
Treat it as a **protocol safety signal**:
- Convene the **multidisciplinary** pathway group and review clinical and financial data
- Identify the at-risk subgroup (**long operative time, diverticulitis**)
- Review fluid and vasopressor practice; introduce **goal-directed fluid therapy** during and after surgery for high-risk cases
- Review nephrotoxins and postoperative monitoring of urine output and creatinine
- **Re-audit** after the change and keep collecting outcomes
cards.e: This mirrors Miller's example and shows that ERAS is an iterative quality-improvement process. Intraoperative fluid and vasopressor management affects postoperative renal function.

cards.q: A 55-year-old man is discharged the same day after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. He had a difficult intubation (grade 3 view, needed a bougie) and complains of a sore throat and difficulty swallowing. The surgeon's discharge letter covers only the operation. What is your responsibility?
cards.a:
Take responsibility for **anaesthesia-related follow-up and handover**:
- Tell the patient about the **difficult airway** and give written documentation (difficult airway letter or alert)
- Explain that **post-extubation dysphagia** can last days and impair airway protection, especially when asleep. Give advice on warning signs (stridor, fever, cough) for aspiration or pneumonia
- Send a letter to the **primary care provider** covering the airway, analgesia and the dysphagia
- Arrange **telephone follow-up** or a postoperative clinic visit
cards.e: Miller notes that operative notes rarely cover airway or anaesthetic sequelae, and that patients often cannot retain discharge instructions. He raises the question of whether dysphagia contributes to pneumonia that only appears after discharge.

cards.q: Your hospital joins a bundled-payment scheme for total hip and knee arthroplasty. The chief executive asks how anaesthesia can help the programme succeed financially and clinically. What do you propose?
cards.a:
Set up a **PSH-style pathway** for the joint replacement episode:
- **Preoperative clinic**: standardised low-value test reduction, anaemia and diabetes optimisation, education, risk stratification
- **Intraoperative**: regional and opioid-sparing analgesia, PONV prophylaxis, protocolised fluids
- **Postoperative**: early mobilisation, multimodal analgesia, VTE prophylaxis, planned discharge home
- **Co-management** with hospitalists for comorbid patients
- **Data**: track length of stay, complications, readmissions, discharge destination and cost, and report them
- Negotiate the anaesthesia **share of the bundle** using the data
cards.e: Under bundling the hospital is paid one sum per episode, so avoided complications and readmissions become savings. Miller cites PSH arthroplasty programmes with reduced cost, shorter stays and fewer readmissions, and notes that data on value strengthen negotiations over bundled payments. Oxford Handbook notes that regional anaesthesia may protect against VTE in hip and knee replacement.

cards.q: A 76-year-old woman attends pre-assessment for total hip replacement. She had a coronary stent 6 months ago, has stable angina relieved by sublingual nitrate, an EF of 30% on recent echo, and is on metoprolol. A trainee suggests repeat coronary angiography to see if she needs CABG first. How do you respond?
cards.a:
**Do not order further coronary intervention** without a new indication:
- Indications for cardiac investigation are the **same as outside surgery**
- Revascularisation before surgery is justified only if the combined risk of intervention plus surgery is **lower** than surgery alone
- Instead: **communicate with her cardiologist** to confirm she is optimised, **continue her beta-blocker**, check her antiplatelet plan with respect to stent type and timing
- Plan **haemodynamic stability** intraoperatively and appropriate postoperative monitoring
cards.e: This is a Lippincott scenario showing the perioperative medicine principle of avoiding low-value testing. Oxford Handbook advises continuing existing beta-blockers and not starting them on the day of surgery. Lippincott adds that elective surgery is usually delayed about 1 year after a drug-eluting stent and about 4 weeks after a bare-metal stent.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 3 · Lippincott Ch 21 · Lippincott Ch 1 · Oxford Handbook Ch 1

cards.q: What is informatics, and what is it called when applied to health care?
cards.a:
The discipline that studies how information is **created, stored, handled, manipulated and presented**.
- In health care it is called **medical, biomedical or clinical informatics**
- Perioperative informatics covers the anaesthesia record, decision support, data exchange and secondary use of data
cards.e: At the hardware level every computer only retrieves data from memory, performs an arithmetic or comparison operation in the processor and stores the result, repeated millions of times a second. The operating system schedules these tasks, allocates memory, organises files and controls access, while application software performs the specific job (e.g. the EHR).

cards.q: Compare wired and wireless networks in the hospital setting.
cards.a:
Most hospitals use a **blend** of both to balance their strengths.
- **Wired**: needs a physical cable to a fixed, preplanned connection point; inflexible to move, but data cannot be intercepted without physical access to cables or ports; fastest
- **Wireless**: mobile and convenient, but may be **an order of magnitude slower**, prone to poor reception and interference, and its coverage cannot be confined precisely to the building
- Wireless therefore requires **access control and encryption** of transmitted data
cards.e: Every device needs a unique network address so that data reach the right computer. The security trade-off is the key exam point: wireless signals leak outside the walls, so authentication and encryption are mandatory rather than optional.

cards.q: What is the client–server model, and why are many EHRs deployed with application virtualisation?
cards.a:
The **server** hosts shared resources and the **client** accesses them; the server checks the client is authorised (**access control**) and stops any one client monopolising the resource.
- **Application virtualisation**: the application runs centrally on the server and clients simply connect to it whatever their configuration
- Advantages: tight control of availability, easy maintenance, compatibility, and the **data stay on the server inside the institutional network** rather than on the client
cards.e: Because the client only displays the session, little local computing power is needed and patient data are not scattered across workstations. This separation of data from client devices is a security as well as a maintenance benefit.

cards.q: What are "cloud" services, and what do they offer a hospital?
cards.a:
Computing resources supplied by an external vendor over the Internet, used **on demand and scalably**.
- Paid for by time used or amount stored; capacity can be added flexibly
- Accessible from anywhere with an Internet connection
- Transfers management of specialised hardware to another party
cards.e: The Internet is a network of networks; routers choose the fastest of many interconnected paths, so data cross the world in hundreds of milliseconds or less. Low-resource sites (e.g. office-based anaesthesia) may use cloud documentation without a monitor interface.

cards.q: Define information security, and explain why data sent over the Internet are not inherently private.
cards.a:
Information security means the **correct information** reaches **only the correct users** at the **correct time**.
- Unprotected Internet traffic is like a **postcard** (readable by anyone handling it) rather than a sealed **envelope**
- Safeguards (encryption, VPN, firewalls, authentication) are needed for private, secure delivery of care
cards.e: Note that availability is part of the definition: an attack that blocks legitimate users (e.g. ransomware) is a security failure just as much as a data leak. Remote care (e.g. the rapid growth of video "virtual visits" during COVID-19) also raises access and equity concerns.

cards.q: List the internal and external threats to health care information security.
cards.a:
Threats can arise inside or outside the organisation.
- **Internal**: staff accessing records they are not authorised to see; storing or transferring data insecurely; using apps that send data outside; connecting unauthorised personal devices
- **External**: **hacking**; **phishing** to steal passwords or identities; **ransomware** that disables systems to extort payment
- Targets include non-clinical systems too: power, heating/cooling, email, asset management
cards.e: Highly publicised attacks on large health systems have caused prolonged outages and impaired clinical care. Any Internet-connected device is a potential entry point, so the attack surface in a hospital is very broad.

cards.q: What is role-based security?
cards.a:
Access is granted through **users and accounts**: each user maps to a real person and may belong to **groups** that share privileges.
- A group with a similar functional role (e.g. anaesthesia providers) is given a defined set of resource privileges, e.g. the departmental policy folder
- Individuals may also have personal access (e.g. their own private files)
- Changing a group's privileges changes access for **every member** at once
cards.e: Which resources each user or group should reach must be decided in advance. Role-based design makes it simple to grant and remove access when staff join, change roles or leave.

cards.q: What are the benefits and drawbacks of strict password policies?
cards.a:
Policies enforce **complexity** (minimum length, mixed letters, numbers, special characters), **expiry dates** and **no reuse**, to make passwords harder to guess or exploit if stolen.
- Drawback: increasing complexity and frequent forced changes burden users, who may find them unacceptable
- Such requirements **may not actually reduce risk**
cards.e: Alternatives to passwords now in common use include biometrics (fingerprint, iris or face scan) and physical tokens built into ID badges. Usability matters: if security is too onerous, users find workarounds.

cards.q: Explain two-factor authentication and why it protects remote access.
cards.a:
It requires **"something you know"** (password) plus **"something you have"** (a token code generator, a smartphone app or a phone call).
- An impostor needs both the password and the physical device
- A stolen password can be obtained without the user knowing, but loss of a phone or token is likely to be noticed
- So remote access by an unauthorised person becomes very unlikely
cards.e: The trap is to call two passwords "two-factor": both are things you know. The second factor must be a different category, such as a possession or biometric.

cards.q: Why is physical security part of information security, and how is it achieved?
cards.a:
Someone with physical access to hardware or network points can bypass many software controls.
- Locked rooms and doors, devices that stop hardware being moved
- **Disconnecting unused network ports**
- Not siting computers holding controlled information in public areas
- Balanced against the need for usable, portable devices at the point of care
cards.e: This tension between security and usability recurs throughout the chapter. A workstation on the anaesthesia machine is convenient but must still be protected and cleanable to infection-control standards.

cards.q: How does encryption work, and why is it hard to break?
cards.a:
Encryption transforms readable information into a meaningless form and back again using an **encryption key**.
- Easy to reverse **with** the key, computationally infeasible **without** it
- Current methods rely on mathematics involving **multiplication of very large numbers**, which yields so many possible factor combinations that trying them all is impractical
cards.e: Encryption protects data in transit over wireless links and the Internet. It underpins VPNs and secure web traffic.

cards.q: Distinguish a firewall from a virtual private network (VPN).
cards.a:
Both control the boundary between the hospital network and the Internet.
- **Firewall**: hardware or software that blocks unauthorised connections **from outside** to internal systems and can restrict traffic leaving the network
- **VPN**: after authentication, creates an **encrypted tunnel** from an external computer to the internal network, so the remote computer behaves as if physically connected
- A hospital may require VPN use to reach the EHR from outside
cards.e: The firewall keeps strangers out, while the VPN lets trusted users in safely. Both are needed because hospitals must stay connected to the Internet for information exchange.

cards.q: What should a hospital's business continuity plan for information systems include?
cards.a:
Plans to keep care going when equipment fails or systems are attacked or damaged (fire, flood, malicious acts).
- **Redundant** physical plant (power, HVAC)
- Redundant network and server infrastructure that can take over automatically
- Robust **backups** onsite and **offsite** for rapid restoration
- Alternative software and **paper-based processes** for downtime
cards.e: Like an operating room, the perioperative information system must always be available for emergencies. Planned maintenance and unplanned failures both require a defined downtime process and a plan for reconciling records made during it.

cards.q: Compare the HL7 and FHIR data exchange standards.
cards.a:
Both let devices and clinical systems from different vendors exchange data in a standard way.
- **HL7 (Health Level-7)**: from the late 1980s, still widely used; messages are tied to a specific patient, typed (labs, monitor data, billing) and can trigger actions in the receiving system; designed for exchange **within an institution**
- **FHIR (Fast Health Interoperability Resources)**: newer; modelled on modern Internet applications making simple standard requests to a central resource; easier integration across software, **built-in security** for mobile devices; handles anything from a single vital sign to a scanned document
cards.e: HL7 did not anticipate many Internet-connected devices remotely accessing shared resources across organisations, which drove the creation of FHIR. Proprietary interfaces quickly become unmanageable across a whole hospital, hence the need for common standards.

cards.q: What does HIPAA regulate, and what are its four major rules?
cards.a:
HIPAA (US, **1996**) created a common framework defining health information, how it may be stored and transferred, and powers to investigate non-compliance.
- **Privacy Rule**: allowable uses and disclosures of **protected health information (PHI)**, covered entities, business partners, research use
- **Security Rule**: electronic PHI must be handled confidentially with **integrity and availability**; threats must be monitored and mitigated (physical, technical, procedural, administrative)
- **Enforcement Rule**: investigation and sanctions by the **Office of Civil Rights** (HHS); criminal cases may go to the Department of Justice
- **Breach Notification Rule**: breaches must be reported to the OCR, affected individuals and, depending on numbers, the media
cards.e: The rules are complex, so professional advice is recommended for specific situations. The Security Rule applies only to electronic PHI, while the Privacy Rule covers all identifiable health information.

cards.q: Give examples of HIPAA identifiers that make data protected health information.
cards.a:
Any element allowing a patient to be identified, for example:
- Names; geographic units smaller than a state (street, city, ZIP code)
- All date elements except year; **ages over 89**
- Phone, fax, email, social security, medical record, health plan, account and licence numbers
- Vehicle and device serial numbers, URLs, **IP addresses**
- **Biometrics**, full-face photographs, and any other unique code
cards.e: De-identifying a research dataset means removing all of these. A common trap is forgetting that exact dates (e.g. date of surgery) and ages above 89 are themselves identifiers.

cards.q: What must every entry in an electronic health record establish?
cards.a:
Each record must show:
- **Which patient** it belongs to, with a robust way to detect and **merge duplicate records** (e.g. an unidentified emergency patient)
- **When** it was created and a full **audit history** of later changes
- **Who** created or modified it, individually identifiable
- **Non-repudiation**: proof that the named clinician really made the entry
cards.e: Unique identification over time is difficult because name, date of birth, address and social security number each have limitations. These requirements shape how documentation must be completed.

cards.q: Why is anaesthesia information particularly suited to electronic records?
cards.a:
Anaesthesia data are **highly structured, limited in options and predictably repeated**, yet voluminous.
- Preoperative items fall into small sets of options (e.g. **Mallampati class**)
