- Intraoperative data recur at fixed intervals and can be captured automatically (e.g. NIBP every **3 minutes**)
- **More than 50 parameters** may describe a single minute of anaesthesia
cards.e: Contrast a primary care visit, where the issues to document cannot be defined or structured in advance. The combination of structure and volume is exactly what automated capture handles best.

cards.q: Outline the history of anaesthesia information management systems (AIMS).
cards.a:
Automated recording has a long history.
- **1934**: McKesson's apparatus integrated a monitor with a vital-sign recorder
- **DAME** and microDAME (Duke): monitoring platform with networked central recording
- **ARKIVE** (Diatek, **1982**): voice recognition and touch screen
- Terminology moved from "anaesthesia record keeping" (ARK) to **AIMS** as integration grew
- Limited use in early 2000s; market penetration estimated at **84%** of US medical centres by 2020
- Now usually an integral part of the enterprise EHR
cards.e: The ASA has issued a statement on documentation of anaesthesia care. The chapter stresses that the real promise lies in integration and secondary use, not in replacing paper alone.

cards.q: What are the three minimum requirements of an electronic anaesthesia documentation system?
cards.a:
A mature system must:
- **Record the whole encounter** (preoperative, intraoperative, PACU), implying a networked central server with workstations at each care location
- **Automatically capture** high-fidelity data from monitors and anaesthesia machines via an interface or **gateway device**
- Allow the provider to **annotate** events, drugs, procedures and attestations
cards.e: These are minimum requisites only; a system offering just these is not high value. The OR workstation should allow contemporaneous charting without leaving the patient and must be cleanable to infection-control standards.

cards.q: How are continuous monitoring signals stored in the anaesthesia record, and why?
cards.a:
As **sampled values at a prespecified frequency**, not as full waveforms.
- ECG, SpO₂, invasive BP and EtCO₂ are continuous sources transformed into lower-frequency recorded measures (e.g. ECG → heart rate and ST analysis)
- Storing full continuous streams is technically possible but hard to present, archive and review
- Sources: core physiological monitor (BP, CVP, PA pressure, PPV/SPV, temperature), stand-alone devices (acceleromyography, NIRS, depth of anaesthesia, SvO₂), anaesthesia workstation (FiO₂, gas flows, agent concentrations, PIP, PEEP, VT, mode)
cards.e: Because everything electronically generated could be recorded, the department must decide how much to include. The sampling choice affects later research, e.g. how hypotension is defined.

cards.q: What are documentation templates (macros), and what is their purpose?
cards.a:
Predefined groups of charting elements tailored to a case type, also called scripts or macros.
- Make relevant items easy to select (e.g. bypass events prominent in a cardiac template)
- **Reduce free-text entries**, which are often left incomplete
- Customisable at each site for local practice
- A spinal template need not ask for intubation details
cards.e: The order of elements can act as a simple prompt, e.g. after "full bypass" is charted, the next element may be stopping ventilation. This makes templates a form of passive decision support.

cards.q: What are the advantages of electronic over handwritten anaesthesia records?
cards.a:
Electronic records are more complete for physiological data and unbiased.
- **Vigilance is not reduced** by removing manual charting, and time is freed for other tasks
- Independent, unbiased record of monitor and machine data
- No legibility problems
- Handwritten charts show a **"smoothing effect"**: lower maximum systolic and higher minimum diastolic pressures than automated data
- Handwritten errors cluster at **induction, emergence and critical events**
cards.e: Smoothing may lose clinically meaningful extremes, which matters for both quality review and medicolegal defence. The trap is assuming the electronic record is complete in every respect; see the limitations of free-text and drug entries.

cards.q: What are the limitations of electronic anaesthesia documentation, and how can completeness be improved?
cards.a:
Non-automated fields, especially **free text**, and **drug administrations** are often incomplete, with errors again clustering in busy periods.
- Mandatory fields help, but too many cause **"clicking through"** (arbitrary data entry) and frustration
- **Context-sensitive (adaptive) mandatory fields**: e.g. breath sounds required with an ETT but not an LMA
- **Real-time text pages** for missing items (e.g. allergy, procedure notes) improve completion
- Non-real-time dashboards, email feedback and campaigns also help, with effects that may persist
cards.e: System design, defaults and required elements strongly shape record quality. Forcing completion of items that have legitimate exceptions can undermine trust in the whole record.

cards.q: How does electronic documentation support anaesthesia billing and supervision?
cards.a:
It captures billing elements automatically and enables real-time compliance checks.
- Start and stop times, procedure, type of anaesthesia, separately billable procedures, providers, ASA status
- **Concurrency checking at sign-in**: no in-room provider in two ORs at once and no supervisor exceeding the allowed **supervision ratio**
- Automated text and email alerts reduce documentation errors, shorten time to billing and increased capture of **arterial line** placement
- Concurrent access lets supervisors and OR managers follow each case remotely
cards.e: In the US, professional charges depend on the duration of care and the procedure. Some designs unhelpfully shift administrative work onto clinicians at the point of care.

cards.q: Distinguish block scheduling from case scheduling in OR management systems.
cards.a:
ORs are finite, costly resources whose allocation is coordinated centrally.
- **Block scheduling**: general allocation, e.g. OR 6 every Monday for thoracic surgery
- **Case scheduling**: a specific patient, procedure, surgeon and time, with staff and equipment allocated; durations estimated from historical data by surgeon and procedure; surgeon preference lists generated
- Integration with the anaesthesia record gives a unified case list and shared phase-of-care timestamps
cards.e: Because ORs incur enormous fixed costs before any surgery starts, much literature analyses procedure-time variability, turnover time and anaesthesia-related timings. Newer models add patient factors and live intraoperative data to predict remaining case duration.

cards.q: Why is medication documentation in the OR different from the ward, and what safety features are lost?
cards.a:
In the OR one clinician **decides, selects from a pre-stocked cart and gives** the drug, usually documenting **retrospectively**.
- On the ward: order → pharmacy verification → nurse administration, with barcode scanning of patient and drug
- In the OR, barcode linking to an order is typically not done, and automated **interaction, dose and allergy checks may not work**
- Patients are positively identified (sometimes by barcode) at the start of the anaesthetic
cards.e: OR drugs can matter long after the case: neuromuscular blockers, long-acting opioids and local anaesthetics, and antibiotics. A shared EHR lets ward teams see them; similarly a **difficult airway** documented in theatre helps future providers.

cards.q: What are health information exchanges (HIEs), and what is their key risk?
cards.a:
Systems that transfer records between **separate health systems' EHRs**, organised regionally or through a shared vendor platform.
- Avoid reliance on fax, paper or the patient's memory when presenting to an unaffiliated hospital
- Must **match the same patient correctly across institutions**: false matches or missed matches could be catastrophic
- Local medical record numbers are not suitable; social security numbers have accuracy and privacy problems
- Even revealing that a record exists (e.g. at a specialist clinic) may disclose a diagnosis
cards.e: Data sharing always trades information availability against privacy. Aggregation of practices into large health systems with one EHR has reduced, but not removed, the problem.

cards.q: Distinguish active and passive clinical decision support, with examples.
cards.a:
Decision support forms a hierarchy that trades burden against likelihood of changing practice.
- **Passive**: default doses, units and range checks; suggested next steps in templates; dose charts or policies shown at order entry
- **Active**: notifications about important updated trends or results, and **alerts that integrate several data items** (e.g. tidal volume above 6–8 mL/kg ideal body weight, glucose above a threshold, gap in BP recording)
- Both can highlight patterns not apparent to the clinician
cards.e: Defaults work through the **anchoring effect**, so they must be reviewed against actual local practice over time. Too many active alerts cause alert fatigue, so design and priority matter.

cards.q: Describe the architecture of an active decision support system.
cards.a:
It runs in parallel with documentation, built into the EHR or as separate software, and adds three modules:
- **Rules module**: defines the population (e.g. adults in main ORs), the rule (e.g. glucose above 300 mg/dL) and the action (page or pop-up)
- **Surveillance module**: repeatedly checks new labs, charting and device data against the rules
- **Notification module**: alerts the user within the EHR, on separate workstation software, or by text, push notification or phone call
cards.e: Examples include AlertWatch OR, a multiparameter display combining monitor and EHR data. Separating the modules makes systems easier to design, test and modify.

cards.q: Why are EHR-based alerts unsuitable for rapidly changing events such as desaturation?
cards.a:
Because of **latency**: data may update only every minute, rules need repeated values to exclude artefact, and notification adds further delay.
- Second-to-second changes (e.g. SpO₂) translate poorly into systems with delays of minutes
- Rapid or extreme events are better handled by **alarms built into monitors** at the point of care
- Alert content should suit the recipient: decision support for the in-room provider, situational awareness for the supervisor, resource and schedule issues for the OR manager
cards.e: Desaturation alerts sent to supervising anaesthesiologists had often resolved before arrival. Matching priority and intrusiveness to the clinical problem is a key design principle.

cards.q: What is the evidence for decision support in anaesthesia?
cards.a:
Strong for **processes of care**, limited for **patient outcomes**.
- Improved ventilation settings, beta-blockade documentation, antibiotic timing and redosing, BP management, PONV prophylaxis, and reduced agent use via lower fresh gas flow
- Single-centre glucose management support improved glucose control and reduced **surgical site infection**
- A multiparameter system reduced hospital charges
- Outcome benefit is more likely from **multiple combined rules** than from any single rule
cards.e: Process improvements do not automatically translate into outcome changes. Multiparameter systems are not yet widely implemented or studied.

cards.q: What are the challenges of implementing an AIMS?
cards.a:
Reliability, partial failures, archiving and coverage.
- **Downtime**: need paper backup and a plan for those records
- **Partial failure**, e.g. loss of the monitor-to-EHR link, must be recognised; manual entry is less complete and raises **legal liability** concerns
- **Retention**: often up to **10 years** after last contact for adults, and for minors until about **age 30**, potentially outliving the software
- Paper documents (consents, outside records) must be scanned or archived
- Separate perioperative systems **silo** information; infrequently used non-OR sites may not justify the cost and need paper charting
cards.e: Siloing makes the perioperative period look separate from the rest of the admission, which can cause communication failures and harm. Each paper location adds business processes for billing and quality review.

cards.q: Explain the DIKW model in the secondary use of EHR data.
cards.a:
A pyramid in which raw material is turned into practice change: **Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom**.
- **Data**: raw observations (e.g. monitor values)
- **Information**: inferred from data (e.g. surgery start, extubation)
- **Knowledge**: associations synthesised across records (e.g. practice variation)
- **Wisdom**: turning that into actionable change in systems and practice
cards.e: Secondary use (research, quality measurement, operations) is part of the value proposition of EHRs. The goal is to climb the pyramid, not merely to accumulate data.

cards.q: Why have large and multicentre EHR databases become central to perioperative research?
cards.a:
Queries are faster and broader than paper review, allowing **tens of thousands** of records per study.
- Large samples are needed for rare events (difficult airway, epidural haematoma) and to model common ones (AKI, intraoperative hypotension)
- Single-centre results generalise poorly because practice varies between institutions
- **MPOG** (Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group) pools and standardises **over 20 million** records from dozens of US institutions
cards.e: Major intraoperative complications are rare, but postoperative complications are common and the whole-hospital record is needed to capture them. Multicentre networks aim to produce generalisable knowledge.

cards.q: What methodological problems arise when using intraoperative EHR data to study hypotension?
cards.a:
The main problem is **abstraction**: hours of granular BP data must be summarised into a few biologically plausible variables.
- A 3-hour case may have **60 or more** NIBP readings
- Options: mean BP, time or fraction below an **absolute** threshold (e.g. MAP below 65 mm Hg) or a **relative** drop (e.g. 20% below baseline)
- Different definitions give different results and interpretations
- **Artefacts** pass automatically into the record and must be handled
- Define the hypothesis and analysis **a priori** to avoid post hoc fishing
cards.e: EHRs are also being used for prospective trials and **embedded pragmatic trials**, where institutions standardise a usual-care choice and rely on EHR data (and sometimes decision support) for delivery and follow-up.

cards.q: How can the EHR be used to measure quality of care?
cards.a:
By **automated derivation** of process and outcome measures instead of trained abstractors reviewing charts.
- Process example: antibiotic prophylaxis timing; outcome example: surgical site infection
- Feedback near the time of care: emails, provider dashboards, real-time pages
- Central registries reduce the technical burden on each site but limit local flexibility and add delay
cards.e: Manual abstraction is accurate but does not scale to high-volume practice because of time and staffing cost. Automated feedback can change behaviour quickly when measures are carefully designed.

cards.q: Distinguish supervised from unsupervised models and list the pitfalls of machine learning on EHR data.
cards.a:
**Supervised** models learn from known inputs and known outputs (a category such as complication or not, or a continuous value such as surgical duration); **unsupervised** models find groups with similar features (e.g. postoperative pain trajectories).
- Training data must represent the population where the model will be used, or **generalisability** is lost
- Models can propagate **historical biases**
- **Overfitting** (learning features unique to the training set) or **underfitting** (missing real relationships), tested by splitting data into training, validation and test sets
- Performance can **drift** after deployment as populations, risk relationships or outcome incidence change
cards.e: A model that performed well at derivation must be monitored over time. Bias in training data is an ethical as well as a statistical problem.

cards.q: How do workload and distractions relate to electronic devices during anaesthesia?
cards.a:
Workload is high and **clusters at induction and emergence**; distractions are common.
- Sources: unrelated conversation, preparing the next case, reference look-up, education, personal matters
- One study found personal distractions in **49%** and educational ones in **24%** of cases
- Professional societies (ASA, ACS, AANA) recommend **local policies** separating clinical, educational and personal device use
- Device use is often **logged**, allowing later medicolegal review
cards.e: Workload depends on the task, the situation and the operator. Whether providers can safely take on additional tasks is debated, so managing distraction is regarded as a required skill.

cards.q: What is meant by secondary use of EHR data, and what are its main purposes?
cards.a:
Using data collected for clinical care for other purposes:
- **Research**, often by building statistical models to identify associations or predict outcomes
- **Operational analytics** (OR utilisation, case duration prediction, staffing)
- **Quality measurement** and feedback
cards.e: Operational models increasingly combine surgeon and facility averages with patient factors and live intraoperative data. This reuse of single-patient data for business processes depends on integrated, interoperable EHRs.

cards.q: Your department finds that intraoperative antibiotic redosing is often missed in long cases. How could informatics fix this?
cards.a:
Use **active decision support** with measurement and feedback.
- Measure baseline compliance from EHR data (secondary use)
- Build a rule: population (cases with prophylactic antibiotic), trigger (elapsed time since last dose exceeds the drug's redosing interval), action (pop-up or text page to the in-room provider)
- Add passive support: redosing interval displayed at administration, template prompt
- Feed back compliance via dashboards or emails; audit after introduction
cards.e: Studies of automated reminders have improved redosing and timely prophylaxis, showing decision support reliably changes processes of care. Keep the alert specific to avoid alert fatigue, and remember a process gain may not by itself prove an outcome benefit.

cards.q: Halfway through a 4-hour laparotomy you notice the electronic record has shown no new vital signs for 25 minutes, although the monitor is working normally. What do you do?
cards.a:
Recognise a **partial system failure** (monitor-to-EHR interface) and protect both patient and record.
- Confirm the patient is stable on the monitor; patient care comes first
- Start **manual documentation** of vital signs (in the EHR or on paper per the downtime policy), with a note of the time of failure
- Inform IT/biomedical support and the supervising anaesthesiologist
- After restoration, reconcile the gap per policy; do not back-fill with invented values
cards.e: Failure to recognise loss of incoming data in a record-keeping system has been linked to increased medicolegal liability. Manual entry is unlikely to match automated completeness, which is why the gap must be clearly documented.

cards.q: A supervising anaesthesiologist covering four rooms asks for EHR text pages whenever any patient's SpO₂ falls below 90%. The EHR receives monitor data once a minute and requires two consecutive values. How do you advise?
cards.a:
This alert is **poorly suited** to the EHR decision support system.
- Latency: at least 2 minutes of data plus notification delay; many desaturations resolve before the page arrives
- Rapid events belong to **monitor alarms** and the in-room provider
- Better supervisor alerts: situational-awareness information such as **prolonged hypotension**, gaps in BP measurement, case progress, emergencies
- Target rules to events that evolve over minutes and calibrate intrusiveness
cards.e: Desaturation alerts to supervisors have been shown to be of limited use because hypoxaemia had often resolved. Matching the event's time course to the system's latency is the key design principle.

cards.q: You plan a retrospective study of intraoperative hypotension and postoperative acute kidney injury using your hospital's EHR (12,000 cases). What are the key design issues?
cards.a:
Address exposure definition, data quality, generalisability and analysis plan.
- Define hypotension **a priori**: absolute (e.g. MAP below 65 mm Hg) or relative (20% below baseline), as cumulative time, fraction of case or area under threshold
- Build **artefact filters** (e.g. flushes, transducer height, cuff errors)
- Extract the outcome from whole-hospital data (creatinine) and adjust for confounders
- Pre-register the hypothesis to avoid post hoc testing
- Consider a **multicentre** database (e.g. MPOG) to improve generalisability
- De-identify data, removing HIPAA identifiers
cards.e: Different summary definitions of BP can change the result, so sensitivity analyses are wise. Single-centre findings may reflect local practice patterns and fail to generalise.

cards.q: A 40-year-old unidentified trauma patient is registered as "Unknown Male" and anaesthetised for emergency surgery. Two days later he is identified and has an existing record noting a severe penicillin allergy and difficult intubation. What informatics issues arise?
cards.a:
A **duplicate record** has created a safety hazard.
- The EHR must detect and **merge** the temporary and existing records, preserving the audit history of who documented what and when
- Allergy and airway alerts must be visible on the merged record
- Review drugs already given (e.g. antibiotics) against the allergy
- Document the difficult airway prominently for future anaesthetics
cards.e: Robust patient identification over time is a core requirement of any EHR. Airway information gathered perioperatively has lasting value to ICU and future teams, and the same matching problem across hospitals is the main risk of health information exchanges.

cards.q: A ransomware attack takes the hospital EHR offline at 07:30 on a weekday. The first cases are due to start. How should the anaesthesia department respond?
cards.a:
Activate the **downtime and business continuity plan**.
- Switch to **paper anaesthesia records** and downtime order forms; ensure standalone monitors and machines are working
- Obtain allergy, medication and lab information from printed downtime reports or backup systems; prioritise urgent cases
- Do not connect personal devices or unapproved apps to work around the outage
- Report through the security incident process
- After recovery, scan or enter paper records according to policy
cards.e: Ransomware attacks on health systems have caused prolonged outages and impaired care. Redundancy, offsite backups and rehearsed paper processes reduce harm, and preventing access by legitimate users is itself a breach of information security.

cards.q: A resident is seen using a personal smartphone for social media during maintenance of a stable general anaesthetic. A complication occurs later in the case. What are the issues and how should the department respond?
cards.a:
Distraction during care and potential medicolegal exposure.
- Anaesthesia workload varies and peaks at induction and emergence, but vigilance is required throughout
- Personal and educational activities are common distractions in studies
- Device activity is often **logged** and may be reviewed medicolegally
- Department should have a **local policy** (per ASA/ACS/AANA statements) distinguishing clinical, educational and personal device use
- Address through education and a just, non-punitive review of the event
cards.e: Whether providers can safely multitask is debated; mitigating distraction is regarded as a core anaesthetic skill. Clinical use of devices (reference look-up, EHR) is often appropriate, so policies should not ban all device use.

cards.q: How did Deming and the Institute of Medicine (now NAM) define quality?
cards.a:
Two definitions, industrial and health care.
- **Deming**: a predictable degree of uniformity and dependability, with a standard suited to the customer (from industrial production)
- **IOM 1990** (Medicare: A Strategy for Quality Assurance): the extent to which care for individuals and populations **makes desired health outcomes more likely** and **matches current professional knowledge**
cards.e: The IOM definition contains measurement, goal orientation, process and outcome, individual and societal preferences, and evolving professional knowledge, and is now widely accepted. Quality means different things to a relative (dignity), a surgeon (functional result), an employer (cost and timeliness) and society (access).

cards.q: List the six aims for quality from Crossing the Quality Chasm (2001).
cards.a:
Care should be **Safe, Effective, Patient-centred, Timely, Efficient and Equitable** (STEEEP).
- **Safe**: no harm to patients or staff, including during handovers and off-hours
- **Effective**: evidence-based; avoid both **underuse** and **overuse**
- **Patient-centred**: respects preferences, needs and values (shared decision-making, family involvement)
- **Timely**: reduced waits and harmful delays
- **Efficient**: less waste of labour, capital, equipment, supplies, ideas and energy
- **Equitable**: quality does not vary by personal characteristics
cards.e: These aims extended the safety focus of To Err Is Human and are used by the IHI. They map onto the six ACGME core competencies in residency training via the Healthcare Matrix.

cards.q: How are errors categorised in the safety domain?
cards.a:
Two types:
- **Execution failure**: the planned action does not occur as intended (e.g. wrong drug given)
- **Planning failure**: the plan itself is wrong (e.g. misdiagnosis leading to wrong treatment)
cards.e: This distinction (from To Err Is Human) matters for prevention: execution failures respond to standardisation, labelling and checks, while planning failures need better knowledge, decision support and debiasing.

cards.q: Compare Safety-I and Safety-II.
cards.a:
Two views of what safety means.
- **Safety-I**: as few things as possible go wrong; incidents come from failure of components (technology, procedures, people, organisation) that function in a **bimodal** right-or-wrong way; used in nuclear and aviation from the 1960s to 1980s
- **Safety-II**: as many things as possible go **right**; the system's ability to **succeed under varying conditions**
cards.e: Safety-I assumptions fitted simpler, less interdependent systems with lower performance demands. Modern health care is complex and adaptive, so studying why things usually go right is also needed.

cards.q: What are the two levels of equitable care defined by the NAM?
cards.a:
Equity applies at population and individual level.
- **Population**: reduce or eliminate **disparities between subgroups**
- **Individual**: no discrimination by age, gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, education, sexual orientation, disability or geography
cards.e: Equity also features in the CMS National Quality Strategy. Unequal access to IT and measurement resources within a system can itself create disparities.

cards.q: What is the Quadruple Aim?
cards.a:
Proposed by Bodenheimer and Sinsky and adopted by the IHI:
- Better care
- Better outcomes
- Lower cost
- **Better work life for the health care workforce**
cards.e: The fourth aim was added to the earlier Triple Aim because clinician **burnout** threatens high-quality care. Exam trap: the Triple Aim lacks the workforce element.

cards.q: Outline the CMS National Quality Strategy (2022).
cards.a:
A person-centred approach across the whole care journey and all payer types, with **four priority areas, each with two goals**:
- **Aligned and improved outcomes**: outcomes; alignment across programmes and settings
- **Equity and engagement**: health equity and whole-person care; engaging individuals as partners
- **Safe and resilient systems**: **zero preventable harm**; resiliency
- **Interoperability and innovation**: digital, data-driven care; science, analytics and technology
cards.e: It spans care from birth to end of life and settings from home to post-acute care. Note the explicit safety goal of zero preventable harm.

cards.q: Compare quality assurance (QA) with continuous quality improvement (CQI).
cards.a:
QA measures compliance against **standards**; CQI improves **processes** continuously.
- **QA**: standards define "acceptable" performance (e.g. cardiac surgery mortality below 3%, CT within 4 hours of head injury) but are often **arbitrary**; reacts only when a standard is breached; flags "bad apples" (peer review, M&M); can feel punitive and blame people for random variation
- **CQI**: assumes systems cannot be built perfectly; uses **specifications** (measurable statements of key attributes, without set limits) and evaluates **all cases**, not just failures; **fixes the process, not the people**; aims to prevent failures by building improvement into the process
cards.e: Most medical CQI systems grew out of QA foundations. Excellence is rarely identified by QA, which only finds failure.

cards.q: How does CMS define quality improvement?
cards.a: A framework to **systematically improve care** using **standardised structures and processes** to **reduce variation** and produce **predictable results**.
cards.e: Crosby's maxim summarises the philosophy: quality is caused by prevention rather than appraisal. The best opportunities often lie in delivering known effective therapies more reliably rather than discovering new ones.

cards.q: What was Shewhart's contribution to QI, and how did it lead to PDSA?
cards.a:
In **1939** Shewhart introduced a three-step scientific process: **specification**, **production**, **inspection**, which must go **in a circle** rather than a line.
- His protégé **Deming** applied this in government and industry in the 1940s and developed the **Plan–Do–Study–Act** cycle
- Shewhart also introduced the control chart and the idea that data contain **signal and noise**
cards.e: The circularity is the key concept: learning from inspection feeds the next specification. This is the origin of iterative small tests of change.

cards.q: Describe each step of the PDSA cycle.
cards.a:
An iterative four-stage framework for testing changes.
- **Plan**: plan the test, **predict** results and decide how data will be collected
- **Do**: test on a **small scale**; document data, observations and problems
- **Study**: compare data with predictions to build knowledge, from both success and failure
- **Act**: **adopt**, **adapt** or **abandon**, then plan the next cycle
cards.e: Small-scale testing limits risk and reduces resistance to change. PDSA was reintroduced in the 1980s and modified in 1993, and supports both informal and complex projects.

cards.q: What is Deming's System of Profound Knowledge?
cards.a:
Improvement occurs where **subject-matter knowledge** (e.g. anaesthesiology) overlaps with **profound knowledge**, which has four parts:
- **Appreciation of a system**: any system yields exactly the results its design produces
- **Theory of knowledge**: information is not knowledge; improvement needs a theory, not just data
- **Understanding variation**: distinguish common-cause from special-cause variation
- **Psychology**: intrinsic motivation and joy in work; often the hardest part
cards.e: Two classic errors are treating common-cause variation as special cause and vice versa. If a system underperforms, it has unintentionally been designed to do so and must be managed differently.

cards.q: List Kotter's eight steps to change.
cards.a:
From The Heart of Change:
- Increase **urgency**
- Build the **guiding team**
- Get the **vision** right
- **Communicate** for buy-in
- **Empower** action
- Create **short-term wins**
- Don't let up
- Make change **stick**
cards.e: Kotter's model addresses the human and organisational side of change, which complements technical tools such as PDSA. Short-term wins sustain momentum in long projects.

cards.q: What is the Model for Improvement, and what are its three questions?
cards.a:
Developed by Associates in Process Improvement and used by the IHI: three questions followed by PDSA cycles.
- **Aim**: What are we trying to accomplish? (a **SMART** aim: specific, measurable, actionable, relevant, time-specific)
- **Measure**: How will we know a change is an improvement? (quantitative where possible, plotted on run or control charts)
- **Changes**: Which changes could we make that would lead to improvement? (observation, copying others' success, brainstorming)
cards.e: Successful changes are then tested on a larger scale and in other areas. A deep understanding of the process and its key drivers makes successful change ideas more likely.

cards.q: How is value defined in health care, and what are the problems in measuring its components?
cards.a:
**Value = patient health outcomes achieved per dollar spent**, measured over the full cycle of care.
- Outcome problems: no consensus on what an outcome is; EMRs poor at longitudinal capture; outcomes vary by condition; high cost of follow-up due to fragmentation
- Cost problems: **cost aggregation** by department or line item, and **cost allocation** as averages of shared resources (e.g. hourly OR charge)
- True costs should be aggregated around the **patient** and allocated by actual resource use; patient costs (e.g. lost work) are often omitted
cards.e: Outcomes and costs should be measured separately. Focusing on cost containment rather than value improvement has hampered understanding of real costs.

cards.q: State the five principles of Lean methodology.
cards.a:
Lean (from the Toyota Production System) creates more value for the patient with fewer resources by eliminating waste.
- **Define value** from the customer's view (e.g. Virginia Mason's patient-first focus)
- **Map the value stream**, timing every step
- **Smooth flow** by removing non-value-adding steps (e.g. unnecessary preoperative tests)
- Create **pull**: downstream demand triggers upstream work (e.g. open ORs according to surgical demand)
- **Pursue perfection** until there is no waste
cards.e: Lean also aims to reduce unevenness of workflow (e.g. ICU admissions, emergency cases) and avoid overburdening people and equipment.

cards.q: What is Six Sigma, and how did Chassin compare health care and anaesthesia with it?
cards.a:
A method from **Motorola** (1980s) aiming at near error-free processes and reduced variation; Six Sigma corresponds to **3.4 errors per million**.
- Negligent harm in hospital: about **Four Sigma** (10,000 per million)
- Inadequate depression treatment: **Two Sigma**
- Missed beta-blockers after MI: **One Sigma**
- **Anaesthesia** approached Six Sigma: deaths due to anaesthesia as low as **5.4 per million**
- Airline fatalities (1998 report): Two Sigma
cards.e: Six Sigma uses the **DMAIC** cycle: Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control. Lean Six Sigma combines flow and value improvement with reduced error and variation.

cards.q: Describe the DMAIC steps.
cards.a:
The Six Sigma improvement framework:
- **Define** goals, gain support and resources, form the team
- **Measure**: set metrics and baseline performance
- **Analyse** the system for improvement opportunities
- **Improve** by implementing ideas and statistically validating them
- **Control**: institutionalise the new system and monitor its stability
cards.e: Like the Model for Improvement it is a simple guiding framework; tools from different methods (PDSA, DMAIC) can be mixed as appropriate.

cards.q: Who were the historical pioneers of measurement in health care quality?
cards.a:
Measurement to drive improvement has a long history.
- **Florence Nightingale**: soldiers' mortality data to improve field hospital sanitation
- **John Snow**: mapped cholera to the Broad Street pump
- **Ernest Codman**: early 20th century surgeon who advocated tracking outcomes to identify adverse events
- **Donabedian** (1960s): structure–process–outcome model
- **Batalden and Berwick** (1991): founded the IHI
cards.e: These names commonly appear as one-line exam questions. Codman's end-result idea is the ancestor of modern outcome registries.

cards.q: Describe Donabedian's framework and the role of balancing measures.
cards.a:
A balanced set of measures is needed.
- **Structure**: how care is organised (e.g. ICU nurse-to-physician ratio)
- **Process**: what we do (e.g. hand hygiene and chlorhexidine before CVC insertion)
- **Outcome**: results for the patient's health over time (e.g. CRBSI, mortality, function)
- **Balancing**: unintended effects elsewhere (e.g. shorter length of stay worsening satisfaction)
- A comprehensive set has at least one process, one outcome and one balancing measure
cards.e: In-hospital mortality alone is an incomplete picture: it ignores many quality domains and the success of the whole care cycle. Balancing measures answer whether we are improving one part of the system at the expense of another.

cards.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of process measures?
cards.a:
They show whether patients reliably receive **evidence-based interventions**.
- Advantages: rapid feedback (CRBSI process compliance visible within **a week**, whereas outcome change may need **12–24 months**); **face validity** for clinicians; less need for **risk adjustment**; clinicians feel accountable for them
- Validity requires a **causal link** to an important outcome
- Disadvantages: need frequent updating as evidence changes; **measurement fixation**; can script care and stifle innovation; may ignore patient preferences
cards.e: Every patient can be assessed for a process, whereas rare outcomes give too few events for timely feedback. Clinicians are more accountable for processes because outcomes are influenced by many other variables.

cards.q: Is patient satisfaction a process or an outcome measure?
cards.a:
It depends what is being rated.
- Satisfaction **with care** is a **process** measure
- Satisfaction **with health** is an **outcome** measure
- Outcome measures include survival, functional status, sustainability of recovery, morbidity, length of stay, quality of life
cards.e: A classic trap. Current outcome measures often focus on immediate procedural results rather than the success of the entire cycle of care.

cards.q: What is measurement fixation?
cards.a:
An unintended effect of process measures in which **meeting the measure becomes the priority** rather than the intended outcome.
- Example: counting the percentage of diabetic patients given an action plan instead of measuring improved patient understanding
- Other aspects of care may be neglected
cards.e: Related risks are stifled innovation from over-scripted processes and conflict with patient preferences, which can reduce trust and satisfaction. Selecting measures is a balancing act.

cards.q: State the principles of effective measurement in QI.
cards.a:
Measurement should support, not overwhelm, change.
- Focus on what the team **can change**; start simple, small-scale and on the **process, not people**
- Be **practical**: usefulness, not perfection
- Make data **easy to collect**, built into daily work
- Combine **qualitative** with quantitative data
- Keep the set **balanced**
cards.e: Manual chart review is costly; EMRs reduce the burden but are expensive and unevenly available. Measures should have face validity for the frontline clinicians whose behaviour they aim to change.

cards.q: What is the CMS Quality Payment Program?
cards.a:
A US scheme requiring providers to demonstrate quality, linking payment to performance.
- Either through an **Advanced Alternative Payment Model** (e.g. bundled payments, quality collaboratives)
- Or by accumulating points in the **Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS)**
- UK analogue: the **Quality and Outcomes Framework**
cards.e: CMS is the largest single US health care purchaser, so these mandates have changed how hospitals and clinicians engage in and report QI.

cards.q: Distinguish common-cause from special-cause variation and define "tampering".
cards.a:
Data contain **signal** and **noise** (Shewhart).
- **Common-cause (random)**: inherent to the process, always present; a process with only this is **stable / in statistical control**
- **Special-cause (specific, assignable)**: arises from causes outside the usual system; makes the process **unstable** and should be investigated
- **Tampering**: trying to correct random variation, which inevitably fails and can worsen performance
- To improve a stable but poor process, **change the process** (often by standardisation) to shift the average
cards.e: A standards-based QA system cannot distinguish the two types and tries to correct all variation. Aggregate summary statistics do not filter noise, which is why time-series charts are preferred.

cards.q: What are the rules for interpreting a run chart?
cards.a:
A run chart plots the measure against time with the **median** as centre line.
- Baseline needs at least **12 points**; **20–25** to detect patterns
- **Shift**: **6 or more** consecutive points above or below the median
- **Trend**: **5 or more** points all increasing or all decreasing
- **Run**: consecutive points that all fall on one side of the median
- **Astronomical point**: an obvious outlier
- Annotate the chart with tests of change
cards.e: Run and control charts are the best tools for judging whether a change has had an effect, because change is temporal.

cards.q: How does a control chart differ from a run chart?
cards.a:
A control (Shewhart) chart distinguishes special from common-cause variation statistically.
- Centre line is the **mean**, not the median
- **Upper and lower control limits** at **±3 sigma** from the mean
- Points within limits: stable process; points **beyond limits**: special-cause variation, unstable process
cards.e: Reacting to a single in-limit dip as though it were special cause is tampering. Non-random patterns within the limits can also indicate special causes.

cards.q: What is a Failure Modes and Effects Analysis, and how is it simplified?
cards.a:
A **prospective** tool to find where a process could fail **before** harm occurs, especially before introducing a new process.
- For each step list **failure modes** (what could go wrong), **causes** (why) and **effects** (consequences)
- Score **likelihood of occurrence**, **likelihood of detection** and **severity** to calculate a **risk profile number**; target the highest scores
- **Simplified FMEA**: list steps, list potential failures, brainstorm interventions (e.g. infusion pump programming)
cards.e: Contrast with root cause analysis, which is retrospective after an event. FMEA tells you where to focus effort first.

cards.q: What are dashboards, balanced scorecards, flow charts, key driver diagrams and Pareto charts?
cards.a:
QI tools for display and organisation.
- **Dashboard**: real-time measures, like an aircraft instrument panel
- **Balanced scorecard** (Kaplan and Norton): whole-system measures linked to organisational strategy
- **Flow chart / process map**: visual map of every step, showing complexity and opportunities
- **Key driver diagram**: aim, theories (key drivers) and interventions; a shared mental model that evolves from descriptive to predictive theory
- **Pareto chart**: bar chart of categories in descending order, showing the few causes responsible for most problems
cards.e: In the chapter's medication-error example, three categories (infusion pumps, acetaminophen, antibiotics) caused about 80% of errors. A balanced set prevents improvement in one area from harming another.

cards.q: What is a daily goals sheet, and what results did it achieve?
cards.a:
A one-page checklist completed on ICU rounds to set the care plan, goals and safety risks for each patient.
- Before: **under 10%** of residents and nurses knew the day's plan
- About 4 weeks after: **95%** understood the goals
- Surgical ICU length of stay fell from **2.2 to 1.1 days**
- Brazil, 118 ICUs: better low tidal volume use, less heavy sedation, better teamwork and safety climate, but **no fall in hospital mortality**
- Paediatric cardiac ICU whiteboard: team agreement on goals **62% → over 87%**
cards.e: Traditional rounds focused on teaching disease rather than the work needed for the patient. The tool prompts discussion of sedation, weaning and medications.

cards.q: Why do checklists improve safety? Give the evidence for central line insertion checklists.
cards.a:
They ensure essential steps are not forgotten by **standardising practice, reducing complexity and adding a redundant check**.
- A designated reader (nurse or doctor) is **empowered to stop** the procedure if steps are missed or sterility is broken
- Central line checklist and bundle: **66%** reduction in CLABSI; median rate from **2.7 per 1000 catheter-days to zero** by month 3, sustained to month 18
- FDA recommends a checklist for anaesthesia machine checkout
cards.e: Hand hygiene and chlorhexidine skin preparation are two of the five evidence-based processes known to reduce CRBSI. These three principles are the same ones borrowed from aviation.

cards.q: What does the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist contain, and what limits its effectiveness?
cards.a:
Three phases:
- **Sign in** (before induction; at least nurse and anaesthetist): identity, site, procedure, consent; site marked; machine and drug check; **pulse oximeter** working; allergy; difficult airway/aspiration risk; risk of **over 500 mL blood loss (7 mL/kg in children)**
- **Time out** (before incision; whole team): introductions by name and role; confirm patient, procedure and incision site; **antibiotic within the last 60 minutes**; anticipated critical events; imaging displayed
- **Sign out** (before leaving OR): procedure recorded; instrument, swab and needle counts; specimen labelling; equipment problems; recovery concerns
- Haynes showed reduced **mortality and complications**; impact varies with environment, staffing, timing, relationships and **culture**
cards.e: Postoperative mortality remains two to three times higher in developing countries despite the checklist (Oxford). The checklist is meant to be adapted locally, not treated as comprehensive.

cards.q: What are briefings and debriefings, and what is TeamSTEPPS?
cards.a:
Structured team communication before and after a procedure.
- **Briefing**: introductions (first and last names, roles), patient, site, procedure, equipment, antibiotics, blood availability, and **"If something went wrong, what would it be?"**
- **Debriefing**: what went well, what failed, what could be better; handover plan; specimen and instrument issues
- Briefings improve communication, best-practice compliance and perceived safety climate
- **TeamSTEPPS**: AHRQ and Department of Defense evidence-based programme adapting **crew resource management** to health care
cards.e: The checklist is part of the Universal Protocol against wrong patient, procedure and site surgery; briefings extend this to issues such as DVT prophylaxis, fire risk and blood availability.

cards.q: Why is voluntary incident reporting valuable, and what are its limitations?
cards.a:
It identifies **hazards**, including **near misses** that caused no harm, for QI to mitigate.
- Should be **non-punitive** and focused on **systems**, not individuals
- Frequent low-harm events (skin abrasions, specimen mislabelling) can matter as much as rare severe events at local level
- Many incidents still go **unreported**; staff safety surveys asking how the next patient will be harmed fill the gap
- Rare events need **multi-institutional** systems: **AIRS** (Anesthesia Quality Institute), **Wake Up Safe** (paediatric), Vizient, UK and Australian incident systems
cards.e: Reports need not represent human error or preventable events. When staff identify the issue themselves they are more invested in fixing it.

cards.q: What national resources and registries support anaesthesia QI?
cards.a:
Guidelines, metrics and outcome registries.
- **AHRQ**, **ASA** and WFSA guidelines (e.g. central venous access, OSA, fasting)
- CMS measures (QPP, SCIP), **Joint Commission** National Patient Safety Goals, **NQF**-endorsed consensus standards
- Most **SCIP** process measures are "topped out" (near 100%) and retired
- Registries: **STS** (cardiac surgery, robust risk models), **NSQIP** (VA origin, now ACS, over 350 centres), **AQI/NACOR**, **MPOG**, **Wake Up Safe** (about 40 members, apparent cause analysis of each event)
cards.e: Risk adjustment is the key issue in outcomes research; administrative data are limited, so purpose-built registries are preferred. STS findings promoted perioperative beta-blockers, aspirin and internal mammary artery grafts.

cards.q: How can real-time EMR data support QI? Give an example.
cards.a:
Dashboards of run and control charts update automatically, enabling **rapid tests of change**, earlier detection of disruption, and visible results that motivate teams.
- Example: during the **2018 opioid shortage**, Seattle Children's used warehouse data to cut intraoperative opioid use at an ambulatory centre
- Primary measure: percentage of patients given intraoperative opioids; balancing measures: PACU rescue opioids, PACU minutes, PONV rescue, analgesic cost
- Result: less opioid use **without worse outcomes**
cards.e: This illustrates a full measure set with process, outcome and balancing measures. Real-time data are especially useful for departments without dedicated QI analysts.

cards.q: What is the IHI Breakthrough Series collaborative model?
cards.a:
A collaborative of **12 to 160 teams** across organisations working on one topic.
- Topic selected and teams enrolled; expert faculty create a **change package** of evidence-based interventions
- Alternating **learning sessions** and **action periods** with PDSA cycles, supported by calls, visits and reports
- Ends with summative congresses and publications
- Successes: waiting times down 50%, ICU costs down 25%, heart failure admissions down 50%
cards.e: Collaboratives work by shared learning and momentum, which increases sustainability. The leading team chooses interventions and defines data collection and feedback.

cards.q: Describe the TRIP model for translating evidence into practice.
cards.a:
A collaborative approach (Sawyer and Pronovost group) to ensure every patient receives evidence-based care.
- Identify evidence-based interventions linked to better outcomes
- Select those with the **strongest effect (smallest NNT)** and **lowest barrier**, and turn them into behaviours
- Develop **process or outcome measures**
- Measure **baseline** and provide timely feedback
- Ensure all patients receive the interventions through the **four Es**: **Engage, Educate, Execute, Evaluate**
cards.e: In the CRBSI example: engage by comparing local and national rates; educate all staff; execute by reducing complexity (all line supplies in one place), adding redundancy (checklists) and assigning tasks; evaluate with real-time visible feedback.

cards.q: What are the five steps of the Comprehensive Unit-based Safety Program (CUSP)?
cards.a:
A unit-level programme to improve safety culture and learn from mistakes.
- **Educate** staff on the science of safety
- **Identify hazards**: ask "How will the next patient be harmed?" and "How can we prevent it?"; review incidents, claims and sentinel events
- Assign a **senior executive** to the unit to prioritise, remove barriers, provide resources and show commitment
- **Learn from defects** (one per month), keeping fixes simple: reduce complexity, create independent redundancy
- **Implement teamwork tools** (checklists, daily goals, training)
cards.e: Safety culture is surveyed at baseline and after one year. CUSP has been used in ICUs, inpatient units, primary care and the perioperative setting.

cards.q: Why do QI projects fail?
cards.a:
Common causes:
- Inadequate resources and **lack of leadership support**
- Vague expectations and objectives
- Poor communication; overly complex plans
- Poor data management
- **Reinventing the wheel** instead of adopting proven practices
- A local culture **not ready for change**
cards.e: Success needs a shared view of safety and understanding of the science of quality and safety. CUSP is often used as a primer to create a receptive culture before specific interventions.

cards.q: Distinguish QI operations, improvement science and implementation science.
cards.a:
Three overlapping fields on a spectrum (Koczwara).
- **QI**: timely, context-dependent, local team improvement; may be criticised as unscientific
- **Improvement science**: uses QI methods but seeks **generalisable** knowledge with attention to internal and external validity; less timely
- **Implementation science** (knowledge translation in Canada): narrows the **evidence-to-practice gap**; relies on **evidence-based interventions** and explicit **theories, frameworks and models**; greatest emphasis on generalisability
cards.e: Where no evidence exists but quality is clearly poor, rapid small-scale QI tests are appropriate. Implementation science is a major focus of US and Canadian research funders.

cards.q: When should a QI project undergo formal ethical review?
cards.a:
QI is usually exempt from human-subjects review, but the Hastings Center suggests review when the project:
- Uses a **randomised** design
- Uses **novel treatments**
- Involves **researchers**
- Has **delayed feedback** of monitoring
- Is **externally funded**
cards.e: Reporting QI work with internal review board approval and a standardised format is encouraged, supporting quality delivery as a science as well as an art.

cards.q: Around which three areas should quality and safety work be organised, and which aviation principles has anaesthesia adopted?
cards.a:
Three key areas:
- **Translating evidence into practice**
- **Identifying and mitigating hazards**
- **Improving culture and communication**
- Aviation principles: **standardisation** of routine tasks, **reduction of unnecessary complexity**, and **redundancy**
cards.e: Each area needs different tools (TRIP, incident reporting and FMEA, CUSP and teamwork tools). Frontline staff must view hazards as features of systems rather than incompetent people.

cards.q: Which factors do national mortality studies repeatedly identify as contributing to anaesthesia-related death?
cards.a:
Factors in the quality of care delivery:
- Inadequate **preoperative assessment**
- Inadequate **preparation and resuscitation**
- Inappropriate **technique**
- Inadequate **monitoring**
- Lack of **supervision**
- Poor **postoperative care**
cards.e: Oxford quotes anaesthesia-associated death in ASA 1–2 adults at about 1 in 100,000, with 5–10 times higher risk in ASA 3–4 or emergency surgery. These recurrent system themes are natural targets for QI and audit.

cards.q: Your hospital has a high rate of surgical site infection after orthopaedic surgery. Design a QI project using Miller's tools.
cards.a:
Use the **Model for Improvement** with a balanced measure set.
- Form a multidisciplinary team; set a **SMART aim** (e.g. reduce SSI by 30% within 12 months)
- Measures: outcome (SSI rate), process (antibiotic **within 60 minutes** before incision, timely redosing, normothermia, skin preparation), balancing (e.g. antibiotic reactions, OR delays)
- Map the process; build a **key driver diagram**
- Test changes in small **PDSA cycles**; plot data on a **run chart** (12 baseline points) or control chart
- Spread successful changes; sustain with audit and feedback
cards.e: Process measures give feedback within weeks, whereas a fall in infection rate may take many months to show. In-hospital outcomes alone miss infections diagnosed after discharge, so follow-up must cover the whole cycle of care.

cards.q: A syringe swap leads to a patient receiving a neuromuscular blocker instead of an antiemetic at the end of a case. The error is recognised and no harm occurs. How should the department respond?
cards.a:
Treat it as a **system** problem in a non-punitive culture.
- Immediate: support ventilation and sedation until full recovery; disclose to the patient
- Report it as an incident (a **near miss/no-harm event** is still valuable)
- Analyse contributing factors (look-alike syringes, tray layout, labelling, fatigue)
- Mitigate hazards: standardised colour-coded labels, barcode checks, separate storage of paralysing agents, double-checks; consider a prospective **FMEA** of drug preparation
- Feed lessons back to staff and monitor recurrence
cards.e: Miller's three areas apply: identify and mitigate hazards, translate evidence into practice, and improve culture so staff report near misses. A QA approach that blames the individual misses the system causes and discourages reporting.

cards.q: A monthly run chart of PACU hypothermia (temperature below 36°C) has a median of 18%. After introducing forced-air warming, the last 7 consecutive points are all below the baseline median, though none is below 10%. The department chair says nothing has changed because no single month looks dramatic. Interpret this.
cards.a:
This is a **shift**: **6 or more** consecutive points on one side of the median indicates a **non-random change**, so the intervention is likely effective.
- No single astronomical point is needed
- Confirm data quality and that nothing else changed at the same time
- Annotate the chart, then recalculate a new median
- Continue PDSA cycles toward the aim; add a balancing measure (e.g. burns, OR time)
cards.e: Judging improvement by single months reacts to noise. Run chart rules separate signal from noise; a control chart (mean ± 3 sigma) could also be used once enough data exist. Lippincott notes forced-air warming as one of the best ways to prevent hypothermia and shivering, giving the change a sound theory.

cards.q: The chief executive wants to rank anaesthesiologists by their patients' 30-day mortality and publicly flag anyone above 2%. Advise.
cards.a:
This is a QA, outcome-only approach with major flaws.
- Mortality alone gives an **incomplete picture** and is strongly affected by case mix; it needs robust **risk adjustment**
- Deaths are rare, so individual rates are dominated by **random (common-cause) variation**; flagging people is tampering and blames individuals for chance
- Fixed thresholds are **arbitrary**
- Better: a balanced set of **structure, process, outcome and balancing** measures; control charts at the system level; feedback for learning, not punishment; use registries for benchmarking
cards.e: Clinicians accept process measures more readily because they control them, and CQI fixes processes rather than people. A punitive approach also discourages incident reporting.

cards.q: Your department records about 3 medication errors per month. Outline a QI project to reduce them.
cards.a:
Follow the Model for Improvement.
- Team: anaesthesiologist, nurse anaesthetist, resident, **pharmacist**
- SMART aim: from 3 to 1 error per month within 12 months
- Measure: run chart of monthly errors from the reporting system
- Understand: categorise errors in a **Pareto chart** (e.g. infusion pumps, acetaminophen, antibiotics about 80%); process maps; **key driver diagram**
- Change: PDSA tests (pharmacy stickers, two-person infusion pump checks); adopt, adapt or abandon
- Review run chart rules; continue testing until the median reaches the aim
cards.e: Focusing on the vital few categories gives the most benefit for effort. In the chapter example the median fell from 3 to 2, a significant change by run chart rules but short of the aim, so testing continued.

cards.q: An ICU has a CLABSI rate of 3 per 1000 catheter-days, above the national benchmark. The unit director asks you to lead a programme. What would you do?
cards.a:
Combine **TRIP** with **CUSP**.
- **Engage**: show staff the local rate versus the national rate
- **Educate** all team members on evidence-based practices (e.g. hand hygiene and chlorhexidine skin preparation)
- **Execute**: all insertion supplies in one cart; insertion **checklist** with a nurse empowered to stop the procedure; one to two tasks per week with named owners
- **Evaluate**: track CLABSI rate and checklist compliance, give real-time visible feedback, investigate each infection
- CUSP: safety culture survey, senior executive partner, learn from one defect per month
cards.e: A checklist and bundle reduced CLABSI by 66%, from a median 2.7 per 1000 catheter-days to zero within 3 months, sustained to 18 months. Collaborative participation across units increases momentum and sustainability.

cards.q: What contributes to patient safety errors in the perioperative environment?
cards.a:
Usually several **interacting factors** in a dynamic, high-stakes setting:
- Reliance on large volumes of **monitor and equipment data**
- The **complexity** (sometimes chaos) of the OR environment
- Skills and **interpersonal interactions** among staff
- **Personal factors**: expertise and familiarity with the procedure, distraction, fatigue, **production pressure**
- Cognitive errors, miscommunication, poor use of resources, reluctance to admit limits and seek help
cards.e: Clinical performance depends on knowledge and skills but also on these human factors at individual, team and organisational level. Recognising them is the basis of crisis resource management and simulation training.

cards.q: What do medicolegal and closed claims analyses show about human factors in airway harm?
cards.a:
Provider factors dominate.
- Canadian airway medicolegal review (2021): faulty **clinical decision-making 54%**, **procedural violations 22%**, poor **situational awareness 20%**; team and system factors far less often identified
- ASA Closed Claims difficult intubation analysis: **errors of judgement in 73%** (no plan for a known difficult airway, not using a supraglottic airway as a bridge, persisting with one technique)
- Closed claims with brain damage or death: situational awareness errors possibly contributed in **74%**
cards.e: The Canadian methodology was poorly suited to detecting team and system factors, so these may be under-represented. Perseveration with a failing airway technique is a classic fixation error.

cards.q: How does fatigue affect anaesthesia practice, and have duty-hour limits solved it?
cards.a:
Fatigue remains a significant safety issue.
- Causes: high clinical demand, call obligations, rising acuity, working at **non-physiological times** (circadian disruption), chronic sleep debt in residents
- **ACGME duty-hour limits** (including moonlighting) are in place
- Despite these, **perceived quality of care has not improved**
- Workforce shortages make the problem harder
cards.e: Simulation and experiential learning help clinicians assess and adapt practice habits to the effects of fatigue. The trap is assuming duty-hour regulation alone ensures safety.

cards.q: What are the sources of distraction for the anaesthesiologist in the OR?
cards.a:
Many, environmental and self-initiated:
- **Noise and alarms**, people moving in and out, background music
- Expectation to oversee the whole OR while caring for the patient
- Phone calls (PACU, next case, future patients), pharmacy and blood bank calls
- Preparing unavailable drugs urgently; troubleshooting equipment; complex **EMR documentation**
- Social media and internet use, clinical or non-clinical
cards.e: Simulation and experiential learning can teach strategies to maintain vigilant monitoring despite distractions. Oxford advises reducing background noise (e.g. turning off the radio) so commands are heard during a crisis.

cards.q: What is production pressure, and when is OR efficiency most achievable safely?
cards.a:
Time pressure (turnover times, keeping the surgeon on schedule) that pushes the anaesthesiologist to rush pre-induction tasks and may lead to **deviation from the standard of care**.
- Efficiency is most realistic when a **stable team** works together regularly on similar, common procedures (e.g. cardiac, neuro, transplant) and patients have low disease burden
- Collaboration is harder for providers who do not regularly work with the same surgical team, increasing pressure
cards.e: Patient safety should take precedence over efficiency, but competing pressures on each team member are hard to manage even in collaborative environments.

cards.q: What is the "second victim" phenomenon, and why is the term contested?
cards.a:
The impact of an adverse event or error on the **clinicians involved**.
- They may second-guess their judgement and competence, feel remorse, lose self-confidence, and avoid similar cases; duration is undefined
- Also affects staff less directly involved
- Likelihood of experiencing it over a career is **high**, especially where a relationship with the patient or family exists
- Term criticised because it may **diminish the patient and family** as the true victims and undermine systematic review of events
cards.e: Support for clinicians cannot replace analysing why the event occurred and fixing the system. Clinicians should still be encouraged to ask what went wrong and how it could be prevented.

cards.q: How should an organisation support clinicians after an adverse event?
cards.a:
Identify affected staff early and offer **individualised** support.
- **Peer support**
- **Case review** to understand whether and how the outcome could have been avoided
- Access to social workers, psychologists, psychiatrists or clergy for those who want it
- Recognise that some decline help initially
cards.e: Providing resources demonstrates organisational acknowledgement of the phenomenon. Responses differ widely between individuals, so a single standard response is inadequate.

cards.q: Define cognitive bias and cognitive error.
cards.a:
**Cognitive bias** is a tendency to think or act in a particular way; it becomes **cognitive error** when the bias misleads.
- Also called cognitive disposition to respond or recognition-primed decision-making
- Systematic cognitive errors are **predictable** deviations from reality
- Apply to clinical decisions and to judgements about people (patients, trainees)
cards.e: Croskerry observed that almost every cognitive error looks preventable in hindsight. Bias also distorts our thinking about bias itself, which makes self-detection difficult.

cards.q: Compare type 1 and type 2 thinking in dual process theory.
cards.a:
Two modes of decision-making.
- **Type 1**: fast, intuitive, automatic, low effort, parallel, **heuristic-based**, highly context-bound (workload, interruptions, emotion); mostly unconscious (about **95%** of our time); the **"story" system** that fills gaps and jumps to conclusions; efficient but error-prone
- **Type 2**: slow, analytical, logical, effortful; **less error-prone** but degraded by **fatigue, distraction and inattention**
- With experience, type 2 tasks become type 1 (e.g. correcting respiratory acidosis on a ventilator)
- Clinicians switch between modes
cards.e: Novices may lack the experience on which type 2 reasoning depends, yet often default to type 1 to save effort (**cognitive indolence**). Debiasing requires deliberately engaging type 2 thinking.

cards.q: What are heuristics? Give anaesthesia examples and their drawback.
cards.a:
**Mental shortcuts (rules of thumb)** that reduce cognitive load; a feature of type 1 thinking.
- "Arrives intubated, leaves intubated"
- "Every after-hours case gets an endotracheal tube"
- "Supraglottic airway only for cases under two hours"
- "Always check potassium before surgery in haemodialysis patients"
- Drawback: they ignore the **individual patient's risk–benefit** and specific context, so may not be optimal
cards.e: Heuristics preserve mental resources for difficult decisions and are often correct, but are not guaranteed to be rational or nuanced. The three main categories are anchoring, availability and affective heuristics.

cards.q: Explain the anchoring, availability and affective heuristics.
cards.a:
Three broad groups of bias.
- **Anchoring**: overvaluing **early information** (first impression); e.g. estimating 8×7×6×5×4×3×2×1 as larger than 1×2×3×…×8
- **Availability**: judging frequency by **how easily examples come to mind**; e.g. vivid media events seem commoner than they are
- **Affective**: emotion distorts decisions; e.g. a VIP patient, one resembling a relative, or one the clinician wishes to distance from (homelessness, incarceration)
cards.e: Related biases include confirmation, diagnosis momentum, framing and search satisfaction (anchoring group); feedback and gambler's fallacy (availability group); and overconfidence, visceral, commission and fundamental attribution error (affective group).

cards.q: Define confirmation bias, diagnosis momentum, framing effect and search satisfaction, with anaesthesia examples.
cards.a:
All overweight early or salient information.
- **Confirmation**: seeking evidence that supports rather than refutes a belief (noticing only a "weak" resident's errors after being warned)
- **Diagnosis momentum**: a label passed between providers becomes fixed (trauma patient labelled "lung and cardiac contusion" whose **tension pneumothorax** is missed)
- **Framing**: how information is presented alters judgement ("anxiety, depression, 23 allergies, chest pain" versus a hypertensive diabetic with chest pain)
- **Search satisfaction**: stopping the search once one finding is made (the **second fracture** is most often missed)
cards.e: Handovers are particularly vulnerable to diagnosis momentum. Graber's checklist asks whether the diagnosis was suggested by someone else or accepted as a hand-off.

cards.q: Explain feedback bias, gambler's fallacy, commission bias, overconfidence and fundamental attribution error.
cards.a:
These biases distort judgement about frequency, action and motive.
- **Feedback bias**: treating absence of feedback as good news ("never had awareness because nobody complained")
- **Gambler's fallacy**: believing independent events balance out ("I've already had my difficult airway today")
- **Commission bias**: favouring action over inaction (repeated vasopressor boluses before the first has acted)
- **Overconfidence**: believing we know more than we do; dismissing checklists and cognitive aids; acting on hunches
- **Fundamental attribution error**: assuming bad motives rather than error (labelling a patient "drug-seeking")
cards.e: Other named biases are visceral bias (countertransference) and the "yin-yang" bias (believing a patient has been fully worked up, so nothing more can be done). Overconfidence includes believing biases affect others but not oneself.

cards.q: What is the horns versus halos effect?
cards.a:
Physical characteristics (gender, height, attractiveness) wrongly suggest **incompetence or competence**.
- Example: a patient defers to the male resident rather than the female attending when asked about a nerve block
cards.e: This belongs to the anchoring group and affects evaluation of trainees and colleagues as well as patient interactions. Awareness of such biases is part of fair assessment of trainees.

cards.q: What system strategies reduce the impact of cognitive bias?
cards.a:
A multi-pronged approach that engages type 2 thinking.
- Teaching cognitive theory and biases; team-based learning; **cognitive aids**; inferential rules
- **Structured data acquisition**: review every image or echo systematically, reporting all structures (avoids missing an unrelated lung mass)
- **"Slow down" strategies**: time-outs before procedures, debriefs afterwards
- **SBAR** (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) to create a **shared mental model**
- Effective group interaction with shared decision strategy, accountability, feedback and **psychological safety**
- Decision support, alerts and reminders in the EMR that do not distract
cards.e: Data on effective debiasing are limited. Debriefing, after-action reflection and metacognition all increase awareness of compromised decisions.

cards.q: List Graber's questions that suggest an increased risk of bias.
cards.a:
Ask yourself:
- Was the diagnosis **suggested by someone else** (patient, nurse, colleague)?
- Did I accept the patient as a **hand-off**?
- Did I consider **other organ systems**?
- Do I **dislike, or like too much**, this patient?
- Was I **interrupted or distracted**?
- Am I **cognitively overloaded**?
- Am I **stereotyping** the patient or the presentation?
cards.e: These questions are a metacognitive pause that switches thinking from type 1 to type 2. They target diagnosis momentum, affective bias and distraction specifically.

cards.q: Describe the individual debiasing strategies "prospective hindsight", "rule out worst case", "don't just do something, stand there" and "my working diagnosis is".
cards.a:
Practical tools to engage analytical thinking.
- **Prospective hindsight**: imagine the decision proved wrong and ask what was missed
- **Rule out worst case**: exclude the most dangerous cause first, then the most likely
- **Don't just do something, stand there**: when feasible, pause and reassess before acting, especially when treatment carries risk
- **"My working diagnosis is…"**: signals uncertainty and keeps the differential open
cards.e: In thoracic surgery with bleeding and hypotension, hypovolaemia is likely, but pneumothorax, air embolism, tamponade and MI must be considered; treat the likely cause but change course rapidly if the response is not as expected. Experienced clinicians are more comfortable delaying action; simulation lets residents practise this.

cards.q: Name common human-performance pitfalls that lead to adverse events.
cards.a: **Fixation errors**, medication errors, misunderstandings, poor team communication, erroneous assumptions and unclear task management.
cards.e: Fixation can mean focusing on one problem while missing the real one, refusing to consider a diagnosis, or believing all is well despite warning signs. Perseverance with one airway technique in closed claims is a typical example.

cards.q: What is a high-reliability organisation (HRO), and what are its key features (AHRQ)?
cards.a:
An organisation in a hazardous environment that does not prevent every error but **anticipates, detects and contains** errors so they do not disable it; the concept dates from **1987** (airlines, aircraft carriers).
- Acknowledges the **high-risk** nature of its work and is determined to operate safely
- **Blame-free** reporting of errors and near misses
- **Collaboration across ranks and disciplines**
- **Resources committed** to safety
cards.e: The hallmark is not being error-free but that errors do not cripple the organisation. HROs also value open dialogue, respect and trust.

cards.q: What are the four structural pillars of an HRO?
cards.a:
Anchor points for systematic improvement:
- Creating and sustaining a **culture of safety**
- Organisational learning, including **incident reporting systems**
- **Continuous training** of individuals and teams, including regular **simulation**
- Continuous optimisation of safety-relevant **structures and processes**
cards.e: Simulation lets an HRO test whether its policies actually prevent the problems they target, and refine them if not.

cards.q: List the five HRO organising principles with an example of each.
cards.a:
From Sutcliffe:
- **Preoccupation with failure** (most important): chronic wariness; discuss what must not go wrong preoperatively and at handover
- **Reluctance to simplify interpretations**: question assumptions; seek alternative views
- **Sensitivity to operations**: frequent information sharing to keep a current big picture and make small corrections
- **Commitment to resilience**: build capability to contain and recover from mishaps; talk about them constantly
- **Deference to expertise**: in a crisis decisions migrate to the person with most relevant expertise, **regardless of rank**
cards.e: HROs examine even small, inconsequential problems because they are precursors of larger failures. The first three principles relate to anticipation, the last two to containment.

cards.q: Compare prevention and resilience in high-reliability organisations.
cards.a:
Two competing but necessary approaches.
- **Prevention (anticipation)**: foresee events, define causes, create standardised policies, protocols, guidelines and checklists; review events by QI and **root cause analysis**; effective against **"never events"**
- Limits: cannot prevent unanticipated events; overly complex rules reduce compliance; rigid adherence stops capable staff adapting to atypical situations
- **Resilience**: ability to **absorb strain** and keep functioning, to **recover** (bounce back), and to **learn and grow** from previous episodes
cards.e: An HRO must both prevent and contain mishaps before they spread. This mirrors the Safety-I versus Safety-II debate in quality improvement.

cards.q: Outline the history of medical simulation.
cards.a:
Key milestones:
- **Mrs Chase** (1911): first doll designed for training carers, made by Martha Jenks Chase for a nursing school
- **Resusci Anne**: Laerdal, with Peter Safar and James Elam, for mouth-to-mouth resuscitation
- **Sim One** (1969, University of Southern California, with an aerospace company): first electromechanical manikin; intubation and induction
- **Harvey** (1976): cardiology simulator of pulses, JVP, precordium and heart sounds
- **CASE** (1986, Gaba and DeAnda, Stanford): full-scale simulator to study decision-making in critical events, leading to **ACRM**
- Commercial full-scale manikins in anaesthesia from about **1995**
cards.e: In the early 2000s simulation was recognised as a means to reduce harm and described as an ethical imperative. Modern manikins can recognise drugs and interventions and respond physiologically.

cards.q: Which types of simulators are used in health care, and which are most widely used?
cards.a:
**Screen-based** computer simulators are most widely used; **manikins** are most often used for resuscitation; **high-fidelity (full-scale)** manikins for complex team training.
- Also: tabletop single-skill trainers; synthetic models, animals, fruit and vegetables; cadavers; plasticised human models; **standardised patients**; hybrid models; VR and robotic trainers (fibreoptic intubation, echo, endoscopy); virtual and augmented reality
cards.e: The best simulator is the one that meets the learning objective; not every teaching or assessment task needs simulation. The overarching goal is improved patient outcomes.

cards.q: What are the major roles of simulation in anaesthesiology (Box 6.1)?
cards.a:
Three tiers across a career.
- **Preparation and introduction**: procedural skills, common events, teamwork and communication
- **Growth and improvement**: new skills, **rare events**, crisis resource management
- **Leadership and consultant practice**: system integration, leading a team, process improvement, liability and morbidity/mortality reduction
cards.e: Experience is hard to replace, and "see one, do one, teach one" does not ensure competence. Simulation provides experience of rare crises safely.

cards.q: Which education theories underpin simulation?
cards.a:
No single theory covers all of simulation; key ones are:
- **Behaviourism** (Pavlov): repeated practice produces **automaticity** (skills, closed-loop communication, time-outs)
