- It is useful in **refractory status epilepticus** (effective in about **56%**, better in children)
cards.e: Miller's recommendation is to **avoid ketamine as the sole anesthetic** when intracranial compliance is impaired, but it may be given cautiously with adjunctive sedation. This is a classic area where newer and older texts disagree.

cards.q: How does lidocaine affect cerebral physiology, and how is it used in neuroanesthesia?
cards.a:
It lowers CBF and CMR: **5 mg/kg over 30 min then 45 µg/kg/min** lowered CBF by **24%** and CMR by **20%**.
- In very large doses (160 mg/kg on bypass in dogs), the CMRO2 fall exceeds that of barbiturates, because **membrane stabilization** reduces housekeeping energy use
- A **1.5 mg/kg bolus** was **as effective as thiopental 3 mg/kg** in blunting the ICP rise from pin-holder placement or skin incision, with **less hypotension**
- It also prevents ICP rises during **tracheal suctioning**
- Seizure threshold in awake humans is about **5–10 µg/mL**; a 2 mg/kg bolus gives peaks of 6.6–8.5 µg/mL, so use **1.5–2 mg/kg**
cards.e: Lidocaine-induced seizures have not been reported in anesthetized patients, but keep doses within this range. Oxford also recommends local anesthetic infiltration of pin sites.

cards.q: Explain the dose-dependent effect of volatile anesthetics on CBF.
cards.a:
Net CBF reflects **two opposing actions**: **CMR suppression** (coupled vasoconstriction) and **direct vasodilation** of smooth muscle.
- **0.5 MAC**: CMR suppression dominates, so CBF **falls** compared with awake
- **1 MAC** (iso, sevo, des): the two effects **balance**, so CBF is **unchanged**
- **> 1 MAC**: vasodilation dominates, so CBF and CBV **rise** even though CMR is much lower
- Most CMR suppression has already happened by 1 MAC, so extra agent adds mostly vasodilation
cards.e: Stoelting places the turning point at 0.6–1.0 MAC. Oxford: ICP is unaffected by less than 1 MAC iso, sevo or des. Hence the common craniotomy advice to keep volatile agents below 1 MAC.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: Do volatile anesthetics "uncouple" flow and metabolism?
cards.a:
**Not strictly.** Coupling (CBF tracking CMR changes) **persists** under volatile anesthesia. What changes is the **CBF/CMR ratio**, which **rises in a dose-dependent way**.
- Higher MAC gives more **"luxury perfusion"** (flow in excess of need)
- At large doses autoregulation is lost and flow becomes **pressure-passive**; both the lower and upper limits shift **to the left**
cards.e: Oxford and many exam answers say volatiles "uncouple" flow and metabolism. Miller argues the better wording is "reset the ratio". Either way, the clinical result is the same: higher CBF and CBV for a given metabolic rate.

cards.q: Rank the volatile anesthetics by cerebral vasodilating potency, and give their CBF and CMR effects in humans.
cards.a:
**Halothane ≫ enflurane > desflurane ≈ isoflurane > sevoflurane.**
- **Halothane** 1.1 MAC (MAP held at 80): CBF up to **+191%**, CMR about −10%
- **Enflurane** 1.2 MAC: CBF **+45%**, CMR −15%
- **Isoflurane** 1.1 MAC: CBF about **+19%**, CMR about −45%
- **Sevoflurane** 1 MAC: CBF **−38%**, CMR −39%; **desflurane** 1 MAC: CBF −22%, CMR −35% (Kety–Schmidt, mostly cortical)
- PET: 1 MAC sevoflurane lowered CBF by about 50% and CMRO2 by 50–60%, **but not CBV**
cards.e: Methods that sample mainly the cortex underestimate global CBF, and BP was not always held constant, so exact comparisons between newer agents are uncertain; TCD studies show only modest differences. Stoelting: at equal MAC, desflurane raises ICP more than isoflurane, and halothane is unsuitable when ICP matters.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: How do volatile anesthetics affect CMRO2, and how is halothane different?
cards.a:
All lower CMR in a **dose-related** way.
- At 1 MAC, CMRO2 falls by about **25% (iso), 38% (sevo), 22% (des)**; sevo is similar to iso, and des slightly less, especially above 1 MAC
- The maximum fall coincides with **EEG suppression at 1.5–2 MAC**; isoflurane up to 6% end-tidal gives no further fall and **no metabolic toxicity**
- The dose–response is **non-linear**: a sharp fall at the onset of anesthesia, then a slower decline
- **Halothane** needs **> 4 MAC** for EEG suppression, and more halothane lowers CMRO2 further with reversible **energy-charge changes**, implying interference with **oxidative phosphorylation**
cards.e: Lippincott: isoflurane gives an isoelectric EEG at about 2–2.5 MAC; halothane slows the EEG up to 4 MAC; enflurane produces spike-and-wave activity; sevoflurane at 2–5 MAC moves from slow waves to burst suppression and then isoelectric EEG with spikes.

cards.q: How do volatile anesthetics redistribute CBF regionally?
cards.a:
The pattern varies by agent.
- **Halothane**: **homogeneous**, with a global rise in CBF and a global fall in CMR
- **Isoflurane**: **heterogeneous**: CBF rises most in **subcortical and hindbrain** areas; CMR falls most in the **neocortex**
- **Sevoflurane** (PET): cortical CBF falls with dose, but **cerebellar CBF rises above 1.5 MAC**; similar to isoflurane
- **Propofol**: uniform fall, no redistribution
cards.e: This explains conflicting older data: a cortical xenon-washout method showed **no rise in CBF** with isoflurane at craniotomy, whereas global methods showed rises. Desflurane is assumed to behave like isoflurane because its EEG effects are similar.

cards.q: Compare the effects of volatile anesthetics and propofol on CBV, and explain why this matters.
cards.a:
**CBV, not CBF, sets ICP**, and the two can diverge.
- CBV is **considerably higher with isoflurane** than with propofol or pentobarbital
- In volunteers, **1 MAC sevoflurane lowered regional CBF but not regional CBV**; **propofol lowered both**
- Adding N2O to sevoflurane did not change CBV
- CBV follows PaCO2 (falls with hypocapnia) but by less than CBF does
cards.e: This explains why isoflurane at doses that should lower CBF still raised ICP in some patients, and why hypocapnia did not always reverse it in tumor patients. Do not assume that a fall in CBF means a fall in ICP.

cards.q: How do volatile anesthetics affect autoregulation and CO2 reactivity?
cards.a:
**CO2 reactivity is well preserved** with all volatile agents.
- During **hypotension**, CBF is maintained to lower MAP values (as with any vasodilator), with no clear differences between agents
- The response to **rising BP** is **impaired**, in proportion to dose and vasodilating potency
- **Sevoflurane** impairs it least: at 1.2–1.5 MAC, phenylephrine-induced rises in MAP did not change CBF velocity
- With high doses, autoregulation is abolished and CBF becomes pressure-passive
cards.e: Loss of protection against hypertension matters during **laryngoscopy, pinning or a mismatch between stimulus and depth**. Stoelting and Oxford list volatile anesthesia among the causes of impaired autoregulation.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: What does the evidence show when volatile-based and propofol-based anesthesia are compared in craniotomy, and when should TIVA be preferred?
cards.a:
A **meta-analysis** found only **small differences in ICP and CPP (about 5 mm Hg)** and **no difference in brain relaxation scores**, so **either technique is safe in most patients**.
- Prefer a **mainly IV technique** until the dura is open with: large or rapidly expanding masses (especially **acute TBI**), unstable ICP, impaired CO2 reactivity or coupling
- Clinical warning signs: drowsy, vomiting patient with **papilledema**; large mass; **compressed basal cisterns**
cards.e: Hypocapnia does not always reverse isoflurane-induced ICP rises in tumor patients, and in injury models it did not help at all. Oxford and Stoelting accept low-dose (< 1 MAC) sevoflurane or isoflurane, usually combined with IV vasoconstricting agents.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13

cards.q: Why does prior CMR suppression increase the vasodilating effect of a volatile anesthetic?
cards.a:
At low doses, the volatile agent's direct vasodilation is partly **offset by coupled vasoconstriction** from CMR suppression. If CMR is **already low**, this offset is lost and **vasodilation predominates**.
- On a background of morphine (little CMR suppression), isoflurane does not raise CBF significantly
- On a background of **thiopental** or **propofol** (near-maximal suppression), adding isoflurane or any volatile agent **raises CBF significantly**
- The same applies to disease states with low CMR, such as **TBI**
cards.e: Classic "unmasking" question. It is the reason for caution with volatile agents in brain-injured patients whose metabolism is already depressed, even though their CO2 reactivity may seem normal.

cards.q: Do the CBF effects of volatile anesthetics change over time?
cards.a:
**In animals, yes**: after an initial rise, CBF falls back to near pre-exposure levels over **2.5–5 hours**.
- The mechanism is unknown
- **In humans** this was **not seen** during 3- or 6-hour exposures to halothane, isoflurane, desflurane or sevoflurane
cards.e: Do not rely on time to lessen volatile-induced vasodilation in a patient with a tight brain. If the field stays tight, change technique rather than wait.

cards.q: Describe the cerebral effects of xenon and argon.
cards.a:
**Xenon**: MAC about **63–71%** (about **51% in women**); acts by **non-competitive NMDA antagonism**, possibly also via TREK K+ channels.
- At 1 MAC: CBF falls about **15% in cortex** and **35% in cerebellum**, but **rises 22% in white matter**; CMRglucose falls about **26%**
- Autoregulation and CO2 reactivity preserved (animals); did not raise ICP in an intracranial hypertension model
- It diffuses into air spaces **less than N2O**, but caution is still needed with **intracranial air**
- **Argon** 70%: no change in CBF or CMR on fentanyl–midazolam, so **not a vasodilator**
cards.e: Xenon's neurovascular profile suits neuroanesthesia, and both noble gases protect in experimental ischemia (xenon more than argon). Neither has human outcome data yet.

cards.q: What are the cerebral effects of nitrous oxide?
cards.a:
N2O can **raise CBF, CMR and ICP**, partly through **sympathoadrenal stimulation**. The size of the effect depends on the **background anesthetic**.
- **Alone** or with little else: large rises; **66% N2O raised mean ICP from 13 to 40 mm Hg** in tumor patients
- With **IV agents** (barbiturates, benzodiazepines, opioids, propofol): the effect is **attenuated or abolished** (e.g., 50% N2O during barbiturate anesthesia with hypocapnia: negligible ICP change)
- **Added to ≥ 1 MAC volatile**: **substantial additive rise** in CBF (0.75 MAC iso + 65% N2O gave 43% more CBF than 1.5 MAC iso)
- **CBV changes little**; 70% N2O modestly raises **CMRO2**; CO2 reactivity is preserved
cards.e: Do not ban N2O routinely, but suspect it when ICP stays high or the field stays tight. **Avoid** it when there is a **closed intracranial gas space** (pneumocephalus) or concern about venous air. Lippincott: N2O is about 33 times more soluble than nitrogen and expands air spaces quickly. Stoelting: it causes tension pneumocephalus after dural closure.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Lippincott Ch 13 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: How do non-depolarizing relaxants affect cerebral physiology?
cards.a:
The only direct effect is through **histamine release**, which raises ICP (cerebral vasodilation) and lowers MAP, so **CPP falls**.
- Histamine release: **d-tubocurarine** most; metocurine, atracurium and mivacurium less; **cisatracurium least** (none at 0.15 mg/kg in neuro-ICU patients)
- **Vecuronium, rocuronium, pipecuronium**: no direct cerebral effect
- Indirect benefit: relaxation prevents coughing and straining, which lowers CVP and cerebral venous outflow resistance
- **Laudanosine** (atracurium metabolite) is theoretically epileptogenic, but this is unlikely at clinical doses
cards.e: Pancuronium is acceptable if acute rises in MAP are prevented. Limit doses of histamine-releasers to avoid hypotension. Lippincott and Stoelting favor rocuronium or vecuronium for stability. The cerebral effects of sugammadex have not been studied.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Lippincott Ch 13 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13

cards.q: Does succinylcholine raise ICP, and can it be used in head injury?
cards.a:
It can cause a **modest (≈5 mm Hg) ICP rise** in **lightly anesthetized** patients.
- Mechanism: **cerebral arousal** (EEG activation, higher CBF) from **muscle spindle afferent** input, not fasciculation itself
- Prevented by **deep anesthesia**, by paralysis with vecuronium, and by **defasciculation** (metocurine 0.03 mg/kg)
- In ventilated neuro-ICU patients (mostly head-injured), **1 mg/kg caused no ICP change**, perhaps because the reduced conscious level blunts arousal
- With attention to PaCO2, BP, depth and defasciculation, it is safe for **rapid-sequence induction**
cards.e: Note: Oxford attributes the rise to fasciculation and venous pressure; follow Miller. All books agree it should still be used when rapid intubation is needed with a full stomach. The question is how it is used, not whether.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13

cards.q: How do anesthetics affect CSF formation and absorption, and what is the practical point?
cards.a:
The data are **from animals only**.
- **Halothane**: secretion ↓, absorption ↓
- **Enflurane**: secretion ↑, absorption ↓ (the **worst combination**)
- **Isoflurane**: secretion unchanged, absorption ↑
- **Desflurane**: secretion ↑, absorption unchanged
- **Fentanyl**: secretion unchanged, absorption ↑
- **Etomidate**: secretion ↓, absorption ↑
cards.e: The theoretical concern is a long closed-cranium procedure in a patient with poor compliance. More production plus less absorption is the worst case, so if a volatile agent is used, isoflurane (minimal effect) is the logical choice. Clinical relevance is probably small.

cards.q: How does the blood–brain barrier differ from other capillary beds, and what do anesthetics do to it?
cards.a:
Systemic capillary fenestrations are about **65 Å**; cerebral **tight junctions** reduce the pores to about **8 Å**, which excludes large molecules and most ions.
- **No BBB** at the **choroid plexus, pituitary and area postrema**
- In animals, **1% isoflurane** lets albumin leak into the **thalamus**; **3%** causes more leakage, including into the cortex, similar to **mannitol**
- In injury models, isoflurane has been reported both to worsen and to reduce edema; there are no human data
cards.e: The BBB explains why metabolic acidosis does not change CBF while CO2 does, and why β-agonists affect metabolism only when the barrier is damaged. Stoelting: mannitol needs an intact BBB for its full effect.

cards.q: Why does anesthetic epileptogenicity matter? Discuss enflurane, isoflurane and sevoflurane.
cards.a:
Concerns: an **unrecognized seizure** in a paralyzed patient can cause injury if CMR exceeds supply, and seizures may continue **after surgery** in a less controlled setting.
- **Enflurane**: genuinely epileptogenic, especially at **high dose with hypocapnia**. 3% lowered CMRO2 by 50%, which **returned to normal** with seizures (coupling intact). Seizures can raise CMR by up to **400%**. It has been used to **activate foci**
- **Isoflurane**: spikes and myoclonus but essentially no clinical seizures; used to **treat refractory status epilepticus**
- **Sevoflurane**: seizures during high-concentration **inductions in children**; epileptiform discharges at 2 MAC in volunteers; widespread paroxysms at 1.5 MAC in temporal lobe epilepsy (**not useful for localizing foci**); tonic–clonic movements at emergence
cards.e: Avoid enflurane (Oxford: "no place in neuroanaesthesia") and use sevoflurane with care in epileptic patients. No adverse outcomes have been reported from sevoflurane-related seizures.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Lippincott Ch 13

cards.q: Which IV anesthetics and opioids can activate seizure foci, and which are anticonvulsant?
cards.a:
Proconvulsant potential:
- **Methohexital**: myoclonus; used to **activate foci** for mapping; risk in **temporal lobe (psychomotor) epilepsy** and with large doses
- **Etomidate**: myoclonus **without EEG seizure activity** in most patients; generalizes epileptic activity in epileptics; **0.1 mg/kg** activates a quiet focus selectively; gives **longer ECT seizures**, with no dose-related inhibition at 0.15–0.3 mg/kg
- **Ketamine**: seizures in patients with an epileptic diathesis, starting in **limbic and thalamic** regions and possibly **invisible on surface EEG**
- **Opioids**: in temporal lobe epilepsy, fentanyl (mean **26 µg/kg**) and alfentanil **50 µg/kg** increased spike activity
Anticonvulsant: **propofol** (shorter ECT seizures; dystonic movements but not proconvulsant), thiopental.
cards.e: Lippincott: propofol raises seizure threshold and shortens ECT seizures, whereas etomidate, caffeine and hyperventilation lengthen them. Ketamine, etomidate and enflurane can produce seizure-like EEG activity. In neurologically normal patients, none of these drugs needs to be restricted for this reason.

cards.q: State the CBF thresholds for cerebral ischemia.
cards.a:
Function fails **progressively**, not all at once.
- **≈50** mL/100 g/min: normal
- **≈30** (35–40% fall): **clinical symptoms** in awake humans
- **≈20**: **EEG slowing** begins
- **≈15**: cortical EEG **isoelectric**
- **10–20**: the **ischemic penumbra**: neurons are electrically silent but viable for a time, and die if flow is not restored
- **≈6–10**: **membrane failure** (K+ efflux, loss of direct cortical response) and **rapid neuronal death**
cards.e: The EEG threshold under halothane–N2O in humans matches the primate data, which is why EEG is used during carotid cross-clamping. Small gains in CBF in the penumbra can greatly extend neuronal survival, which is the rationale for supporting BP. Lippincott: CBF < 20 = ischemia.

cards.q: Why does the brain tolerate focal (incomplete) ischemia better than complete global ischemia?
cards.a:
**Residual collateral flow** in incomplete ischemia delivers enough O2 for some **ATP production**.
- This **delays energy failure**: ATP falls within minutes after decapitation or cardiac arrest, but much more slowly after MCA occlusion
- So irreversible **membrane failure** happens much later in focal ischemia
cards.e: For the same reason, interventions that increase collateral flow (BP support, hematocrit near 30–34%) matter in focal ischemia. CMR suppression helps only where some electrical activity continues, i.e., in an abnormal but not flat EEG.

cards.q: Describe energy failure and excitotoxicity in cerebral ischemia.
cards.a:
**ATP depletion** is the central event.
- Ion pumps fail, so the membrane **depolarizes** and **Na+ and Ca2+ flood in**; voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open
- Presynaptic depolarization releases large amounts of **glutamate**
- **NMDA and AMPA** receptors let more Na+ and Ca2+ in; **mGluR** produces **IP3**, releasing Ca2+ from the ER
- Water follows the ions, so neurons **swell** (cytotoxic edema)
- Injury caused by excess glutamate activity is called **excitotoxicity**
cards.e: Uncontrolled cytosolic Ca2+ is the trigger for the downstream damage. Xenon (an NMDA antagonist) protects in models, and anesthetics that suppress glutamatergic transmission are logical candidates, but no human benefit has been shown.

cards.q: What downstream processes does calcium overload set off in ischemic neurons?
cards.a:
Ca2+ activates **destructive enzymes**:
- **Proteases** break down the cytoskeleton (e.g., actin) and other proteins
- **Lipases** (PLA2) damage membranes and release **arachidonic acid**, which COX and LOX convert to prostaglandins and leukotrienes, producing **superoxide** (lipid peroxidation, inflammation, chemotaxis)
- **NOS** makes NO, which forms **peroxynitrite**
- **Endonucleases** cause DNA strand breaks
- **PARP** overactivation for DNA repair **depletes NAD+**, which **worsens energy failure**
- Platelet activation and leukocyte influx block microvessels
cards.e: Mitochondrial injury adds free radicals and releases cytochrome c, which starts apoptosis. **Lactic acidosis** from anaerobic glycolysis worsens the intracellular environment, and **hyperglycemia** feeds it. NO is "friend and foe": endothelial NO helps collateral flow during ischemia, while neuronal and macrophage NO harms afterwards.

cards.q: Compare necrotic and apoptotic neuronal death.
cards.a:
**Necrosis** (excitotoxic):
- Rapid cell **swelling**, nuclear pyknosis, swollen mitochondria and ER, **acidophilic cytoplasm**
- Causes **inflammatory infiltration**, with considerable collateral damage
**Apoptosis** (programmed cell death):
- Chromatin condensation, membrane involution, mitochondrial swelling, **cell shrinkage**, fragmentation into **apoptotic bodies** that are cleared
- **Little inflammation**, so less harm to surviving neighbors
cards.e: In reality, ischemic death is a **spectrum**: some cells show necrosis, some apoptosis and some features of both. Apoptosis can continue for days after the insult, which helps explain delayed neuronal death.

cards.q: Outline the biochemical pathways of neuronal apoptosis.
cards.a:
**Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway**:
- Injured mitochondria release **cytochrome c** through outer-membrane pores; **Bax promotes** and **Bcl prevents** this
- Cytochrome c + **APAF** + procaspase-9 form the **apoptosome**, activating **caspase-9** and then **caspase-3** (the executioner)
- Caspase-3 cleaves essential proteins, including DNA-repair enzymes such as **PARP**
**Extrinsic pathway**:
- **TNF-α** activates **caspase-8**, which activates caspase-3 directly or cleaves **Bid** to trigger cytochrome c release
cards.e: These pathways are targets for experimental neuroprotection. The key exam point is that apoptosis continues long after reperfusion, so short-term infarct-size studies overestimate protection.

cards.q: What is delayed neuronal death, and why does it matter for neuroprotection research?
cards.a:
Neurons **keep dying long after** the initial insult, not only during ischemia and early reperfusion.
- After severe ischemia most neurons die quickly; after **moderate** ischemia, survivors die **later**
- Infarcts **gradually expand**; inflammation has been seen **6–8 months** later
- Timeline: excitotoxicity (minutes–hours), inflammation (hours–days), apoptosis (days–weeks), then repair and scarring (weeks–months)
cards.e: Many drugs that reduced injury at **3–4 days** showed no benefit at longer follow-up. For example, isoflurane's protection was clear at 2 days and gone by 14 days. Studies need **more than 1 month** of follow-up to claim neuroprotection.

cards.q: What are the reperfusion strategies for acute ischemic stroke, and what are their time windows?
cards.a:
**Reperfusion is the main treatment**; no neuroprotective drug has been proven.
- **IV alteplase** within **3 h** of symptom onset, extendable to **4.5 h** in selected patients
- Contraindications: **unknown onset time**, intracranial hemorrhage, head trauma or stroke within **3 months**, recent spinal or intracranial surgery, GI bleeding or malignancy, coagulopathy
- **Mechanical thrombectomy** for large-vessel occlusion: previously up to **6 h**; now up to **16 h (DEFUSE 3)** and **24 h (DAWN)** from last known well, if there is **mismatch** (salvageable penumbra)
- DAWN used **clinical–core mismatch** (NIHSS vs infarct volume); DEFUSE 3 used **imaging mismatch** (CT perfusion or MRI diffusion–perfusion)
cards.e: Wider eligibility means anesthetists are more often involved in thrombectomy. BP targets: < 185/110 before treatment, < 180/105 during and after. Stoelting notes that the tPA window is limited by the risk of hemorrhagic transformation.

cards.q: What are the management priorities for the brain after resuscitation from cardiac arrest?
cards.a:
**Physiological support** matters most.
- **Prevent hypotension**: it worsens microcirculatory and vasospastic problems (target MAP > 65, SBP > 90)
- Keep **normocapnia** and normal pH; **avoid hyperthermia**; **detect and treat seizures**
- Late intracranial hypertension comes from extensive (vasogenic + cytotoxic) edema with necrosis; **osmotherapy usually fails**, and ICP monitoring is not routine because the damage is already massive
- **Barbiturates are ineffective**; nimodipine improved CBF but not outcome (a subgroup with ALS delayed > 10 min benefited); the lidoflazine trial was negative
cards.e: Hyperoxia: PaO2 **> 300 mm Hg** after arrest is linked to higher mortality (100–300 is not), so avoid it. The EXACT trial of O2 titration was ongoing when Miller was written.

cards.q: Summarize the evidence on targeted temperature management after cardiac arrest.
cards.a:
Early trials were positive; later ones were neutral.
- Early trials: **32–34°C for 12–24 h** in comatose survivors (**GCS ≤ 7**) improved outcome at discharge and 6 months; passive rewarming over about 8 h
- Neonatal HIE: **33.5°C for 72 h** reduced mortality, with long-term benefit
- **TTM**: **33 vs 36°C**, no difference
- **TTM2**: hypothermia vs **normothermia (< 37.8°C)**, no benefit
- Guidelines still support **32–36°C**, with an **individualized** target; at a minimum, **strict avoidance of hyperthermia**
cards.e: Hypothermia helps both functional and integrity metabolism, but its clinical benefit depends on context. Exam answer: TTM remains standard, the exact target is debated, and fever must always be prevented.

cards.q: What is the evidence for barbiturates as neuroprotective agents in focal ischemia?
cards.a:
**Effective in animals, but not proven in humans.**
- Mechanism: mainly **CMR suppression**, plus CBF redistribution and free-radical scavenging. CMR suppression is not the whole story
- Early animal studies probably **overestimated** benefit because of unrecognized **hypothermia**; with temperature control, the effect is modest
- **One-third of the burst-suppression dose** gave the **same** reduction in infarct size
- Barbiturates differ: **methohexital and thiopental** protected but **pentobarbital** did not
- **IHAST**: thiopental to suppress EEG during aneurysm clipping did **not improve outcome**
cards.e: Barbiturate EEG suppression may still be reasonable **before or early in temporary focal ischemia** (e.g., temporary clipping), weighed against cardiovascular depression and delayed emergence. Oxford describes thiopental 3–5 mg/kg plus an infusion to burst suppression for temporary clipping; Stoelting also accepts it for prolonged occlusion.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13

cards.q: What is the evidence on neuroprotection by volatile anesthetics, propofol and etomidate?
cards.a:
Results differ by agent.
- **Volatiles** (isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, halothane): reduce injury compared with the awake or N2O–fentanyl state, with **no difference between agents**. Protection at **2 days is lost by 14 days**, except with **mild** ischemia and complete reperfusion
- **Propofol**: as protective as halothane or pentobarbital; better than awake; durable only with **mild** insults
- **Etomidate**: **larger** infarcts than halothane; more tissue hypoxia and acidosis than desflurane during temporary occlusion. Possible mechanisms: **NO scavenging by hemolysis** and **direct NOS inhibition**. Not supported for protection
cards.e: Anesthesia itself protects compared with a stressed awake state, so beware studies whose control group was "high-stress" (N2O sedation). No specific agent can be recommended for neuroprotection.

cards.q: What are the neuroprotective properties of xenon and argon, and how does xenon differ from other NMDA antagonists in the developing brain?
cards.a:
**Xenon** (non-competitive NMDA blocker) protects in vitro (O2–glucose deprivation), in focal ischemia and in bypass-related cognitive dysfunction in animals.
- **Subanesthetic xenon plus hypothermia or isoflurane** reduced injury in **neonatal hypoxia–ischemia**, with benefit lasting to **30 days**
- It has a **preconditioning** effect
- Unlike **ketamine** and GABA-A agents, xenon **does not appear to cause apoptosis** in the developing brain
- **Argon** also protects (stroke, TBI, bypass models) and is cheap, plentiful and non-toxic, but is **less effective** than xenon
cards.e: Long-term protection in adult models and human outcome data are still lacking, so neither gas is in routine use for neuroprotection.

cards.q: What is the role of calcium channel blockers in neuroprotection?
cards.a:
**Oral nimodipine for 21 days**, started as early as possible after **aneurysmal SAH**, is established practice. IV nimodipine is not approved in North America.
- Other CCBs reduce angiographic vasospasm but **do not improve outcome**, which suggests nimodipine works at a **cellular** rather than vascular level
- Routine nimodipine after stroke is **not** standard; trials are inconsistent
- After cardiac arrest: no overall benefit
cards.e: Stoelting: nimodipine improves outcome without widening vessels on angiography, which points to direct neuronal protection. Oxford: watch for nimodipine-induced hypotension and treat it with fluids and vasopressors. Apart from tPA, thrombectomy and CCBs in SAH, there is no proven neuroprotective drug.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: How should blood pressure and PaCO2 be managed in a patient at risk of cerebral ischemia?
cards.a:
**BP**: maintain **high-normal CPP** to improve collateral perfusion of the penumbra; treat falls promptly.
- In acute stroke trials, a **10–20% BP fall** made death or dependency **four times more likely**
- Intraoperative hypotension is associated with perioperative stroke
- For most patients without acute ischemia and with normal or controlled BP, **MAP ≈ 75 mm Hg** is adequate
**PaCO2**: keep **normocapnia**.
- Hypercapnia can cause **intracerebral steal** and intracellular acidosis
- Hypocapnia's hoped-for **"Robin Hood" (inverse steal)** has not proven useful in the laboratory or clinically
cards.e: There is no way to check the perfusion response to PaCO2 changes at the bedside, so normocapnia is the safe default. Hyperventilation is reserved as a temporary measure for raised ICP (Lippincott, Oxford).
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Lippincott Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: What is the current guidance on oxygen targets in brain injury?
cards.a:
**Treat hypoxemia aggressively and avoid hyperoxia** (PaO2 **> 300 mm Hg**) when oxygenation is otherwise normal; tailor the target to each patient.
- Hyperoxia causes **vasoconstriction**, lower microvascular flow, **reactive oxygen species** and inflammation
- After cardiac arrest, PaO2 **> 300** was linked to higher mortality (100–300 was not), though long-term outcome in survivors was unaffected
- In TBI, hyperoxia helps metabolism only in regions with very low metabolism; PaO2 **> 487** was linked to worse outcome in one study, while others found no effect
- Supplemental O2 in acute stroke and SAH did not change outcome
cards.e: The evidence conflicts, so no single target PaO2 exists. The key exam points are that hypoxia is harmful and very high PaO2 is not harmless.

cards.q: What is the evidence on intraoperative and post-injury hypothermia for brain protection?
cards.a:
Mild hypothermia (**2–4°C**) protects strongly in the laboratory, even when started after ischemia, but **clinical trials have been negative**.
- **IHAST** (aneurysm clipping): **no benefit**, but most patients were WFNS grade I–III and few had temporary clips for **> 20 min**. It may still be **considered** for high-grade aneurysms or complex clipping, and must be planned in advance
- **TBI**: helpful in pilot trials (lower ICP) but the multicenter trial was negative, so **not recommended**
- **Stroke**: feasible (33–35°C) and improves ICP and CPP, but complications are common: **thrombocytopenia, bradycardia, ventricular ectopy, hypotension, infection, ICP rebound on rewarming**. Efficacy uncertain
cards.e: Stoelting: no benefit from intraoperative hypothermia for aneurysm clipping, and none for adult TBI. Oxford: hypothermia is rarely indicated at craniotomy. Deep hypothermia for circulatory arrest is the exception, because it clearly increases ischemic tolerance.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: How should blood glucose be managed in patients at risk of cerebral ischemia?
cards.a:
**Avoid hyperglycemia and avoid hypoglycemia.**
- High glucose before ischemia **worsens injury** (more substrate for anaerobic glycolysis, more lactic acidosis); it independently predicts poor outcome, and in the NINDS tPA trial it was linked to worse outcome and **intracranial hemorrhage**
- Insulin trials in stroke: **intensive (80–130 mg/dL) was no better than standard (80–179)**; hypoglycemia occurred only with insulin
- Target **140–180 mg/dL**; the authors would not give acute insulin for glucose **< 180** in the surgical setting
- **Hypoglycemia**: EEG slows at about **40 mg/dL** and is **flat below 20**; persistent hypoglycemia causes seizures and **hippocampal** injury
- **Avoid glucose-containing IV fluids** unless treating hypoglycemia
cards.e: High glucose may be a marker of the severity of the insult rather than its cause. Lippincott and Oxford: use glucose-free isotonic fluids at craniotomy; dexamethasone can raise glucose. Stoelting: keep glucose ≤ 180 mg/dL.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Lippincott Ch 13 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: According to Miller, what should brain protection focus on, and what did the GALA trial show?
cards.a:
**Physiological homeostasis, not pharmacology.**
- No anesthetic or regimen has been shown superior; drugs that produce burst suppression (thiopental, etomidate, propofol in IHAST) gave **no added benefit**
- **GALA** (CEA under general vs local anesthesia): **same outcome**, so the anesthetized state itself gave no protection
- Experimental protection depends on strict homeostasis, and poor physiological management harms far more than drugs can protect
- Priorities: **perfusion pressure, oxygenation, normocapnia, temperature (no hyperthermia), avoiding excessive hyperglycemia, treating seizures**
cards.e: Seizures greatly increase CMR and CBF and should be treated promptly after stroke, but **prophylactic** antiepileptics are not recommended. Oxford's list of systemic secondary insults (hypotension, hypoxia, hypercapnia, pyrexia, hyperglycemia, hyponatremia, anemia) covers the same ground.

cards.q: How long should elective surgery be delayed after a stroke, and what are the exceptions?
cards.a:
The authors suggest deferring elective surgery for **9 months**.
- Regional CBF and CMR stabilize by about **2 weeks**; loss of CO2 reactivity and autoregulation can last longer; **BBB changes persist at 4 weeks**; large infarcts take months to resolve
- 30-day mortality risk is highest in the **first 3 months** and does not plateau until **9 months**
- **Early CEA**: recurrent stroke risk is about **12% within 4 weeks**; for **non-disabling** strokes, CEA **within 2 weeks** appears safe (small infarct, symptoms resolved, ipsilateral stenosis). Early CEA after **large disabling** strokes increases the risk of **intracerebral hemorrhage**
- **Emergency surgery**: MACE risk was higher at **3–14 days** but lower **within 3 days**, so if surgery is urgent, there may be no gain from a short delay
cards.e: Lippincott's older answer (stabilization at 2 weeks, BBB changes beyond 4 weeks, delay at least 6 weeks) is superseded by the 9-month figure, which Stoelting also gives.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Lippincott Ch 13

cards.q: How does chronic hypertension affect cerebral autoregulation, and how far may MAP safely be lowered?
cards.a:
Traditionally, **both limits shift to the right**, so a higher MAP is needed to maintain CBF. Newer data show **static and dynamic autoregulation are preserved** in treated and untreated hypertension, and acute SBP reduction from **220 to 150** over an hour did not change CBF.
- A **25% fall in MAP** brings both normotensive and hypertensive patients to the **LLA**
- A **50% fall** often causes **reversible symptoms** of cerebral hypoperfusion in awake patients
- Therefore limit the fall to **20–35% of baseline** (the authors' practice: no more than 20% below baseline measured at head level)
- Treatment can **restore the LLA** toward normal, though in humans this may be incomplete even after 12 months; **ACE inhibitors lower the LLA acutely**
cards.e: Stoelting: lowering BP quickly to "normal" values with vasodilators can cause ischemia in chronic hypertensives, while gradual treatment shifts the curve back. Lippincott: the curve shifts right in chronic hypertension. The margin shrinks further with anemia or unrecognized cerebrovascular disease.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Lippincott Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: What is known about the physiology of brain tumors and peritumoral edema, and how is the edema treated?
cards.a:
Tumors generally have **lower CBF** than normal brain; autoregulation is only occasionally present, while **CO2 and O2 reactivity are usually preserved** in gliomas.
- Hyperventilation can sometimes **paradoxically raise MCA velocity** on the tumor side
- **High-grade gliomas** have higher regional CBF and CBV
- Edema types: **vasogenic** (protein leak), **hydrocephalic** (CSF obstruction), **static** (venous obstruction). Mechanisms include tight-junction loss, **VEGF** and **leukotriene C4**
- More edema on imaging predicts a bigger ICP rise with **intubation-related hypertension**
- **Mannitol** works, but with a leaky BBB it can enter the peritumoral space and cause **rebound edema** (not a concern for acute intraoperative use)
- **Dexamethasone**: reduces edema formation and BBB permeability **within about 1 hour**, and shrinks the tumor slightly
cards.e: Stoelting: mannitol 0.25–0.5 g/kg, effective within 30 min, peak at 1–2 h; stop if osmolality > 320 mOsm/L; it needs an intact BBB. Steroids help tumor edema but have **no role in head injury** (Oxford).
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: A 68-year-old man with treated hypertension (baseline BP 160/90) has shoulder arthroscopy in the beach-chair position under GA. The arm cuff reads 90/50 (MAP 63), and his external auditory meatus is about 30 cm (12 inches) above the cuff. Interpret this and manage it.
cards.a:
**Brain perfusion is probably inadequate.** Pressure at the circle of Willis is about **24 mm Hg lower** than at the cuff, so the MAP at the brain is roughly **39 mm Hg**.
- His baseline MAP is about 113; the target is no more than a **20–30% fall**, i.e., a MAP of **≈80–90 at head level**
- Reduce anesthetic depth if possible; give fluid
- Raise MAP with a vasopressor, preferably one that keeps up CO (**ephedrine**) or as an **infusion** rather than repeated phenylephrine boluses
- Consider lowering the head-up angle; measure invasively with the transducer **zeroed at the external auditory meatus**
- Consider cerebral oximetry, but remember its extracranial contamination
cards.e: The hydrostatic correction is about 2 mm Hg per inch. Do not rely on the siphon argument, because cerebral vessels are collapsible. Chronic hypertension may shift the LLA rightwards, and treatment may restore it only partly, so his margin is small. Lippincott: zero at the ear for seated patients.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Lippincott Ch 13 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13

cards.q: A 25-year-old with severe TBI has been hyperventilated to PaCO2 25 mm Hg for 36 hours in ICU. ICP is now controlled, and the team wants to return PaCO2 to 40 mm Hg straight away. What do you advise?
cards.a:
**Normalize PaCO2 slowly** (over many hours), watching ICP.
- After 6–8 h, CSF bicarbonate has fallen and CSF pH has returned to normal, so the vasoconstriction has **already faded**
- A sudden rise in PaCO2 now causes **CSF acidosis**, leading to **cerebral vasodilation and a rebound rise in CBF, CBV and ICP**
- Raise PaCO2 in small steps, ready to treat ICP with osmotherapy, sedation and CSF drainage
- In future, use hyperventilation only **briefly** for acute ICP crises, not as routine sustained therapy (it also risks ischemia in the injured brain)
cards.e: Stoelting, Lippincott and Oxford all note that hyperventilation's effect lasts at most about 6–24 h and that rebound intracranial hypertension follows rapid normalization. Oxford: excessive hyperventilation causes ischemia and loss of autoregulation.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Lippincott Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: During craniotomy for a large frontal glioma with midline shift, anesthesia is maintained with 1.5 MAC sevoflurane and 60% N2O. After the bone flap is removed, the dura is tense and the brain bulges. PaCO2 is 42 mm Hg, MAP 85. How do you manage this?
cards.a:
**Remove the vasodilators and lower CBV.**
- **Stop N2O** (it adds to volatile vasodilation and may raise CMR)
- **Switch to propofol TIVA** (lowers both CBF and CBV) or at least reduce sevoflurane to **< 1 MAC**
- **Moderate hyperventilation** to PaCO2 about 30–35 mm Hg
- **Mannitol** 0.25–1 g/kg (or hypertonic saline); head-up about 30° with the neck free of venous obstruction; check that MAP and CPP are maintained
- Ensure depth and relaxation (no straining); consider a bolus of thiopental or propofol
cards.e: Above 1 MAC, volatile vasodilation outweighs CMR suppression, and N2O on top of a volatile agent gives a substantial additive rise in CBF. Miller advises a mainly IV technique for large masses until the dura is open and the brain can be seen. The meta-analysis showing equivalence applies to typical elective cases, not this one.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13

cards.q: A 40-year-old with TBI is sedated with midazolam in ICU; ICP has been difficult to control (22–28 mm Hg). The neurosurgeon asks for 0.5 mg flumazenil to allow a neurological examination. How do you respond?
cards.a:
**Advise against a rapid flumazenil bolus.**
- Rapid reversal can cause a **CBF and ICP overshoot well above pre-sedation levels** (animal data: CBF +44–56%, ICP +180–217%), which is **not matched by CMR** and is probably a neurogenic arousal response
- In head-injured patients with poorly controlled ICP, severe ICP rises have been reported
- Alternatives: stop midazolam and wait, or switch to a short-acting agent (propofol, remifentanil) for daily sedation holds
- If flumazenil must be used, give it **slowly in small increments or by infusion**, with ICP and CPP monitored and treatment ready
cards.e: Flumazenil alone does not change CBF in volunteers, and after routine tumor craniotomy it was harmless. The danger is specifically **rapid reversal when compliance is poor**.

cards.q: A 52-year-old woman (WFNS grade IV SAH) is having clipping of a complex MCA aneurysm. The surgeon expects temporary clipping for more than 20 minutes. What can you do to protect her brain?
cards.a:
Focus on **physiology first**, then consider pharmacological suppression.
- **Before the clip goes on**, raise **MAP to high-normal or slightly above** to improve collateral flow; avoid any hypotension
- **Normocapnia**, normal PaO2 (avoid hypoxia and gross hyperoxia), **glucose 140–180 mg/dL**, no hyperthermia; avoid hemoconcentration (Hct 30–35% is the theoretical optimum, but routine hemodilution is not justified)
- **Optional EEG burst suppression** with thiopental (Oxford: 3–5 mg/kg bolus then 3–5 mg/kg/h) or propofol, **titrated on EEG**, given **before or early** in the occlusion; expect a vasopressor requirement and delayed emergence
- **Mild hypothermia** may be considered in high-grade or complex cases (IHAST excluded few such patients), but **decide early** because cooling takes time; avoid hyperthermia on rewarming
- **Avoid etomidate** (worsens tissue hypoxia during temporary occlusion)
- Continue **nimodipine** and manage its hypotension
cards.e: Thiopental and hypothermia did not improve outcome in IHAST, so neither is mandatory. Oxford and Stoelting still accept them for long temporary occlusions. A lower dose (about one-third of the burst-suppression dose) gave equal infarct reduction in animals.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Lippincott Ch 13

cards.q: A 60-year-old man is admitted to ICU after out-of-hospital VF arrest with ROSC at 20 minutes. GCS is 5; temperature 38.2°C; PaO2 410 mm Hg on FiO2 1.0; PaCO2 30 mm Hg; MAP 58 mm Hg; glucose 260 mg/dL. What are your neuroprotective priorities?
cards.a:
Correct each harmful variable.
- **Hypotension**: restore MAP **> 65** (SBP > 90) with fluids and vasopressors/inotropes, because hypotension worsens post-arrest microcirculatory injury
- **Hyperthermia**: start **targeted temperature management** at 32–36°C (target individualized), and **strictly prevent fever**
- **Hyperoxia**: reduce FiO2 to keep PaO2 in the normal range, at least **< 300 mm Hg** (linked to higher mortality)
- **Hypocapnia**: aim for **normocapnia** (vasoconstriction risks ischemia)
- **Glucose**: bring to **140–180 mg/dL** with careful insulin, avoiding hypoglycemia
- **Seizures**: EEG monitoring and treatment
- Do **not** give barbiturates or calcium channel blockers for protection (ineffective)
cards.e: TTM (33 vs 36°C) and TTM2 (vs normothermia) found no benefit from deeper cooling, but guidelines keep 32–36°C and insist on avoiding hyperthermia. Late intracranial hypertension from global edema responds poorly to osmotherapy.

cards.q: A 71-year-old had a left MCA ischemic stroke 6 weeks ago with mild residual weakness. He is listed for elective total knee replacement next week. What do you advise?
cards.a:
**Postpone elective surgery** until about **9 months** after the stroke, if possible.
- Perioperative death and MACE risk is highest in the **first 3 months** and does not plateau until **9 months**
- Autoregulation and CO2 reactivity can stay impaired beyond 2 weeks; BBB changes persist at 4 weeks or more; large infarcts take months to resolve
- Use the delay to **find and treat the cause** (carotid, cardiac source) and control risk factors
- If surgery cannot wait: keep MAP near baseline (tolerate little hypotension), normocapnia, normoglycemia, normothermia
cards.e: Stoelting also recommends a delay of up to 9 months for autoregulation to return and for risk factor management. Contrast an **urgent** case, where surgery within 3 days was not worse than at 3–14 days.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Lippincott Ch 13

cards.q: A 74-year-old woman with a right MCA occlusion (NIHSS 16) arrives 10 hours after she was last known well. CT perfusion shows a small core with a large penumbra. She is agitated, and BP is 200/105. What is the plan for anesthetic management of thrombectomy?
cards.a:
She is a thrombectomy candidate under **DEFUSE 3 / DAWN** criteria (up to 16–24 h with mismatch).
- **BP**: lower to **< 185/110** before the procedure (e.g., small titrated IV labetalol doses; avoid overshooting, since nicardipine-induced BP falls lowered CBF in acute stroke), then keep **< 180/105** during it; **avoid hypotension**, because the penumbra depends on collateral pressure
- After successful recanalization, a lower target (SBP **< 140**) is reasonable; after incomplete recanalization, < 180/105
- Technique: sedation or GA as suits the patient (agitation, airway, cooperation); induce with careful hemodynamic control and have a vasopressor ready
- **Normocapnia**, treat hypoxemia but avoid hyperoxia, **glucose 140–180**, normothermia
- Treat seizures if they occur
cards.e: In stroke, a 10–20% BP fall made a poor outcome four times more likely. Small CBF gains in the penumbra (10–20 mL/100 g/min) extend neuronal survival. Stoelting stresses managing airway, oxygenation, ventilation, BP, glucose and temperature together.

cards.q: A 30-year-old motorcyclist with a GCS of 8, a suspected acute subdural hematoma and a full stomach needs emergency intubation and craniotomy. BP is 150/90. Choose your induction drugs and justify them.
cards.a:
**Rapid-sequence induction that protects CPP and avoids ICP surges.**
- Induction agent: **propofol or thiopental** titrated to avoid hypotension (they lower CMR, CBF and ICP); **etomidate** is acceptable for hemodynamic stability (lowers ICP, keeps CPP); **ketamine** is acceptable if combined with other sedatives, not as the sole agent
- Opioid: modest fentanyl or remifentanil, avoiding a sudden fall in MAP
- Lidocaine **1.5 mg/kg** IV may blunt the ICP response
- Relaxant: **rocuronium** (fast, no ICP effect) or **succinylcholine 1 mg/kg**. The small ICP rise from succinylcholine is an arousal effect, blunted by adequate depth, and absent in ventilated head-injured patients
- Afterwards: PaCO2 about 35 (brief hyperventilation only for herniation), maintain MAP so that **CPP is 60–70** (assume ICP is about 20, so MAP ≥ 80), **avoid N2O**, use a mainly IV technique until the dura is open
cards.e: Oxford: succinylcholine should still be used when rapid intubation is needed with a full stomach in head injury, and minimum MAP should be 80 mm Hg if ICP is assumed to be 20. Miller: how succinylcholine is used matters more than whether it is used.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Lippincott Ch 13

cards.q: During resection of a meningioma, a 65-year-old with an ejection fraction of 30% becomes hypotensive (MAP 55) after blood loss. Cardiac index is low. The trainee plans repeated 100 µg phenylephrine boluses. What would you do instead, and why?
cards.a:
**Restore volume first**, then use an agent that **supports cardiac output**.
- Give fluid or blood to correct preload
- In poor LV function, bolus **phenylephrine** raises afterload, which can **lower CO**, and **CO may contribute to CBF** independently of MAP
- Prefer **ephedrine**, or an **inotrope** (dobutamine raised CBF independently of MAP in SAH and TBI), or a vasopressor as an **infusion** rather than boluses
- Target MAP ≥ 70 (CPP 60–65), considering retractor pressure, which makes local perfusion pressure **MAP − tissue pressure**
cards.e: Heart failure limits autoregulatory defense against hypotension. In tumor patients, ephedrine kept local CBF and microcirculatory flow better than phenylephrine at the same MAP.

cards.q: A 35-year-old with drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy is having resection with intraoperative electrocorticography. The surgeon asks you to "bring out" the seizure focus. Which drugs would you use, and which should you avoid during recording?
cards.a:
**Activate gently, then suppress less.**
- Activating options: **etomidate about 0.1 mg/kg** (selective activation of a quiet focus; larger doses generalize), **methohexital** (used for cortical mapping), **alfentanil 50 µg/kg** (increases temporal spikes)
- **Sevoflurane** at 1.5 MAC causes **widespread** paroxysms that **do not localize** the focus
- Avoid deep **propofol** or benzodiazepines during recording, as they suppress spikes; reduce depth with light volatile plus remifentanil
- Be ready to treat a generalized seizure (propofol or thiopental bolus, benzodiazepine)
cards.e: Enflurane and hypocapnia also activate the EEG, but enflurane is obsolete. Ketamine-induced seizures may arise from limbic and thalamic regions and not show on surface recordings, so it is a poor activating agent.

cards.q: A 58-year-old with a large left frontal glioblastoma (surrounding edema, 6 mm midline shift, drowsy, vomiting) is listed for craniotomy tomorrow. How do you optimize him before surgery and during induction?
cards.a:
Treat the **vasogenic edema** and plan an ICP-protective induction.
- **Dexamethasone** (Oxford: 4 mg 6-hourly) to reduce edema and BBB permeability (effect begins within about 1 h); monitor and control the resulting **hyperglycemia** (target ≤ 180 mg/dL)
- **Mannitol** in theatre if needed (0.25–1 g/kg); with a leaky BBB it can enter the peritumoral space and cause rebound edema
- **Avoid sedative premedication** that could cause hypercapnia
- Induction: propofol or thiopental + opioid titrated to avoid **intubation hypertension** (extensive edema predicts a larger ICP rise); consider lidocaine 1.5 mg/kg; rocuronium
- Maintenance: **propofol TIVA** or < 1 MAC volatile, **no N2O**, PaCO2 about 35; glucose-free isotonic fluids
cards.e: Hyperventilation is usually effective because CO2 reactivity is generally preserved in gliomas, but paradoxical ipsilateral rises in MCA velocity have been reported, so check the effect clinically. Clinical signs of a tight brain favor an IV technique.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Lippincott Ch 13

cards.q: After hypothermic cardiopulmonary bypass for CABG, a 66-year-old is being rewarmed; nasopharyngeal temperature reaches 38.6°C and glucose is 290 mg/dL. Why does this matter to the brain, and what do you do?
cards.a:
**Both hyperthermia and hyperglycemia worsen ischemic brain injury**, and the brain is at risk of ischemia around bypass.
- Stop active warming and **keep core temperature at or below 37–38°C** (avoid overshoot during rewarming)
- Treat glucose with insulin to **140–180 mg/dL**, watching for hypoglycemia
- Keep MAP adequate (the ULA on bypass may be only about 90, and the LLA varies), keep normocapnia
cards.e: An increase of only 1°C during or after ischemia can turn scattered neuronal necrosis into infarction. Hyperglycemia increases lactic acidosis during anaerobic glycolysis. Stoelting recommends monitoring nasopharyngeal or esophageal temperature to avoid hyperthermia.

cards.q: A 70-year-old with long-standing untreated hypertension (BP 190/105) needs urgent laparotomy. His MAP after induction is 75 mm Hg, and the surgical team say this "looks fine". Is it? Justify your target.
cards.a:
**Probably not fine**: a MAP of 75 is about **45% below his baseline of about 133**.
- In untreated chronic hypertension the LLA may be shifted **to the right**, so a population-normal MAP can approach his LLA
- A **25% fall** reaches the LLA even in normotensive people; a **50% fall** commonly causes hypoperfusion symptoms in awake patients
- Aim to keep MAP within **20–30% of baseline** (about **95–105**), using lighter anesthesia, fluid and a vasopressor
- Avoid hypocapnia and anemia, which shrink the margin further
cards.e: Newer evidence shows autoregulation is preserved in hypertension, and gradual treatment can move the LLA back. But he is **untreated** and the fall is **acute**. Stoelting warns that rapid lowering to "normal" values in chronic hypertensives can cause cerebral ischemia.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Lippincott Ch 13

cards.q: A 45-year-old is admitted to ICU after a cerebellar hemorrhage with external ventricular drainage. She is breathing spontaneously, sedated with midazolam boluses, and her PaCO2 is rising (52 mm Hg). ICP has risen from 15 to 26 mm Hg. Explain the physiology and outline management.
cards.a:
**Hypercapnia** (from benzodiazepine respiratory depression) causes cerebral vasodilation, so **CBF and CBV rise and ICP rises**.
- CBF rises by about 1–2 mL/100 g/min for each mm Hg of PaCO2; CBV rises by about 0.05 mL/100 g per mm Hg
- Hypercapnia also **weakens autoregulation**, so BP surges pass straight to the brain
- Management: secure the airway and **ventilate to normocapnia** (about 35–40 mm Hg); continue sedation with ventilation controlled (propofol)
- Head-up 30°, neck neutral, drain CSF via the EVD, osmotherapy if ICP stays raised; keep CPP above 60
cards.e: Benzodiazepines are safe with raised ICP only if hypercapnia and hypotension are prevented. Lippincott: the fastest way to lower ICP is hyperventilation (to about PaCO2 25, briefly), but in this case the first goal is to correct the hypercapnia.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 10 · Lippincott Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13

cards.q: Describe the structure of the adult neuromuscular junction (NMJ). Where are the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) and sodium channels located?
cards.a:
The NMJ is a synapse made of **three cells**: the motor nerve terminal, the muscle fibre and the **Schwann cell** covering the terminal.
- The nerve loses its myelin near the muscle and branches into boutons over the end plate
- **Synaptic cleft about 50 nm** wide, bridged by basal lamina; the muscle surface folds into primary and secondary clefts
- **AChRs sit densely on the shoulders (crests) of the folds**, about **5 million per junction**, and are sparse in the depths
- **Voltage-gated Na+ channels sit in the depths of the folds** and throughout the muscle membrane
- Acetylcholinesterase is anchored in the cleft
cards.e: Placing receptors on the crests, directly opposite the release sites, means little ACh is wasted. Na+ channels in the troughs then turn the end-plate potential into a propagated action potential. Each adult muscle fibre normally has only one end plate. The main exception is the extraocular muscles.

cards.q: What is a motor unit, and why does succinylcholine cause fasciculations? Why do nondepolarizing relaxants (NDMRs) prevent them?
cards.a:
A **motor unit** is one motor neuron plus all the muscle fibres its branches supply. **Fasciculation** is the **synchronous contraction of all the fibres in one motor unit**.
- Only the nerve can synchronise a whole unit, so succinylcholine must act **prejunctionally**: it depolarises nicotinic receptors on the nerve terminal and causes repetitive firing
- Small doses of NDMR occupy the same prejunctional receptors and stop that firing, which is why **precurarisation abolishes fasciculations**
cards.e: This reasoning was the first evidence for prejunctional nicotinic receptors. The fasciculations are often strong enough to be seen through the skin. Remember that the prejunctional receptor is a neuronal subtype, which is different from the postjunctional muscle receptor.

cards.q: Why do the extraocular muscles respond differently to succinylcholine, and what is the clinical relevance?
cards.a:
Extraocular muscles are **tonic, multiply innervated** fibres with many NMJs along each fibre, and they express **both mature and immature (fetal) AChRs** even in adults.
- They are chemically excitable along most of their surface, so **accommodation does not occur**
- Their receptors **resist desensitisation**
- Succinylcholine therefore causes a **sustained contracture** lasting **1–2 minutes**, with more than **12 g** of tension per muscle, which pulls the globe against the orbit and helps **raise intraocular pressure**
cards.e: Miller says reports of vitreous extrusion are largely anecdotal, but because of the contracture it still advises that succinylcholine probably should not be used for **open eye injuries**. A standard exam trap is to attribute the rise in IOP only to raised venous pressure, when the extraocular contracture is the specific NMJ mechanism.

cards.q: What is the perijunctional zone and why does it matter?
cards.a:
It is the band of muscle membrane **just beyond the end plate**. It has fewer AChRs but the **highest density of Na+ channels** in the muscle.
- It converts the end-plate potential into a **propagated muscle action potential**
- During depolarising block its Na+ channels become fixed in the inactivated state, so it **acts as a buffer** that isolates the rest of the fibre
- Isoforms of AChRs and Na+ channels expressed here change with age and with reduced nerve activity, which helps explain why relaxant responses differ in disease
cards.e: The perijunctional zone links chemical transmission to electrical propagation. It is the site of accommodation during succinylcholine block, and it is where immature receptors appear in denervation states.

cards.q: Explain the quantal theory of acetylcholine release. Give the key numbers.
cards.a:
ACh is released in **packets (quanta)** of fixed size, each corresponding to one vesicle.
- **Miniature end-plate potentials (MEPPs)** are spontaneous depolarisations about **1/100 the amplitude** of an evoked end-plate potential. They are too large to come from one ACh molecule, so each one must be a quantum
- The evoked end-plate potential is the **sum of the synchronous release of several hundred vesicles**
- One nerve impulse releases **at least 200 quanta of about 5000 ACh molecules each** and activates about **500,000 AChRs**
- Release happens within about **200 μs**, which suggests that Ca2+ channels lie right next to the release sites (active zones)
cards.e: The release sites face the postjunctional receptors directly, so transmission is tightly coupled and very little transmitter is wasted. These numbers form the basis of the margin of safety.

cards.q: What is the margin of safety of neuromuscular transmission, and what is its clinical consequence?
cards.a:
The nerve releases **more ACh than needed**, and that ACh activates **more receptors than needed**. The end-plate potential therefore comfortably exceeds threshold, while each impulse uses just a **small fraction** of the vesicles and receptors on hand.
- Consequence: a **large proportion of receptors must be blocked before twitch height falls**, so twitch monitoring is insensitive to partial receptor occupancy
- Anything that reduces the margin increases sensitivity to NDMRs and causes weakness: fewer receptors (myasthenia, newborn), less release (LEMS, magnesium, aminoglycosides) or desensitised receptors
cards.e: Miller describes the system as having both excess signal and reserve capacity. Desensitising drugs such as volatile agents reduce this margin without competing with ACh, which is why they potentiate NDMRs. The elderly keep a better margin of safety than neonates.

cards.q: How is acetylcholine synthesised in the motor nerve terminal, and what is the rate-limiting step?
cards.a:
**Choline + acetyl-CoA → ACh**, catalysed by **choline acetyltransferase**.
- Choline is taken up from extracellular fluid by a dedicated transporter
- Acetyl-CoA comes from **mitochondria**
- Enzymes, channels and other proteins are made in the cell body and carried down by **axonal transport**
- **Choline uptake and choline acetyltransferase activity** are probably rate-limiting
cards.e: Mobilisation means all the steps that keep the terminal able to release transmitter during repeated stimulation, from choline uptake to moving filled vesicles to release sites. ACh is stored in the cytoplasm before it is packaged into vesicles.

cards.q: What is the role of calcium in transmitter release, and what is the quantitative relationship?
cards.a:
The nerve action potential (Na+ influx) opens **voltage-gated Ca2+ channels** beside the active zones. Ca2+ entry triggers vesicle fusion.
- Without extracellular Ca2+, even electrical stimulation of the nerve releases **no transmitter**
- **Doubling extracellular Ca2+ increases quantal content about 16-fold**
- Voltage-gated and Ca2+-activated **K+ channels** repolarise the terminal and so limit Ca2+ entry
- **K+ channel blockers (4-aminopyridine, tetraethylammonium)** prolong the Ca2+ current and greatly increase release
cards.e: Because release depends so steeply on Ca2+, small changes in Ca2+ entry have large effects. This explains the potentiation of NDMRs by magnesium and the temporary reversal of aminoglycoside-induced weakness by calcium (Lippincott).

cards.q: Explain the mechanism of post-tetanic potentiation (facilitation).
cards.a:
It is a **prejunctional calcium phenomenon**.
- Ca2+ enters the nerve terminal with each stimulus during tetanic (high-frequency) stimulation
- Ca2+ **accumulates** because it cannot be removed as fast as it enters
- For a period after the tetanus, a single stimulus therefore releases **more ACh than normal**
- This extra ACh temporarily overcomes the competitive NDMR and **twitch height increases**
cards.e: This is the basis of the post-tetanic count used to quantify deep block. It is seen during nondepolarising block, and Lippincott notes that fade and post-tetanic facilitation are the hallmarks of nondepolarising block.

cards.q: Which calcium channels control ACh release? Why do magnesium and verapamil differ in their effect on the NMJ?
cards.a:
**P-type channels** (found only in nerve terminals) are the main channels for normal transmitter release. Slower **L-type channels** are also present.
- **Magnesium, cadmium and manganese** (divalent cations) block Ca2+ entry through **P channels** and can profoundly impair transmission. This explains maternal and neonatal weakness and potentiation of relaxants when MgSO4 is given for pre-eclampsia
- **Verapamil, diltiazem and nifedipine** act on **L channels** (cardiovascular). At therapeutic doses they do not affect normal ACh release, although they may slightly increase NDMR block, possibly through L channels in the nerve ending
cards.e: Lippincott stresses that magnesium potentiates **both depolarising and nondepolarising** relaxants and lowers MAC, so doses must be reduced and recovery confirmed carefully. It does not alter local anaesthetic dose requirements.

cards.q: What is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS)? How does it differ from myasthenia gravis in mechanism and in response to relaxants?
cards.a:
LEMS is an **acquired autoimmune disease** with **antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels**, so **less ACh is released**. In myasthenia gravis the defect is fewer **postjunctional AChRs**.
- LEMS: **increased sensitivity to both depolarising and nondepolarising** relaxants
- Myasthenia gravis: fewer AChRs, so less efficient transmission and altered sensitivity to relaxants
cards.e: Stoelting notes that LEMS is often **paraneoplastic**, especially with lung carcinoma. The examiner's trap is to assume that LEMS, like myasthenia, is resistant to succinylcholine. It is sensitive to both classes.

cards.q: Describe the two vesicle pools and the ways in which vesicles release their contents.
cards.a:
Vesicles exist in two pools.
- **Reserve pool (VP1)**: the majority, deeper in the terminal, tethered to the cytoskeleton by actin, **synapsin**, synaptotagmin and spectrin. It is mobilised during intense or prolonged stimulation, when Ca2+-dependent enzymes break the synapsin links
- **Readily releasable pool (VP2)**: smaller vesicles bound to the active zones. These are the ones normally released
- Modes of release: **"kiss and run"** (brief opening, then retrieval), **compensatory** (open longer, incomplete collapse) and **stranded** (full collapse, retrieved only with the next stimulus)
cards.e: Replenishing releasable vesicles during sustained activity is called mobilisation. Its limits contribute to fade during high-frequency stimulation when the margin of safety is reduced.

cards.q: Describe the SNARE-mediated exocytosis of ACh.
cards.a:
Exocytosis needs **SNARE proteins** plus a calcium sensor.
- **Synaptobrevin (VAMP)** on the vesicle membrane
- **Syntaxin** and **SNAP-25** on the nerve terminal membrane
- When Ca2+ enters, **synapsin is phosphorylated** and frees the vesicle from the cytoskeleton
- Synaptobrevin forms a **ternary complex** with syntaxin and SNAP-25, which pulls the vesicle against the active zone
- **Synaptotagmin** is the vesicle's **Ca2+ sensor**. It localises vesicles near Ca2+ channels and stabilises docking
- A fusion pore forms, ACh is released, and the complex disassembles so the vesicle can be recycled
cards.e: Synaptophysin is a vesicle membrane glycoprotein. Because the release sites, Ca2+ channels and Ca2+ sensor are so close together, release is fast and synchronous with the stimulus. These proteins are the targets of clostridial toxins.

cards.q: How does botulinum toxin cause paralysis? What are its clinical uses and anaesthetic implications?
cards.a:
Botulinum toxin has a **heavy chain and a light chain**.
- The **heavy chain** binds polysialogangliosides and synaptotagmin, and the toxin is internalised
- The **light chain** is released and **cleaves SNARE proteins** (which ones depends on the toxin type), so vesicle fusion and **ACh release are blocked**
- The result is weakness or paralysis, which amounts to a **chemical denervation**
- Uses: spasticity, focal spasm, hyperhidrosis, cosmetic wrinkle treatment
- Systemic paralysis can follow clostridial infection (trauma, drug users, musculoskeletal allografts). Local injection can occasionally have distant effects
cards.e: Chemical denervation can upregulate AChRs, and botulism is listed among the causes of re-expression of immature receptors. Stoelting notes botulinum toxin injection as a treatment for hyperhidrosis.

cards.q: Describe junctional acetylcholinesterase and how quickly it terminates ACh action.
cards.a:
Junctional acetylcholinesterase is the **asymmetric A12 form**, a **type B carboxylesterase** made by the muscle under the end plate and attached by **collagen stalks** to the basement membrane.
- Normally each ACh molecule reacts with **only one receptor** before it is hydrolysed
- ACh is destroyed **within 1 ms** of release
- Smaller amounts of the enzyme are found extrajunctionally. **Denervation decreases** the enzyme
- Chronic inhibition (organophosphates, nerve gas, **prophylactic pyridostigmine**) can cause fatigue and weakness through **AChR downregulation** and receptor-independent effects
cards.e: Rapid hydrolysis lets the end plate reset long before the next impulse. Succinylcholine does not have this advantage because acetylcholinesterase does not hydrolyse it, so it persists in the cleft. Congenital abnormalities of the enzyme produce myasthenia-like syndromes.

cards.q: Describe the molecular structure of the mature, immature and α7 nicotinic AChRs.
cards.a:
All are **pentamers** (about **250 kDa**) arranged like barrel staves around a central cation channel.
- **Mature (junctional)**: 2 **α1** + β1 + δ + **ε**
- **Immature (fetal, extrajunctional)**: 2 α1 + β1 + δ + **γ**
- **Neuronal α7**: **five α7 subunits** (homomeric)
- The ACh binding site is on the extracellular part of each α subunit, near cysteines at positions **192–193**. α-Bungarotoxin binds residues 185–199
- AChRs are anchored to the end plate by **rapsyn** (43 kDa, 1:1 ratio)
cards.e: γ, δ and ε subunits occur **only in muscle**. Nerve receptors are built only from α and β subunits. Swapping γ for ε changes the channel's kinetics and pharmacology even though the subunits are very similar.

cards.q: Explain how the AChR channel opens. Which ions flow, and how big is the current?
cards.a:
**Both α subunits must be occupied by agonist at the same time**. The protein then twists and opens the central pore.
- **Na+ and Ca2+ flow in, K+ flows out**. The channel passes cations and some neutral molecules but **excludes anions** such as Cl−
- Each open channel carries only a **few picoamperes** (about 10^4 ions/ms)
- One nerve impulse opens about **500,000 channels**, so the summed current is easily enough to depolarise the end plate
- The end-plate potential is a graded sum of many **all-or-none** single-channel events
cards.e: Because two agonist molecules are needed, a single antagonist molecule on either α subunit is enough to keep the channel shut. This asymmetry is the basis of competitive block.

cards.q: Explain why competitive NDMR block is biased in favour of the antagonist, and why neostigmine should not be given at deep block.
cards.a:
Opening the channel needs **two ACh molecules**, but **one NDMR molecule** is enough to keep it closed.
- If the NDMR concentration **doubles**, the ACh concentration must rise **fourfold** to stay competitive
- Neostigmine raises ACh only to a limited extent, so at high NDMR concentrations (deep block) it may **fail to reverse** until redistribution or elimination lowers the relaxant concentration
- **Sugammadex** encapsulates steroidal relaxants (rocuronium, vecuronium) whatever the concentration, so it can reverse **any depth of block** if the dose is large enough
cards.e: This is the molecular reason not to give anticholinesterases too early. Lippincott adds that clinicians cannot reliably detect TOF fade once the ratio is above about 0.4, so quantitative monitoring is needed to confirm adequate reversal.

cards.q: How do anticholinesterases reverse NDMR block, and what other effects do they have at the NMJ?
cards.a:
Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase **raises the cleft ACh concentration**, which shifts the competition (law of mass action) so that two ACh molecules are more likely to occupy a receptor.
- They also have **allosteric effects** on the nerve terminal and receptor
- Neostigmine can cause **channel block** and **desensitisation**
- A large bolus or prolonged use can **impair neuromuscular function** in healthy patients
cards.e: Neostigmine and edrophonium appear in Miller's list of drugs that promote desensitisation. Giving neostigmine after full spontaneous recovery may therefore paradoxically cause weakness.

cards.q: How does succinylcholine produce depolarising block? Explain the three zones of the muscle membrane and accommodation.
cards.a:
Succinylcholine is **two ACh molecules joined together**. It opens AChR channels, but **acetylcholinesterase does not hydrolyse it**, so the end plate stays **persistently depolarised**.
- The Na+ channel has a **voltage-dependent activation gate** and a **time-dependent inactivation gate**
- Initial depolarisation opens perijunctional Na+ channels, causing a propagated action potential and contraction (fasciculation)
- With continuing depolarisation the inactivation gates **stay closed**
- The three zones are: (1) the **depolarised end plate**; (2) the **perijunctional zone**, where Na+ channels are fixed in the inactivated state; (3) the **distal membrane**, where Na+ channels are at rest
- ACh released from the nerve cannot overcome the inactivated perijunctional channels, so transmission fails (**accommodation**). **Direct muscle stimulation still causes contraction**
cards.e: The duration of depolarising block is set by **clearance from plasma** (plasma cholinesterase), not by acetylcholinesterase. Lippincott notes that only a fraction of an injected dose reaches the junction because plasma cholinesterase hydrolyses so much of it on the way.

cards.q: What is the effect of plasma cholinesterase variants on succinylcholine, and how is atypical enzyme diagnosed?
cards.a:
Succinylcholine's action ends when the drug diffuses back into plasma and is hydrolysed by **plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase**. When the enzyme is abnormal, more drug reaches the junction and stays there longer.
- Normal enzyme: block lasts about **5–10 min**
- **Homozygous atypical** enzyme: block lasts **60–180 min**
- **Dibucaine number**: dibucaine inhibits normal enzyme by about **80%**, but homozygous atypical enzyme by only about **20%**. Heterozygotes are intermediate
- Atypical enzyme also hydrolyses other ester drugs poorly
cards.e: Lippincott's explanation for prolonged block is that a greater proportion of the dose reaches the NMJ, not a reduction in hepatic clearance. Miller refers the details to Chapter 24 but notes that whole-body clearance is the main determinant of duration.

cards.q: What are the nonclassic (noncompetitive) actions of drugs at the AChR? Why can anticholinesterases not reverse them?
cards.a:
Some drugs alter receptor function **without acting at the ACh binding site**, either directly or by changing the surrounding membrane lipid.
- Channels may open more slowly, stay open longer, close in several steps or flicker
- Examples include procaine, ketamine and inhaled anaesthetics
- If channel opening is prevented, transmission is weakened. If closing is slowed, transmission may be enhanced
- The two clinically important forms are **desensitisation** (a receptor state) and **channel block** (in the pore)
- Because they are **not competitive with ACh**, raising ACh with an anticholinesterase does not reverse them
cards.e: Miller also notes that NDMRs bind outside muscle. At the **carotid body** they reduce the **hypoxic ventilatory response**, and on immune cells' **α7 receptors** they may have anti-inflammatory effects. Residual block therefore impairs the response to hypoxaemia as well as respiratory muscle strength.

cards.q: What is receptor desensitisation, and which anaesthetic drugs promote it?
cards.a:
A desensitised receptor **binds agonist very tightly but its channel does not open**. Receptors shift constantly between resting and desensitised states. Agonists, and NDMRs too, can trap receptors in the desensitised state. Desensitisation is accompanied by tyrosine phosphorylation.
- Drugs that promote it (Miller Box 11.1): **volatile agents** (halothane, isoflurane, sevoflurane), **barbiturates** (thiopental), **local anaesthetics** (lidocaine, dibucaine, prilocaine), **anticholinesterases** (neostigmine, pyridostigmine, edrophonium), **agonists** (succinylcholine, ACh), alcohols, phenothiazines, **verapamil**, polymyxin B, cocaine
- Effect: fewer functional channels, so a **reduced margin of safety** and **enhanced NDMR block**
cards.e: Rapid desensitisation may explain why an NDMR is more potent after a prior dose of succinylcholine. Miller warns that phase II block should not simply be called a desensitisation block, because desensitisation is only one of several contributing processes.

cards.q: Compare open-channel and closed-channel block at the AChR. Give examples.
cards.a:
Both are **noncompetitive** blocks of ion flow through the pore.
- **Closed-channel block**: the drug sits in the mouth of the channel and stops ions passing, **even when the channel is not open**
- **Open-channel block**: the drug enters a channel **only after ACh has opened it**, so it is **use-dependent**. Raising ACh opens more channels and can **increase** the block
- Neither is reversed by anticholinesterases. **Neostigmine itself can block channels**
- Implicated drugs: some **antibiotics**, cocaine, quinidine, **tricyclic antidepressants**, naloxone, naltrexone
- Relaxants: **pancuronium** acts mainly at the recognition site. **Tubocurarine** at high doses also blocks the channel. Succinylcholine and decamethonium can open the channel and then enter and block it
cards.e: This explains why some drug interactions (for example antibiotic-potentiated block) respond poorly to neostigmine. Lippincott adds that aminoglycosides also reduce prejunctional ACh release, and calcium temporarily antagonises this.

cards.q: What is phase II block? What factors cause it and how should it be managed?
cards.a:
Phase II block is the change in a depolarising block to one with **fade on TOF and tetanus**, resembling nondepolarising block, during **prolonged or high-dose exposure** to succinylcholine.
- Mechanism: complex. It probably includes **prejunctional effects** of high succinylcholine concentrations on transmitter mobilisation and release, desensitisation, and secondary changes in nerve and muscle homeostasis
- Contributing factors: **duration of exposure, dose and concentration**, the drug used, **muscle type** (fast or slow twitch), and interactions with anaesthetics
- Management: the response to anticholinesterases is **unpredictable**, so Miller advises **not attempting reversal**. Continue ventilation and monitor until recovery
