cards.q: How does hydrophobicity affect local anaesthetic potency and duration? Give the classic example.
cards.a:
Bigger alkyl groups on the amine or ring make the drug **more hydrophobic**, which makes it **more potent and longer acting**.
- **Etidocaine** has 3 more carbons at the amine end than lidocaine. On isolated sciatic nerve it is about **4 times as potent** and lasts about **5 times as long**
- Hydrophobicity is measured as the **octanol:buffer partition coefficient** of the uncharged base
- Octanol is a fair model for the base but **underestimates membrane uptake of the charged form**, which gathers near the polar membrane surface
cards.e: The drug has to enter the membrane and reach a partly hydrophobic site on the Na+ channel, so lipid solubility is the main driver of intrinsic potency. In living tissue the link is looser: highly hydrophobic drugs stick to tissue and are given at lower concentrations, and vascular effects alter how fast the drug is removed. Approximate hydrophobicity values: procaine 100, lidocaine 366, ropivacaine 775, bupivacaine 3420, tetracaine 5822.

cards.q: Explain the role of pKa in local anaesthetic action using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.
cards.a:
Local anaesthetics are **weak bases**. They switch very rapidly between the uncharged base (B) and the protonated cation (BH+).
- For a base: **pH = pKa + log([B]/[BH+])**
- pKa is the pH at which B and BH+ are present in equal amounts
- At pH 7.4, the **lower the pKa, the more drug is in the uncharged base form**
- Of the drugs plotted in Miller, **lidocaine (pKa 7.8)** has the least protonated drug and **chloroprocaine (9.1)** the most. Bupivacaine and ropivacaine are 8.1, tetracaine 8.4, procaine 8.9
- Inside the non-polar membrane the **effective pKa is lower**, so the membrane takes up more base than cation
cards.e: All clinical local anaesthetics have a pKa above 7.4, so at body pH most of the drug is charged. Oxford uses this to explain why lidocaine and prilocaine start working quickly: more of the drug is un-ionised and can cross the membrane. Temperature, ionic strength and the surrounding medium also change how much drug is protonated.

cards.q: Which form of local anaesthetic, the base or the cation, actually blocks the sodium channel? Explain the evidence.
cards.a:
**Both forms matter, but at different steps.**
- The **uncharged base crosses membranes**. That is why alkaline solutions block faster on nerves without a sheath
- The **cation is the more potent blocking species**. It acts from the **cytoplasmic (inner) side** of the channel
- Evidence: changing axoplasmic pH, and perfusing the inside of the axon with permanently charged **quaternary** derivatives, both show block coming from the inner side
- The base has some activity of its own, which explains why **benzocaine** (always uncharged) works topically
- The aromatic end anchors at the binding site, and the charged amine sits in the channel pore
cards.e: A useful phrase: lipid solubility gets the drug to the receptor, and the charge holds it there. The charged form leaves closed and inactivated channels much more slowly than the base does. Ion trapping in acidic tissue follows from this. Drug that becomes protonated inside an acidic cell cannot easily get back out.

cards.q: Why are local anaesthetics supplied as hydrochloride salts, and why does injecting them hurt?
cards.a:
The free bases dissolve poorly in water, so they are made into **acidic hydrochloride salts**. This gives solubility and **shelf life**.
- Injection pain comes from **the acidity of the solution**
- Lidocaine also briefly **activates TRPV1 and TRPA1** channels on nociceptors before the Na+ channel block silences the nerve
- **Adding sodium bicarbonate** just before skin infiltration reduces the pain and may speed onset
cards.e: Once injected, tissue buffers raise the pH and free up more base. Tissue uptake, mostly by binding to lipids, also lowers the apparent pKa and slows spread away from the injection site. Commercial solutions containing adrenaline are made more acidic, because adrenaline is more stable at low pH. Oxford also notes that these solutions contain preservative.

cards.q: At the same concentration, why does a moderately hydrophobic drug like lidocaine block faster than either a hydrophilic drug (2-chloroprocaine) or a highly hydrophobic one (tetracaine)? Why is chloroprocaine still fast clinically?
cards.a:
Onset depends on balancing **how easily the drug crosses membranes** against **how much it binds to tissue**.
- Very hydrophilic drugs (chloroprocaine) **cross membranes poorly**
- Very hydrophobic drugs (tetracaine, bupivacaine) **bind heavily to tissue** and, being potent, are **given at low concentrations**, so the diffusion gradient driving onset is smaller
- Lidocaine is in the middle: it is less tissue-bound but still crosses membranes well
- In patients, **chloroprocaine starts fast** because its low systemic toxicity allows a **high concentration (3%)**
cards.e: In vivo, onset also depends on dose: 0.75% bupivacaine starts faster than 0.25%. Do not answer "lowest pKa means fastest onset" without adding the effect of concentration. Chloroprocaine has the highest pKa yet starts quickly because so much drug is given.

cards.q: Describe the connective tissue layers of a peripheral nerve. Which is the main diffusion barrier, and why does nerve make-up matter for onset?
cards.a:
From inside out: **endoneurium** (around each axon), then **perineurium** (around each fascicle), then **epineurium** (around the whole nerve), with a **paraneurium** around some nerves such as the distal sciatic.
- The **perineurium is the main barrier** to local anaesthetic diffusion
- Nerves also contain non-nerve tissue: fat, connective tissue and blood vessels
- At the **popliteal sciatic**, about **60% of the cross-section is non-neural**, which affects how the drug spreads and how fast the block starts
cards.e: To reach the axolemma, the drug has to cross every one of these layers. That is why diffusion, not binding to the channel, sets the clinical onset time. Unmyelinated C fibres run in bundles of 5–10 axons wrapped by Schwann cells. Myelinated fibres each have their own myelin sheath made by Schwann cells.

cards.q: Classify peripheral nerve fibres by size, myelination, conduction velocity and function.
cards.a:
Use the **A, B and C classification**:
- **Aα**: 6–22 µm, myelinated, 30–120 m/s. Motor efferents, plus proprioception
- **Aβ**: 6–22 µm, myelinated, 30–120 m/s. Touch and pressure afferents from skin and joints
- **Aγ**: 3–6 µm, myelinated, 15–35 m/s. Efferents to muscle spindles (muscle tone)
- **Aδ**: 1–4 µm, myelinated, 5–25 m/s. **Fast pain, cold** and touch
- **B**: under 3 µm, lightly myelinated, 3–15 m/s. **Preganglionic sympathetic**
- **C**: 0.3–1.3 µm, unmyelinated, 0.1–2 m/s. **Postganglionic sympathetic** fibres and dorsal root afferents for **slow pain and warmth**
cards.e: Fibre classes also differ in their membranes and in which ion channels they carry, not only in size. Newer work groups sensory neurons by function, for example several types of cold-sensing and mechano-heat neurons, and most neurons serve more than one sensation. This may change how local anaesthetic targets are thought about in future.

cards.q: Which nerve fibres are most and least susceptible to local anaesthetic block? How does this compare with traditional teaching?
cards.a:
When drug is applied in vivo, the order runs **against the old "small fibres first" rule**:
- **Most susceptible: small myelinated fibres (Aγ motor, Aδ sensory)**
- Next: **large myelinated fibres (Aα, Aβ)**
- **Least susceptible: unmyelinated C fibres**. The slowest-conducting C fibres resist block the most
- Clinical point: checking cold or pinprick tests **Aδ function**. Losing these sensations **does not prove** that every sensory modality is blocked
cards.e: Older books say C fibres are blocked first, but measurements in single fibres show the reverse. When clinicians see differential block, possible explanations include the length of nerve exposed to drug (as in the spinal and epidural space), the drug spreading along the nerve, and different proportions of Na+ and K+ channels in different fibres. Miller warns against working out which fibre types drive chronic pain from the dose that a diagnostic block needs.

cards.q: Outline the ionic basis of the resting membrane potential and the action potential in nerve.
cards.a:
Resting potential is **−60 to −90 mV**. At rest the membrane lets K+ through but **not Na+**.
- The Na+/K+-ATPase keeps intracellular K+ at about 150 mM against 5 mM outside, a **30:1 ratio**
- Nernst: **E(K) = −58 log 30 ≈ −86 mV**. **E(Na) ≈ +60 mV**
- When the membrane depolarises, Na+ channels open faster than K+ channels. Na+ flowing in depolarises the membrane further, which opens more Na+ channels (**positive feedback**)
- **Na+ channel inactivation** and **K+ outflow** then bring the membrane back to resting potential
- Just after an impulse, the membrane is **refractory**, so the impulse can only travel one way
cards.e: A single impulse barely changes ion concentrations in large fibres, but can change them by up to 10% in small unmyelinated axons. Local anaesthetics hardly alter the resting potential. They slow the rate of depolarisation and lower the peak of the action potential until the impulse fails.

cards.q: What is meant by saltatory conduction, and how many nodes of Ranvier must be blocked to stop an impulse?
cards.a:
In myelinated fibres the impulse is regenerated only at the **nodes of Ranvier**, where **Na+ channels are packed together**. Current flows through the axoplasm and quickly charges up the insulated stretch of axon to the next node.
- Several centimetres of the largest axons are depolarised **at the same time**. The impulse does not jump from one node to the next as a single event
- The local current is strong enough to **skip 2 fully blocked nodes** and still fire a third
- If channels are only partly blocked, the impulse **shrinks node by node** (decremental conduction) and may fail only after many centimetres
cards.e: This is why drug must cover a long enough stretch of nerve (about three nodes in the classic teaching) for the block to be reliable. Miller describes block as a dynamic balance between how strong the impulse is and how much drug is present. Strichartz compared it to a car getting stuck in a muddy patch of road, not a locked door.

cards.q: Distinguish tonic from phasic (use-dependent) local anaesthetic block, with numbers from voltage-clamp studies.
cards.a:
**Tonic block** is the reduction in Na+ current when the nerve is stimulated rarely. **Phasic block** is extra block that builds up with repeated firing.
- Phasic block appears at frequencies **above 5 Hz** and builds with each pulse until it reaches a new steady state
- 0.2 mM lidocaine (subclinical) cuts tonic current by about **30%**. A 10 Hz train cuts it by about **75%**
- A clinical **1% lidocaine solution is about 40 mM**, enough to abolish current completely
- Phasic block reverses within seconds once firing slows
cards.e: The cause is that the drug binds more tightly to **open and inactivated** channels than to resting ones. It also leaves them more slowly than the channel normally recovers from inactivation, so bound channels pile up with repeated firing. This use-dependence explains why lidocaine is a class Ib antiarrhythmic and why rapidly firing ectopic neurons in neuropathic pain are especially sensitive.

cards.q: Explain the modulated receptor and guarded receptor hypotheses of local anaesthetic binding.
cards.a:
Both explain why **depolarisation increases local anaesthetic binding**.
- **Guarded receptor**: the binding site is easier to reach when the channel **opens**, because the gate stops guarding it
- **Modulated receptor**: the drug's **affinity depends on the channel state** (inactivated or open greater than resting). Binding **stabilises the inactivated state** and slows dissociation
- There appears to be **one binding site**, with low affinity at rest (tonic) and higher affinity after depolarisation (phasic)
cards.e: The two models fit together: more sites become available, and drug stays bound longer. Potency for both tonic and phasic block depends on structure, hydrophobicity and pKa in the same way. When asked "where do local anaesthetics bind?", say the inner vestibule of the Na+ channel, reached from the cytoplasmic side.

cards.q: Describe the structure of the voltage-gated Na+ channel and the local anaesthetic binding site.
cards.a:
The main **α subunit has 4 homologous domains (D1–D4), each with 6 membrane-spanning helices (S1–S6)**.
- The **P loop** between S5 and S6 of each domain dips into the membrane. The four P loops form the **ion selectivity filter**
- The positively charged **S4 segments are the voltage sensors**. They move outward when the membrane depolarises
- **S6 segments form the inner gate**. Fast inactivation happens when the **cytoplasmic loop between D3 and D4** plugs the inner opening
- Local anaesthetics bind in the **inner vestibule**, touching **S6 of D1, D3 and D4** (Site 9)
- **Tetrodotoxin and saxitoxin** bind at the **outer pore, Site 1**
cards.e: Drug can reach its site through a hydrophilic route (through the open pore) or a hydrophobic route (sideways through the membrane). The second route explains why very lipophilic drugs can block closed channels. Extracellular H+ ions passing slowly through the pore can protonate or deprotonate the bound drug and so control how quickly it leaves. Na+ ions compete with the drug.

cards.q: Why do current local anaesthetics fail to block specific Na+ channel isoforms selectively? What do Nav1.7, 1.8 and 1.9 do?
cards.a:
There are **nine mammalian Na+ channel isoforms**. At least four occur in peripheral neurons, and some are found only in nociceptors.
- Local anaesthetics hardly discriminate, because the **binding pocket is very similar across isoforms** and the drug molecule is **flexible** (it can rotate around several bonds), so it is a poor template for any one pocket
- **Nav1.7**: amplifies signals at sensory nerve terminals
- **Nav1.8**: needed for **repetitive firing** of nociceptors
- **Nav1.9**: carries **persistent currents** that raise excitability. It seems important in **visceral pain**
cards.e: Natural peptide toxins can block single isoforms, which proves selective block is possible. A monoclonal antibody about 1000 times more potent at Nav1.7 than at other isoforms has been described. In animal models of visceral pain such as cystitis, drugs aimed at Nav1.7 failed but blocking Nav1.9 worked.

cards.q: Give examples of Na+ channelopathies relevant to pain and to muscle.
cards.a:
**Nav1.7**:
- Loss of function leads to **congenital insensitivity to pain**
- Gain of function leads to **erythromelalgia** and **paroxysmal extreme pain disorder**
**Nav1.4** (skeletal muscle): **myotonia, periodic paralysis, congenital myasthenia**
- In one erythromelalgia mutation, **mexiletine** brought Na+ currents back to normal
cards.e: Abnormal repetitive firing, as seen in neuropathic pain or inherited myotonia, can be stopped by systemic lidocaine at doses that leave normal impulses alone. The selectivity comes from the firing pattern on top of slow depolarisation, not from one channel subtype being more sensitive to the drug.

cards.q: Summarise the sequence of events in local anaesthetic nerve block. What sets the clinical onset and offset times?
cards.a:
The steps are:
- Drug is placed near the nerve. Some is lost to **tissue binding, removal by the circulation** and, for esters, local hydrolysis
- The free drug crosses the nerve sheath and then the axonal membrane. Speed depends on **pKa and lipophilicity**
- It binds to the Na+ channel and **stops the shape change that opens the channel**
- During onset and recovery, partly blocked fibres are blocked further by repeated firing (**use-dependence**)
- **One binding site** explains both tonic and phasic block
- **Onset and offset are set by slow diffusion into and out of the whole nerve**, not by binding to the channel
cards.e: Drugs that leave the channel within seconds can still give blocks lasting hours, because the drug left in and around the nerve keeps re-binding. This is why changing the dose, volume, additives and injection site changes block duration so much.

cards.q: Why does intrinsic (in vitro) local anaesthetic potency not match clinical potency exactly?
cards.a:
Hydrophobicity predicts potency in isolated nerve, but in patients other factors act too:
- **Charge and hydrophobicity** change how the drug partitions into and crosses tissues and membranes
- **Vasodilator or vasoconstrictor action** changes how fast the drug is taken up into the blood from the injection site
- **Tissue binding** and the concentration that can be given safely
- Relative in vitro potency: procaine 1, mepivacaine 1.5, prilocaine 1.8, lidocaine 2, chloroprocaine 3, ropivacaine 5.5, **tetracaine, bupivacaine and etidocaine 8**
cards.e: The potency groups (low: procaine; intermediate: lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, chloroprocaine; high: tetracaine, bupivacaine, etidocaine, ropivacaine) roughly match duration groups. Clinically, ropivacaine is about 1.3–1.5 times less potent than bupivacaine.

cards.q: Classify local anaesthetics by duration and explain how vascular effects change duration.
cards.a:
Duration classes:
- **Short**: procaine, chloroprocaine
- **Intermediate**: lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine
- **Long**: tetracaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, etidocaine
Vascular effects:
- Most drugs act on vessels in two ways: **constriction at low concentrations and dilation at clinical concentrations**
- More dilation means faster removal and a shorter block
- **EMLA** constricts skin vessels for about the first hour, then dilates them **after 2 h or more**
- **Cocaine** constricts at **every concentration** because it **blocks noradrenaline reuptake**
cards.e: Oxford adds that duration also depends on how much drug binds to protein at the site of action. Prilocaine causes little vasodilatation, which partly explains its low toxicity. Lidocaine dilates vessels moderately, so adrenaline prolongs lidocaine more than any other drug.

cards.q: What is differential sensory–motor block? Which drug made it clinically useful, and how is it explained?
cards.a:
Differential block means **pain relief with little motor block**.
- **Bupivacaine** became popular in the 1980s for epidurals because **dilute solutions** gave good analgesia with only mild weakness. Etidocaine, the other long-acting option, caused dense motor block
- Possible explanations:
  - a **longer length of nerve exposed** in the neuraxial space, so lower concentrations still block
  - spread of drug **along the nerve**
  - different **Na+ versus K+ channel** block in different fibre types
- **Single enantiomers** were developed partly to improve sensory selectivity, but **genuine sensory selectivity remains out of reach**
cards.e: Length of exposed nerve can explain differential spinal or epidural block, but not differential block after peripheral nerve blocks. At equal potency the motor profiles of ropivacaine and bupivacaine are nearly the same. Note: Oxford says ropivacaine causes less motor block; follow Miller.

cards.q: How do dose, volume and concentration affect block characteristics? Give the trial data.
cards.a:
A **higher dose** makes success more likely, **shortens onset** and **lengthens the block**.
- Epidural bupivacaine 10 mL at **0.5% versus 0.125%** gave faster onset, better analgesia and longer sensory block
- **Volume affects spread**: 30 mL of 1% epidural lidocaine reached **more than 4 dermatomes higher** than 10 mL of 3%, although the dose was the same
- Choose doses by the **ED95, not the ED50**, within toxic limits
- With **ultrasound**, the femoral block volumes for 50% and 95% success were about **57% and 54%** of those needed with nerve stimulation
- The minimum effective volume is about **0.1–0.15 mL per mm² of nerve cross-sectional area**
cards.e: Trap: the smallest volume that gives a successful block at 30 minutes may also give a **shorter block**. That matters if the painful period after surgery lasts longer than the block. Lippincott's rule of thumb for epidural dosing is about 1–2 mL of solution per segment to be blocked.

cards.q: Discuss adrenaline as a local anaesthetic additive: concentration, benefits, limits and how to prepare it.
cards.a:
The usual concentration is **5 µg/mL (1:200,000)**.
- It **slows absorption into the blood**, which **deepens and prolongs** the block and **lowers peak plasma levels**, especially of **lidocaine and mepivacaine**
- It greatly prolongs **short- and intermediate-acting** drugs, but gives only **mild intensification and little prolongation with bupivacaine**
- In the epidural space it may add analgesia by acting on **spinal α2 receptors**
- It acts as a **marker of intravascular injection**. Lippincott: 15 µg IV raises heart rate by about 20% or more within about 30 s. False results occur in **labour, under general anaesthesia and with β-blockers**
- Oxford: adult total **no more than 200 µg**. **Do not use for digital or penile blocks**. 0.1 mL of 1:1000 added to 20 mL of local anaesthetic gives 1:200,000
cards.e: Local anaesthetics are absorbed in two phases: a fast peak from the fluid phase, then a slower one from fat. Adrenaline slows the first phase, so the block is denser and blood levels are lower. Higher concentrations add vasoconstriction and systemic side effects without much extra benefit, which is why 1:200,000 is the usual compromise.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42 · Lippincott Ch 7

cards.q: Compare clonidine and dexmedetomidine as perineural adjuvants.
cards.a:
Both are **α2 agonists** that also **block the hyperpolarisation-activated cation current** (Ih).
- **Clonidine** prolongs the block by about **2 h**, but results vary widely and many studies are negative. Suggested dose limit **0.5–1 µg/kg ideal body weight**
- **Dexmedetomidine** is more α2-selective and prolongs **sensory and motor** block from long-acting drugs by about **4 h**. Its best dose is not known
- Side effects: **hypotension, bradycardia, sedation**
- **No added neurotoxicity** has been found with either drug
cards.e: Blocking Ih stops neurons from returning to resting potential normally after firing, which helps keep them blocked. Oxford quotes clonidine at 1–2 µg/kg for neuraxial and peripheral use, limited by hypotension and sedation. Lippincott lists α2 agonists among the usual neuraxial adjuvants and notes that indirect-acting vasopressors add nothing.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42 · Lippincott Ch 7, 8

cards.q: Compare buprenorphine and dexamethasone as adjuvants for prolonging peripheral nerve block.
cards.a:
**Buprenorphine** (partial μ agonist):
- Acts as an antagonist at κ and δ receptors and also **blocks Na+ channels**
- Prolongs long-acting blocks by about **6 h**, at the cost of **more PONV**. It is thought not to be neurotoxic
**Dexamethasone**:
- Early reviews: about 2–3 h extra with intermediate-acting drugs and up to 10 h with long-acting ones. Newer estimate with bupivacaine: about **4 h**
- Works **IV or perineurally**. Perineural is somewhat better, but many clinicians give it IV to avoid off-label mixing and to get the antiemetic effect
- Typical adult dose **4–10 mg**
- Its **mechanism is unknown** and its **neurotoxicity has not been studied enough**
cards.e: In a study in healthy volunteers (Marhofer), perineural dexamethasone did not prolong the block. This suggests its effect after surgery is systemic or anti-inflammatory rather than a local nerve effect. Lippincott notes that ketamine added to peripheral blocks gives little or no benefit.

cards.q: How does the injection site affect onset and duration? Compare spinal with brachial plexus bupivacaine.
cards.a:
**Spinal and subcutaneous injection** give the **fastest onset and shortest duration**. **Large-volume brachial plexus blocks** (without ultrasound) give the **slowest onset and longest duration**.
- Intrathecal bupivacaine: onset within about **5 min**, lasting **3–4 h**
- Brachial plexus bupivacaine: onset about **20–30 min**, analgesia averaging about **10 h**
- Spinal is fast because there is **no nerve sheath** and the drug sits right next to the cord and roots. It is short because the **dose is small**
- The plexus is slow because the drug must **diffuse through tissue** to reach the nerve. It lasts long because **uptake into blood is slow**, the **dose is larger** and **longer lengths of nerve** are exposed
cards.e: These differences come from anatomy affecting diffusion and uptake into blood. The same reasoning explains why blood levels differ so much between block sites for the same dose (see the absorption card).

cards.q: What is the rationale for alkalinising or carbonating local anaesthetics, and what are the limitations?
cards.a:
Adding bicarbonate **raises the pH**, so more drug is **uncharged base** and enters the nerve faster. On isolated nerve this **speeds onset and lowers the minimum blocking concentration (Cm)**.
- Clinical benefit is **disputed**. Ultrasound guidance has made it less relevant for peripheral blocks
- It **reduces pain on skin infiltration**
- **Risk of precipitation**, especially with **long-acting drugs**. Lippincott: bupivacaine precipitates above about **pH 6.8**
- Oxford mix: **1 mL of 8.4% bicarbonate per 10 mL of lidocaine or per 20 mL of bupivacaine**. Throw the mixture away if it precipitates
cards.e: Carbon dioxide works in a similar way. It crosses into the axon and lowers the internal pH, which traps more active cation inside. Lippincott's MCQ catch: bicarbonate speeds onset of lidocaine, chloroprocaine and mepivacaine, but is not used with bupivacaine.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42, 43 · Lippincott Ch 7

cards.q: Discuss mixing local anaesthetics: rationale, evidence and the key safety warning.
cards.a:
Mixing aims to combine the **fast onset** of chloroprocaine or lidocaine with the **long duration** of bupivacaine or tetracaine.
- Clinical studies of mixtures have given **mixed results**
- Catheter techniques allow an alternative: **start with a fast drug, then infuse a long-acting one**
- Ultrasound has shortened onset times, so mixing matters less. It remains an option when surgery must start soon
- **Toxicity is additive.** Never give the maximum dose of each drug on the assumption that their toxicities are independent
cards.e: Oxford agrees and adds that using several drugs raises the risk of drug errors. When working out a safe total, treat each drug's dose as a fraction of its own maximum and keep the fractions added together at or below 1.

cards.q: How does pregnancy change local anaesthetic requirements and toxicity?
cards.a:
Spinal and epidural blocks **spread further and are denser** in pregnancy.
- **Mechanical cause**: engorged epidural veins reduce the volume of the epidural and subarachnoid spaces
- **Hormonal cause**: **progesterone** makes nerves more sensitive to block. This is probably the **more important** cause, because spread is already greater in the **first trimester**, before the veins enlarge
- **Reduce doses** at every stage of pregnancy
- Animal data suggest pregnant patients are **more sensitive to bupivacaine cardiotoxicity**. Ropivacaine's toxicity was **the same** in pregnant and non-pregnant ewes
cards.e: Lippincott lists pregnancy, ascites, large abdominal tumours and old age as conditions that reduce CSF volume and exaggerate neuraxial spread. Height, age, volume and position matter more than weight alone. A large bolus can give an unexpectedly high block with bradycardia when the T1–T4 cardioaccelerator fibres are blocked.

cards.q: Describe intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier block): drugs, doses, safety rules and complications.
cards.a:
Local anaesthetic is injected IV into a limb with a tourniquet inflated. It **diffuses from the vessels to nerve endings and axons**.
- Drugs: **lidocaine or prilocaine**, without preservative or adrenaline. **Never bupivacaine** (cardiotoxic)
- Upper limb: about **3 mg/kg**, which is **40 mL of 0.5% lidocaine** for a 65–70 kg ideal body weight. Lower limb: 50–100 mL of 0.25%
- Chloroprocaine has caused **thrombophlebitis**
- Safety depends on the **tourniquet staying inflated** and being **released gradually**
- Lidocaine has caused seizures at doses of only **1.4 mg/kg**. Cardiovascular collapse can occur
- Oxford: inflate the cuff **50–100 mmHg above systolic pressure**. Do not deflate before **15 min (prilocaine) or 20 min (lidocaine)**
cards.e: Oxford prefers 0.5% prilocaine (40/50/60 mL for small, medium and large arms) because it is metabolised quickly and is less toxic. The lidocaine maximum is 250 mg. Lippincott adds that tourniquet pain can start at about 20 min, and that even after 15–20 min the cuff should be released slowly and in steps. Contraindications include crush injury, sickle cell disease and peripheral vascular disease.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42 · Lippincott Ch 8

cards.q: State the maximum doses and durations for infiltration anaesthesia, plain and with adrenaline (Miller Table 25.4, adult).
cards.e: Onset is almost immediate after intradermal or subcutaneous injection, so choose the drug by how long it needs to last. Adrenaline prolongs every drug, most of all lidocaine. Oxford gives weight-based limits: lidocaine 3 mg/kg (7 with adrenaline), prilocaine 6 (8), bupivacaine and levobupivacaine 2, ropivacaine 3. Its formulary quotes lidocaine 6 mg/kg with adrenaline.

cards.q: A 4-kg infant needs infiltration with lidocaine. Work out the maximum volume and explain why dilute solution is better.
cards.a:
Using Miller's ceiling of **5 mg/kg**, the maximum dose is **20 mg**.
- That is **1 mL of 2%** (20 mg/mL) or **4 mL of 0.5%** (5 mg/mL)
- Lidocaine works for infiltration at **0.3–0.5%**, so the **dilute solution covers a bigger area for the same dose**
- To cover a large area, use **large volumes of dilute solution**
cards.e: Remember that 1% equals 10 mg/mL. Convert every dose into mg/kg before injecting, especially in small children, where the safe volume of concentrated solution is tiny.

cards.q: Summarise Miller's recommendations for major peripheral nerve blocks (Table 25.6) and the rule for combining blocks.
cards.a:
Usual concentration, maximum dose without/with adrenaline (mg), onset and duration (min):
- **Lidocaine** 1–2%: 350/500. Onset 10–20, duration 120–240
- **Mepivacaine** 1–1.5%: 350/500. 10–20, 180–300
- **Prilocaine** 1–2%: 400/600. 10–20, 180–300
- **Bupivacaine** 0.25–0.5%: **175/225**. 20–30, **360–720**
- **Levobupivacaine** 0.25–0.5%: 200/225. 20–30, 360–720
- **Ropivacaine** 0.2–0.5%: **200/250**. 20–30, 360–720
- Usual volume 30–50 mL. Intermediate-potency drugs start faster than the potent ones
- If several blocks are done together, the **total of all doses must not exceed the listed maximum**
cards.e: Lower the dose for children, for patients with risk factors and for high-risk sites such as interscalene. Minor blocks of a single nerve (for example ulnar or radial) start quickly with most drugs, so the choice depends mainly on duration: bupivacaine and ropivacaine last 180–360 min plain and 240–420 min with adrenaline.

cards.q: What does Miller say about truncal blocks and continuous perineural infusions?
cards.a:
**Truncal blocks**:
- For breast surgery: **PECS I and II and serratus plane** blocks. Proximal intercostal and **paravertebral** blocks are also used
- Paravertebral block is **non-inferior to epidural** for VATS and thoracotomy pain and has **fewer side effects**
**Perineural infusions**:
- Can run for days after surgery, or for weeks to months for chronic pain
- Poor sensory selectivity can **conflict with early mobilisation**
- Accumulation is a theoretical risk, but the **acute-phase rise in α1-acid glycoprotein** after surgery **binds free drug** and lowers this risk
cards.e: Lippincott notes that paravertebral blocks cause less sympathectomy than neuraxial blocks and less toxicity than intercostal blocks. They mainly cover somatic, not visceral, pain, and bilateral blocks can spread to the epidural space and lower blood pressure. Oxford lists bupivacaine 0.1% or ropivacaine 0.2% as common infusion solutions.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Lippincott Ch 8 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42

cards.q: Summarise local anaesthetic choice and dosing for epidural anaesthesia and analgesia.
cards.a:
Any drug can be used. **Procaine and tetracaine** are rarely used because they **start slowly**.
- **Chloroprocaine, lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine**: onset **5–15 min**. Intermediate drugs give 1–2 h of surgical block (Table 25.7: 60–180 min with adrenaline)
- **Bupivacaine, levobupivacaine, ropivacaine**: onset **15–20 min**, lasting about **180–350 min**
- Adrenaline (1:200,000) **greatly prolongs short and intermediate** drugs but barely changes long-acting ones
- Bupivacaine: **0.0625–0.1%** infusions for labour (with opioid and adrenaline); **0.125%** boluses for postoperative pain; **0.25%** for denser analgesia with moderate motor block; **0.5–0.75%** for surgery
- **Do not use 0.25% bupivacaine as the first-choice infusion**. **Boluses spread further** than infusions
cards.e: Concentrated infusions risk long, unwanted motor block. Patients vary widely in how much motor block they get. Maximum doses (mg, plain/with adrenaline): chloroprocaine 700/900; lidocaine, mepivacaine and prilocaine 350/500; bupivacaine 175/225; levobupivacaine and ropivacaine 200/250.

cards.q: Summarise drugs for spinal anaesthesia, baricity and the effect of vasoconstrictors.
cards.a:
Main options (Miller Table 25.8, 70-kg adult):
- **Bupivacaine** 0.75% **hyperbaric with 8.25% dextrose** (2–3 mL), or 0.5% isobaric (actually **slightly hypobaric**) (3–4 mL). Dose 15–20 mg, lasting 90–200 min. Its profile resembles tetracaine
- **Lidocaine** 1.5 or 5% hyperbaric, 30–100 mg, 30–90 min
- **Tetracaine** 5–20 mg (hyper-, hypo- or isobaric), 90–200 min
- **Procaine** 10%, 100–200 mg, 30–60 min
- **Adrenaline 0.2–0.3 mg** prolonged blocks by up to **50%** in early studies, more in **lumbosacral than thoracic** segments, but such doses are no longer used
cards.e: Oxford (UK practice): heavy bupivacaine 0.5% contains about 8% glucose (80 mg/mL). 2.5–3 mL of hyperbaric solution reaches T6–T10 in most young adults lying flat. Chloroprocaine 1% (40–50 mg) is licensed for short spinals. Manufacturers advise against lidocaine because of cauda equina and TNS risk, and ropivacaine is not licensed for intrathecal use. Reduce doses in pregnancy and with age.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42 · Lippincott Ch 7

cards.q: Describe the main topical local anaesthetic preparations and their cautions.
cards.a:
**EMLA**:
- A **eutectic mixture of lidocaine base 2.5% and prilocaine base 2.5%**
- Needs **45–60 min under an occlusive dressing**. Longer application gives deeper analgesia
- Safe in term newborns. Methaemoglobinaemia is very rare. Better than placebo for circumcision but **worse than dorsal penile nerve block**
**Tetracaine (Ametop 4% gel)**:
- Oxford: apply 30 min before venepuncture or 45 min before cannulation. Lasts 4–6 h
**TAC** (tetracaine, adrenaline, cocaine):
- Works only on **cut skin**. Rapid absorption from **mucosa can be fatal**
- Alternatives: **LET** (lidocaine 4%, adrenaline 1:20,000, tetracaine 0.5%) or liposomal lidocaine
**Synera** (lidocaine with tetracaine):
- A heating element speeds onset and causes vasodilatation
**Airway**:
- Prefer **cocaine-free** mixtures, such as an α1 agonist (oxymetazoline or phenylephrine) with **2–4% lidocaine**
cards.e: "Eutectic" means the mixture melts at a lower temperature than either drug alone, so a high concentration of base can be applied as an oil. Oxford's product advice (avoid under 1 year, on broken skin or mucosa) is more cautious than Miller's data on neonates. Answer with both views. Cocaine: 4–10% solution, maximum topical dose 3 mg/kg. It causes hypertension and arrhythmias and can be misused.

cards.q: What is tumescent anaesthesia, and what are its pharmacokinetic hazards?
cards.a:
Plastic surgeons, mainly for **liposuction**, inject **large volumes of dilute lidocaine with adrenaline** under the skin.
- Total lidocaine doses up to **45 mg/kg** have given plasma levels **at or below about 5 µg/mL**
- **Peak levels may occur up to 20 h later**, depending on the site
- Large case series report good safety, but **cardiac arrests and deaths** have happened in patients with several risk factors, high drug concentrations and **added sedatives**
cards.e: Strong vasoconstriction and slow uptake from fat explain why such large doses can be tolerated. The late peak means monitoring has to continue long after the patient leaves the operating room. Sedatives can hide early central nervous system warning signs.

cards.q: What is the role of systemic (IV) lidocaine in perioperative and neuropathic pain?
cards.a:
**Perioperative use**:
- Lidocaine acts on **G protein-coupled receptors (Gαq family)** and has strong **anti-inflammatory** effects
- A Cochrane review found clear benefit mainly in **visceral (abdominal) surgery**. A later meta-analysis found a **smaller effect** than once thought
**Neuropathic pain**:
- IV lidocaine works at plasma levels **50–100 times lower** than those needed to block normal nerves, and normal sensation is unaffected
- **Ectopic impulses** from injured nerve or dorsal root ganglia are very sensitive to **use-dependent** Na+ channel blockers
- Relief can last **days to months** after a single infusion, by an unknown mechanism
- A good response may lead to **oral mexiletine**, which many patients tolerate poorly
cards.e: This links basic pharmacology to clinical use. Phasic block means that rapidly firing abnormal neurons are suppressed at concentrations that leave normal conduction alone. Results vary between patients and pain conditions.

cards.q: Rank block sites by peak plasma local anaesthetic level and give the lidocaine example.
cards.a:
From highest to lowest plasma level: **intercostal, caudal, lumbar epidural, brachial plexus, subcutaneous**.
- **400 mg lidocaine** without adrenaline gives a mean peak of about **7 µg/mL after intercostal block**. That is enough to cause CNS toxicity in some patients
- The same dose for **brachial plexus** block gives about **3 µg/mL**, which rarely causes toxicity
- More vascular tissue means faster and greater absorption
- For a given site, **peak level rises in proportion to total dose**
cards.e: So a "maximum dose" only makes sense for a given site and patient. Oxford adds that maximum doses vary with age, size, site, vascularity and technique. Adrenaline at 5 µg/mL lowers peak levels of lidocaine and mepivacaine at every site. Lippincott notes that intercostal blocks cause more toxicity than paravertebral blocks.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42 · Lippincott Ch 8

cards.q: Describe the distribution, metabolism and excretion of local anaesthetics.
cards.a:
**Distribution**:
- Fits a **two-compartment model**. A fast phase reflects uptake into well-perfused tissues, and a slow phase depends on the drug itself
- Well-perfused organs reach higher concentrations
- The **lung takes up** a lot of drug on first pass. The **liver** is the main site of extraction
**Metabolism**:
- **Esters** are hydrolysed by **plasma pseudocholinesterase**. **Chloroprocaine is cleared fastest**
- **Amides** are broken down in the liver: **lidocaine faster than mepivacaine, which is faster than bupivacaine**
**Excretion**:
- Metabolites are excreted by the kidney. **Less than 5%** is excreted unchanged in urine
cards.e: Uptake by the lung buffers the brain and heart against an IV bolus. This buffering is lost with right-to-left shunts. Chloroprocaine is broken down so fast that it suits neonatal epidural infusions. Prilocaine is the amide metabolised most quickly, which is why Oxford favours it for Bier blocks.

cards.q: How do age, liver disease and heart failure change amide local anaesthetic pharmacokinetics?
cards.a:
**Age**:
- Lidocaine half-life after an IV dose was about **80 min at age 22–26** and **138 min at age 61–71**
**Liver disease**:
- Lidocaine half-life about **1.5 h if the liver is normal** and **5.0 h with liver disease**
**Congestive heart failure**:
- Lidocaine clearance is **markedly prolonged**, because less blood reaches the liver
**Neonates**:
- Immature liver enzymes prolong elimination of lidocaine, bupivacaine and ropivacaine
cards.e: Lidocaine has a high hepatic extraction, so its clearance depends mainly on liver blood flow. Low cardiac output, β-blockade and liver disease all reduce it. Single doses are usually fine, but infusions and repeated doses need to be reduced.

cards.q: State the safe infusion limits for epidural bupivacaine and lidocaine in infants and children, and why they matter.
cards.a:
Bupivacaine terminal half-life is about **3.5 h in adults** and **8–12 h in neonates**.
- **Bupivacaine infusion maximum: 0.4 mg/kg/h** for children and adults, and **0.2 mg/kg/h** for neonates and young infants
- Even at 0.2 mg/kg/h, blood levels in some infants were **still rising toward toxic levels after 48 h**
- **Lidocaine infusions in neonates: no more than 0.8 mg/kg/h**. The metabolite **MEGX** builds up and can cause **seizures**
- **Chloroprocaine** suits neonatal infusions because it is cleared quickly, even in preterm babies
cards.e: Seizures have been reported with high bupivacaine infusion rates in infants. Infants also have low α1-acid glycoprotein, so more drug is free. Reassess infusions daily and be suspicious of new irritability or seizures in a baby with a catheter infusion.

cards.q: Describe the presentation and incidence of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST).
cards.a:
The CNS is **more sensitive** than the cardiovascular system, so CNS toxicity usually starts at **lower levels** than circulatory collapse.
- **Early symptoms**: light-headedness, dizziness, **perioral tingling, metallic taste, tinnitus**, difficulty focusing, disorientation, drowsiness
- **Excitation**: shivering, **twitching and tremor** in the face and hands and feet, then **generalised tonic–clonic seizures**
- **Depression**: seizures stop, followed by respiratory depression or arrest
- **Cardiovascular**: hypotension, arrhythmia, AV block, collapse
- In a review of 93 cases only **about 60%** followed the classic order. Some patients go straight to CNS depression, especially if they have had sedatives
- Incidence: about **1:1000 with nerve stimulator** guidance and **1:1600 with ultrasound**
cards.e: Oxford's list of ECG signs: longer PR and QRS, AV block and changes in T-wave size. Lippincott warns that LAST is under-reported and that a negative epinephrine test dose and aspiration do not fully protect, so dose in small increments. Symptoms appearing within about 30 s of an epidural bolus suggest intravascular injection.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42 · Lippincott Ch 7

cards.q: Explain why local anaesthetic CNS toxicity shows excitation first and then depression. How are seizures treated?
cards.a:
At first the drug **blocks inhibitory cortical pathways**, so excitatory neurons fire unopposed and seizures follow. Effects on **glutamate** signalling add to this.
- Higher levels block **both inhibitory and excitatory** circuits, causing global CNS depression
- CNS toxicity rises with **potency**
- **Treatment**: small IV doses of **benzodiazepine** (midazolam) or **small doses of propofol**. Propofol acts faster but **avoid large doses**, especially if the patient is haemodynamically unstable
- Always have ready: monitoring, oxygen, rescue airway equipment and anticonvulsants (midazolam, thiopental, propofol)
cards.e: Oxford gives doses: midazolam 3–10 mg, propofol 20–60 mg, thiopental 50–150 mg, titrated to effect. It also stresses that propofol does not replace lipid emulsion. Seizures quickly cause hypoxia and acidosis, so control of the airway is part of treating the seizure.

cards.q: Why do hypercapnia, acidosis and hypoxia worsen local anaesthetic toxicity? What should you do about it?
cards.a:
Several mechanisms add together:
- **High PaCO2 raises cerebral blood flow**, so more drug reaches the brain faster
- CO2 diffuses into neurons and **lowers intracellular pH**, which **traps the cation** inside (**ion trapping**)
- Acidosis and hypercapnia **reduce plasma protein binding**, so more drug is free
- **Hypoxia and acidosis** strongly increase **bupivacaine's cardiac depression** and arrhythmias. In sheep they increased arrhythmias and deaths
- Seizures cause **hypoventilation and mixed acidosis**, which creates a vicious circle
- Action: **ventilate promptly to normocapnia** and give 100% oxygen
cards.e: Some patients become severely acidotic and hypoxic within seconds of a seizure. This may explain much of the cardiovascular collapse seen after accidental IV bupivacaine. Oxford suggests that mild hyperventilation may help by correcting metabolic acidosis. Miller's target is normocapnia.

cards.q: Describe the direct cardiac effects of local anaesthetics and why bupivacaine is more arrhythmogenic than lidocaine.
cards.a:
The main mechanism is **block of cardiac Na+ channels**, causing **arrhythmia and reduced contractility**.
- **Vmax (phase 0) falls** in Purkinje fibres and ventricular muscle. Conduction slows, giving **longer PR and wider QRS**
- Very high levels depress the **sinus node**, causing bradycardia or sinus arrest
- Other effects: altered **Ca2+ handling** (influx and SR release), **mitochondrial and fatty acid metabolism** inhibition (bupivacaine more than ropivacaine, much more than lidocaine)
- **Bupivacaine** depresses Vmax more and **recovers from use-dependent block slowly**, so Na+ channels are not fully free between beats, especially at **fast heart rates**. This makes it **arrhythmogenic**
- **Lidocaine** dissociates quickly and is **antiarrhythmic**
- Loss of contractility tracks **conduction-blocking potency** (bupivacaine and tetracaine more than lidocaine)
cards.e: This is the "fast-in, slow-out" behaviour of bupivacaine. Oxford adds that the **R-enantiomer** binds the myocardium more tightly and leaves it more slowly, which is the reason single S-enantiomers were developed. Tachycardia makes bupivacaine toxicity worse, which is one reason adrenaline must be given in small, careful doses.

cards.q: List the ways bupivacaine cardiotoxicity differs from lidocaine's, including the CC/CNS ratio.
cards.a:
There are four main differences:
- The **CC/CNS ratio** (dose causing irreversible cardiovascular collapse divided by dose causing seizures) is **lower** for bupivacaine and etidocaine than for lidocaine. Collapse can follow CNS signs with little warning, or even come first
- **Ventricular arrhythmias and VF** are more common after a rapid large IV dose of bupivacaine
- **Pregnancy** may increase sensitivity to bupivacaine (animal data)
- **Resuscitation is harder**, and **hypoxia and acidosis** strongly worsen toxicity. Lipid emulsion seems most effective against bupivacaine
cards.e: Lippincott summarises that bupivacaine is best known for cardiotoxicity, and that other agents tend to cause neurological toxicity before collapse. With lidocaine there is usually a wider margin between seizures and circulatory arrest.

cards.q: What do current guidelines say about drug therapy during resuscitation from LAST? What must be avoided?
cards.a:
Start with **standard CPR and ACLS**: airway, oxygen, ventilation and chest compressions.
- Give **adrenaline in small titrated doses**, not the fixed full doses of the arrest algorithm
- Give **lipid emulsion early**
- **Avoid propofol** if the patient is haemodynamically unstable
- For ventricular arrhythmias, **avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, β-blockers and other local anaesthetic antiarrhythmics (lidocaine)**
- No drug works reliably, so **prevention** is essential
cards.e: Lippincott's answer key also says vasopressin and standard-dose adrenaline should be avoided because they have not improved outcome, while ALS continues alongside lipid. Large adrenaline doses can make arrhythmias worse and cause lactic acidosis. Be prepared for a long resuscitation, as the drug needs time to wash out of the heart.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Lippincott Ch 7 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42

cards.q: Give the lipid emulsion regimen for LAST and discuss how it works.
cards.a:
**Miller (ASRA-based)**:
- **20% lipid 1.5 mL/kg ideal body weight IV bolus** (maximum **100 mL** in adults)
- Then **0.25 mL/kg/min**, up to about **200–250 mL**
- Repeat according to clinical response. **Continue for 10 min after the circulation is stable**
**Oxford (AAGBI)**:
- 1.5 mL/kg over 1 min
- Then **15 mL/kg/h**
- Repeat the bolus up to twice at 5-min intervals, and double the infusion rate after 5 min if the circulation is still inadequate
**How it may work**:
- The "**lipid sink**" pulls drug out of tissues. Models suggest heart bupivacaine falls about **11% in 3 min** and brain content about **18% in 15 min**
- It may also **improve heart metabolism** (fatty acid use) and act directly at the Na+ channel
cards.e: A volunteer study did not show a meaningful lipid sink effect, so lipid is **not a full antidote**. It helps but does not replace careful technique. Every site that does major blocks or large-volume infiltration should keep 20% lipid on hand. 0.25 mL/kg/min equals 15 mL/kg/h, so the two guidelines match.

cards.q: How can local anaesthetic systemic toxicity be prevented?
cards.a:
Prevention matters most because resuscitation is so difficult.
- **Aspirate first, but a negative aspirate does not rule out intravascular placement**
- **Give the dose in small increments** for every major block
- **Watch the ECG continuously** for changes in QRS or T-wave shape, rate, rhythm or ectopic beats, and stop injecting if they appear
- Use an **adrenaline marker** where it can be interpreted
- **Ultrasound guidance** lowers the incidence and allows smaller volumes
- **Calculate the dose** for the site and patient, add together doses of different drugs, and take care with infusions in infants and patients with liver or heart failure
- Choose **less cardiotoxic drugs** (ropivacaine, levobupivacaine) for large doses or sites with fast uptake
cards.e: Oxford: inject slowly in small amounts with frequent gentle aspiration, especially when giving a large dose at one site. ECG changes often, but not always, come before collapse. Have lipid, airway equipment and anticonvulsants ready before starting.

cards.q: Compare ropivacaine and levobupivacaine with racemic bupivacaine.
cards.a:
**Bupivacaine** is a **racemic mixture of R and S** forms.
- **Levobupivacaine**: the pure **S-enantiomer** of bupivacaine
- **Ropivacaine**: a pure **S-enantiomer** with a **propyl group instead of butyl** on the piperidine ring
- Ropivacaine **releases the Na+ channel faster** after each beat and **depresses contractility less**. Bupivacaine also selectively blocks Ca2+ currents
- Potency: ropivacaine is about **1.3–1.5 times less potent**. Studies of brachial plexus and epidural blocks show **nearly identical** profiles. 0.75% ropivacaine matched 0.5% bupivacaine
- Animal data: bupivacaine causes conduction block, collapse and VF more easily, and **resuscitation succeeds more often after ropivacaine**
- S-enantiomers of bupivacaine and mepivacaine are **metabolised more slowly**, so they may build up more during infusions
- **Levobupivacaine is labelled by weight of free base**, whereas most other drugs are labelled by weight of hydrochloride salt
cards.e: Oxford: the R-enantiomer binds the myocardium more firmly. Ropivacaine is the least cardiotoxic of the three and lasts slightly less long. Studies disagree on how levobupivacaine compares with the others in potency and duration. Use the safer drugs for large doses or when absorption is fast.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42, 43 · Lippincott Ch 8

cards.q: Describe the indirect cardiovascular effects of neuraxial block and how to treat severe bradycardia with hypotension.
cards.a:
**High spinal or epidural blocks** cause **sympathectomy**, which can lead to severe hypotension.
- Closed-claims data describe **cardiac arrest in healthy patients** under neuraxial block. Common features: **high block, liberal sedation**, hypotension with **bradycardia**, and **delays** in noticing the problem, supporting the airway and giving adrenaline
- **Mild to moderate hypotension**: **ephedrine** or small doses of **phenylephrine**
- **Severe hypotension with severe bradycardia**: give **adrenaline** early in increments, starting at **0.1–1 µg/kg**. This is about **20 to 200 times less** than arrest doses
cards.e: Lippincott: blocking the **T1–T4 cardioaccelerator fibres** causes bradycardia. Phenylephrine is the least useful drug here because it does not raise heart rate. Dyspnoea in high block is usually from hypotension reducing brainstem blood flow, not from phrenic nerve block.

cards.q: Explain prilocaine-induced methaemoglobinaemia: dose, mechanism and treatment.
cards.a:
Clinically important methaemoglobinaemia usually needs about **600 mg of prilocaine** in an adult.
- The liver metabolises prilocaine to **o-toluidine**, which **oxidises haemoglobin** to methaemoglobin
- Treat severe cases with **IV methylene blue**. Oxford gives **1–2 mg/kg** (methylthioninium chloride)
- Normal-dose **EMLA in term newborns** makes very little methaemoglobin. Risk rises with rare metabolic disorders or **other drugs that impair methaemoglobin reduction**
cards.e: Methaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve to the left. The patient looks cyanosed and pulse oximetry reads around 85% whatever the oxygen given. Oxford advises caution in pregnancy and anaemia. Prilocaine is otherwise the least toxic amide, which is why it is used for Bier blocks.

cards.q: Discuss allergy to local anaesthetics: frequency, causes and how to manage a patient with suspected allergy.
cards.a:
**True allergy is rare.** Stoelting estimates that only about **1% of reported reactions** are truly allergic.
- **Esters** cause allergy more often because they are metabolised to **PABA**, which acts as a hapten
- Amide reactions may come from **methylparaben** (structurally like PABA) or other preservatives (propylparaben, metabisulfite). **Latex** contamination of vials has been suspected
- Most "allergies" are really **intravascular injection** (seizures, hypotension), **adrenaline effects** (tachycardia, hypertension) or anxiety or vasovagal reactions
- Urticaria, laryngeal oedema and bronchospasm suggest true allergy
- Management: take a careful history and review records. Use **preservative-free** solutions. Esters and amides do **not cross-react**. Consider **intradermal testing** with preservative-free drug
- If allergy to both classes is confirmed, **meperidine (pethidine)** can be used for spinal anaesthesia
cards.e: Oxford notes that esters also cross-react with **sulphonamides**. The exam point is that being "allergic to the dentist's injection" is usually an epinephrine reaction or a vasovagal faint, and should not stop you using an amide regional technique after proper assessment.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Stoelting 7e Ch 27 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42

cards.q: Explain how local anaesthetics cause direct nerve toxicity. What clinical events showed this?
cards.a:
**At the concentrations in commercial vials, all local anaesthetics are toxic to nerve.** They are safe only because they are **diluted in tissue** before reaching the nerve.
- **5% lidocaine (about 200 mM)**, a dense viscous solution given through **narrow intrathecal microcatheters**, caused radicular symptoms and **cauda equina syndrome**, because the drug pooled on the sacral roots without mixing
- Applied straight to bare nerve, such concentrations cause **irreversible block within 5 min**
- Toxicity is **separate from conduction block**: tetrodotoxin, saxitoxin and neosaxitoxin cause intense block **without nerve damage**
- Injecting into a **confined tissue space** increases the risk
cards.e: Lippincott: cauda equina syndrome gives saddle anaesthesia, bladder and bowel problems, and weakness in sacral-root muscles. The quadriceps (lumbar plexus) is spared. Oxford notes that small spinal catheters became less popular after these reports.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Lippincott Ch 7 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42

cards.q: What are transient neurological symptoms (TNS)? Give the risk factors and data.
cards.a:
TNS is **temporary radicular irritation** after a single-shot spinal. Symptoms are **back or buttock pain radiating to the legs**, paraesthesia or hypoaesthesia, with a **normal neurological examination**.
- **Lidocaine and mepivacaine** cause it more often than bupivacaine and prilocaine
- Pooled relative risk with lidocaine: **6.7 times bupivacaine** and **5.5 times prilocaine**
- **Diluting lidocaine from 5% to 1–2% does not lower the risk**
- **Positioning** (for example **lithotomy**) affects it
- Adding a vasoconstrictor may add risk in theory, but current doses appear safe
cards.e: It sits at the mild end of a spectrum that has cauda equina syndrome at the other. Lippincott's classic MCQ is buttock pain after 5% lidocaine spinal in lithotomy with a normal neurological exam, which is TNS. It usually resolves on its own; treat with NSAIDs and reassurance. Exclude haematoma or abscess if there are neurological deficits.

cards.q: Do local anaesthetics damage skeletal muscle?
cards.a:
Yes. **Myotoxicity** has been shown after injection of lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, bupivacaine and etidocaine.
- The **more potent, long-acting drugs (bupivacaine, etidocaine)** cause **more local muscle damage** than lidocaine or prilocaine
- It is **reversible**, because muscle regenerates well and only a small area is affected. It is usually **not noticed clinically**
cards.e: Site 1 toxins are attractive for long blocks partly because they appear not to damage muscle. Muscle damage is a recognised cause of temporary weakness after high-concentration infiltration or continuous perineural techniques near muscle.

cards.q: What approaches are being developed to give prolonged-duration or sensory-selective local anaesthesia?
cards.a:
**Slow-release formulations**:
- **Liposomal bupivacaine (Exparel)** is licensed for infiltration and some nerve blocks
- Systematic reviews **question whether it beats plain bupivacaine**
- Others: bone wax, polylactic or polyglycolic acid polymers, proliposomes, on-demand release
**Site 1 blockers**:
- e.g. **neosaxitoxin** (phase 1–2 trials)
- No local nerve or muscle toxicity, little cardiotoxicity
- Combining with local anaesthetic or adrenaline lengthens the block and improves the therapeutic index
**Isoform targeting**:
- e.g. a Nav1.7 antibody; Nav1.9 for visceral pain
**Nociceptor targeting**:
- A **quaternary lidocaine derivative** enters pain fibres through **TRPV1** channels opened by lidocaine or capsaicin
- Stopped by **neurotoxicity**
cards.e: Tricyclic antidepressants and quaternary derivatives used as long-acting drugs were also limited by neurotoxicity. So far only liposomal bupivacaine has reached practice. The goal remains a surgical block followed by long sensory (or pain-only) block without weakness.

cards.q: Why do local anaesthetics fail in inflamed or infected tissue?
cards.a:
Both **pharmacokinetic** and **pharmacodynamic** factors contribute.
**Pharmacokinetic**:
- **Higher local blood flow** removes drug faster
- **Tissue acidosis** means more drug is charged, so less crosses membranes
- **Oedema** lengthens the distance the drug must diffuse
**Pharmacodynamic**:
- **Peripheral and central sensitisation**
- Dental failure rates with an abscess or pulpitis reach **70%**
- Even an **inferior alveolar nerve block** placed far from the infection often fails
- **Higher concentrations** can still work, though the block may be shorter
cards.e: Oxford notes that the acidic surroundings of an abscess impair local anaesthetics. The failure of a distant inferior alveolar block shows that acidity at the injection site cannot be the whole explanation, so sensitisation must play a part. In practice, give a larger dose or use a block farther from the infected area.

cards.q: What is tachyphylaxis to local anaesthetics? What causes it, and how can it be prevented?
cards.a:
Tachyphylaxis is a **loss of effect with repeated doses or infusions**.
- Some apparent cases have other causes: **catheter displacement** or a **change in the source or intensity of pain**
- In labour, **letting pain return before the next top-up** shortened and weakened later blocks. **Re-dosing before pain returned** prevented this
- **Systemic opioids** stopped segmental regression during thoracic epidural bupivacaine infusions
- In rats, tachyphylaxis was linked to **hyperalgesia**. **NMDA antagonists and nitric oxide synthase inhibitors** prevented it
- Pharmacokinetic factors play a part too: repeated injections left **less lidocaine inside the nerve**
cards.e: The exact mechanism is unknown, and its importance with continuous long-acting infusions is unclear. Practical points: top up on a schedule rather than waiting for pain, check the catheter, and add multimodal analgesia.

cards.q: Can patients be genetically or acquired-resistant to local anaesthetics?
cards.a:
Yes, though it is rare.
- Mutations in **segment IIIS6** of the Na+ channel α subunit (and in Nav1.7 and Nav1.5) **reduce the affinity** of local anaesthetics and anticonvulsants
- Different mutations change the response to particular drugs, which suggests the binding site is **dynamic**
- A family with **inherited resistance** has been studied genetically. In a clinical study, some patients who reported failed blocks did show partial or **drug-specific resistance**
- **Acquired** resistance has been reported after **repeated scorpion stings**. Scorpion toxins act at **sites 3 and 4**, not site 9
cards.e: When a patient says "local anaesthetics never work on me", first rule out technical failure. Then consider true resistance, and possibly try a different drug, since resistance can be selective.

cards.q: What actions do local anaesthetics have besides Na+ channel block?
cards.a:
They also:
- **Block various receptors** and other ion channels, including **K+ and Ca2+ channels**
- **Change glutamate release and its downstream effects**
- **Depress certain intracellular signalling pathways**, including **Gαq-coupled GPCRs**
- Have **anti-inflammatory** effects
- **Activate TRPV1 and TRPA1**, which causes injection pain and allows targeting of pain fibres
- When given systemically, they affect **cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle**, the CNS and the conducting system of the heart
cards.e: Effects other than Na+ channel block help explain IV lidocaine's analgesic and anti-inflammatory actions, part of its CNS toxicity (glutamate), and its cardiac toxicity (Ca2+ and mitochondria). Stoelting notes that lidocaine and ropivacaine slow tumour cell growth in the laboratory, which is one proposed link between regional anaesthesia and cancer outcome.

cards.q: A 70-kg woman has a thoracic epidural for laparotomy. After a negative lidocaine–adrenaline test dose and negative aspiration, 10 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine is given. Within 30 s she complains of tinnitus and light-headedness and becomes agitated. BP falls from 150/70 to 100/45 and HR from 85 to 55. She then has a generalised seizure. What is the diagnosis and how do you manage it?
cards.a:
**Diagnosis: local anaesthetic systemic toxicity from intravascular injection** through the catheter. The CNS signs came within seconds of the bolus, which rules out a high block or anaphylaxis.
- **Stop the injection** and call for help and the lipid kit
- **Airway**: 100% O2. Ventilate to **normocapnia** and intubate if needed to prevent hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis
- **Seizures**: small doses of **midazolam**. Avoid large doses of propofol while she is unstable
- **Lipid 20%**: 1.5 mL/kg IBW (about 100 mL) bolus, then 0.25 mL/kg/min (about 15 mL/kg/h). Repeat the bolus and increase the rate if she stays unstable
- **If she arrests**: CPR with **small adrenaline doses (≤1 µg/kg)**. **No vasopressin, calcium channel blocker, β-blocker or lidocaine**. Expect a long resuscitation. Consider cardiopulmonary bypass if it fails
- **Afterwards**: monitor for several hours (lipid can be followed by recurrence), check the catheter position, report the event
cards.e: A negative test dose and aspiration do not protect against intravascular placement. Every bolus should be given in small increments. Bupivacaine has a low CC/CNS ratio, and hypoxia and acidosis from the seizure strongly increase its cardiotoxicity, so early airway control and lipid are what decide the outcome.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Lippincott Ch 7 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42

cards.q: A 58-year-old man (ideal body weight 70 kg) is having an awake shoulder procedure. He suddenly loses consciousness and develops broad-complex VT 2 minutes after an interscalene block with 30 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine. A pulse is present but BP is 60/30. Outline your lipid and drug plan with doses.
cards.a:
Treat as **LAST with cardiovascular involvement**.
- **ABC**: 100% O2. Secure the airway and **avoid hypercapnia**
- **Lipid 20%**:
  - **bolus 1.5 mL/kg IBW, about 105 mL** (Miller caps the adult bolus at 100 mL)
  - then **infusion 0.25 mL/kg/min, about 17.5 mL/min** (about 1000 mL/h, matching the AAGBI 15 mL/kg/h)
  - **repeat the bolus up to twice at 5 min** and **double the rate** if he stays unstable
  - continue **10 min after stability**, keeping within the upper dose limits of your guideline
- **VT with a pulse**: synchronised cardioversion if unstable. **Do not give lidocaine, amiodarone-type drugs that block Na+ or β channels, calcium channel blockers or vasopressin**. If he arrests, use **small adrenaline doses**
- **Supportive**: careful vasopressor titration. Watch for lipid-related problems (pancreatitis, interference with blood tests)
cards.e: Bupivacaine's slow release from cardiac Na+ channels causes re-entrant broad-complex arrhythmias. Adding another Na+ channel blocker makes them worse. Lipid draws drug out of the heart, but it is not a complete antidote, so good CPR and patience still matter most.

cards.q: A 30-year-old, 70-kg man has a forearm fracture reduced under a Bier block with 40 mL of 0.5% lidocaine. Ten minutes after injection the cuff accidentally deflates. He reports circumoral tingling and tinnitus and then twitches. What happened, and how could it have been prevented?
cards.a:
**Systemic toxicity** from a sudden release of the full lidocaine dose (200 mg, about 3 mg/kg) into the circulation before it was bound to tissue.
- **Management**: stop, give O2 and support the airway. **Midazolam** for twitching or seizures. Lipid emulsion if toxicity progresses. Monitor ECG and BP
- **Prevention**:
  - **reliable double-cuff tourniquet** checked beforehand; pressure **50–100 mmHg above systolic**
  - **keep the cuff inflated at least 20 min for lidocaine (15 min for prilocaine)**
  - **release in steps**, re-inflating between releases
  - use **prilocaine 0.5%** where available
  - **never bupivacaine**
  - IV access in the other arm and resuscitation equipment ready
cards.e: Seizures have been reported with as little as 1.4 mg/kg in IVRA. Lippincott stresses keeping the tourniquet on for at least 15–20 min even if surgery finishes early, and then releasing it slowly in steps. Contraindications include crush injury, sickle cell disease and peripheral vascular disease.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42 · Lippincott Ch 8

cards.q: A 25-year-old man has a spinal with 1.5 mL of 5% hyperbaric lidocaine for ureteric stenting in the lithotomy position. Surgery is uneventful. In recovery he has severe bilateral buttock pain radiating to the thighs. Power, sensation and sphincter function are normal. What is the diagnosis and what is your plan?
cards.a:
**Transient neurological symptoms (TNS).**
- Risk factors present: **lidocaine** (pooled risk about 6.7 times that of bupivacaine) and **lithotomy**
- **Neurological examination is normal**, which separates TNS from haematoma, abscess or cauda equina syndrome
- **Management**:
  - reassure him that it usually **resolves within days**
  - NSAIDs and simple analgesia
  - **reassess** for any new weakness, numbness or sphincter problem; image urgently if these appear
- **Future prevention**: use **bupivacaine, prilocaine or chloroprocaine** for short spinals. **Diluting lidocaine does not reduce TNS**
cards.e: Lippincott uses this exact vignette to test TNS. Oxford notes that manufacturers now advise against spinal lidocaine because of cauda equina and TNS risk, and that 1% chloroprocaine (40–50 mg) is an option for short procedures.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Lippincott Ch 7 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42

cards.q: A 75-kg woman receives 900 mg of prilocaine for multiple infiltrations during a long dermatological procedure. Two hours later she looks grey-blue and her SpO2 is 86% on 10 L/min oxygen. Her chest is clear and her ABG PaO2 is 28 kPa. What is the likely diagnosis, how do you confirm it, and how do you treat it?
cards.a:
**Methaemoglobinaemia** caused by prilocaine. The dose was over the usual 600 mg threshold and the metabolite o-toluidine oxidised haemoglobin.
- **Clue**: the **gap between a high PaO2 and a low SpO2** that does not improve with oxygen. Blood may look chocolate-brown
- **Confirm** with **co-oximetry** (methaemoglobin fraction)
- **Treat**:
  - stop further prilocaine and give 100% O2
  - **IV methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg** if she has symptoms or the level is high
  - repeat the co-oximetry
  - look for other oxidising drugs or reduced reductase activity
cards.e: Pulse oximeters cannot measure methaemoglobin correctly and tend to read about 85%. Methylene blue speeds up NADPH-dependent reduction of methaemoglobin. Oxford advises caution with prilocaine in pregnancy and anaemia, where loss of oxygen-carrying capacity is tolerated poorly.

cards.q: A 3-week-old, 3.5-kg infant has an epidural catheter after laparotomy and is on a bupivacaine infusion. On day 2 the baby becomes irritable and then has a seizure. The infusion has been running at 0.4 mg/kg/h. Explain the problem and how you would set up epidural infusions in neonates.
cards.a:
**Bupivacaine accumulation and toxicity.** 0.4 mg/kg/h is the limit for older children and adults. **Neonates should get no more than 0.2 mg/kg/h.**
- Reasons: **immature liver enzymes** (half-life 8–12 h compared with 3.5 h in adults) and low α1-acid glycoprotein, so more drug is free
- **Immediate**: stop the infusion, ABC, benzodiazepine for the seizure. Lipid if there are cardiovascular signs. Check plasma level if available
- **Future plan**:
  - bupivacaine **at most 0.2 mg/kg/h**, and limit duration (levels can still rise after 48 h)
  - or **chloroprocaine**, which is cleared quickly even in preterm babies
  - lidocaine at most **0.8 mg/kg/h** (the metabolite MEGX can cause seizures)
  - review the dose daily
cards.e: Seizures in infants on high-rate bupivacaine infusions are exactly the cases that led to these limits. Early CNS signs in babies are subtle, so irritability or apnoea in a baby on an infusion should be treated as toxicity until proven otherwise.

cards.q: A 40-year-old man needs drainage of a large dental abscess. Two standard inferior alveolar nerve blocks with 2% lidocaine and adrenaline have failed. The dentist asks why, and what to do next.
cards.a:
**Local anaesthetic failure in inflamed tissue.** Failure rates with an abscess or pulpitis reach about 70%.
- **Why it fails**:
  - more blood flow removes the drug
  - **acidosis** keeps more drug charged so less enters the nerve
  - **oedema** lengthens the diffusion distance
  - **peripheral and central sensitisation**, which explains why even a distant inferior alveolar block fails
- **Options**:
  - a **higher dose or concentration**, within maximum dose limits
  - a block **farther from the inflamed area**
  - allow more time
  - add systemic analgesia or sedation
  - consider general anaesthesia if a large dose would be needed
- Avoid injecting into the pus itself
cards.e: Adding bicarbonate does not overcome the tissue acidity once injected. Keep track of the total lidocaine dose: about 7 mg/kg with adrenaline per Oxford, 500 mg in Miller's infiltration table.

cards.q: A 55-year-old woman is listed for carpal tunnel release under regional anaesthesia. She says she is "allergic to local anaesthetic" because her heart raced and she felt faint after a dental injection 10 years ago. How do you assess her and what do you advise?
cards.a:
The history suggests a **non-allergic reaction**. **Palpitations and faintness** fit **systemic adrenaline** or a **vasovagal** reaction. Fewer than about 1% of reported local anaesthetic "allergies" are real.
- **History and records**:
  - which drug was used
  - whether there was **urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm or hypotension needing treatment** (these suggest true allergy)
  - when symptoms started
- **If true allergy is unlikely**: proceed with a **preservative-free amide** (dental drugs are usually amides with adrenaline). Give a small test dose with full monitoring
- **If doubtful**: refer to an allergist. Consider **intradermal or provocation testing** with preservative-free drug before the operation
- Remember possible **preservative (methylparaben, metabisulfite) or latex** causes. Esters and amides **do not cross-react**
cards.e: Labelling her as allergic would deny her a safe and suitable anaesthetic. Ester allergy is linked to PABA. Amide reactions are usually to preservatives. If allergy to both classes is confirmed, meperidine can be used for a spinal.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Stoelting 7e Ch 27 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42

cards.q: A 70-kg man needs femoral and sciatic blocks for below-knee amputation, plus surgeon infiltration of the wound. You plan 0.5% ropivacaine 20 mL for each block. The surgeon wants to add 20 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine. Is this safe?
cards.a:
**No. Toxicities add together, and the combined dose goes over the limits.**
- Ropivacaine: 2 × 20 mL × 5 mg/mL = **200 mg**, which is **100% of the plain maximum** (200 mg; 250 mg with adrenaline; about 3 mg/kg)
- Bupivacaine: 20 mL × 5 mg/mL = **100 mg**, about **57% of its 175 mg maximum**
- Total is about **157% of a maximum dose**, well over 100%
- **Options**:
  - lower the block concentration or volume with ultrasound (minimum effective volume is about 0.1–0.15 mL/mm² of nerve)
  - use **0.2–0.375% ropivacaine**
  - remove the infiltration or use a small dilute volume
  - add adrenaline as a marker and to slow absorption
  - give in small increments and keep lipid available
cards.e: Miller says that when blocks are combined, the total must not exceed the listed maximum, and that adding maximum doses of two drugs is a recognised mistake. Oxford adds that using several drugs raises the risk of error. Lippincott suggests femoral plus proximal sciatic blocks as an option when neuraxial block is contraindicated.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42 · Lippincott Ch 8

cards.q: A 32-year-old woman at term has an emergency caesarean. A spinal of 2.5 mL of 0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine is given. Five minutes later she says her hands are tingling and she feels breathless. BP is 65/30, HR 42, and her voice is weak. What is happening and how do you manage it?
cards.a:
**High (approaching total) spinal block.** Pregnancy increases spread through engorged epidural veins and progesterone, and **T1–T4 cardioaccelerator fibres** are blocked, causing bradycardia.
- **Call for help** and give 100% O2. Keep her **left lateral tilt**, but **do not put her head-down**
- **Severe hypotension with bradycardia**: give **adrenaline early in increments, starting at about 0.1–1 µg/kg** (roughly 10–50 µg). Atropine or ephedrine may help. **Phenylephrine alone is the least useful**
- **Airway**: if she loses consciousness, cannot speak or her breathing becomes inadequate, intubate (rapid sequence) and ventilate. Keep her blood pressure up to maintain brainstem perfusion
- Deliver the baby once the mother is stable. Monitor the fetus
cards.e: Closed-claims cardiac arrests under neuraxial block share delays in recognising the problem, in supporting the airway and in giving adrenaline. Lippincott notes that breathlessness in high block is mainly due to brainstem hypoperfusion, so restoring blood pressure treats the breathing problem too.

cards.q: What is the central premise examined in Miller's chapter on immune implications of anaesthesia?
cards.a: That the reported effects of anaesthetics on immune cells mean **perioperative anaesthetic exposure affects the patient's immune system and therefore outcomes**.
cards.e: The premise implies further assumptions: that anaesthesia alters immunity, that perioperative immunosuppression should and can be prevented, that anaesthetic choice can modulate it, and that it could be harnessed for patient benefit. The chapter concludes that current evidence does not support most of these assumptions clinically.

cards.q: After decades of research, what is Miller's overall conclusion on choosing anaesthetics to protect immune function?
cards.a: No anaesthetic can currently be recommended over another for protecting immune function or improving outcomes: the integrated evidence (animal, human, in silico) is **insufficient**. Commonly used anaesthetics appear **broadly safe**.
cards.e: Miller's practical advice is twofold: keep the whole perioperative episode safe, and get patients into the best possible health before surgery.

cards.q: Which factor has the greatest influence on perioperative immune function?
cards.a: The **surgical stress response** (neuroendocrine activation of the sympathetic nervous system and hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis), which outweighs the effect of any anaesthetic drug.
cards.e: Stoelting explains that catecholamines and cortisol act on β2-adrenergic and glucocorticoid receptors on immune cells, shifting cytokine balance from TH1 (cell-mediated) towards TH2 (anti-inflammatory) responses.

cards.q: What benefit and what cost does perioperative immunosuppression carry?
cards.a: Benefit: it limits the **inflammatory response** to surgical tissue injury. Cost: increased vulnerability to **infection** and possibly **tumour proliferation**.
cards.e: Cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α released by activated monocytes and macrophages further stimulate the HPA axis, amplifying the response.

cards.q: Besides drugs, which perioperative factors weaken immunity?
cards.a:
- **Acute pain** (suppresses NK cell activity)
- **Hypothermia** (amplifies stress response, suppresses NK and lymphocyte function)
- **Tissue hypoxia** (impairs neutrophil oxidative killing, delays wound healing)
- **Hyperglycaemia** from stress hormones
- **Allogeneic blood transfusion**
cards.e: Most of these are modifiable by good anaesthetic care (analgesia, warming, oxygenation, glucose control, blood conservation), which is the practical way to support immunity.

cards.q: What is transfusion-related immunomodulation (TRIM)?
cards.a: Measurable immune effects of allogeneic blood: **increased infection risk** and possible **tumour growth**, but improved renal allograft survival.
