- Nondepolarising NMBAs cause **prolonged, profound block**: use objective monitoring; **sugammadex** reversal reported; ulnar TOF may be unreliable if those muscles are affected
- General and **epidural** anaesthesia used successfully; **spinal often avoided**
cards.e: Monitoring at a clinically weak muscle can overestimate block depth, so interpret TOF in light of the individual pattern of weakness. Plan for possible postoperative ventilation.

cards.q: Describe Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease (hereditary motor-sensory neuropathy).
cards.a:
The commonest HMSN: a chronic, symmetric, slowly progressive **distal motor and sensory polyneuropathy** from defective **myelin genes**.
- Distal weakness and wasting, weak ankle dorsiflexion, reduced reflexes, **pes cavus**, falls, neuropathic pain, sometimes deafness
- **CMT1A**: **PMP22 duplication on 17p11.2**; PMP22, GJB1, MFN2 and MPZ account for 90%
- Types 1 and 2 most common (about **40 per 100,000**); **type 3 (Dejerine–Sottas)** is severe with infant hypotonia
- Markedly slowed nerve conduction with prolonged distal motor and F-wave latencies
cards.e: Pregnancy, diabetes, chemotherapy and trauma can accelerate progression. Stoelting describes CMT as the most common inherited cause of chronic motor and sensory neuropathy; exercise is encouraged and cAMP-targeted therapy that lowers PMP22 expression is emerging.

cards.q: What are the anaesthetic considerations in Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease?
cards.a:
- **Positioning**: sensory loss and deformities raise injury risk
- **CMT1**: increased sensitivity to **thiopental**, proportional to motor and sensory deficit
- Reduced AChRs: **raised sensitivity to nondepolarising NMBAs** (prolonged vecuronium reported; atracurium and mivacurium normal); assess baseline function and monitor
- **Succinylcholine** has been used without problems, but exaggerated hyperkalaemia is possible during **acute exacerbation**
- **TIVA and volatiles** both used safely
- **Neuraxial** used in obstetrics, but worsening neurology is debated
- Obstetrics: degeneration of uterine adrenergic nerves may cause **uterine hypotonia and PPH**
cards.e: Responses vary because of the limited case experience, so titrate relaxants to objective monitoring. Oxford Ch 13 lists hyperkalaemia risk and possible respiratory muscle involvement for CMT.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Oxford Handbook Ch 13 · Stoelting 7e Ch 15

cards.q: What is fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP)?
cards.a:
A rare **autosomal dominant** disease of progressive **heterotopic ossification** of muscle, fascia, tendon and ligament.
- About **97%** carry the **ACVR1 R206H** gain-of-function variant (BMP type I receptor), which signals constitutively and treats Activin A as a BMP
- Early clues: **deformed big toes** from birth plus soft tissue swellings that come and go; initial misdiagnosis in up to **90%**, and biopsy can provoke ossification
- Ossification starts in the **upper back and neck**, then trunk and limbs; **TMJ ankylosis** limits mouth opening
- Death usually from **thoracic insufficiency** (restrictive lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure) or pneumonia
- Chronic pain in **86%**; neuronal hyperexcitability linked to the same variant
cards.e: Any tissue trauma, including biopsy, IM injection or surgical retraction, can trigger a flare. FOP is therefore a multisystem disease and the airway is the main anaesthetic hazard.

cards.q: What are the perioperative considerations for patients with FOP?
cards.a:
- **Multidisciplinary planning** for all elective procedures; general anaesthesia commonly recommended
- **Awake nasal fibreoptic intubation** is first choice when non-urgent (laryngoscopy stretching the TMJ may cause permanent ankylosis); **ENT ready for tracheostomy**; HFNC suggested as an alternative
- **Pad all pressure points**
- **Avoid IM injections**; IV and arterial lines are safe (may be technically hard)
- **Regional anaesthesia relatively contraindicated** (needles through muscle and fascia can trigger flares; mandibular block caused jaw ankylosis); neuraxial is also technically difficult
- **Perioperative corticosteroid prophylaxis** against flares
cards.e: Cervical fusion, TMJ ankylosis and restrictive lung disease make airway management very difficult. A distal ultrasound-guided ankle block has been reported without problems, but the general rule is to avoid penetrating muscle.

cards.q: Describe the genetics and pathophysiology of Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy.
cards.a:
**X-linked recessive** defects of **dystrophin** (Dp427) at **Xp21**.
- DMD **1 in 3500** male births; BMD about **1.53 per 100,000** males
- **Deletions** cause 65–70% of DMD and > 80% of BMD; about **one-third are new mutations**
- **Out-of-frame** mutations (no dystrophin) cause DMD; **in-frame** mutations (partly functional protein) cause milder BMD
- Dystrophin links **actin** (N terminus) to the **dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex** (C terminus) and laminin, stabilising the sarcolemma
- Loss causes membrane leak, **CK rise**, necrosis and fibrofatty replacement (**pseudohypertrophy**)
cards.e: Dystrophin is also present in cardiac and smooth muscle and brain, explaining cardiomyopathy, GI dysmotility and higher rates of intellectual impairment. Female cases occur with 45,X or skewed 46,XX patterns, and female carriers can develop cardiomyopathy.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11

cards.q: What is the clinical course of Duchenne muscular dystrophy compared with Becker?
cards.a:
**DMD**:
- Symptoms by **4 years** in 74%; walking delayed to **≥ 18 months**
- Waddling gait, falls, stair difficulty, **Gowers manoeuvre**; pseudohypertrophy of calves (**60%**), **macroglossia (30%)**
- Loss of ambulation by **9–11 years**; scoliosis **> 20°** in 90% within 3–4 years of wheelchair use
- Proximal reflexes lost; **Achilles reflex preserved**
- Death usually in the **30s** from cardiorespiratory failure
**BMD**: onset in the **second or third decade**, wider severity range, survival to the early 40s
cards.e: Earlier onset predicts faster progression. Perioperative complications do not track disease severity and occur even in mildly affected patients, so every patient needs full assessment.

cards.q: Describe respiratory involvement in DMD.
cards.a:
Pulmonary insufficiency is the leading cause of morbidity; **pneumonia** is the commonest cause of death and respiratory failure typically occurs in the **20s**.
- **Expiratory** muscles (abdominal) weaken first; inspiratory function and the diaphragm relatively spared early
- **VC rises** with growth in the first decade, **plateaus** in early adolescence, then **falls** steeply as the diaphragm weakens
- Loss of VC and TLC is disproportionate due to chest wall mechanics, surfactant changes, microatelectasis, fibrosis after pneumonia and **scoliosis**
- Sleep apnoea may lead to pulmonary hypertension
cards.e: Weak expiratory muscles mean a poor cough and retained secretions, which explains the high rate of postoperative chest infection. About 30% of DMD deaths are respiratory.

cards.q: Describe cardiac involvement in DMD and BMD.
cards.a:
Myocardium is replaced by fibrous tissue and fat, causing **dilated cardiomyopathy**, starting in the **posterobasal and lateral LV wall**.
- ECG: sinus tachycardia, **tall R waves in right precordial leads**, deep **Q waves in left precordial leads**, increased QT dispersion, inverted T waves
- Echo: normal or regional wall motion abnormality early, then LV dysfunction and ventricular arrhythmias; **MVP in 10–25%**
- About **90%** have subclinical or overt heart disease, yet the heart is the cause of death in just **20%** (DMD) and **50%** (BMD)
- Cardiac severity **does not correlate** with skeletal weakness
- Treatment: early **ACE inhibitors**, then beta blockers, even LVAD
cards.e: Preoperatively 50–70% show some cardiac abnormality but only 10% are clinically significant. A resting echo may not show how the heart responds to stress; stress echo, Holter and troponin I have been advocated.

cards.q: How is muscular dystrophy diagnosed, and what are the pitfalls of CK measurement?
cards.a:
- **CK** rises to **50–300 × normal** early; three raised values a month apart support the diagnosis; levels **fall as muscle mass is lost** and do not track severity
- **CK-MB** is raised from skeletal muscle, so it is useless as a cardiac injury marker (use troponin)
- **MLPA/array CGH** for exon copy number gives results within about 24 h, largely replacing biopsy with dystrophin immunostaining
- **Corticosteroids** are the mainstay of treatment; gene therapy and utrophin up-regulation are under trial
cards.e: Early genetic diagnosis via newborn screening will matter more as exon-targeted therapies arrive. Corticosteroid therapy means considering perioperative steroid cover.

cards.q: What are the intraoperative anaesthetic considerations in DMD/BMD?
cards.a:
- **Succinylcholine contraindicated**: rhabdomyolysis and **hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest** from unstable sarcolemma (resuscitation often fails)
- **Volatile agents** can cause life-threatening rhabdomyolysis: **TIVA recommended**
- MH-like events: **0.002 (DMD)** and **0.00036 (BMD)**, though true MH mutation risk equals the general population
- Nondepolarising NMBAs: **deeper and longer block**; reverse with **sugammadex**
- Small doses of short-acting opioids
- **Aspiration risk** (weak laryngeal reflexes, slow gastric emptying); masseter spasm possible; difficult airway possible (macroglossia)
- **Regional anaesthesia** is a good alternative or adjunct (avoids triggers, provides analgesia, helps physiotherapy)
cards.e: The reactions are not true MH but anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis, which is why the same agents are avoided. Stoelting confirms rhabdomyolysis with or without cardiac arrest after volatiles even without succinylcholine.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11

cards.q: What pulmonary function thresholds predict postoperative respiratory problems in DMD?
cards.a:
- Preoperative **FVC < 40% predicted**: highest incidence of **prolonged ventilation (> 36 h)**
- **VC > 30% predicted**: usually extubated immediately after surgery
- **Delayed respiratory insufficiency** can appear up to **36 h** postoperatively despite apparent recovery of strength
- **CPAP or BiPAP** effectively manage postoperative respiratory depression
- **Peak expiratory flow** is easy and correlates with functional tests (VC and FEV1 did not)
cards.e: Plan postoperative HDU/ICU care and NIV availability for patients near these thresholds. A poor cough plus slow recovery of weakness explains the delayed deterioration.

cards.q: Describe limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD) and its anaesthetic implications.
cards.a:
A heterogeneous group with progressive **shoulder and pelvic girdle** weakness; most lose ambulation within 20 years of onset. Prevalence about **1–6.5 per 100,000**.
- **LGMD1**: autosomal dominant; **LGMD2**: autosomal recessive and about **10 × more common**
- Common genes: **FKRP** and **CAPN3**; diagnosis now needs genotyping (ENMC 2018: raised CK, imaging degeneration, dystrophic histology)
- Anaesthesia as for DMD/BMD: cardiac and respiratory involvement, **rhabdomyolysis** risk
- **Sensitive to opioids and muscle relaxants**: use short-acting agents and sugammadex
- Consider **local anaesthetic myotoxicity** with regional techniques
cards.e: Oxford groups limb-girdle among the autosomal recessive dystrophies, which are less severe and later in onset than Duchenne. Respiratory impairment is common, so plan postoperative monitoring.

cards.q: Compare myotonic dystrophy types 1 and 2.
cards.a:
Both are **autosomal dominant**, multisystem disorders (prevalence about **1 in 8000**).
- **DM1 (Steinert)**: about **98%** of cases; **CTG repeat** in **DMPK** on **19q13.3**; repeat expands in successive generations (**anticipation**); distal and cranial weakness
- **DM2 (PROMM)**: **CCTG repeat** in **CNBP** on **3q21**; later onset, milder, **proximal** weakness; myotonia in 90%; tolerates GA better
- Both: insulin resistance from **INSR mis-splicing**
- DM1 features: facial, temporalis, masseter and sternomastoid wasting, myotonia, **cardiac conduction defects**, cataracts, frontal balding, testicular atrophy, cognitive impairment
cards.e: Stoelting describes DM1 as the most common and serious adult form. Antimyotonic drugs include phenytoin, quinine and mexiletine; Stoelting warns that quinine and procainamide can worsen conduction defects.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11

cards.q: What cardiac and respiratory features of myotonic dystrophy matter to the anaesthetist?
cards.a:
**Cardiac**:
- **First-degree AV block** is common even before symptoms; progressive AV and intraventricular block; **MVP in 20%**
- AV block may **not respond to atropine**: have **pacing** available; ECG and echo screening; monitor into the postoperative period
**Respiratory**:
- Pulmonary complications dominate, especially after **upper abdominal surgery** and with proximal limb weakness
- Causes: hypotonia, **chronic aspiration** (smooth muscle atrophy, poor gastric motility, weak cough), central and peripheral hypoventilation
cards.e: Even asymptomatic patients have some cardiomyopathy, so volatile myocardial depression may be exaggerated (Stoelting). Also check glucose, thyroid function and calcium preoperatively.

cards.q: Which drugs and stimuli provoke myotonic contractures in myotonic dystrophy, and how are they managed?
cards.a:
- **Succinylcholine**: contracture lasting minutes that can make intubation and ventilation impossible; **not relieved by nondepolarising NMBAs**
- **Hypothermia, shivering**, surgical manipulation and **electrocautery**
- **Neostigmine**, methohexital, etomidate and propofol have been implicated
- Patients are **sensitive to sedatives, opioids and hypnotics** (hypersomnolence, CO2 retention): titrate short-acting agents
- Rocuronium with **sugammadex** gives normal reversal
- Keep **normothermic**; extend recovery monitoring
cards.e: Stoelting notes that neither regional nor general anaesthesia nor neuromuscular blockade reliably abolishes the contracture; high volatile concentrations can, but at the cost of myocardial depression. There is no proven link between DM and MH. Pregnancy can unmask DM, with uterine atony and retained placenta.

cards.q: What are the challenges of regional anaesthesia in myotonic dystrophy?
cards.a:
- **Neuraxial block** is used frequently to reduce opioid requirements
- **Peripheral nerve blocks** can be difficult: needle stimulation may trigger myotonia, and ultrasound images are altered
- Degenerated bundles may look **hypoechoic**; atrophic muscle overall is **hyperechoic**, reflecting energy and limiting deep penetration
cards.e: Regional techniques avoid the respiratory depression these patients are prone to, but they do not prevent myotonic contractures. Plan for longer imaging time and lower-frequency probes where needed.

cards.q: Describe myotonia congenita and its anaesthetic implications.
cards.a:
A **chloride channelopathy** (**CLCN1**, ClC-1) reducing sarcolemmal Cl- conductance and delaying relaxation.
- **Thomsen** (dominant, infancy onset, about 1:23,000) and **Becker** (recessive, onset 10–14 years, more severe, about 1:50,000, yet described as 10 × more common than Thomsen)
- Stiffness after rest that **improves with repeated contraction** ("warm-up"); muscle hypertrophy, percussion myotonia, lid lag; Becker may be mistaken for epilepsy
- First-line treatment: **mexiletine** (others: lamotrigine, ranolazine)
- Anaesthesia: **normothermia** (shivering triggers myotonia); **avoid succinylcholine** (severe masseter spasm); caution with high-dose **β-agonists** and **propranolol**
- Generalised spasm resembling MH may impair ventilation; **dantrolene** usually abolishes it
cards.e: An MH link has been suggested but not confirmed. Dantrolene works because it inhibits SR Ca2+ release downstream of the membrane defect. Oxford manages myotonia congenita as for myotonic dystrophy.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11

cards.q: Describe X-linked myotubular myopathy and its anaesthetic considerations.
cards.a:
Severe congenital myopathy with **central nuclei** resembling fetal myotubes; **MTM1** on **Xq28**; about **1 in 50,000** male births.
- Polyhydramnios and reduced fetal movement; severe floppiness and **respiratory failure at birth**; reflexes absent; heart usually spared
- Survivors are often **ventilator dependent**; **hepatobiliary disease/cholestasis** common
- Surgery: tracheostomy, gastrostomy, scoliosis and hip procedures
- **Non-triggering** anaesthesia used (propofol, fentanyl, remifentanil, N2O); NMBA effect may be prolonged and intubation is often possible **without relaxant**
- Higher ventilator pressures can reduce RV preload and raise afterload
cards.e: Defects in membrane remodelling (MTM1, BIN1, DNM2) impair T-tubule ECC. Anticholinesterases can relieve fatigability. Postoperative ventilation is often needed because of chronic respiratory failure.

cards.q: Describe glycogen storage disease type I and its anaesthetic implications.
cards.a:
**Autosomal recessive** deficiency of **glucose-6-phosphatase** (Ia, von Gierke, > 80%) or the **G6P transporter** (Ib); incidence about **1 in 100,000**.
- **Fasting hypoglycaemia**, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatomegaly, renomegaly; doll-like face, short stature
- Type Ib: **neutropenia**, recurrent infection, IBD
- Anaesthesia: **IV glucose during fasting**, **frequent glucose checks**, **avoid lactate-containing fluids** (cannot convert lactate to glycogen)
- **Platelet dysfunction**: bleeding risk; screen for renal disease, seizures, hypertension
cards.e: Stoelting stresses that even a short fast can cause hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis, so fasting should be minimised and arterial pH monitored. Counter-regulatory hormones release lactate and fatty acids, worsening acidosis.

cards.q: Describe glycogen storage disease type II (acid maltase deficiency/Pompe disease).
cards.a:
**Lysosomal acid α-glucosidase (GAA)** deficiency with glycogen accumulating in skeletal, respiratory and cardiac muscle; about **1 in 14,000–40,000** births; mostly autosomal recessive.
- **Infantile (Pompe)**: hypotonia, **macroglossia**, **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** (walls up to **25 mm**, LVOT obstruction), hepatomegaly; death from heart failure within a year if untreated
- **Childhood**: slower myopathy, selective respiratory muscle involvement, vascular smooth muscle glycogen (basilar aneurysms)
- **Adult**: after age 20; proximal weakness, **diaphragmatic weakness** and restrictive respiratory failure in a third
- ECG: **short PR**, very large QRS; WPW possible
- **Enzyme replacement therapy** with recombinant GAA
cards.e: Stoelting lists Pompe among disorders of carbohydrate metabolism. Glycogen in the conduction system explains SVT and VT risk.

cards.q: How should anaesthesia be managed in Pompe disease with cardiomyopathy?
cards.a:
Aim to preserve **coronary perfusion** in a thick, stiff ventricle prone to **subendocardial ischaemia**.
- Maintain **adequate filling** and **normal-to-high SVR**; avoid tachycardia
- **Ketamine or etomidate** preferred; **propofol** may reduce afterload and cause ischaemia
- Halothane has been associated with cardiac arrest in infants; sevoflurane used without problems
- **Avoid succinylcholine** (hyperkalaemia, rhabdomyolysis)
- **Low-dose rocuronium 0.5 mg/kg** with monitoring and **sugammadex**
- Assess diaphragm (imaging, PFTs, ultrasound): risk of **postoperative respiratory failure**
- Consider local anaesthetic techniques in severe cardiomyopathy
cards.e: Increased LVEDP at small volumes means hypovolaemia and vasodilatation quickly compromise subendocardial flow. A CVC or PA catheter is not essential if normovolaemic and without failure.

cards.q: What are the key features of mitochondrial disease relevant to diagnosis?
cards.a:
Defects in substrate transport or use, the Krebs cycle, the **electron transport chain** (complexes I–V plus CoQ10 and cytochrome c) or oxidative phosphorylation coupling.
- Of > 80 respiratory chain proteins, only **13 are mtDNA-encoded**
- mtDNA: **circular, no introns**, many copies, high mutation rate, **maternal inheritance**
- Lab: **lactate:pyruvate ratio 50–250:1** (normal < 25:1), raised free carnitine
- Biopsy hallmark: **ragged red fibres** on modified Gomori trichrome
- Point mutations: MERRF, MELAS, NARP, Leigh, Leber optic neuropathy; large deletions: **Kearns–Sayre**, PEO, Pearson
cards.e: Every tissue can be affected, so the high-energy organs (brain, muscle, heart) dominate the phenotype. Oxford Ch 13 notes Kearns–Sayre carries conduction defects ranging up to complete heart block and sudden death.

cards.q: Compare MELAS and MERRF.
cards.a:
**MELAS**:
- Commonest mitochondrial encephalomyopathy; prevalence 3.5 per 100,000; onset usually before 20
- Reversible **stroke-like episodes** not following vascular territories, migraine-like headache, seizures, lactic acidosis, cortical blindness
- **MTTL1** (tRNA-Leu); complex I and IV deficits; diabetes, deafness, endocrine failure
- Work up any **stroke under 40**; L-arginine or taurine may prevent episodes
**MERRF**:
- About 1 in 100,000; childhood onset; **myoclonus**, epilepsy, ataxia, **ragged red fibres** (> 90%)
- **A8344G in MT-TK** (tRNA-Lys) in about 80%
- **Cardiomyopathy, WPW**, sudden death; raised CK and lactate
- CoQ10, B vitamins, L-carnitine
cards.e: Severity depends on the proportion of mutant mtDNA in each tissue (heteroplasmy). Basal ganglia calcification and symmetric infarct-like lesions on MRI support MELAS.

cards.q: How do anaesthetic drugs affect mitochondrial function?
cards.a:
- **Propofol, barbiturates, midazolam** inhibit the respiratory chain (complex I) dose-dependently; mitochondrial dysfunction may underlie **propofol infusion syndrome**
- **Volatile agents** inhibit complex I (also the basis of preconditioning); children with complex I defects may be **more sensitive**
- Nondepolarising NMBAs: increased sensitivity reported (mivacurium, atracurium, rocuronium) but also normal responses: **monitor**
- **Local anaesthetics** impair oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid transport
- **Opioids**: risk of respiratory acidosis added to metabolic acidosis
cards.e: Despite these theoretical effects, almost every technique, including sevoflurane, propofol, ketamine, remifentanil and dexmedetomidine, has been used safely. The patient's comorbidities and metabolic status matter more than the choice of agent.

cards.q: List the perioperative principles for patients with mitochondrial disease.
cards.a:
- Document organ involvement, including **conduction defects** (e.g. Kearns–Sayre); have **pacing** available
- **Minimise fasting**; avoid hypovolaemia and glycogen depletion; give **glucose-containing fluids**
- **Avoid lactate-containing fluids** (Hartmann's/lactated Ringer's), especially in children
- Minimise metabolic stress; prevent **shivering, hypothermia, hypoxia, hypotension** (all worsen lactic acidosis)
- **Avoid succinylcholine** (no MH link, but myopathy hyperkalaemia risk)
- Neuraxial techniques acceptable after neurological and coagulation assessment
- Watch for hyponatraemia, adrenal insufficiency (hypotension) and **infection**
cards.e: The respiratory chain generates body heat, so these patients cannot defend temperature well. Initial workup includes glucose, anion gap, lactate, pyruvate, ammonia, CK and acylcarnitines.

cards.q: Classify the skeletal muscle channelopathies.
cards.a:
- **Chloride channelopathies**: myotonia **without** paralysis (myotonia congenita)
- **Sodium channelopathies**: myotonia **with** paralysis (hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis)
- **Other cation channelopathies**: paralysis **without** myotonia (hypokalaemic periodic paralysis)
cards.e: Stoelting gives serum K+ during attacks as < 3.0 mmol/L for hypokalaemic and > 5.5 mmol/L for hyperkalaemic forms, and states that hypothermia must be avoided in every form of periodic paralysis.

cards.q: Describe hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis (HyperPP).
cards.a:
**Autosomal dominant** **SCN4A** (NaV1.4) mutation; prevalence about **0.17 per 100,000**.
- Excess Na+ current depolarises the fibre, K+ leaves (**hyperkalaemia**), then myotonia, inactivation and **flaccid paralysis**
- Attacks last **15 min to 1 h**; mild myotonia between attacks
- Triggers: **K+-rich food, rest after exercise, cold, stress, fasting, glucocorticoids, pregnancy**
- CK may be **5–10 ×** normal; Na+ and K+ normal between attacks; up to **20%** gene-negative
- Treatment: **acetazolamide, mexiletine**, trigger avoidance
- **Normokalaemic periodic paralysis** is a variant of HyperPP (same gene)
cards.e: Stoelting notes that weakness after oral potassium confirms the hyperkalaemic form and that paramyotonia congenita may belong to the same spectrum.

cards.q: What are the anaesthetic considerations for hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis?
cards.a:
- **Avoid potassium**, **succinylcholine** and **anticholinesterases** (neostigmine): they worsen myotonia; succinylcholine can cause masseter spasm and prolonged weakness
- Admit preoperatively for **dextrose-containing, K+-free fluids** during fasting; avoid hypoglycaemia
- Maintain **normothermia**; keep K+ low-normal; monitor ECG, K+ and acid–base
- Volatiles, propofol and nondepolarising NMBAs are safe; regional acceptable
- **No increased MH risk**
- Paralysis may persist for **several hours** postoperatively
cards.e: Even patients without clinical myotonia (one-third) can develop stiffness of jaw or respiratory muscles at intubation. Glucose and insulin move K+ into cells, which is why dextrose is protective here but harmful in HypoPP.

cards.q: Compare hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (HypoPP) with HyperPP.
cards.a:
HypoPP: **no myotonia**; attacks come with **hypokalaemia**; **potassium treats** them; **glucose triggers** them.
- Genes: **CACNA1S** (CaV1.1, type 1) or **SCN4A** (type 2); autosomal dominant, higher penetrance in males
- Attacks are **more severe** than HyperPP and can involve swallowing and breathing
- Triggers: vigorous exercise, stress, **carbohydrate or salt loads**, pregnancy, menstruation, **hypothermia, insulin**
- Prophylaxis: **acetazolamide** for type 1 (it may **worsen type 2**, which responds to spironolactone); **dichlorphenamide** is the only FDA-approved drug
cards.e: Stoelting notes that weakness provoked by a glucose–insulin infusion confirms the hypokalaemic form. Between attacks K+ is normal and EMG shows no myotonia.

cards.q: What are the anaesthetic considerations for hypokalaemic periodic paralysis?
cards.a:
- Avoid triggers and drugs that shift K+ into cells: **glucose and saline infusions**, cold, stress, **adrenaline-containing local anaesthetic**
- **Monitor K+ closely** throughout the perioperative period
- Use intermediate-acting NMBAs (atracurium, mivacurium reported safe); **avoid long-acting NMBAs**
- **Epidural analgesia** reduces pain-related hyperventilation and catecholamines, stabilising K+
- Expect possible **postoperative weakness and respiratory distress**
- MH link cannot be fully excluded (CACNA1S overlap, MH-like crises reported): non-triggering technique is safest; extra vigilance if volatiles used
cards.e: Overall MH risk is thought similar to the general population, but one reported patient seemed to carry separate HypoPP and MH variants. Stoelting adds maintaining carbohydrate balance and correcting electrolytes before surgery.

cards.q: What is thyrotoxic periodic paralysis and how is it treated?
cards.a:
Recurrent weakness with **profound hypokalaemia** in hyperthyroid patients, appearing later in life than familial HypoPP; strong **male** and **East Asian** predominance.
- Mechanism: thyroid hormone over-stimulates the **Na+/K+-ATPase**, driving K+ into cells (also activated by **β-agonists and insulin**); Kir2.6 loss-of-function in some
- Severity relates to K+, not to the degree of hyperthyroidism
- **Non-selective β-blockers (propranolol)** are first-line; antithyroid drugs (methimazole) prevent recurrence
- Large K+ doses risk **rebound hyperkalaemia and dysrhythmias**
cards.e: The K+ is redistributed rather than lost, so aggressive replacement overshoots once the shift reverses. Look for thyrotoxicosis in a young man with sudden flaccid weakness and low K+.

cards.q: Describe multiple sclerosis and its main disease-modifying therapies.
cards.a:
Chronic inflammatory **demyelinating and neurodegenerative CNS** disease; onset 20–30 years; **female:male 3:1**; risks include HLA-DRB1, low vitamin D, EBV, smoking.
- Optic neuritis, partial myelitis, ataxia, sensory disturbance, brainstem syndromes, **autonomic dysfunction**
- Diagnosis: MRI lesions disseminated in **space and time**, evoked potentials, CSF **oligoclonal bands**
- Types: **relapsing–remitting**; **secondary progressive** (up to 50% untreated within 10–15 years); **primary progressive** (10–15%)
- DMTs: IFN-β, **fingolimod** (S1P analogue), teriflunomide, cladribine, **natalizumab** (α4 integrin), alemtuzumab (CD52), **rituximab/ocrelizumab** (CD20; ocrelizumab licensed for PPMS)
- Steroids for acute relapses
cards.e: Most DMTs are immunosuppressive, so consider infection risk and continue them perioperatively. Oxford notes that GA does not affect the course of MS.

cards.q: What are the anaesthetic considerations in multiple sclerosis?
cards.a:
- Surgery and anaesthesia **do not increase relapse risk**, but inform the patient of possible postoperative relapse; document deficits; **continue DMTs**
- **Avoid hyperthermia**: heat blocks conduction in demyelinated axons
- **Autonomic dysfunction**: careful fluids and cautious vasodilators/sympathomimetics
- **Avoid succinylcholine** (AChR upregulation, hyperkalaemic arrest)
- Nondepolarising NMBAs: both **sensitivity and resistance** reported; monitor objectively; rocuronium with sugammadex suggested
- **Epidural** with low-concentration LA is safe and does not affect postpartum relapse; **spinal** traditionally discouraged (possible LA neurotoxicity, impaired BBB), though recent cohorts show no excess relapse
- Peripheral nerve blocks generally safe; reduce LA concentration
cards.e: Oxford reports widespread UK use of spinal anaesthesia for caesarean section in MS and recommends documenting a risk discussion before regional techniques. Severe weakness or bulbar dysfunction may need extended monitoring and NIV postoperatively.

cards.q: Describe Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS).
cards.a:
Immune-mediated **acute polyradiculopathy** and the commonest cause of **acute flaccid paralysis** worldwide.
- **Ascending, symmetrical** weakness with **areflexia**, possibly involving facial, bulbar and respiratory muscles
- Antecedent infection: **Campylobacter jejuni**, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, H. influenzae, hepatitis E, influenza A, Zika; also vaccines, checkpoint inhibitors and surgery
- **Autonomic dysfunction**: labile BP, arrhythmias, sudden circulatory collapse
- CSF: **raised protein with normal cell count**; nerve studies may be normal early, showing demyelination and slow conduction after 1–2 weeks; **AIDP** is the commonest subtype
- **IVIG and plasma exchange** equally effective and safe in pregnancy
cards.e: Up to two-thirds of deaths during recovery are cardiovascular or respiratory, and at least a third have chronic pain at one year. Stoelting quotes 3–8% mortality, mainly from sepsis, respiratory failure, PE or cardiac arrest.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 15 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11

cards.q: What are the anaesthetic considerations in Guillain–Barré syndrome?
cards.a:
- **Aspiration risk** (cranial nerve palsy, autonomic gut dysfunction): decompress stomach before induction
- **Autonomic instability**: exaggerated **hypotension** at induction or with hypovolaemia; **hypertension** with laryngoscopy; use small doses of short-acting vasoactive drugs; arterial line
- **Avoid succinylcholine**, even after recovery (lasting hyperkalaemia risk)
- Nondepolarising NMBAs may cause **prolonged weakness**: use objective monitoring
- Possible prolonged ventilation
- GA is well tolerated; **regional is controversial** (may worsen symptoms)
cards.e: Denervated receptors exaggerate responses to direct-acting vasopressors, so start with small doses (Stoelting makes the same point for phenylephrine in autonomic failure). Oxford notes epidural opioids have been used for troublesome paraesthesiae.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 15 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11

cards.q: Compare critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP) and critical illness myopathy (CIM).
cards.a:
The commonest acquired neuromuscular problems in ICU, affecting up to **50%** of patients staying **> 2 weeks**.
- **CIP**: distal **axonal** sensorimotor neuropathy; reduced motor and sensory action potential amplitudes
- **CIM**: primary myopathy with **loss of myosin thick filaments**, atrophy, necrosis, Na+ channel dysfunction; **normal nerve conduction**, abnormal spontaneous EMG potentials
- Both: symmetric limb weakness, reduced reflexes, **diaphragm involvement** (weaning failure); **face and eye movements spared**; autonomic function normal; CK normal or raised
- Risks: **female sex, sepsis, ICU stay, multiorgan failure**
- Prevention: limit sedation, paralytics and steroids; **tight glucose control** cut CIP by 44%; early mobilisation
cards.e: The two often coexist, so electrophysiology may show both patterns. Diagnosis needs clinical strength assessment plus full nerve and muscle studies; treatment is supportive rehabilitation.

cards.q: What are the anaesthetic considerations in CIP/CIM?
cards.a:
- Protect compression-prone nerves (**ulnar, peroneal**)
- Immobility increases **immature (extrajunctional) AChRs**: **resistance to nondepolarising NMBAs**
- **Succinylcholine contraindicated**: increased sensitivity and **hyperkalaemia**
- Monitor and correct electrolytes and glucose
- **Avoid steroids** (implicated in pathogenesis)
- Avoid NMBAs where possible; if needed, nondepolarising only, guided by objective monitoring
cards.e: Immature receptors spread across the muscle membrane and release large amounts of K+ when depolarised. This is a frequent exam trap: a long-stay ICU patient needing re-intubation should not receive succinylcholine.

cards.q: Describe the pathophysiology and epidemiology of myasthenia gravis.
cards.a:
**Autoimmune** disease of the NMJ with fluctuating, fatigable weakness of ocular, bulbar, limb and respiratory muscles; incidence **7–23 per million** per year.
- Antibodies against muscle **nAChRs** (80–90%) block ACh binding, cross-link and internalise receptors, and trigger **complement lysis**
- **Anti-MuSK** antibodies in some seronegative patients
- Bimodal: **young women** (20s–30s) and **older men** (60s–80s)
- **Thymic hyperplasia > 70%**, **thymoma 10%**; associated with thyroid disease, SLE, RA
- Ptosis and diplopia first, then dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal regurgitation, aspiration; worse with exercise and later in the day
cards.e: Stoelting describes fewer receptors, simplified folds and wider synaptic clefts, with up to 80% of functional receptors lost. Oxford notes consensus now favours thymectomy in adults with generalised disease.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11

cards.q: How is myasthenia gravis diagnosed, and when should intubation be considered in respiratory weakness?
cards.a:
- **Antibody testing** (anti-AChR, anti-MuSK) confirms most cases
- **Repetitive nerve stimulation**: **decrement** in CMAP in seronegative patients
- **Edrophonium (Tensilon) test** is now largely abandoned (poor accuracy, adverse effects)
- Low threshold for elective intubation if serial **VC < 15–20 mL/kg** or **MIP weaker than −25 to −30 cmH2O**
cards.e: Noninvasive ventilation can help, but bulbar weakness and aspiration limit it. Serial trends matter more than single values because weakness fluctuates.

cards.q: What preoperative factors predict postoperative ventilation or ICU admission in myasthenia gravis?
cards.a:
Miller lists:
- **VC < 2 L**
- **Pyridostigmine > 750 mg/day**
- **Bulbar symptoms**
- **High anti-AChR titre**
- **Previous myasthenic crisis**
- **Expected blood loss > 1 L**
cards.e: Oxford's list is similar: major body cavity surgery, disease > 6 years, chronic respiratory disease, pyridostigmine > 750 mg/day, VC < 2.9 L and blood loss > 1000 mL. Continue anticholinesterases, warn the patient about possible postoperative ventilation and involve neurology. Immunomodulators can be held on the morning of surgery.

cards.q: How do patients with myasthenia gravis respond to neuromuscular blocking drugs, and how should these be used?
cards.a:
Fewer functional AChRs: **very sensitive to nondepolarising NMBAs** and **resistant to succinylcholine**.
- RSI succinylcholine: **1.5–2.0 mg/kg** may be needed
- But anticholinesterase therapy reduces cholinesterase activity, so **succinylcholine and mivacurium can be prolonged**
- Avoid NMBAs when possible; **volatile agents** often provide enough relaxation
- If needed: **rocuronium or vecuronium** in increments of **0.1–0.2 × ED50**, titrated to objective monitoring
- **Sugammadex** preferred for reversal; neostigmine response is unpredictable and risks cholinergic crisis
cards.e: Oxford notes inhaled agents can reduce neuromuscular transmission by up to 50% and that plasmapheresis lowers plasma esterases, prolonging succinylcholine, mivacurium, ester LAs and remifentanil. For conversion, Oxford equates 30 mg oral pyridostigmine with about 1 mg parenteral neostigmine.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25

cards.q: What regional anaesthesia cautions apply in myasthenia gravis, and how do you distinguish myasthenic from cholinergic crisis?
cards.a:
**Regional**: epidural and spinal acceptable with monitoring, but **high blocks** affecting accessory muscles and **interscalene or supraclavicular** blocks (phrenic palsy) are poorly tolerated.
**Crisis**:
- **Myasthenic**: under-treatment or disease exacerbation; weakness improves with anticholinesterase
- **Cholinergic**: excess anticholinesterase (e.g. after reversal) causing paradoxical weakness plus **SLUDGE** (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis)
- Treat cholinergic features with **atropine or glycopyrrolate**; neurophysiology can help distinguish
cards.e: Both present as postoperative weakness, so a recent large dose of neostigmine with muscarinic signs points to cholinergic crisis. Assess bulbar and respiratory function closely after surgery.

cards.q: Describe Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS).
cards.a:
Autoimmune **presynaptic** disorder: antibodies to **P/Q-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels** reduce **ACh release**.
- Often **paraneoplastic** (**small cell lung cancer**, whose cells express VGCCs); otherwise linked with other autoimmune disease
- **Proximal limb weakness, legs > arms**; ocular and bulbar signs uncommon; minor autonomic features
- **Worse in the morning**, **improves with exercise** (presynaptic Ca2+ accumulates)
- EMG: **facilitation** with high-frequency stimulation (**30–50 Hz**)
- Treatment: treat the tumour, **3,4-diaminopyridine**, IVIG/plasmapheresis, steroids; **anticholinesterases help little**
cards.e: The improvement with repeated effort is the key clinical contrast with myasthenia. Stoelting notes LEMS was first described with small cell carcinoma but occurs without cancer too.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11

cards.q: What are the anaesthetic considerations in LEMS, and how does NMBA sensitivity compare with myasthenia gravis?
cards.a:
- LEMS: **increased sensitivity to both succinylcholine and nondepolarising NMBAs**; avoid them when possible
- MG: sensitive to nondepolarisers but **resistant to succinylcholine**
- In LEMS, reversal with anticholinesterases may **fail**, especially if on DAP or pyridostigmine
- If an NMBA is essential: **incremental rocuronium**, objective monitoring, **sugammadex** reversal
- Assess risk of **postoperative respiratory failure**; plan monitoring
cards.e: Suspect undiagnosed LEMS in a smoker with lung cancer and proximal weakness presenting for bronchoscopy or mediastinoscopy. Oxford Ch 13 lists impaired oesophageal motility and relaxant sensitivity in LEMS.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Oxford Handbook Ch 13 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25

cards.q: What general themes apply to anaesthesia for patients with neuromuscular disease?
cards.a:
- Take a careful history of **previous anaesthetic events** and **family history**
- **Avoid succinylcholine** in denervating, dystrophic and immobilised states (hyperkalaemia, rhabdomyolysis)
- **Titrate** sedatives, hypnotics, opioids and NMBAs; use **objective monitoring**
- **Rocuronium/vecuronium with sugammadex** has simplified management of many disorders
- Plan for **postoperative respiratory insufficiency** and **cardiac** complications
- Use **non-triggering** anaesthesia when MH risk is plausible; keep emergency drugs including dantrolene
cards.e: Some diseases first present during the perioperative period, so unexplained weakness, rhabdomyolysis or hyperkalaemia should prompt consideration of an undiagnosed myopathy. Multidisciplinary planning and simulation training are recommended.

cards.q: A 9-year-old boy is having strabismus surgery under sevoflurane. After 40 min, ETCO2 rises from 5.0 to 9.5 kPa despite increased minute ventilation, HR is 160/min, the jaw and limbs are rigid and temperature has risen from 36.8 to 38.4°C. What is your diagnosis and immediate management?
cards.a:
**Probable malignant hyperthermia**: several signs together (hypercarbia resistant to ventilation, tachycardia, rigidity, rising temperature).
- Call for help and the MH kit; tell the surgeon to finish quickly
- **Stop sevoflurane**; switch to TIVA (propofol, opioid); fit **activated charcoal filters**; **100% O2 at ≥ 10 L/min** and hyperventilate
- **Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV** (sterile water; prewarmed; large-bore line), repeat to effect up to **10 mg/kg**
- Arterial line, ABG, K+, CK, coagulation, urine catheter
- **Bicarbonate 1–4 mEq/kg** guided by gases; treat hyperkalaemia (insulin/dextrose, calcium if severe)
- **Active cooling**, stop at 38°C; urine > 1–2 mL/kg/h
- ICU for 24–48 h; dantrolene 1 mg/kg every 4–6 h for 24 h
cards.e: Children account for about half of MH reactions. Before committing, quickly exclude hypoventilation and equipment problems, but do not delay dantrolene when the picture is this clear. Afterwards, refer the child and family to an MH unit for contracture or genetic testing and give warning documentation (Oxford).

cards.q: A 6-year-old girl receives propofol and succinylcholine for urgent tonsillar abscess drainage. Her jaw becomes very tight and intubation is difficult, but her limbs are flaccid. HR and ETCO2 are normal. How do you proceed?
cards.a:
**Isolated masseter spasm** after succinylcholine.
- Secure the airway (deeper anaesthesia, wait; usually intubation becomes possible)
- Check for **rigidity of other muscles**, rising ETCO2 or tachycardia: if present, treat as **MH**
- If isolated: proceed only if urgent, using a **non-triggering technique** (TIVA, no volatile)
- Monitor ETCO2 and temperature; consider arterial line
- Send **CK** (initial and 24 h), **K+**, acid–base; inspect the first urine for **myoglobinuria**
- Observe postoperatively; refer for MH assessment if CK rise or metabolic signs
cards.e: Over 80% of isolated trismus is a normal variant of succinylcholine's effect on slow tonic jaw fibres, but Oxford quotes about 30% proving MHS, rising to 50–60% with metabolic signs and 70–80% with muscle signs. Document clearly and counsel the family.

cards.q: A 70-kg man was treated for MH 4 hours ago with 5 mg/kg dantrolene and is now in ICU. His ETCO2 rises again, HR is 130/min with ventricular ectopics, and K+ is 6.8 mmol/L. A junior suggests IV verapamil for the arrhythmia. What is happening and what do you do?
cards.a:
**MH recrudescence** (up to 50%, usually within 6.5 h, possibly up to 16 h).
- Give further **dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg** boluses until signs settle, then **1 mg/kg every 4–6 h for 24 h** (total may reach 30 mg/kg)
- **Do not give verapamil** (or other calcium channel blockers): with dantrolene they can worsen hyperkalaemia and cause cardiac arrest
- Treat K+: **insulin 10 units with 50 mL 50% dextrose**, bicarbonate, **calcium chloride**; dantrolene itself is the most effective K+-lowering therapy
- Check Mg2+, ABG, CK, coagulation; maintain urine output with alkalinisation
- Treat arrhythmias by ACLS (calcium and digoxin are acceptable in recrudescence)
cards.e: Maintenance dantrolene is given precisely because recrudescence is common. Calcium channel blockers increase Ca2+ in human muscle cells (nifedipine most potently), so they work against dantrolene.

cards.q: A 32-year-old woman whose brother had a confirmed MH reaction and who carries the family RYR1 variant needs a laparoscopic cholecystectomy as a day case. How will you plan her anaesthetic?
cards.a:
She is **MH-susceptible**; plan a **non-triggering** anaesthetic.
- Reassure her; first case of the day if possible; no prophylactic dantrolene
- **Prepare the machine**: remove vaporisers, new absorbent and circuit, flush to **< 5 ppm** per manufacturer (or dedicated machine), **charcoal filters on both limbs**, keep FGF **≥ 10 L/min**
- **TIVA** (propofol, remifentanil/opioid), **rocuronium** (reverse with neostigmine or sugammadex); no succinylcholine, no volatiles
- Local anaesthetic infiltration and amides are safe; standard monitoring including **ETCO2 and core temperature**
- **Dantrolene** available within 10 min (36 × 20 mg or 3 × 250 mg Ryanodex)
- Day-case discharge by normal criteria
cards.e: A laparoscopic case adds a confounder, since CO2 insufflation raises ETCO2; watch for other signs before suspecting MH. The workstation flush time varies widely (10–104 min), so plan it in advance. Oxford stresses MHS patients should not be denied surgery and lists all NDMRs, LAs and reversal agents as safe.

cards.q: A 14-year-old boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, wheelchair bound, is listed for posterior spinal fusion for a 60° scoliosis. FVC is 35% predicted, echo shows posterobasal hypokinesis with EF 45%, and he takes prednisolone. Outline your perioperative plan.
cards.a:
**High-risk case** needing multidisciplinary planning (cardiology, respiratory, ICU).
- **Cardiac**: ECG, echo, consider Holter and troponin; optimise ACE inhibitor/beta blocker; expect arrhythmias and heart failure; invasive monitoring
- **Respiratory**: FVC 35% (below 40%) predicts **prolonged ventilation**; plan ICU, **NIV (CPAP/BiPAP)** after extubation, physiotherapy, cough assist; delayed insufficiency up to **36 h**
- **Airway/aspiration**: possible macroglossia, weak laryngeal reflexes, slow gastric emptying
- **No succinylcholine** and **no volatile agents**: **TIVA** with propofol and remifentanil
- Nondepolarising NMBA in small doses with monitoring; **sugammadex** reversal
- Steroid cover; careful positioning and temperature control; blood loss strategy
- CK and urine for rhabdomyolysis; regional/neuraxial analgesia where feasible
cards.e: Unstable dystrophic membranes make succinylcholine and volatile agents risk rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemic arrest, which is often refractory to resuscitation. CK-MB is unreliable here, so use troponin for myocardial injury. Stoelting confirms rhabdomyolysis has occurred with volatiles alone.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11

cards.q: A 45-year-old man with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (first-degree heart block, daytime somnolence) needs an open upper abdominal procedure. What are the main risks and your anaesthetic plan?
cards.a:
Risks: **conduction block and arrhythmia**, **sensitivity to respiratory depressants**, **aspiration**, **myotonic contractures** and **postoperative pulmonary complications** (worse with upper abdominal surgery).
- Preop: ECG, echo, consider Holter/cardiology; glucose, thyroid function, calcium; sleep and respiratory assessment
- **External pacing** available (AV block may not respond to atropine)
- Aspiration prophylaxis; RSI using **rocuronium**, not **succinylcholine** (contracture could prevent ventilation and is not reversed by NDMRs)
- Titrate short-acting agents (propofol, remifentanil); objective NM monitoring; **sugammadex** rather than neostigmine
- **Warm patient and fluids**; prevent shivering; warn surgeon about diathermy-induced myotonia
- Epidural analgesia to spare opioids
- Extended recovery with ECG and SpO2 monitoring; HDU
cards.e: Myotonia can be triggered by cold, shivering, mechanical or electrical stimulation and some drugs, and neither regional anaesthesia nor NMBAs reliably stop it (Stoelting). Cardiac conduction disease can progress silently, so monitoring continues postoperatively.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11

cards.q: A 35-year-old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis (pyridostigmine 120 mg five times daily, VC 1.8 L, mild dysphagia) is scheduled for thymectomy. How will you manage her?
cards.a:
High risk of **postoperative ventilation** (VC < 2 L, bulbar symptoms; pyridostigmine 600 mg/day is near the 750 mg threshold).
- Neurology input; optimise (consider IVIG or plasma exchange preoperatively); continue pyridostigmine; arrange ICU
- Aspiration precautions
- Induction with propofol and remifentanil; intubate **without NMBA** or with small **rocuronium increments (0.1–0.2 × ED50)** guided by quantitative monitoring
- If RSI needed: succinylcholine **1.5–2 mg/kg** (resistance), but block may be prolonged by cholinesterase inhibition
- Volatile agent can supply relaxation
- Reverse with **sugammadex**; avoid large neostigmine doses
- Postop: watch bulbar and respiratory function, VC trends; distinguish **myasthenic vs cholinergic crisis**; resume anticholinesterase (Oxford: about 1 mg IV neostigmine per 30 mg oral pyridostigmine if NBM)
cards.e: Plasmapheresis lowers plasma cholinesterase, prolonging succinylcholine, mivacurium and remifentanil (Oxford). Oxford advises avoiding drugs that impair transmission, such as aminoglycosides, and notes magnesium and beta-blockers also have effects. Oxford notes thymectomy is now favoured for adults with generalised disease.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25

cards.q: A 62-year-old heavy smoker with a hilar mass is listed for mediastinoscopy. He reports leg weakness that improves after walking for a while, a dry mouth, and worse strength in the morning. Tendon reflexes are reduced. What do you suspect and how does it change your anaesthetic?
cards.a:
**Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome**, likely **paraneoplastic** from **small cell lung cancer**.
- Confirm if time allows: P/Q-type VGCC antibodies; EMG facilitation at 30–50 Hz; neurology input
- Expect **increased sensitivity to both succinylcholine and nondepolarising NMBAs**
- Avoid NMBAs if possible; otherwise small **rocuronium** increments with quantitative TOF and **sugammadex** reversal (anticholinesterases may not work, particularly on DAP)
- Plan for **postoperative respiratory failure** and extended monitoring
cards.e: Improvement with exercise and morning weakness contrast with myasthenia gravis, where weakness worsens with effort and through the day. Dry mouth reflects mild autonomic involvement. Unrecognised LEMS is a classic cause of prolonged paralysis after thoracic procedures in lung cancer.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 25 · Oxford Handbook Ch 13

cards.q: A 58-year-old man has been in ICU for 3 weeks with septic shock and multiorgan failure. He was extubated 2 days ago but now has hypercapnic respiratory failure and needs re-intubation. He has symmetric flaccid limb weakness with absent reflexes, but normal facial and eye movements. What is the likely diagnosis and how will you intubate him?
cards.a:
**Critical illness polyneuropathy and/or myopathy** (sepsis, MOF, long ICU stay; face and eyes spared; diaphragm weakness causing weaning failure).
- **Do not use succinylcholine**: upregulated immature AChRs risk **life-threatening hyperkalaemia**
- Use **rocuronium** (may need a higher dose due to resistance), with sugammadex available
- Expect hypotension from sepsis; prepare vasopressor
- Afterwards: nerve conduction and EMG to distinguish CIP from CIM; limit sedation, NMBAs and steroids; glucose control; early rehabilitation; protect ulnar and peroneal nerves
cards.e: Immobilisation alone increases extrajunctional receptors, causing resistance to nondepolarisers but sensitivity to succinylcholine. GBS is less likely given the timing, intact cranial nerves and lack of autonomic features, but nerve studies help exclude it.

cards.q: A 25-year-old man with known hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (CACNA1S variant) is scheduled for knee arthroscopy. Preoperative K+ is 3.8 mmol/L. How will you minimise the risk of a perioperative attack?
cards.a:
Avoid factors that **shift K+ into cells** and maintain normokalaemia.
- Short fast but **avoid glucose loads** and large **saline** volumes
- **Measure K+** regularly perioperatively; give K+ for falls
- Keep warm; reduce anxiety and pain (stress catecholamines drive K+ uptake)
- Prefer regional/spinal or GA with **intermediate-acting NMBA** (e.g. atracurium) and monitoring; **no long-acting NMBAs**
- Avoid **adrenaline-containing local anaesthetic** and β-agonists
- MH link not fully excluded: a **non-triggering** technique (TIVA) is the safest choice
- Monitor for postoperative weakness and respiratory compromise
cards.e: In HypoPP, glucose and insulin precipitate attacks, the opposite of HyperPP, where dextrose infusions are protective. Acetazolamide prophylaxis suits type 1 (CACNA1S) but can worsen type 2 (SCN4A). Stoelting stresses avoiding hypothermia and carbohydrate loads.

cards.q: A 4-year-old child with suspected mitochondrial myopathy (raised lactate, lactate:pyruvate ratio 80:1, exercise intolerance) is booked for a diagnostic muscle biopsy. Outline your anaesthetic plan.
cards.a:
Focus on **metabolic stability** rather than any single agent.
- Assess heart (ECG for conduction defects, echo for cardiomyopathy), respiration, swallowing, glucose, electrolytes, lactate
- **Minimise fasting**; start **glucose-containing IV fluid**; **avoid lactated Ringer's/Hartmann's**
- Maintain **normothermia**; avoid shivering, hypoxia, hypotension and hypovolaemia (all worsen lactic acidosis)
- Sevoflurane induction or titrated propofol (single doses acceptable; avoid prolonged infusion); possible increased sensitivity
- **Avoid succinylcholine**; if NMBA needed, small doses with monitoring
- Local anaesthetic infiltration at biopsy site; cautious opioids
- Pacing available if conduction disease; monitor glucose and lactate postoperatively
cards.e: Barbiturates, propofol and volatiles all inhibit complex I, yet nearly every technique has been used safely, so careful titration and metabolic care are what matter. There is no evidence linking mitochondrial disease with MH, but succinylcholine is still avoided because of hyperkalaemia risk in extensive myopathy.

cards.q: A 30-year-old woman with Guillain–Barré syndrome, ventilated for 10 days, needs a surgical tracheostomy. Her BP swings from 80/40 to 190/110 mmHg and she has episodes of bradycardia. How will you manage the anaesthetic?
cards.a:
**Autonomic dysfunction** with lower motor neuron disease.
- **Arterial line**; atropine and external pacing available
- Ensure normovolaemia; **titrate induction agents** in small doses (exaggerated hypotension)
- Blunt the response to stimulation (opioid); treat swings with **small doses of short-acting vasoactive drugs** (direct agents may cause exaggerated response)
- **No succinylcholine** (denervation hyperkalaemia, even after recovery)
- If NMBA needed, reduced-dose nondepolariser with **quantitative monitoring**; expect prolonged weakness
- Gastric decompression/aspiration precautions; continue IVIG/plasma exchange plan
- Postoperative ventilation; DVT prophylaxis and pain management
cards.e: Loss of compensatory reflexes causes hypotension with induction or position change, while noxious stimuli provoke hypertensive surges; these are usually brief and self-limiting. Stoelting reports profuse sweating, tachycardia and conduction abnormalities, and warns that denervation hypersensitivity exaggerates responses to vasopressors.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 31 · Stoelting 7e Ch 15 · Oxford Handbook Ch 11

cards.q: Distinguish heart rate from pulse rate. What is a pulse deficit and give clinical examples?
cards.a:
**Heart rate** counts electrical depolarizations (ECG R-R interval); **pulse rate** counts peripheral pulsations that actually reach the arterial tree (pulse oximeter plethysmogram or arterial line).
- **Pulse deficit** = amount by which pulse rate falls short of heart rate
- Classic cause: **atrial fibrillation**, where a very short R-R interval gives a beat with too little stroke volume to produce a palpable pulse
- Extreme form: **pulseless electrical activity** (electromechanical dissociation)
- Monitors usually update the digital rate every **5–15 s**
cards.e: Displaying both the ECG-derived and the pleth/arterial-derived rates lets the clinician cross-check each against the other, which reduces false alarms and errors (e.g. ESU artifact on the ECG while the pleth continues to show a normal rate). A rate that is normal on the ECG but absent on the pleth must prompt a pulse check, not reassurance.

cards.q: What are the three primary purposes of intraoperative ECG monitoring, and what technical settings must the anesthesiologist attend to?
cards.a:
Continuous **heart rate**, detection of **arrhythmias and conduction defects**, and detection of **myocardial ischemia** (plus checking function of pacemakers/ICDs).
- Technical details: **lead placement and selection**, **filter mode**, **gain** setting, pacing-detection mode
- ASA basic monitoring standard: ECG continuously displayed from start of anesthesia until leaving the anesthetizing location
cards.e: The ECG is a mandatory ASA monitor, and blood pressure and heart rate must be evaluated at least every 5 minutes (Lippincott). Most monitoring errors come from wrong lead position, inappropriate filter or gain rather than from the device itself, so these settings are frequent viva questions.

cards.q: Describe the standard 5-lead operating-room ECG system: which leads can be displayed, the AHA color code, and where the electrodes are placed.
cards.a:
Five electrodes give the **six limb leads** (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) plus **one precordial lead** (any of V1–V6); usually two leads are displayed at once.
- AHA colors: RA **white**, LA **black**, RL **green**, LL **red**, chest **brown** (IEC international colors differ)
- Limb electrodes are moved onto the **torso** (Mason-Likar): arm leads just below the clavicles, leg leads above the hips
- The **RL (green) is a ground** and may be placed anywhere without altering any lead
- The AHA now regards all leads as effectively bipolar (old unipolar/bipolar distinction discouraged)
cards.e: Torso placement (introduced by Mason and Likar in 1966 for exercise testing) reduces motion artifact; QRS amplitude and axis change slightly but ST measurements are comparable to the standard 12-lead. Limb electrodes must stay outside the cardiac borders (above/below and left/right of the heart), otherwise the tracing becomes distorted. Lead II = RA negative, LL positive; lead I = RA negative, LA positive; lead III = LA negative, LL positive (Lippincott).

cards.q: Which precordial lead should be monitored for perioperative ischemia, and how do you place it accurately?
cards.a:
An **anterolateral mid-precordial lead: V3, V4 or V5**, chosen so it does not interfere with the surgical field.
- **V5** is the classic choice (most sensitive in exercise testing and early anesthesia studies; compatible with sternotomy)
- **V3/V4** were more sensitive than V5 for prolonged postoperative ischemia in vascular surgery
- Landmarks: find the **angle of Louis** → 2nd interspace below it → count down to 4th and 5th spaces
- **V4**: 5th interspace, mid-clavicular line; **V5**: same level, anterior axillary line; **V6**: mid-axillary line
cards.e: The chest lead is the electrode most often misplaced, usually too lateral, which reduces sensitivity. When V3–V5 positions are impossible (e.g. left thoracotomy), another lead such as V1 may be used, accepting that ischemia detection will be less sensitive.

cards.q: What is lead V4R, where is it placed, and when is it useful?
cards.a:
A **right-sided mirror image of V4**: 4th–5th intercostal space at the **right mid-clavicular line**.
- **Best lead for right ventricular ischemia/infarction**
- Consider in patients at risk of **inferior LV ischemia**, which often involves the RV (RCA territory)
- Not used for routine ischemia monitoring
cards.e: Inferior ischemia (leads II, III, aVF) usually reflects the right coronary artery in a right-dominant system (about 80% of people, Lippincott), and the RCA also supplies the RV; V4R picks up RV involvement that the standard left-sided leads miss.

cards.q: What can a 3-lead ECG system do, and what is the modified lead MCL1?
cards.a:
A 3-electrode system (RA, LA, LL) reliably gives **heart rate**, **R-wave detection for synchronized cardioversion**, and recognition of **life-threatening arrhythmias** (e.g. VF); it is the standard configuration in **external defibrillators/transcutaneous pacers** and transport monitors.
- **MCL1** (surrogate V1): LA electrode in usual position, **LL electrode at the V1 position**, display **lead III**
- Used where **P-wave morphology and arrhythmia diagnosis** matter most (ICU)
- After cardiac surgery an **epicardial atrial pacing wire** connected to a precordial lead shows P waves that are hard to see on surface leads
cards.e: A 3-lead system cannot provide a true precordial lead, so it is poor for ischemia detection. The atrial-wire electrogram greatly enlarges atrial activity and helps distinguish atrial flutter, junctional rhythm and AV dissociation in the ICU.

cards.q: Explain ECG low-frequency (high-pass) filtering: what artifact does it remove and what is its danger? State the AHA recommended cutoffs.
cards.a:
Removes **baseline wander** caused by respiration and movement; heart rates below 40/min (0.67 Hz) are rare, so analog filters typically cut **below 0.5 Hz**.
- Danger: **phase distortion of the ST segment** where the QRS ends abruptly → false ST deviation
- AHA: low-frequency cutoff **0.05 Hz** for analog filters, or **≤0.67 Hz** for linear digital filters with zero phase distortion
cards.e: The ST segment is a low-frequency component, so an aggressive high-pass filter alters it exactly where ischemia is judged. Remember the naming trap: a low-frequency filter is a high-pass filter (it lets high frequencies through), and vice versa.

cards.q: What does high-frequency (low-pass) ECG filtering remove, what can it hide, and what upper cutoffs does the AHA recommend?
cards.a:
Removes **muscle tremor/fasciculation** and **60-Hz (mains) electromagnetic interference**.
- Can blunt QRS upstroke and R-wave amplitude and, importantly, **eliminate pacemaker spikes** (high frequency, low amplitude)
- AHA: upper cutoff **≥150 Hz** for adults, adolescents and children; **250 Hz** for infants (older 1975 standard was 100 Hz)
cards.e: Loss of pacing spikes makes it difficult to confirm capture at the bedside, so the diagnostic filter should be selected whenever pacemaker function or ST segments matter. Higher-frequency QRS components may also carry clinical information in heart disease.

cards.q: Compare the three ECG filter modes on a typical bedside monitor and state which should be used for ischemia and pacemaker assessment.
cards.a:
**Diagnostic mode ≈ 0.05–150 Hz**, **monitor mode ≈ 0.5–40 Hz**, **filter mode ≈ 0.5–20 Hz** (often with a 60-Hz notch).
- Diagnostic: closest to a 12-lead, **undistorted ST segment and visible pacing spikes** → use for ischemia/pacing
- Monitor: less baseline drift and mains noise, but **ST deviations are often exaggerated** artifactually
- Filter: cleanest-looking trace, most distortion
cards.e: A frequent trap is diagnosing ischemia from ST depression that is purely an artifact of monitor-mode filtering; switching to diagnostic mode before treating avoids this. Exact bandpasses vary between manufacturers.

cards.q: What is the standard ECG gain, and how do gain changes affect interpretation of ST segments and heart rate counting?
cards.a:
Standard gain is **10 mm/mV**, shown by a 1-mV calibration marker on the monitor.
- Changing gain enlarges or shrinks **every** feature equally, including ST deviation
- **Reduced gain can hide** significant ST changes; **increased gain exaggerates** them
- Gain may be reduced deliberately when a **tall T wave is double-counted** as an R wave (displayed HR twice the true rate)
- Autogain fills the display space; check the vertical marker
cards.e: ST shifts are communicated in millimeters, but a "1 mm" depression on a screen at double gain is only 0.05 mV. Always read the calibration marker before calling ischemia.

cards.q: Why do bedside monitors have a pacing mode, and what does the marker on the screen represent?
cards.a:
Pacemaker stimuli last **<0.5 ms** and are low-amplitude, so even with sampling up to **15,000 times/s** they can be missed; pacing mode uses a detection algorithm to **flag** them.
- The displayed spike is a **monitor-generated marker** (often a different color), **not an amplified pacing artifact**
- Detection can fail in some patients or in some leads but not others
cards.e: Because the marker only indicates that the algorithm believes a stimulus occurred, capture must be confirmed by a following QRS and by a pulse on the pleth or arterial trace. Device management is covered in the CIED chapter.

cards.q: State the standard ECG sweep speed and paper grid values, and explain "full disclosure."
cards.a:
Standard sweep **25 mm/s** (same as a 12-lead).
- **1 small box (1 mm) = 40 ms**; **heavy line every 5 mm = 200 ms**
- Vertical: 10 mm = 1 mV, so **1 mm = 0.1 mV**
- **Full disclosure** = continuous storage of ECG and other waveforms for later retrieval, useful to identify and document arrhythmias missed in real time
cards.e: These conversions underpin rate and interval calculations (e.g. PR >5 small boxes = >200 ms) and ST measurements (1 mm = 0.1 mV at standard gain). Bedside recorders usually print a 2-inch two-lead rhythm strip.

cards.q: What is the commonest cause of ECG artifact in the operating room, why can it not be filtered, and how do you keep monitoring the patient? Name other equipment sources.
cards.a:
The **electrosurgical unit (ESU)**: its frequencies overlap the QRS frequency range and its amplitude can reach **~1 kV** (about a million times the 1-mV QRS), so filtering cannot remove it and HR counting may fail.
- Keep monitoring with the **pulse oximeter plethysmogram and arterial waveform** during ESU use
- Other sources: **60-Hz interference** from nearby devices, cardiopulmonary bypass machine, fluid warmers, pressure irrigation pumps, orthopedic shavers, lithotripsy, MRI, nerve stimulators, evoked potential units, HFOV, dialysis machines, mobile phones, faulty monitor insulation
cards.e: Recognizing artifact prevents inappropriate treatment (e.g. defibrillating "VF" that is really shaver artifact). Simultaneously checking a mechanical signal (pleth or arterial trace) is the quickest way to distinguish true arrhythmia from interference.

cards.q: Compare subendocardial (demand) and transmural (supply) ischemia on the ECG. Which is more common perioperatively and which localizes the coronary territory?
cards.a:
**Subendocardial/demand ischemia → ST depression**; **transmural/supply ischemia → ST elevation** (± hyperacute T waves, reciprocal depression).
- Demand ischemia: tachycardia, hypotension, stress in stable CAD; **most common perioperative form**; seen best in **anterolateral leads regardless of territory → non-localizing**
- Supply ischemia: acute coronary occlusion (thrombus, vasospasm/Prinzmetal); **uncommon except in cardiac surgery**; ST elevation **localizes** the artery (e.g. II, III, aVF → RCA/PDA)
cards.e: In subendocardial ischemia the injury current points toward the inner layer, depressing the ST segment in overlying leads; in transmural ischemia it points outward, elevating ST. Lippincott territories: inferior II/III/aVF (RCA), anterior V1–V4 (LAD), lateral I/aVL/V5–V6 (circumflex).

cards.q: How does computerized ST-segment analysis measure ST deviation, and why is it underused outside the OR?
cards.a:
It measures the ST level **60 or 80 ms after the J point (J+60/J+80)** relative to the **isoelectric PR segment**; at standard gain **1 mm = 0.1 mV**, displayed as trends per lead or as summed deviation.
- Clinician can manually reset the J point or measurement point if misidentified
- Advantage: electrodes stay fixed, unlike repeated 12-lead recordings
- Underuse: **frequent false alarms**, lack of training, and **no proven outcome benefit**
cards.e: Trends are useful for alerting, but every alarm must be verified by looking at the actual ECG complexes on screen or on a printed strip, since misplaced measurement points and positional changes produce spurious trends.

cards.q: List the pitfalls that cause false ST-segment changes or reduce specificity of ST monitoring.
cards.a:
**Positional and baseline factors** confound ST analysis.
- **Body position changes** alter ST segments, but are almost always accompanied by **QRS changes**, which distinguishes them from ischemia
- **Cardiac position in the mediastinum**: e.g. sternal retractor reduced V5 R-wave amplitude and ST deviation (R-wave gain factor proposed)
- **Preexisting abnormalities**: early repolarization, intraventricular conduction delay/bundle branch block, **LVH**, **digitalis**, pericarditis
- Filter mode and gain settings (see filters)
cards.e: In patients with baseline ST abnormalities, standard ischemia criteria lose specificity, so a change from the patient's own baseline in the same lead becomes more important than absolute values.

cards.q: State the ECG criteria for stress-induced (demand) ischemia and describe how the ST segment evolves as ischemia worsens.
cards.a:
**≥1 mm (0.1 mV) horizontal or downsloping ST depression measured 60–80 ms after the J point.**
- Progression with rising HR: **J-point depression with upsloping ST** → **horizontal** → **downsloping** with increasing depth
- Landesberg (vascular surgery) used >0.2 mV in one lead or >0.1 mV in two contiguous leads, lasting >10 min
cards.e: Upsloping J-point depression alone is common with tachycardia and is not diagnostic; the change to a flat or downsloping segment marks true ischemia. The criteria come from exercise testing and are extrapolated to perioperative monitoring.

cards.q: What sensitivities for perioperative ischemia detection have been reported for single and combined ECG leads?
cards.a:
**London (high-risk noncardiac surgery)**: V5 **75%**, V4 **61%**; V4+V5 **90%**; II+V5 **80%**; II+V4+V5 **~98%**.
- **Landesberg (major vascular surgery, continuous 12-lead)**: V3 **87%**, V4 **79%**, V5 **66%**
- Exercise testing: V4 and V5 most sensitive (90–100%)
cards.e: The practical conclusion is to monitor one of V3, V4 or V5 (plus lead II for rhythm and inferior ischemia). Lippincott quotes V5 alone detects ~75% of episodes, rising to 90% with V4 and ~96% with II and V4 added: a favorite MCQ number.

cards.q: Compare the auscultatory and oscillometric methods of noninvasive blood pressure measurement. What does each actually measure?
cards.a:
Both occlude flow with an upper-arm cuff and detect its return during deflation.
- **Auscultatory**: Korotkoff sounds from turbulent flow; **SBP = first sound (phase 1)**, **DBP = disappearance (phase 5)**; **MAP cannot be measured**
- **Oscillometric**: senses small pressure oscillations; **point of maximal oscillation = MAP** (measured); **SBP and DBP are calculated** by proprietary algorithms
- Both are confounded by cold, edema, obesity, abnormal tissue compliance, shock/vasoconstriction, arrhythmias and severe bradycardia
cards.e: Lippincott: if phase 5 never occurs, phase 4 (muffling) is used for DBP; phases 2–3 have no clinical use. The trap is that an oscillometric device's most reliable number is the MAP, while its SBP/DBP are derived estimates.

cards.q: What are the cuff-size rules for NIBP, and what errors follow from wrong cuff size or position?
cards.a:
Cuff bladder width ≈ **40% of arm circumference** and length ≈ **80% of upper-arm length**, fitted snugly.
- **Too small → falsely high**; **too large → slightly low** reading
- **Cuff above heart level → falsely low**; below heart level → falsely high (e.g. non-dependent vs dependent arm in lateral position)
- **Obesity**: conical arm, poor transmission, high inflation pressure, overestimation; in morbid obesity the **wrist** performed best and upper arm worst
- **Ankle** is a poor site
cards.e: The upper arm is preferred because it sits nearest heart level. In a beach-chair patient a small cuff overestimates pressure and can mask cerebral hypoperfusion (Lippincott scenario).

cards.q: How well does NIBP agree with invasive arterial pressure, and what validation standard must devices meet?
cards.a:
Agreement is **best for MAP and worst for SBP**.
- NIBP tends to **underestimate SBP and overestimate DBP**, worsening as hypotension deepens; it underestimates high and overestimates low pressures
- **Below MAP ~65 mm Hg NIBP is not a reliable guide to therapy**; agreement also worse in the critically ill and elderly
- AAMI/BHS validation: mean difference **≤ ±5 mm Hg** with SD **≤8 mm Hg**, so errors up to ~20 mm Hg still "pass"
- Devices are validated against auscultation, not invasive pressure
cards.e: Lippincott notes oscillometric DBP runs ~10 mm Hg above direct DBP while SBP and MAP correlate better. Expecting identical numbers from different techniques measuring different signals is unrealistic, particularly in unstable patients.

cards.q: Describe the three approaches to continuous noninvasive blood pressure (C-NIBP) monitoring and their limitations.
cards.a:
All generate a continuous waveform from different signals; some need cuff calibration.
- **Volume clamp / vascular unloading (Peňáz)**: finger cuff with infrared plethysmography adjusts cuff pressure to keep digital artery volume constant; **good precision, poor accuracy** → best for **trending**; overestimates MAP, performs poorly in lability, but detects hypotension more often than intermittent NIBP
- **Applanation tonometry**: radial artery sensor/strain gauge; very **sensitive to sensor position and motion**
- **Pulse wave propagation** (pulse arrival/transit time, pulse wave velocity): least developed; confounded by arterial stiffness and ambient light
cards.e: All perform worse with atherosclerosis, hypertension, neuropathy, movement, cold, in the elderly and obese (overestimate BP, miss hypotension), and with pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg. They are useful when invasive access is difficult but are not interchangeable with an arterial line.

cards.q: List the complications of automated NIBP measurement and the patients in whom caution is required.
cards.a:
Usually safe, but rare serious complications occur with frequent, prolonged cycling.
- **Pain**, bruising/petechiae, **limb swelling**, thrombophlebitis and venous stasis, **nerve injury (neuropathy)**, **compartment syndrome**
- Caution: patients **unable to report arm pain**, **irregular rhythms** causing repeated inflation, **coagulopathy/anticoagulants/thrombolytics**, peripheral neuropathy, arterial or venous insufficiency
cards.e: Compartment syndrome is thought to result from direct trauma plus impaired distal perfusion during repeated inflations. Avoid the cuff on a limb with an IV infusion or AV fistula and rotate sites in long cases.

cards.q: What are the indications for arterial cannulation, and why is it considered the reference standard for BP monitoring?
cards.a:
Indications:
- **Continuous beat-to-beat BP** monitoring
- Anticipated **pharmacologic or mechanical cardiovascular manipulation** (e.g. large swings, vasoactive infusions, CPB)
- **Repeated arterial blood sampling**
- **Failure of indirect (cuff) measurement**
- **Waveform information** (e.g. PPV/SVV, IABP timing from the dicrotic notch)
cards.e: Direct cannulation detects intraoperative hypotension better than oscillometry and has a low complication rate. Lippincott quotes distal ischemia after arterial cannulation at <0.1%.

cards.q: Is the Allen test useful before radial artery cannulation? Summarize the evidence on hand ischemia.
cards.a:
**No: the Allen test does not predict ischemic complications of radial cannulation for monitoring.**
- Slogoff: 1700 cardiac surgical patients, radial occlusion after decannulation in **>25%**, yet **no ischemic complications**
- After radial artery harvest for CABG, hand perfusion is generally unchanged
- An abnormal modified Allen test may still be relevant when choosing a radial artery for **graft harvest or coronary angiography**
cards.e: Collateral flow to the hand is usually generous; Lippincott notes the ulnar artery is the principal supply of the hand, which explains why radial occlusion is usually silent. Risk factors for ischemia lie elsewhere: vasospastic disease, shock, high-dose vasopressors, prolonged cannulation.

cards.q: What is the role of ultrasound in arterial cannulation?
cards.a:
Ultrasound **improves first-pass success and reduces hematoma** (critical-care data), and is especially valuable as a **rescue after a failed attempt**.
- Not proven to improve clinical outcomes or to justify routine intraoperative use
- Benefit is smaller for experienced operators
- **More useful** for non-radial sites and special groups, e.g. **non-pulsatile flow on mechanical circulatory support**
cards.e: Without a palpable pulse (e.g. continuous-flow LVAD) landmark techniques fail, so ultrasound becomes essential. Otherwise, its use reflects operator skill and setting rather than mandatory standard.

cards.q: Compare alternative arterial cannulation sites to the radial artery: ulnar, brachial, axillary, femoral and pedal arteries.
cards.a:
All have acceptable safety when used carefully.
- **Ulnar**: used safely even after failed ipsilateral radial attempts
- **Brachial**: no collateral protection at the elbow, yet large series (cardiac surgery) show few complications; median nerve at risk (Lippincott)
- **Axillary**: comfortable, mobile; complication rate similar to radial/femoral
- Brachial/axillary: use a **longer catheter**; more central → **higher cerebral embolization risk**, so **avoid prolonged high-pressure flushing**
- **Femoral**: largest vessel; guidewire technique; puncture **below the inguinal ligament** to avoid retroperitoneal/pelvic bleeding; CDC prefers brachial/axillary over femoral because of **infection** risk
- **Dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial** (popular in children), superficial temporal
cards.e: Closed-claims data show femoral complications were mainly severe thrombotic or hemorrhagic events, whereas radial claims involved ischemia, median/radial nerve injury or retained wire fragments.
