cards.e: Disease-specific guidelines exist but allow interpretation; for chronic lung disease they include disabling dyspnoea at rest, poor bronchodilator response, resting hypoxaemia and repeated admissions or ED visits. Hence one hospice may accept a patient another declines.

cards.q: Who receives hospice care in the USA, and what is the problem with timing of referral?
cards.a:
Over **half of Medicare decedents** use hospice, but the **median stay is only 18 days**.
- Diagnoses: **cancer ~30%**, heart disease 18%, dementia 15%, respiratory disease (e.g. COPD) 11%
- Neurological disorders: median stay **105 days** vs 18 days in cancer
- **14.3%** of Medicare cancer patients enrolled only in the **last 3 days** of life
- Poor 6-month prognostic criteria for **non-cancer** disease complicate referral timing
cards.e: The pattern shows patients are referred well after they become eligible, limiting benefit. Outcomes support earlier use: lower symptom burden, 98% of families would recommend hospice, and bereaved families rate hospice care excellent far more often than home-health care (70% vs <50%).

cards.q: Is hospice care cost-saving?
cards.a:
Evidence is **mixed**, but **length of hospice use correlates with savings**.
- One study found savings with stays of **53–107 days**; another showed savings with shorter stays too
- Modelling for poor-prognosis cancers: raising hospice use from **60% to 80%** and duration from **2 to 6 weeks** could save about **$1.79 billion per year**
cards.e: Most of the clear benefit is in symptom burden and family satisfaction rather than cost. Very late referral (days before death) limits both clinical and economic benefit.

cards.q: Define palliative surgery and summarise its reported outcomes.
cards.a:
A **deliberate procedure in incurable disease** intended to relieve symptoms, reduce distress and improve quality of life.
- 2004 series (>1000 advanced cancer patients): 30-day **morbidity 29%**, **mortality 11%**, **80%** improved symptoms
- 2011 series (227 patients): **morbidity 20%**, **mortality 4%**, **90%** symptom resolution, attributed partly to better selection via **shared decision-making**
- Veterans study: perioperative specialist palliative care improved end-of-life communication and family support, but few who died received it
cards.e: Risk–benefit trade-offs for palliative or high-risk surgery in seriously ill patients remain poorly studied. Oxford also advises that palliative procedures to improve quality of life be considered in the elderly provided the patient is properly prepared and involved in decisions on futility.

cards.q: What is the "Best Case/Worst Case" tool and why is it useful before high-risk surgery?
cards.a:
A **shared decision-making** framework with a **visual aid** that sets out best-case, worst-case and **most likely** outcomes for **both surgery and non-operative care**.
- Incorporates patient comorbidities and procedure-specific risk
- Patients: frames a real **choice**, shows distinct paths, encourages deliberation
- Surgeons: structures the conversation, invites preferences, and **legitimises non-operative care** as active care rather than "doing nothing"
cards.e: Many high-risk patients do not understand the range of possible outcomes and an implicit commitment to maximal postoperative support can form. Making outcomes explicit allows choices aligned with goals near the end of life.

cards.q: What preoperative issues should the anaesthesiologist address in a patient receiving palliative care?
cards.a:
**Capacity, goals, resuscitation plan, surrogate and disease review.**
- Assess **decision-making capacity** before consent; it can fluctuate during an admission
- If a **DNR order** exists: discuss goals and agree an intra- and postoperative plan; if suspended, set an explicit time for **reinstatement**, shared with surgeon and nurses
- Confirm a **surrogate decision-maker** in case of arrest or prolonged ventilation
- Review **cognition, recent drugs (including chemotherapy), metastases, wounds**, functional status and prognosis
- Expect **high-dose opioids** or **mixed agonist-antagonists**; plan analgesia accordingly
cards.e: Oxford defines capacity as understanding, retaining and weighing information and its consequences, and notes that a valid advance refusal of treatment is legally binding in many jurisdictions. Functional and cognitive baseline also shapes a realistic risk–benefit discussion.

cards.q: What are the intraoperative and postoperative concerns specific to patients receiving palliative care?
cards.a:
Communicate treatment limits and anticipate fragility.
- Share **resuscitation status** with all perioperative staff
- Consider **frailty** and geriatric syndromes, **PONV prophylaxis**, and protection of **fragile skin, muscle and bone**
- **Coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia or neutropenia** may preclude regional or neuraxial techniques
- Postoperatively: standard care usually suffices, but **pain, delirium and PONV** risks may be higher
- State clearly **when limitations revert** to the preoperative status
cards.e: Stoelting lists cancer-related cautions for regional and neuraxial blocks: infection and bleeding risk, raised ICP or cord compression from metastases, and phrenic palsy with SVC syndrome. Chemotherapy-induced subclinical neurotoxicity may also persist for months, relevant to block choice and documentation.

cards.q: Does anaesthetic technique influence cancer recurrence? Summarise the evidence including drug effects on host defences.
cards.a:
Observational data hinted at benefit from regional anaesthesia, but **RCTs have largely been negative**.
- Breast cancer RCT: regional anaesthesia-analgesia vs volatile plus opioid, **no difference in recurrence**
- Lung cancer and abdominal/thoracic surgery: epidural plus GA gave **no improvement** in cancer outcomes or cancer-specific mortality
- Meta-analyses: neither benefit nor harm of regional vs GA
- Lab/animal data: **ketamine and thiopental** reduce NK-cell activity and number; **propofol** reduces NK number; **volatiles** inhibit interferon-driven NK cytotoxicity; **nitrous oxide** accelerated lung and liver metastases in animals but had no effect in colorectal surgery; **lidocaine and ropivacaine** inhibit tumour cell growth in vitro
cards.e: Most systemic-drug data are in vitro or animal, so they should not dictate clinical choice. Stoelting adds that IV opioids blunt NK-cell activity, a proposed immunosuppressive mechanism favouring tumour proliferation.

cards.q: Why does communication matter in serious illness, and what does the American College of Physicians recommend?
cards.a:
Better communication is linked to **better quality of life**, **less life-prolonging treatment** near death, care **matching preferences** and **earlier hospice referral**.
- ACP calls it a cheap, **high-value intervention**
- Start conversations **early** in life-threatening illness, ideally by a physician with an **established relationship**
cards.e: Communication is therefore a treatment, not a courtesy. It also explains why perioperative and ICU teams are expected to revisit goals rather than rely on a single document.

cards.q: What is the Patient Self-Determination Act and what are the limitations of advance directives?
cards.a:
A US law in force since **1991**: hospitals and providers must **tell patients they have a right to make an advance directive**, and must set up policies and staff education on directives.
- Problems: preferences **change** as illness and circumstances change
- Goals need **repeated, open conversations** to stay current
- Documents alone have not been shown to change the care received
cards.e: Oxford notes the UK equivalents: legally binding advance decisions to refuse treatment and lasting powers of attorney for health decisions. In either system, a directive is the start of a conversation, not a substitute for one.

cards.q: Describe the SUPPORT study and its lessons for advance care planning.
cards.a:
1995 US study of **9105 patients** with advanced illness (6-month mortality **45–48%**) in five teaching hospitals: 2-year observation then 2-year RCT.
- Observation: **49%** of patients who did not want CPR had **no written DNR order**; physicians often did not know patients' wishes
- Intervention: prognostic data for physicians plus a facilitating **nurse**; **no improvement** in communication, pain, resource use or other outcomes
- More directives documented, but only **14%** discussed them with a physician and only **25%** of physicians knew of them a week after admission
- In those who died in hospital, half of surrogates reported **moderate-severe pain** at least half the time in the last 3 days
cards.e: The lesson is that increasing the number of advance directives alone does not change care; similar studies agree. Pain assessment in ICU has improved since SUPPORT.

cards.q: What barriers limit advance care planning, particularly around high-risk surgery?
cards.a:
Problems of **timing, setting and quality** of communication, plus surgeon attitudes.
- Discordant understanding: **50–75%** of patients with incurable cancer believed chemotherapy, radiotherapy or surgery might cure them
- Guidance suggests starting end-of-life planning as an **outpatient** when about **1 year** of life remains; in practice it often waits until, e.g., ventilation is needed
- **Over half of surgeons** surveyed would **not operate** on a patient wishing to limit postoperative life support
- Patients after high-risk surgery wanted more emphasis on: **need for surgery vs alternatives**, **expected recovery**, and **perioperative advance directives**
cards.e: Those three points are an opportunity for the anaesthesiologist to help facilitate preoperative conversations. Surgeons' reluctance reflects the implicit postoperative "contract" discussed elsewhere in the chapter.

cards.q: What evidence shows deficiencies in physicians' communication skills?
cards.a:
Training is limited and **self-assessment is unreliable**.
- **40–75%** of physicians rate their knowledge of delivering bad news as inadequate; code status is less comfortable than procedural consent
- Only **9%** of surgical residents felt adequately trained in palliation; up to **90%** of medicine residents want more training on DNR discussions
- ICU study: **90% of surgeons** satisfied with their prognostic communication vs **23% of intensivists** and **3% of nurses**
- Recordings: physicians dominate, focus on **technical detail**, avoid emotion; families are more satisfied when they **speak more**
- Physicians misjudged metastatic cancer patients' CPR preferences **30%** of the time
cards.e: Communication skills are taught in medical school but poorly retained; empathic skill-building in residency improves primary palliative care. Always check the patient's understanding before a procedure or during ICU care.

cards.q: What is the surgical "contract" (covenantal ethic) and what other cultural factors drive aggressive postoperative care?
cards.a:
Many surgeons feel an **implicit agreement** to pursue **maximal life-sustaining treatment** after operating, taking personal responsibility for the patient's life.
- Rarely made **explicit** with patients; preoperative talks focus on "big surgery" and technical detail, not prolonged ventilation or dialysis
- Surgeons focus on the individual and may **delay withdrawal** even when families request it; intensivists weigh wider resource use
- Patients expect surgery to "fix" things rather than risk functional or cognitive decline
- Other drivers: **clinical momentum**, the **"fix-it" model**, **rescue culture**
- Structural factors: ICU bed numbers and occupancy, ICU-to-hospital bed ratio, nurse staffing, ICU strain
cards.e: Patient factors (fear, anxiety, poor understanding) and system factors (time, no prior planning) add to nonbeneficial surgery. Understanding these frames helps anaesthesiologists mediate between patient, family and surgical team.

cards.q: What do families value in end-of-life communication?
cards.a:
**Trust** in the physician and **truthful** communication rank highest.
- Satisfaction rises with more **shared decision-making** and with the number of **empathic statements** made in meetings
- Priorities: honest, clear, **jargon-free** language; information needed for decisions; involving patient and family in planning
- Information preferences vary and may change over the illness; **do not assume** them from race or ethnicity
- Ask how much the person wants to know; caregivers often want more information than patients; some patients delegate to a surrogate
cards.e: The key points of the chapter emphasise that patients want honesty with empathy and accept that prognosis is uncertain. Asking about preferred information is better than guessing.

cards.q: How should spirituality be addressed at the end of life?
cards.a:
**Spirituality** is how a person finds **meaning, purpose and connectedness**; religion may be one part of it.
- Patients and families in ICU often see dying as a **spiritual process**
- Illness raises questions of meaning and about religious teaching on interventions
- Patients usually **want physicians to ask**, yet report unmet spiritual needs
- Simple screen: ask whether religion or spirituality is important in the person's life
- Raise it **without imposing** one's own views
cards.e: Many decisions about life-sustaining treatment are grounded in belief, so knowing the patient's framework helps the team understand and respect choices. Chaplains on the palliative team take on deeper spiritual care.

cards.q: List the elements of the Serious Illness Conversation Guide.
cards.a:
A stepwise structure synthesised from qualitative research.
- **Set up** the conversation (purpose, permission)
- **Assess** understanding and information preferences
- **Share** prognosis (uncertainty, time range, or function framing)
- **Explore**: goals, fears and worries, sources of strength, **critical abilities**, acceptable **trade-offs**, family's awareness
- **Close**: summarise, make a recommendation, check agreement
- **Document** and **communicate** with key clinicians
cards.e: All frameworks share active listening, validating concerns and checking understanding; none has been shown superior in outcome trials. Asking what abilities are so critical that life without them would be unacceptable directly informs perioperative resuscitation and ventilation limits.

cards.q: What is the evidence for ICU family meetings, and what is the VALUE mnemonic?
cards.a:
Family conferences are endorsed by consensus groups; meetings **within 72 h** of admission shortened ICU stay without raising mortality.
- **VALUE**: **V**alue what the family says, **A**cknowledge emotion, **L**isten (allow silence), **U**nderstand the patient as a person, **E**licit questions
- VALUE plus a bereavement brochure reduced family **psychological distress at 3 months**
- Australian Choosing Wisely **5 Questions** increased family inclusion in ICU decisions
- But some studies show more **anxiety, depression and PTSD** after a single prognosis-focused meeting
cards.e: The lesson is that longitudinal communication and post-ICU support matter more than one structured meeting. Barriers include time, competing duties, the belief that meetings are only for decisions, and COVID-era visiting restrictions; useful resources include VitalTalk, Best Case/Worst Case and Ask-Tell-Ask.

cards.q: Describe the SPIKES protocol for breaking bad news.
cards.a:
A **six-step** framework.
- **S**etting: quiet, private room large enough for everyone
- **P**erception: find out what they already understand
- **I**nvitation: ask how much detail they want
- **K**nowledge: give the information plainly, avoiding jargon
- **E**mpathy: acknowledge emotion
- **S**equelae: agree next steps and a follow-up time
cards.e: Qualitative synthesis shows breaking bad news must be adapted to the relationship, the family's reactions, the environment and cultural context, rather than recited as a script. Starting with perception avoids delivering information the family cannot yet absorb.

cards.q: What is the NURSE framework and how should anger from patients or families be handled?
cards.a:
**NURSE** is a framework for **responding to emotion**.
- **N**ame the emotion
- **U**nderstand: empathise and legitimise it
- **R**espect: praise their strength or effort
- **S**upport: state that you want to help
- **E**xplore: invite them to elaborate
- For anger: do not get **defensive** or take it personally; listen respectfully; set **boundaries for safety**; view anger as a **coping** response within grief
cards.e: Anger towards clinicians is common in serious illness. Responding to emotion before giving more facts usually makes the subsequent information easier to hear.

cards.q: How should a family's request not to tell the patient the diagnosis be handled?
cards.a:
Respond with **empathy**, explore the family's concerns, and **ask the patient** how and whether they wish to be involved.
- Disclosure norms vary widely between cultures; in the USA most physicians now expect to disclose
- No trial evidence; recommendations are expert opinion
- Offer the patient a choice: some want all information and to decide themselves, others prefer a relative to receive information and decide
cards.e: This respects autonomy, since the patient may legitimately choose to delegate. It avoids both overriding the family bluntly and colluding in deception without the patient's consent.

cards.q: What is a time-limited trial and what are its benefits?
cards.a:
An agreement between clinicians and patient or family to **deliver an intervention for a defined period** and then **reassess** whether it is helping.
- Gives the family a timeline and sets the expectation of revisiting the decision
- Associated with **shorter ICU stays**, better family meetings, and **less intense and shorter ICU treatment** (e.g. ventilation)
- Useful with **prognostic uncertainty** or unrealistic expectations; respects autonomy while bridging to palliative care if needed
cards.e: It can also apply to artificial hydration or nutrition, e.g. to see whether delirium improves. The essential components are clear success criteria and a fixed review date.

cards.q: Summarise the outcomes of in-hospital and perioperative cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
cards.a:
Over **half** survive initial in-hospital resuscitation and nearly **one-quarter** survive to discharge.
- Survival by rhythm: **shockable 37%**, **PEA 12%**, **asystole 11%**; time to defibrillation is critical
- About **85%** of arrests in surgical patients are **postoperative**; this group may do better than others
- OR/PACU arrest: rare (**5.6 per 10,000**) but mortality **58%**; 30-day mortality after postoperative arrest **71%**
- Older surgical survivors: about **half** have moderate-severe **neurological deficit**; **60%** alive at 1 year
- Targeted temperature management to 33°C showed **no advantage over normothermia** in recent trials and meta-analyses
cards.e: Outcomes also differ by sex and race: women survivors have worse cognitive and functional outcomes, and Black patients have higher in-hospital arrest mortality. These figures inform realistic code-status discussions.

cards.q: How should resuscitation status be discussed, and what is REMAP?
cards.a:
Frame code status **within the patient's overall goals** rather than as an isolated checklist.
- A patient prioritising **longevity** may be advised to accept CPR; one prioritising **independence** may be advised a DNR order to avoid prolonged ICU care
- Evidence for any single approach is weak; "allow natural death" was not preferred over "do not resuscitate"
- **REMAP** (VitalTalk-based): **R**eframe, **E**xpect emotion, **M**ap the future, **A**lign with values, **P**lan treatments that match values
- ASA and ACS publish guidance on perioperative limitations of treatment
cards.e: Making a recommendation based on stated values is legitimate and reduces the burden on patients. Oxford stresses that patients must be involved in discussions about the utility or futility of surgery and resuscitation.

cards.q: How accurate are clinicians at prognostication?
cards.a:
**Inaccurate for individuals**, with direction depending on setting.
- Near death (median survival 4 weeks): physicians **overestimate by ~30%**; hospice study: overestimated by a **factor of 5**, **63%** of predictions too optimistic
- The **longer** a physician knows the patient, the **less accurate** the estimate
- ICU physicians tend to be **pessimistic**: only **71%** of ventilated patients given <10% survival died in ICU
- Physicians beat scoring systems in the first 24 h of ICU, but neither is reliable for one patient; nurses are more pessimistic than doctors
- Best accuracy when **several clinicians agree**; mortality predicted better than cognitive or quality-of-life outcomes
cards.e: Accuracy is better with poorer performance status and nearer death. Prognostic tools including clinician judgement outperform those using objective data alone.

cards.q: Should physicians give a prognosis when uncertain, and how?
cards.a:
**Yes**: most surrogates want one even if uncertain.
- **87%** of 179 surrogates wanted a prognosis and preferred the uncertainty to be made explicit
- It helps families prepare for bereavement and plan work, visitors and finances
- Use **ranges**: hours–days, days–weeks, weeks–months, months–years, roughly tracking **functional status**
- Surrogates interpret prognoses **optimistically**, especially poor ones, so check understanding
cards.e: Avoiding any timeframe to avoid being wrong is a common but unhelpful response to uncertainty. The Serious Illness Conversation Guide offers uncertainty, time and function framings for the same purpose.

cards.q: Describe the four common trajectories of functional decline before death.
cards.a:
Four patterns.
- **Sudden death** or extreme disability from an acute event
- **Good function then rapid, steady decline** (typical of **cancer**)
- **Waxing and waning** with exacerbations and partial recovery (typical of **organ failure**: CHF, COPD)
- **Slow decline from a low baseline** (typical of **frailty and dementia**)
cards.e: Recognising the trajectory helps explain prognosis, especially in conditions such as COPD and heart failure where any single admission may be the last. After critical illness, disability depends strongly on pre-ICU functional impairment.

cards.q: Which cancer presentations predict a median survival of 6 months or less?
cards.a:
In advanced cancer, **patient factors** (function, labs) outweigh **tumour type**; spending **more than half the day in bed** predicts median survival of about 6 months.
- Solid cancers (locally advanced or metastatic) with any of: **>50% of day in bed**, **calcium >11.2 mg/dL**, **VTE or PE**, multiple brain metastases, **cord compression** with reduced walking, **malignant pericardial effusion**
- Unknown primary with: unable to work, hepatic/bone/adrenal metastases, recurrence after chemotherapy, low albumin or significant weight loss
cards.e: Web prognostic tools are usually cancer-specific; ICU scoring systems are better for research than for individual predictions. Stoelting confirms that hypercalcaemia of malignancy is a poor prognostic sign.

cards.q: Which features predict a median survival of ≤6 months in heart failure, and how good is the Seattle model?
cards.a:
In NYHA III–IV heart failure admitted to hospital, **three or more** markers suggest ≤6 months.
- **LVEF ≤20%**; age **>70**; **troponin I >0.4 ng/mL**; **BNP >950 pg/mL**; **CRP >3.5 mg/L**
- **Fourth** HF admission or readmission **within 2 months**; dependence for **≥2 ADLs**
- Weight loss or **albumin <2.5 g/dL**; history of shock, arrhythmia, arrest, CPR or ventilation
- **SBP <110 mmHg**; creatinine >2 mg/dL or BUN >40; **Na <135**; vascular disease or other comorbidity
- **Seattle Heart Failure Model** estimates 1–3-year survival but **cannot identify** the last year of life in an individual
cards.e: HF follows a waxing-waning course, so timing is hard. Poor prognosis is also linked to admission, tachycardia, hypotension, low EF and rising creatinine, and older age and COPD reduce 1-year survival after decompensation. The prognostic accuracy of these listed factors is itself unknown.

cards.q: What predicts poor prognosis in advanced dementia, COPD and liver disease?
cards.a:
Disease-specific markers.
- **Dementia**: 6-month mortality rises with **infection** and **inability to eat**; also age, dyspnoea, immobility, poor intake, pressure ulcer, **feeding tube** for dysphagia or aspiration, male >90 years
- **COPD**: **BODE** index (BMI, obstruction, dyspnoea, exercise capacity) - impractical at the bedside; **>3 days ventilation** and **failed extubation**; right heart failure, readmission within 2 months, malnutrition
- **Liver**: **MELD** (≥21, or ≥18 with liver-related ICU admission); **hepatic encephalopathy** and **hepatorenal syndrome**
cards.e: For COPD, the qualifying admission is a severe exacerbation with PaO2 ≤55 mmHg, PaCO2 ≥50 mmHg and oxygen dependence plus three markers. Lack of reliable non-cancer criteria explains late hospice referral in these conditions.

cards.q: What is the prognosis of patients on dialysis and after dialysis withdrawal?
cards.a:
Dialysis patients live only **16–33%** as long as age- and sex-matched peers.
- **10-year survival** for dialysis patients **>65 years** is only **3.1%**
- Poor function, poor nutrition and comorbidity worsen prognosis
- **Dialysis withdrawal** causes up to **20%** of deaths in dialysis patients each year
- Average survival after withdrawal is **8–12 days**
cards.e: These numbers are useful when counselling about high-risk surgery in elderly dialysis patients. Withdrawal of dialysis is ethically equivalent to withdrawing any other life-sustaining treatment.

cards.q: How is frailty defined and why does it matter in palliative care?
cards.a:
A multisystem syndrome of **physiological decline** with heightened **vulnerability** to adverse outcomes.
- Measured as **physical frailty** (phenotype) or by **deficit accumulation** (illness, functional and cognitive decline)
- Not exclusive to old age; can occur **under 65**
- Strongly associated with **mortality** and poor surgical outcomes
- Increased functional, cognitive and psychosocial needs support **palliative involvement** and may serve as a palliative **trigger**
cards.e: Oxford notes that frailty and comorbidity drive higher perioperative morbidity and mortality in older patients. A frailty assessment therefore informs both risk discussion and referral.

cards.q: Which alternative routes of drug delivery are used in palliative care and why?
cards.a:
Many patients **cannot swallow** and have **poor IV access**, so the **subcutaneous route** is standard.
- SC infusion of **opioids**, benzodiazepines, some antiemetics, antibiotics, neuroleptics and even **fluids**
- Safety is supported partly by evidence that many "intramuscular" injections actually land subcutaneously
- Optimal **route-to-route conversion ratio** is debated
- Also transmucosal, sublingual, rectal opioids; **epidural or intrathecal** delivery for intractable pain
cards.e: Oxford gives a practical equivalence of 10 mg oral morphine ≈ 3 mg SC/IV morphine ≈ 5 mg oral oxycodone, and a 25 microgram/h fentanyl patch ≈ 90 mg oral morphine per day, but stresses allowance for incomplete cross-tolerance and individual variability. Transdermal fentanyl takes about 12 h to reach steady levels and absorption rises with active warming.

cards.q: What is the epidemiology of cancer pain and how effective is the WHO ladder?
cards.a:
**15–90%** of patients with solid tumours have pain, depending on cancer type, stage and demographics.
- Most is due to the **tumour**; about **one-fifth** is due to **treatment** (e.g. chemotherapy neuropathy, radiation neuritis)
- **WHO analgesic ladder**: Zech's study of 2118 patients gave relief in **76%** with few side effects
- Advanced, progressing disease: **60–90%** have pain affecting function, mood and sleep, needing interventional, psychological or oncological (palliative chemo/radiotherapy) approaches
cards.e: Stoelting describes the ladder steps: NSAIDs and paracetamol for mild pain, then codeine-type opioids, then potent opioids such as oral morphine, switching route when oral fails. It classifies cancer pain as nociceptive (somatic or visceral, opioid-responsive) or neuropathic (burning, lancinating, often poorly opioid-responsive).
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 48 · Stoelting 7e Ch 28 · Oxford Handbook Ch 40

cards.q: How is metastatic bone pain managed?
cards.a:
Multimodal; no single best treatment.
- Common sources: **breast, lung, kidney, prostate**; lesions may be **osteoblastic or osteolytic**
- **Palliative radiotherapy** (relief may take **several weeks**)
- **Dexamethasone** (oral, SC or IV) by expert consensus
- **Bisphosphonates** (zoledronic acid, pamidronate): good evidence, first-line; watch **osteonecrosis of the jaw** and **renal impairment**
- **NSAIDs**; **hormonal therapy** for breast, prostate, endometrial cancer
- **Radiopharmaceuticals** (strontium-89, samarium-153): effective but marrow toxicity
- Interventions: epidural steroids, **vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty**, intrathecal pumps, surgery
cards.e: Stoelting states bone pain is the commonest cancer pain and NSAIDs are especially effective for it. Calcitonin has scarce evidence but is well tolerated.

cards.q: How common is neuropathic pain in advanced cancer and what are the first-line drugs?
cards.a:
**17–28%** of patients with advanced cancer; due to tumour invasion of nerves or to chemotherapy or radiation.
- First-line: **neuropathic agents, not opioids**
- **Gabapentin and pregabalin** (first line; act on calcium channels; individual response varies)
- **TCAs** (desipramine, amitriptyline) for opioid-refractory pain, useful with depression; secondary amines have fewer side effects
- **SNRIs** (duloxetine, venlafaxine): less effective than TCAs but better tolerated, often tried first; SSRIs have scarce evidence
- **Methadone** (NMDA antagonism) may help mixed cancer pain; **IV lidocaine** has good evidence; **ketamine** helpful in pain crisis
cards.e: Consider life expectancy, because some adjuvants need weeks of titration. Older anticonvulsants are reserved for failure of antidepressants and gabapentinoids; baclofen and clonazepam have weak evidence.

cards.q: Classify the adjuvant analgesics used in cancer pain (beyond neuropathic agents).
cards.a:
Grouped by purpose.
- **Multipurpose**: glucocorticoids (dexamethasone, prednisone) for bone and neuropathic pain, lymphoedema, headache, bowel obstruction
- **Bupropion**: little analgesic evidence, used when fatigue or somnolence is a problem
- **α2 agonists**: tizanidine (muscle relaxant), **clonidine** (neuraxial)
- **Cannabinoids**: THC/cannabidiol has good evidence in cancer pain
- **Topical**: lidocaine patch, **capsaicin 8% patch** (postherpetic neuralgia), diclofenac, doxepin cream
- **Bowel obstruction**: **anticholinergics** (hyoscine compounds, glycopyrronium) and **octreotide**, each with a glucocorticoid as first-line
cards.e: Stoelting notes corticosteroids reduce pain perception, spare opioids, lift mood and appetite, and that tricyclics may add analgesia by potentiating opioids.

cards.q: How is pain assessed in the ICU and which procedures are most painful?
cards.a:
**Self-report** is the reference standard; when impossible, use **validated behavioural tools**.
- **Behavioral Pain Scale (BPS)** and **Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT)**, endorsed by SCCM **PADIS** guidelines
- They assess **facial expression, body movement and ventilator synchrony**
- Most painful procedures: **chest tube removal**, wound **drain removal**, **arterial line** insertion
- Pain occurs in **40–50%** of ICU patients, also at rest
- Survivors have traumatic stress and frequent **chronic pain** (part of PICS)
cards.e: Intubation, sedation and delirium make assessment difficult, which is why behavioural tools exist. AI analysis of facial expression may in future automate detection.

cards.q: Do opioids hasten death at the end of life? Is the doctrine of double effect needed?
cards.a:
Evidence indicates that **appropriately titrated opioids do not hasten death**.
- Morita (2001): no difference in survival by opioid or sedative dose in the last 48 h
- Portenoy (2006): weak association with total dose, explaining **<10%** of variance
- Opioid use is common: **70%** in the last week, **47%** in the last 24 h
- Most experts hold that double effect **need not usually be invoked**
- Avoid **undertreatment**; titrate to assessed pain; some urge caution in cancer survivors with long life expectancy
cards.e: Lippincott explains double effect: a drug given to relieve pain or dyspnoea is acceptable even if it might shorten life, but giving sedation or a bolus purely to end life is not. Recent opioid-crisis restrictions have reduced opioid use in dying cancer patients, with more pain-related ED visits.

cards.q: What interventional options exist for refractory cancer pain near the end of life?
cards.a:
**10–20%** of cancer pain is refractory to systemic therapy.
- **Coeliac plexus block/neurolysis**: upper abdominal pain, especially **pancreatic cancer**
- **Superior hypogastric block/neurolysis**: **pelvic** pain
- Peripheral nerve blocks, trigger-point injections
- **Neuraxial** (epidural/intrathecal) analgesia: lower pain scores and much **less systemic opioid**, so less constipation and sedation
- RCT (202 patients): **implantable intrathecal pump** vs medical management reduced fatigue and sedation; 6-month survival **53.9% vs 37.2%** (P = .06)
- Caution: **bleeding** (coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia) and **infection** (immunosuppression)
cards.e: Stoelting notes neurolytic coeliac block with alcohol or phenol is the most effective intervention for pancreatic cancer pain, can cause hypotension from sympathetic block in hypovolaemic patients, and benefits from CT guidance. Cordotomy is reserved for unilateral pain unresponsive to less invasive measures.

cards.q: Outline the causes of nausea and vomiting in palliative patients and the receptor targets involved.
cards.a:
Start with a **cause-directed** assessment.
- **Cortex** (anxiety, raised ICP): GABA
- **Chemoreceptor trigger zone** (drugs, biochemical changes): **dopamine, serotonin**
- **Vestibular** (movement): **histamine, acetylcholine**
- **GI tract** (gastric stasis, constipation, obstruction): dopamine, serotonin
- **Vomiting centre**: histamine, acetylcholine, serotonin
- Chemotherapy: **5-HT3 antagonist** ± **dexamethasone**, **olanzapine**, add **NK1 antagonist (aprepitant)** for highly emetogenic regimens; benzodiazepines for **anticipatory** nausea
- Non-chemotherapy palliative nausea: no high-level evidence; use **scheduled** antiemetics with PRN additions
cards.e: Matching the drug to the receptor of the likely pathway is the rational approach. Oxford adds that rescue antiemetics should be from a different class than the prophylactic drug, and that cyclizine (antihistamine) and hyoscine (anticholinergic) suit vestibular causes.

cards.q: How is malignant bowel obstruction managed in palliative care?
cards.a:
Tailor to life expectancy; surgery is **poor** when expected survival is **<2 months**.
- **Self-expanding metallic stents** as an alternative
- **Nasogastric tube** for immediate relief while deciding
- **Venting gastrostomy** for refractory cases (allows tasting food with decompression)
- Medical: antiemetics with **octreotide** and **corticosteroids**; anticholinergics such as **hyoscine** or glycopyrronium
cards.e: Octreotide and anticholinergics, each combined with a glucocorticoid, are listed as first-line adjuvants for non-surgical obstruction. The venting gastrostomy is a palliative procedure where the anaesthesiologist may meet these patients.

cards.q: Should artificial hydration and nutrition be given at the end of life?
cards.a:
It is a **medical intervention**, so weigh **risks and benefits** with patient and family.
- Hunger is uncommon in advanced disease; treat **thirst** with ice chips or mouth swabs
- Risks: **fluid overload** (choking, oedema), diarrhoea, nausea; tube dislodgement and **restraints**
- **Proven benefit**: acute stroke or head injury, persistent vegetative state, oropharyngeal cancer, brief critical illness, and perhaps bulbar ALS
- **No benefit** in advanced cancer at end of life (symptoms, quality of life, delirium, survival)
- **PEG in advanced dementia** does not prevent pneumonia or prolong life: not recommended
- A **time-limited trial** (e.g. for delirium) is reasonable
cards.e: Fear of "starving" a relative and cultural or religious views make this emotive, so explaining it as a treatment with burdens helps families. Oxford notes elderly patients have a blunted thirst response, which explains easy dehydration but not distress.

cards.q: Define dyspnoea and explain its pathophysiology.
cards.a:
A **subjective** experience of breathing discomfort with distinct sensations of varying intensity, separate from what an observer sees.
- Has a **sensory** component and a **perceptual/affective** component, so observer scores may disagree with self-report
- Mechanisms: increased **chemoreceptor drive**; stimulation of upper airway, lung and chest wall **mechanoreceptors**; altered **mechanical load** (resistance, compliance); **neuromechanical dissociation**; impaired O2 delivery or use
- The affective dimension adds fear and anxiety
cards.e: Dyspnoea is the most distressing symptom reported by ICU patients who can self-report, is linked to PTSD in intubated survivors, and increases nearer death even without cardiopulmonary disease. Treat the cause if possible (e.g. drain an effusion), otherwise treat the symptom.

cards.q: How is refractory dyspnoea managed at the end of life?
cards.a:
Combine **non-drug measures** with **low-dose opioids**.
- **Fan** to the face, pulmonary rehabilitation
- **Oxygen** has shown **no symptomatic benefit** in meta-analysis (non-hypoxaemic patients)
- **Low-dose opioids** are safe and effective: in 48 COPD patients, **20 mg/day sustained-release morphine** improved dyspnoea with minimal side effects
- **Benzodiazepines** ± opioids: small, mixed studies, trend to benefit for the affective component
- **Acupuncture** benefit in lung cancer and COPD trials
cards.e: A key chapter point is that small opioid doses relieve dyspnoea without hastening death. Do not assume worsening breathlessness reflects hypoxaemia that oxygen will fix.

cards.q: How are depression and anxiety screened for and treated in palliative patients?
cards.a:
Prevalence: depression **5–30%**, anxiety **7–13%**.
- **Two-question screen** (feeling depressed? loss of interest or pleasure?): sensitivity **91%**, specificity **68%**, validated in palliative care
- Refer positive screens or any **suicidal/homicidal** ideation
- Treatment by life expectancy: **SSRIs or MAOIs** need **1–2 months** to work, so only for longer prognosis
- Weeks to a few months: **methylphenidate**, onset **1–3 days**, helps depression and **fatigue**
cards.e: Oxford reminds that MAOIs interact dangerously with indirect sympathomimetics and pethidine, a perioperative concern. Distinguishing depression from delirium and normal grief is essential before treating.

cards.q: How do you distinguish normal grief from depression in a terminally ill patient?
cards.a:
Grief is **adaptive and focal**; depression is **maladaptive and pervasive**.
- **Focus**: grief relates to specific losses; depression affects all aspects of life
- **Course**: grief comes **in waves** and eases; depression is constant
- **Pleasure**: preserved in grief; **anhedonia** in depression
- **Hope**: episodic loss in grief; **persistent hopelessness** in depression
- **Self-worth**: maintained in grief; **worthlessness** in depression
- **Guilt**: specific regrets vs excessive guilt
- **Death wish**: passive and fleeting vs **preoccupation** with dying
cards.e: Diminishing engagement in grief may simply reflect functional decline rather than anhedonia. Misdiagnosing grief as depression risks unnecessary drugs, while missing depression leaves treatable suffering.

cards.q: Describe delirium at the end of life: incidence, assessment, reversibility and management.
cards.a:
Affects **28–90%** of terminally ill patients, rising as death nears.
- Assess with the **Confusion Assessment Method** (validated in palliative care)
- Up to **half is reversible**; reversibility more likely with **younger age**, milder impairment, **no organ failure**
- **Terminal delirium** signals very short survival
- **Hypoactive** delirium is common, under-recognised and distressing; no consensus on treatment
- Workup should match **goals of care**
- First-line **non-drug** measures (reorientation, sleep, family, glasses/hearing aids); **typical or atypical antipsychotics**; **palliative sedation** for refractory terminal delirium
cards.e: Delirium undermines capacity to consent to surgery, with legal and ethical consequences. Survivors usually remember it and find it distressing, which supports treating it actively when consistent with goals.

cards.q: List causes of delirium in palliative patients and an appropriate stepwise evaluation.
cards.a:
Often **multifactorial**.
- Metabolic: **hypercalcaemia**, hypo/hypernatraemia, dehydration, glucose derangement
- Organ failure: renal, hepatic, respiratory
- Drugs: **opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, steroids**
- Infection: pneumonia, UTI, sepsis
- Brain: tumour, metastases, leptomeningeal disease, **non-convulsive status**
- **Hypoxia**; **withdrawal** (alcohol, benzodiazepines); DIC, anaemia
- Evaluation: set goals, **review medications**, consider withdrawal, then bloods (metabolic panel, FBC), SpO2, cultures and chest X-ray; specialist tests (EEG, ABG, DIC screen, TSH, CT/MRI, LP) only if appropriate
cards.e: Stoelting notes hypercalcaemia of malignancy can present as lethargy or coma, with polyuria and dehydration. Oxford lists pain, infection, electrolyte imbalance, dehydration and substance withdrawal as reversible delirium factors.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 48 · Stoelting 7e Ch 28 · Oxford Handbook Ch 32

cards.q: How is bleeding, including terminal haemorrhage, managed in palliative care?
cards.a:
Depends on cause, goals and life expectancy.
- Options for suitable patients: **tranexamic acid**, **embolisation**, surgery
- Transfusion: individualised, guided by evidence and prognosis
- **Exsanguination**: uncommon but distressing; no RCTs
- Practical: **dark towels**, suction, pressure, **stay with the patient**
- Drugs for sedation and amnesia: **benzodiazepines, opioids, ketamine**
cards.e: Planning ahead for high-risk patients (e.g. tumours near major vessels) lets staff have drugs and towels ready. Stoelting notes post-radiation bleeding can arise from rectum, bladder, vagina, lung and brain.

cards.q: What changes signal that a patient is actively dying?
cards.a:
Predictable but variably timed changes.
- **84%** drowsy or comatose 24 h before death; **acrocyanosis** and loss of **radial pulse** a median **1 h** before death
- Stopping oral intake, unresponsiveness, **death rattle**
- Circulation: tachycardia, hypertension then hypotension, cool peripheries, cyanosis, **mottling**, dark urine, **oliguria/anuria**
- Respiration: rate rises then slows, smaller tidal volumes, **apnoea, Cheyne–Stokes**, agonal breaths; loss of swallow and gag
- Neurological: drowsiness, word-finding difficulty, **terminal delirium** (day–night reversal, restlessness, moaning)
- Others: inability to close eyes, incontinence, skin breakdown; rarely a burst of energy before death
cards.e: More than 500,000 people die in US ICUs yearly, so anaesthesiologists will be asked by families what to expect. Isolation during COVID-19 worsened grief and quality of dying, supporting flexible visiting and digital contact.

cards.q: What are terminal secretions and what is the evidence for antimuscarinic treatment?
cards.a:
Noisy breathing (**death rattle**) from secretions in the **oropharynx and airway** that the patient cannot clear by **coughing or swallowing**.
- Antimuscarinics widely used, with **weak evidence**
- **Atropine, hyoscine butylbromide and scopolamine**: improved symptoms, **no difference between agents**
- **Sublingual atropine** = placebo
- **Prophylactic SC scopolamine** reduced death rattle vs placebo in a multicentre RCT
- Families vary in distress; patients are usually unconscious, though evidence that they are not bothered is lacking
cards.e: Explaining the sound to the family is as important as drugs. Oxford lists hyoscine and glycopyrronium (a quaternary ammonium anticholinergic) among antimuscarinic options.

cards.q: What are the ethical principles and practical steps in withdrawal of life support?
cards.a:
Withdrawal is **ethically acceptable** and respects **autonomy**; it is **not withdrawal of care**.
- Protocols: **opioid** for pain or dyspnoea and **benzodiazepine** for anxiety or agitation
- Attend to non-symptom needs: **family meetings**, **rituals**, emotional and spiritual support for families and staff, chaplain involvement
- Protocolised withdrawal has not improved clinician-rated quality of death
- Anaesthesiologists bring expertise in symptom control during ventilator withdrawal
cards.e: Lippincott emphasises that stopping life-sustaining treatment is equivalent to refusing it initially and is not euthanasia: it ends prolongation of natural dying. The intent of medication is symptom relief, not hastening death.

cards.q: What do studies show about time to death and drug doses after withdrawal of life support?
cards.a:
Time to death depends on what is withdrawn; titrated opioids do not shorten it.
- 471 patients: death fastest (**median 30 min**) when ventilation and **vasoactives stopped together**; **45 min** vasoactives alone; **50 min** extubation alone
- 74 ICU patients: morphine **5.3 mg/h** in the last hour of ventilation, **10.6 mg/h** in the hour before death
- Mean time to death **153 min** after extubation (range 4–934 min)
- Each **1 mg/h morphine** increase was associated with an **8-min delay** in death; **13 min** per 1 mg/h benzodiazepine in an earlier study
- Longer interval to death was linked to **better family satisfaction**
cards.e: These data support that opioid and sedative titration for comfort does not accelerate death. Variability in drug delivery argues for standard protocols.

cards.q: Should neuromuscular blocking drugs be used during withdrawal of ventilation?
cards.a:
**No**: do not paralyse before extubation.
- Paralysis **masks distress**, prevents symptom assessment and risks suffering
- Patients already paralysed should **wait for recovery** of neuromuscular function before extubation
- If waiting imposes undue burden, **reversal** (e.g. **sugammadex**) may be used
cards.e: Neuromuscular blockers have no analgesic or sedative effect. Lippincott marks giving rocuronium to stop breathing, or a bolus to end life, as ethically unacceptable.

cards.q: How does paediatric palliative care differ from adult palliative care?
cards.a:
Principles are similar but care is adapted to the child's **developmental stage**.
- Under **2 years**: no concept of death; around **10 years**: may want details of dying
- Wider range of diagnoses, mostly **congenital and neuromuscular**; chromosomal disorders seldom seen in adults
- Referral ages: about one-third 1–9 years, one-third 10–18 years, **<20%** under 1 year
- Children often **survive longer** after referral than adults
- Different **legal** issues around refusing treatment; prognostication and forgoing cure are hard for families
- Symptoms: parents report suffering from **pain, fatigue, dyspnoea**; **neurological** symptoms more prevalent than in adults
- **Regional anaesthesia** has helped difficult pain; drug choices are largely extrapolated from adults
cards.e: WHO states paediatric palliative care can work even in resource-limited settings. Anaesthesiologists are increasingly involved in perioperative goal discussions for these children.

cards.q: A 72-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer and a DNR order is listed for a venting gastrostomy for inoperable malignant bowel obstruction. She is alert, says she wants comfort and to "taste food again", and does not want a prolonged ICU stay. How do you approach the perioperative DNR order and anaesthetic plan?
cards.a:
Do **not automatically suspend** the DNR: revisit it in the context of her goals, then agree an explicit plan.
- Confirm **capacity**; explore goals and which complications she would accept treating
- Agree which specific resuscitative interventions she would accept or decline, given her wish to avoid prolonged ICU care
- Document the plan and the **time of reinstatement** of the DNR; tell surgeon, nurses and recovery staff
- Name a **surrogate** in case of arrest or failure to extubate
- Review chemotherapy effects, coagulation and counts (may preclude neuraxial), opioid regimen, skin and frailty
- Give **PONV prophylaxis** and plan opioid-tolerant analgesia; continue octreotide/steroids/antiemetics after surgery
cards.e: Miller's ethics chapter states DNAR orders should not be automatically suspended for anaesthesia; doing so ignores her autonomy, while refusing to operate denies symptom relief. Surgery for obstruction has poor outcomes when life expectancy is under 2 months, which is why a venting gastrostomy or stent is preferred. Oxford stresses patients must be part of decisions on the utility of resuscitation.

cards.q: An 86-year-old man with end-stage heart failure and a large subarachnoid haemorrhage has been extubated on a morphine infusion after the family chose comfort care. An hour later his tearful daughter asks if you can "speed things up". How do you respond?
cards.a:
Acknowledge her distress, explain the aim is **comfort, not hastening death**, and titrate drugs **only to symptoms**.
- Use NURSE: name and validate her emotion, offer support
- Explain the expected dying process and the wide range of time to death (mean about 2.5 h, but up to many hours after extubation)
- Increase morphine **if he shows pain or dyspnoea**; add a benzodiazepine for agitation
- Do **not** give extra sedation, a morphine bolus or a neuromuscular blocker to stop breathing
- Offer chaplaincy and support
cards.e: Lippincott identifies titrating the infusion for pain as the correct answer, citing double effect. Data show titrated morphine (about 8 min later death per 1 mg/h) does not shorten dying, and families are more satisfied when the interval is not rushed.

cards.q: A 58-year-old man is on day 10 of ventilation in ICU after a cardiac arrest, still on a rocuronium infusion for ventilator dyssynchrony. The family decides on comfort-focused care and asks to stop the ventilator now. How do you plan the withdrawal?
cards.a:
Ensure comfort and assessable symptoms before extubation.
- **Stop rocuronium** and allow neuromuscular function to return before extubating; use **sugammadex** if waiting is a real burden
- Start or titrate an **opioid** for dyspnoea/pain and a **benzodiazepine** for anxiety, by symptom assessment
- Decide sequencing: stopping vasopressors and ventilation together leads to the fastest death (median ~30 min); prepare the family
- Prepare family: likely changes, secretions, unpredictable timing; arrange rituals and spiritual support
- Stop non-comfort monitoring and treatments; consider glycopyrronium or scopolamine for secretions
cards.e: Paralysis hides distress and prevents relief, so it must not be continued or started at withdrawal, as also stated in the ethics chapter. Withdrawal is not withdrawal of care.

cards.q: A 67-year-old man with severe COPD (home oxygen, PaCO2 52 mmHg) in a hospice is severely breathless at rest despite maximal bronchodilators. SpO2 is 92% on 2 L/min. His wife wants his oxygen "turned up". What do you advise?
cards.a:
Treat the **symptom**: low-dose opioids and simple measures; extra oxygen is unlikely to help.
- Look for reversible causes (infection, effusion, bronchospasm) if consistent with goals
- **Fan** to the face, positioning, calm environment
- **Low-dose oral morphine** (e.g. sustained-release ~20 mg/day equivalent) or SC if unable to swallow; titrate
- Consider a benzodiazepine if anxiety is prominent (mixed evidence)
- Explain that extra oxygen has not shown symptomatic benefit for breathlessness
- Reassure that small opioid doses do **not hasten death**
cards.e: The COPD crossover trial with 20 mg/day SR morphine showed improved dyspnoea with minimal adverse effects. Dyspnoea is subjective; treat what the patient reports, not the SpO2 number.

cards.q: A 62-year-old woman with pancreatic cancer has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back despite 300 mg/day oral morphine equivalent, with sedation and severe constipation. Platelets 140 × 10^9/L, INR 1.1. Expected survival is 3 months. What do you offer?
cards.a:
Offer **neurolytic coeliac plexus block** and consider neuraxial delivery.
- Coeliac plexus neurolysis (alcohol or phenol), ideally **image-guided**; warn about **hypotension** from sympathetic block; ensure euvolaemia
- If inadequate: **intrathecal drug delivery** (implanted pump or tunnelled catheter), which reduces systemic opioid needs and side effects
- Add adjuvants: dexamethasone, neuropathic agents if burning or lancinating features
- Treat constipation; consider opioid rotation (e.g. methadone) with an allowance for incomplete cross-tolerance
- Check coagulation and infection risk before procedures; align with goals
cards.e: 10–20% of cancer pain is refractory to systemic drugs. Stoelting rates coeliac neurolysis as the most effective intervention for pancreatic cancer pain. The intrathecal pump RCT showed less fatigue and sedation and a trend to better 6-month survival.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 48 · Stoelting 7e Ch 28 · Oxford Handbook Ch 40

cards.q: A 74-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer in hospice becomes acutely confused and agitated over 2 days. Until last week he was walking and enjoying family visits. He takes oxycodone, dexamethasone and lorazepam. How do you manage his delirium?
cards.a:
Look for **reversible causes**, since up to half of end-of-life delirium reverses and his baseline was good.
- Confirm with **CAM**; agree workup intensity with family based on goals
- **Review drugs**: opioid accumulation, benzodiazepine, **steroids**; reduce or rotate
- Check calcium (**hypercalcaemia**), sodium, glucose, renal and liver function, SpO2, infection (urine, chest X-ray); consider brain metastases imaging if it would change care
- Non-drug measures: reorientation, sleep, family presence, glasses/hearing aids
- **Antipsychotic** for distressing agitation; reserve **palliative sedation** for refractory terminal delirium
cards.e: Younger age, milder impairment and no organ failure favour reversibility; a patient expected to die within hours would warrant less workup. Delirium impairs capacity, so decisions must involve his surrogate meanwhile.

cards.q: The son of an 80-year-old woman newly diagnosed with metastatic gastric cancer asks you, before her preoperative assessment, not to tell her the diagnosis because "it will kill her". How do you handle this?
cards.a:
Respond empathetically and **ask the patient** how she wants information handled.
- Acknowledge the son's love and fear; explore his concerns and cultural expectations
- Explain that you will ask her, sensitively, how much she wants to know
- Ask her privately: does she want full information and to decide herself, or prefer a relative to receive it and decide?
- If she delegates, document this and her chosen surrogate
- If she wants to know, use **SPIKES** with the son present if she wishes
cards.e: Disclosure norms vary by culture and no trial evidence exists; expert advice is to empathise with the family and let the patient choose her level of involvement. This respects autonomy, including the choice to delegate.

cards.q: A 70-year-old with metastatic breast cancer and 2–3 months to live describes low mood, hopelessness, loss of all interest, and feeling worthless. She wonders if life has any value. How do you assess and treat her?
cards.a:
This suggests **depression**, not normal grief; treat with a **fast-acting** agent and refer.
- Pervasive anhedonia, hopelessness and worthlessness favour depression
- Screen: two-question test (sensitivity 91%, specificity 68%); ask directly about **suicidal ideation** and refer urgently if present
- Exclude **delirium** (CAM)
- Given weeks-to-months prognosis: **methylphenidate** (onset 1–3 days, also helps fatigue) rather than an SSRI taking 1–2 months
- Refer to psychiatry; involve palliative team and chaplain
cards.e: In grief, mood comes in waves, pleasure and self-worth are preserved, and wishes for death are passive and fleeting. Choosing the antidepressant by life expectancy is the key exam point.

cards.q: An 82-year-old frail woman is on day 5 of ventilation in the surgical ICU after emergency laparotomy for perforation, with new AKI on vasopressors. Her surgeon insists on "full support", while her daughter says she would never want long-term dialysis. How would you structure care?
cards.a:
Hold an early **family meeting** and propose a **time-limited trial** tied to her goals.
- Set up: introduce team, ask what the family understands
- Share prognosis with **ranges and explicit uncertainty**; use VALUE and respond to emotion
- Explore her values: abilities she would not live without, acceptable trade-offs
- Agree a trial of current support for a fixed period with defined markers; revisit then
- Discuss code status in light of goals; consider specialist palliative referral (life-threatening illness plus functional decline or ICU stay)
- Acknowledge the surgeon's covenantal sense of responsibility and align the team before meeting
cards.e: Time-limited trials shorten ICU stays and reduce intensity of treatment while respecting autonomy. Frailty predicts poor surgical outcomes and can be a palliative trigger.

cards.q: A 79-year-old man with NYHA IV heart failure (LVEF 18%, BNP 1200 pg/mL, sodium 131 mEq/L, SBP 100 mmHg, third admission in 2 months) asks whether he could have hospice care at home and whether he must sign a DNR form first. How do you answer?
cards.a:
He likely meets hospice criteria; **a DNR is not required**.
- He has ≥3 markers predicting median survival ≤6 months (LVEF ≤20%, BNP >950, Na <135, SBP <110, readmission within 2 months)
- Eligibility needs certification by his **attending physician and hospice medical director** that prognosis is <6 months
- Benefit: home nursing, aide, social work, chaplain, equipment, 24/7 support, respite/inpatient care for uncontrolled symptoms, **1 year of bereavement support** for his family
- Can be **recertified** in 60-day periods if he lives longer
- Explain that HF follows a waxing-waning course, so prognosis is uncertain
cards.e: Heart failure patients are often referred late because criteria for non-cancer disease are weak. Seattle model estimates cannot pinpoint the last year of life for an individual.

cards.q: What are the main causes of perioperative morbidity and mortality after pulmonary resection, and how often do they occur?
cards.a:
**Respiratory complications** dominate, unlike most other surgery, where cardiovascular events lead.
- Major respiratory complications (**atelectasis, pneumonia, respiratory failure**): **15–20%** of patients
- These account for most of the expected **3–4% mortality**
- Cardiac complications (arrhythmia, ischemia): **10–15%**
- "Resectable" = tumour still local/locoregional and removable; "operable" = patient can tolerate the resection at acceptable risk
cards.e: The whole preoperative assessment is therefore built around predicting respiratory risk. Lippincott lists extent of resection (pneumonectomy > lobectomy > wedge), age over 70 and surgical inexperience as risk factors for death; sex is not one. Since 1990 respiratory complications have fallen below 10%, largely from better analgesia, while the cardiac complication rate has not changed.

cards.q: Describe the "three-legged stool" of prethoracotomy respiratory assessment. Give the best test and the risk threshold for each leg.
cards.a:
Respiratory function is judged in three partly independent areas, and no single test is enough.
- **Respiratory mechanics**: best test **ppoFEV1**; increased risk below **30–40%**
- **Lung parenchymal function (gas exchange)**: best test **ppoDLCO**; increased risk below **30–40%**
- **Cardiopulmonary interaction**: best test **VO2max**; increased risk below **15 mL/kg/min**
- Older gas-exchange cutoffs: PaO2 <60 mm Hg or PaCO2 >45 mm Hg are warning signs, not absolute bars
cards.e: Each leg reflects a step in getting oxygen to tissues: into the alveoli, across into the blood, then delivered by the circulation. Lippincott adds the supporting tests in each leg (FVC, MVV, RV/TLC; PaO2/PaCO2; stair climb, 6MWT, exercise desaturation <4%) and stresses that a wedge pressure has no place in this assessment. A history of the patient's quality of life remains the best single overall guide.

cards.q: How is predicted postoperative FEV1 calculated, and how is it interpreted?
cards.a:
**ppoFEV1% = preoperative FEV1% × (1 − % functional lung tissue removed/100)**.
- Functional tissue is estimated by counting the **functioning subsegments** removed (of the total, 42 in Miller's figure)
- **>40%**: low risk of respiratory complications
- **<40%**: increased risk (not all will have complications)
- **<30%**: high risk
- Express as % of predicted for age, sex and height
cards.e: ppoFEV1 is the single most valid mechanical predictor of post-thoracotomy respiratory complications. The same formula is applied to DLCO to give ppoDLCO. Oxford quotes older minimum absolute FEV1 rules (pneumonectomy >55%, lobectomy >40% predicted), but percentage-based ppo values are now preferred.

cards.q: What does DLCO measure, and what is the significance of ppoDLCO in thoracic surgery?
cards.a:
DLCO reflects the **total functioning alveolar–capillary surface area**, so it is the most useful test of lung parenchymal (gas exchange) function.
- **ppoDLCO <40%** predicts both respiratory **and cardiac** complications, largely independent of FEV1 (some use <50%)
- DLCO, but not FEV1, is reduced by **preoperative chemotherapy**, making it the key predictor in that group
- NETT: preoperative **FEV1 or DLCO <20%** carried unacceptable mortality, regarded as the absolute minimum
cards.e: Patients with diffuse parenchymal disease may have badly impaired gas transfer with fairly normal spirometry, so measuring only FEV1 can miss the risk, as Oxford notes. This is why the stool needs all three legs.

cards.q: How is exercise capacity assessed before lung resection? Give the key numbers for METs, stair climbing and the 6-minute walk test.
cards.a:
Exercise capacity tests the **cardiopulmonary interaction**, probably the most important leg of the assessment.
- **1 MET = 3.5 mL O2/kg/min** (sitting quietly); one flight of stairs ≈ **4 METs**
- Ability to climb **2 flights** (about 3 m each) without stopping is the minimum to be considered for resection
- **6MWT** correlates well with VO2max: **VO2max ≈ distance (m)/30** (450 m → 15 mL/kg/min)
- Complications after lobectomy rise when the 6MWT is **<400 m**
- Unreliable historians or those limited by other disease need simple or formal testing
cards.e: The 6MWT is the best validated simple test and needs no laboratory, whereas stair climbing is less standardised. Box 49.5 suggests formal exercise testing when ppoFEV1 or ppoDLCO is below 60%.

cards.q: State the VO2max thresholds that predict outcome after thoracotomy.
cards.a:
Formal cardiopulmonary exercise testing is the **gold standard**, and VO2max is the best predictor of post-thoracotomy outcome.
- **<15 mL/kg/min**: high risk of morbidity and mortality
- **<10 mL/kg/min** (about 35% predicted): very high risk
- **>20 mL/kg/min** (about 75% predicted): respiratory complications are uncommon
cards.e: After resection the right ventricle faces a smaller vascular bed. At rest this is barely noticed, but on exercise pulmonary pressures rise, cardiac output is limited and PVR fails to fall normally. VO2max tests exactly this reserve, which is why exercise capacity predicts outcome so well, especially in the elderly.

cards.q: How has minimally invasive surgery changed risk thresholds and the plan for extubation after lung resection?
cards.a:
VATS and robotic surgery move the risk threshold for ppoFEV1 (and probably ppoDLCO) from about **40% for thoracotomy to about 30%**.
- ppoFEV1 **>40%**: extubate in the OR if **"AWaC"** (alert, warm and comfortable)
- ppoFEV1 **>30%** with exercise and parenchymal function above risk thresholds: OR extubation, depending on other disease
- >30% but failing the other criteria: consider **staged weaning**
- ppoFEV1 **20–30%** with good cardiorespiratory and parenchymal function: early extubation possible if **TEA** is used or surgery is **VATS**
cards.e: Patients judged high risk for thoracotomy may be acceptable for VATS. In patients over 70, major cardiopulmonary complications were 4.3% after minimally invasive resection versus 10% after open surgery. Epidural analgesia and VATS both protect postoperative lung function, which justifies the lower thresholds.

cards.q: What is the role of ventilation–perfusion scintigraphy in assessing a patient for lung resection?
cards.a:
It refines the ppo estimate by measuring how much the region to be removed actually contributes.
- If the region is nonfunctioning or barely functioning, the predicted loss is smaller
- Most useful for **pneumonectomy**: consider when preoperative **FEV1 and/or DLCO <80%**
- Of limited value for predicting function after **lobectomy**
- The fractional perfusion to the non-operative lung also predicts **PaO2 during OLV**
cards.e: A lung already destroyed by central tumour contributes little gas exchange, so removing it costs little and the patient also tolerates OLV well. Subsegment counting assumes uniform function, which is the weakness the V/Q scan corrects.

cards.q: What are the cardiac ischemia considerations in a patient presenting for pulmonary resection?
cards.a:
Lung resection is an **intermediate-risk** procedure for cardiac ischemia.
- Post-thoracotomy ischemia occurs in about **5%**, peaking on **days 2–3**
- Routine screening of all patients is not cost-effective; noninvasive testing for **major** (unstable ischemia, recent MI, severe valve disease, significant arrhythmia) or **intermediate** (stable angina, old MI, previous CHF, diabetes) predictors
- After MI: a delay of **4–6 weeks** is acceptable if stable and optimised
- After stents: **4–6 weeks for bare metal**, **6 months for drug-eluting**; delay until antiplatelets (other than aspirin) can be stopped
- Stable CAD and VATS lobectomy: no excess complications, but 30-day mortality 5% vs 0.9%
cards.e: Smoking gives most of these patients at least one coronary risk factor. Cancer surgery cannot be delayed indefinitely, which is why the stent intervals matter. Intraoperatively, the plan is to protect supply/demand: keep oxygenation and diastolic pressure, avoid tachycardia and unnecessary rises in cardiac output.

cards.q: What is the incidence of arrhythmias after lung resection, what causes them, and how are they prevented?
cards.a:
Arrhythmias occur in **30–50%** in the first week (Holter), and **60–70% are atrial fibrillation**.
- Risk rises with extent of resection (**pneumonectomy 60%**, lobectomy 40%, thoracotomy alone 30%), intrapericardial dissection, blood loss, **age**; extrapleural pneumonectomy is highest risk
- Mechanism: **raised right-heart afterload** (resection, atelectasis, hypoxemia) plus **sympathetic stimulation**, maximal around **day 2**
- TRJ velocity (RV systolic pressure) rises on day 2 and is linked to SVT
- Prophylaxis: **diltiazem** is currently the most useful; β-blockers may be most effective but are a concern with reactive airways
- COPD patients are harder to rate-control and often need several drugs
cards.e: The AF is best seen as a marker of a struggling right heart, so preventing it does not fix the underlying problem. Lippincott makes the point that arrhythmia incidence rises with age (a classic false statement claims the opposite) and attributes SVT to manipulation and distension of the right atrium.

cards.q: Why do patients with heart failure tolerate one-lung ventilation poorly?
cards.a:
OLV imposes an obligatory **20–30% shunt** through the nonventilated lung.
- Shunted blood carries mixed venous oxygen content into the arterial blood
- A **low cardiac output** lowers **SvO2**, so the same shunt causes a much larger fall in SaO2
- These patients need venous saturation monitoring and **inotropic support** of cardiac output
cards.e: This is the same reason cardiac output must be maintained in every OLV case. The arterial effect of a shunt depends on both the shunt fraction and the oxygen content of the venous blood passing through it.

cards.q: How is pulmonary hypertension defined, and what classification matters most to the thoracic anesthesiologist?
cards.a:
PH is a **mean PAP >25 mm Hg** at catheterisation or **systolic PAP >35 mm Hg** (echo).
- Formal classification has five groups; for anesthesia the useful split is **PH due to left heart disease** vs **PH due to lung disease**
- Left heart: systolic/diastolic dysfunction, mitral disease, congenital heart disease
- Lung disease: pulmonary vascular disease, chronic lung disease/hypoxemia/sleep apnea, thromboembolic, miscellaneous
- Noncardiac thoracic patients usually have the **lung-disease** type; prevalence **40–50%** in severe chronic lung disease
cards.e: The distinction matters because the treatments differ: inodilators help left-heart PH but can worsen lung-disease PH. The RV is normally perfused through systole as well as diastole; as PA pressure nears systemic levels, systolic RCA flow is lost, so systemic hypotension quickly causes RV ischemia.

cards.q: Outline the anesthetic management principles for a patient with pulmonary hypertension secondary to lung disease.
cards.a:
The key goal is **avoiding systemic hypotension** so that systemic pressure stays above PA pressure.
- Avoid vasodilating agents where possible; **ketamine or etomidate** suit induction (ketamine does not worsen PH)
- Support pressure with **norepinephrine, phenylephrine or vasopressin** (vasopressin raises systemic pressure without raising PAP)
- Use **inhaled** pulmonary vasodilators rather than IV: **nitric oxide 10–40 ppm** or **nebulised prostacyclin 50 ng/kg/min**
- Use thoracic epidural local anesthetic **cautiously**, with inotropes as needed
- **Monitor cardiac output**
cards.e: Dobutamine and milrinone help PH from left heart disease but their vasodilation and tachycardia can make lung-disease PH worse. These patients depend on tonic cardiac sympathetic tone, which explains the caution with thoracic epidurals.

cards.q: How should pulmonary artery pressure data be interpreted in a pulmonary hypertensive patient during thoracic surgery, and why is a thoracic epidural a concern?
cards.a:
PA pressure alone is misleading and must be read with **cardiac output or SvO2**.
- **Rising PAP** is almost always bad
- **Falling PAP** may mean useful vasodilation, or impending **RV decompensation**
- TEE helps monitor RV function
- Animal work: with lumbar epidural block, RV contractility rises as afterload rises; a **thoracic epidural's cardiac sympathectomy abolishes this response**
- So these patients often need low-dose **inotropes/vasopressors** with TEA, plus a central line and ICU care
cards.e: A failing RV cannot generate pressure, so PAP falls just as output collapses. Paravertebral analgesia gives better hemodynamic stability than TEA in patients with normal hearts, but it has not been specifically studied in PH.

cards.q: What does Miller say about age as a factor in lung resection?
cards.a:
There is **no upper age limit** for pulmonary resection.
- Mortality of 3% reported in patients aged 80–92
- But respiratory complications (40%) about double and cardiac complications (40%, mainly **arrhythmias**) nearly triple those in younger patients
- **Exercise tolerance** is the main determinant of outcome; cardiopulmonary function is the key assessment
- **Pneumonectomy**, especially **right**, carries excessive mortality in the elderly; quality of life is also worse
- Minimum cardiac work-up: **TTE to exclude pulmonary hypertension**
cards.e: This is why lung-sparing operations and minimally invasive approaches are favoured in the elderly; pneumonectomy is now about a third of its share of resections 15 years ago. Oxford also lists age >70 as a risk factor in thoracic surgery.

cards.q: What are the risk factors for renal dysfunction after lung resection, and how important is it?
cards.a:
Older series showed high mortality (19% vs 0%) when creatinine rose after thoracotomy, but **transient** dysfunction is no longer clearly linked to death.
- Predictors: **preoperative hypertension**, **ARBs**, **hydroxyethyl starch**, **open thoracotomy**
- Also beware **cisplatin** chemotherapy plus postoperative **NSAIDs**
cards.e: Patients at renal risk should have creatinine and urea measured at the initial assessment. Because fluids are restricted in lung resection, avoiding nephrotoxins (starches, NSAIDs after cisplatin) becomes more important.

cards.q: How is COPD severity staged in the thoracic surgical population, and why do stage II and III patients need an arterial blood gas?
cards.a:
ATS staging by FEV1 % predicted: **stage I >50%**, **stage II 35–50%**, **stage III <35%**.
- Stage I patients should not be dyspneic, hypoxemic or hypercarbic; if they are, look for another cause
- Many stage II/III patients are **CO2 retainers**, who cannot be identified by history, examination or spirometry
- So **all stage II and III** need an ABG preoperatively
cards.e: COPD (emphysema, peripheral airway disease and chronic bronchitis) is the commonest comorbidity in thoracic surgery. Knowing the baseline PaCO2 lets you set postoperative targets and expect the rise in PaCO2 when oxygen is given.

cards.q: Why does PaCO2 rise when a hypercapnic COPD patient is given high-concentration oxygen?
cards.a:
Mainly because of **V/Q redistribution and the Haldane effect**, not loss of hypoxic drive.
- Minute ventilation hardly changes, so reduced drive plays only a minor part
- High FiO2 **releases regional HPV**, sending blood to low-V/Q units and raising dead space and shunt
- **Haldane effect**: oxygenated hemoglobin carries less CO2
- Retention reflects inability to sustain the high work of breathing, not altered respiratory control
cards.e: The practical point is that oxygen must still be given after surgery, because FRC inevitably falls and hypoxemia is more dangerous. Expect the PaCO2 rise and monitor it rather than withholding oxygen.

cards.q: Describe nocturnal hypoxemia and right ventricular dysfunction in COPD. When is home oxygen indicated?
cards.a:
COPD patients desaturate more often and more deeply in sleep because **REM sleep** produces rapid shallow breathing, raising VD/VT.
- This is **not** sleep apnea; COPD does not increase SAHS
- **RV dysfunction** in up to **50%**; caused by chronic recurrent hypoxemia, leading to cor pulmonale
- The RV tolerates sudden afterload rises poorly, e.g. switching from spontaneous to **controlled ventilation**
- Home O2 if resting **PaO2 <55 mm Hg** or falls **<44 mm Hg on exercise**; target **PaO2 60–65 mm Hg**
- Only **oxygen therapy** improves long-term survival and reduces right-heart strain
cards.e: Emphysematous patients tend to have lower cardiac output and mixed venous PO2 but lower PA pressures than bronchitic patients. Stoelting notes that cor pulmonale alone does not mandate heart-lung transplantation because RV function recovers quickly after lung transplantation.

cards.q: Explain the pressure behaviour of a lung bulla during spontaneous and positive-pressure ventilation.
cards.a:
A bulla is an area of lost structural tissue held open by recoil of surrounding lung; its pressure equals the **mean alveolar pressure averaged over the breathing cycle**.
- Spontaneous breathing: intrabulla pressure is slightly **negative** relative to surrounding lung
- **Positive-pressure ventilation**: pressure becomes **positive** relative to the adjacent lung, so the bulla expands and may **rupture**
- Results: **tension pneumothorax** or **bronchopleural fistula**
- Usually asymptomatic unless >50% of the hemithorax (then restrictive defect is added)
- PPV is acceptable with **low airway pressures** and the ability to place a chest drain and isolate the lung immediately
cards.e: Needle studies found no ball-valve mechanism; bullae communicate with airways, sometimes very slowly. Within normal tidal volumes bullae are more compliant than lung and fill first, but beyond that range they become stiff and their pressure rises steeply. Lippincott warns that nitrous oxide should be avoided for the same reason.

cards.q: What is expiratory flow limitation, and why does it make induction dangerous in severe emphysema?
cards.a:
Flow limitation occurs when an **equal pressure point** forms inside intrathoracic airways during expiration, so more effort does not increase flow.
- Normal people reach it only in **forced** expiration; severe COPD patients may be flow-limited during **quiet tidal breathing**
- Caused mainly by loss of **elastic recoil** (emphysema); it is the main cause of airflow obstruction in emphysema
- PPV, even bag-mask at induction, causes **dynamic hyperinflation**: inspiration is easy, expiration is not
- Result: raised intrathoracic pressure, reduced venous return and **hypotension**; the **"Lazarus" syndrome** (recovery only after stopping ventilation)
cards.e: Lippincott explains that pursed-lip breathing and early termination of expiration move the equal pressure point to larger, non-collapsible airways. If hypotension follows induction in these patients, disconnect the circuit briefly and let the lungs empty before reaching for more vasopressors.

cards.q: What is auto-PEEP, what determines its size, and how is it detected?
cards.a:
Auto-PEEP (intrinsic PEEP) is alveolar pressure left at end-expiration because expiration stops before the lung returns to FRC.
- Causes: flow limitation, high airway resistance, increased work of breathing
- Spontaneously breathing: adds an **inspiratory load** (pleural pressure must first overcome it)
- Under mechanical ventilation it grows with **larger tidal volumes** and with **shorter expiratory times**
- **Not shown** on standard anesthesia ventilator manometers; measured by **end-expiratory flow interruption** (ICU ventilators) or seen as persistent end-expiratory flow on flow–volume loops
- Develops in most COPD patients during **OLV**, typically **4–6 cmH2O**
cards.e: Lowering the I:E ratio (longer expiration), reducing tidal volume and respiratory rate all reduce it. During OLV some auto-PEEP may actually help by holding the dependent lung nearer its FRC, which is why emphysematous patients often oxygenate well.

cards.q: Which treatable complications of COPD must be sought and treated at the initial preoperative assessment?
cards.a:
Four: **atelectasis, bronchospasm, respiratory tract infection and pulmonary edema**.
