- Atelectasis impairs local lymphocyte and macrophage function and predisposes to infection
- Pulmonary edema is hard to hear in COPD and may look atypical on X-ray (unilateral, upper lobe)
- Bronchial hyperreactivity may reflect heart failure or reversible obstruction
- All COPD patients should get **maximal bronchodilator** therapy; only **20–25%** respond to steroids, so try steroids if poorly controlled on sympathomimetic plus anticholinergic drugs
cards.e: These are the modifiable items; the underlying emphysema is not. Physiotherapy is the other main intervention, and benefit takes about a month to appear.

cards.q: What is the evidence for chest physiotherapy and pulmonary rehabilitation before thoracic surgery?
cards.a:
An intensive perioperative **chest physiotherapy** programme started before surgery reduces pulmonary complications in COPD.
- No one modality is clearly best (cough/deep breathing, incentive spirometry, PEEP, CPAP)
- Family or non-physiotherapy staff can be trained to deliver it
- Exercise tolerance improves even in severe COPD, but little change occurs **before one month**
- Patients with **copious sputum** benefit most
- Full rehabilitation programmes take months: generally not feasible for cancer but worth considering for **non-malignant** resections
cards.e: Smoking cessation, physiotherapy and thoracic epidural analgesia are the interventions shown to reduce respiratory complications in high-risk thoracic patients. Delaying cancer surgery for months of rehabilitation is not justified.

cards.q: What does Miller say about the timing and benefits of smoking cessation before thoracic surgery?
cards.a:
Pulmonary complications fall when patients stop smoking for **more than 4 weeks** before thoracic surgery.
- **Carboxyhemoglobin** falls if smoking stops for **>12 hours**
- There is **no rebound increase** in complications with shorter (<8 weeks) abstinence, so stopping at any time is worthwhile
- Smoking causes prolonged tissue hypoxemia, impairing wound healing and infection resistance
- Avoiding smoking **after** surgery is very important; intensive cessation programmes work best
cards.e: Lippincott adds that 12–24 hours of abstinence shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve to the right by removing CO, whereas mucociliary transport, sputum volume and small-airway function need 8–12 weeks. The old fear that short-term cessation increases sputum and complications is not supported.

cards.q: Why are patients with interstitial lung disease a particularly high-risk group for lung resection?
cards.a:
They can develop an **acute exacerbation of ILD** after surgery.
- In one series, 3-month mortality after resection was **5% with ILD vs 0.3% without**
- Gas transfer may be badly reduced while spirometry looks near normal
- Restrictive disease is also a risk factor for **desaturation during OLV**
cards.e: Pulmonary fibrosis is the commonest indication for lung transplantation, and Miller notes fibrotic patients tolerate OLV poorly. Limit FiO2 and airway pressures where possible.

cards.q: Compare the subtypes of non-small cell lung cancer and their anesthetic relevance.
cards.a:
NSCLC makes up **75–80%** of lung cancers; 5-year survival with surgery is about **40%** (vs <10% without).
- **Squamous cell**: strongly smoking-related; large central tumours with endobronchial growth; cavitation, hemoptysis, obstructive pneumonia, **SVC syndrome**, main bronchus/carina involvement; **hypercalcemia** from a PTH-like factor (not bone metastases)
- **Adenocarcinoma**: now the commonest; **peripheral**, early metastasis (brain, bone, liver, adrenal); invades chest wall/pericardium; almost all **Pancoast** tumours; GH/ACTH secretion; **hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy**
- **Bronchioloalveolar carcinoma**: adenocarcinoma subtype not linked to smoking; multifocal disease may be treated by transplantation
- **Large cell**: least common; large peripheral cavitating tumour, spreads early
cards.e: Knowing the tissue type warns of airway problems (squamous) or occult metastases (adenocarcinoma). Tobacco causes about 90% of lung cancer; asbestos and radon act as co-carcinogens.

cards.q: What are the characteristics and paraneoplastic syndromes of small cell lung cancer?
cards.a:
SCLC is a **neuroendocrine** tumour regarded as **metastatic at presentation**, so it is usually treated medically; surgery is rarely indicated.
- Staged simply as **limited** or **extensive**; chemotherapy response >80% in limited disease but it almost always recurs; overall survival ≤10%
- **Hyponatremia** from **SIADH** (commonest syndrome)
- **Cushing syndrome** from ectopic **ACTH**
- **Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome** (rare)
cards.e: Carcinoids lie at the benign end of the same neuroendocrine spectrum. Check sodium and glucose/cortisol status in a patient with SCLC presenting for any procedure, such as mediastinoscopy for staging.

cards.q: What are the anesthetic implications of Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
cards.a:
LEMS is a paraneoplastic disorder (classically SCLC) with **impaired presynaptic acetylcholine release**.
- Presents with **proximal lower-limb weakness** that may briefly improve with exercise
- EMG: action potential amplitude **increases** with high-frequency stimulation
- Patients are **very sensitive to nondepolarizing** relaxants (and to depolarizing ones)
- They respond **poorly to anticholinesterase reversal**
- Subclinical **respiratory muscle** involvement may exist
- TEA has been used safely; weakness may improve after the tumour is removed
cards.e: Contrast myasthenia gravis, where the defect is postsynaptic receptor loss, patients are resistant to succinylcholine and neostigmine reversal works. In LEMS the exercise-related improvement and incremental EMG response separate it from MG.

cards.q: What are the anesthetic concerns with bronchial carcinoid tumours?
cards.a:
Carcinoids are low-grade neuroendocrine tumours; typical carcinoid has **>90% 5-year survival** after resection, atypical ones are more aggressive.
- Carcinoid syndrome is rare from bronchial tumours (usually gut carcinoids with liver metastases)
- They can still cause an **intraoperative hemodynamic crisis** or **coronary spasm**, even during bronchoscopic resection
- Severe hypotension may not respond to usual vasopressors; treat with **octreotide or somatostatin**
cards.e: Have octreotide available for any carcinoid resection, including rigid bronchoscopic debulking. Carcinoid is also a common indication for sleeve lobectomy.

cards.q: Summarise malignant pleural mesothelioma and its anesthetic relevance.
cards.a:
MPM is strongly linked to **asbestos** (up to **80%**), with no clear dose–response and a latency of up to **40–50 years**.
- Grows along the pleura with a **bloody effusion**; presents with dyspnea
- Thoracentesis relieves symptoms but rarely diagnoses; **VATS pleural biopsy** with **talc pleurodesis** in one anesthetic is most efficient
- Median survival **<1 year**
- **Extrapleural pneumonectomy** for early disease: major blood loss from denuded chest wall, plus risks of diaphragm and pericardial resection
cards.e: Localised fibrous tumours of the pleura (formerly "benign mesothelioma") are a different, usually large space-occupying lesion that may be benign or malignant. Extrapleural pneumonectomy is one of the highest-risk operations for arrhythmia and cardiac herniation.

cards.q: What are the "4 M's" to assess in a lung cancer patient?
cards.a:
**Mass effects, Metabolic effects, Metastases and Medications.**
- **Mass**: obstructive pneumonia, abscess, **SVC syndrome**, tracheobronchial distortion, **Pancoast** syndrome, recurrent laryngeal or phrenic palsy, chest wall/mediastinal extension
- **Metabolic**: Lambert–Eaton, **hypercalcemia**, **hyponatremia**, Cushing syndrome
- **Metastases**: brain, bone, liver, adrenal
- **Medications**: lung toxicity from **bleomycin** or **mitomycin**; cardiotoxic **doxorubicin**; nephrotoxic **cisplatin**
cards.e: This is a quick structure for an exam answer on any thoracic cancer patient. Oxford lists the same non-metastatic manifestations (Eaton–Lambert, ectopic hormones) in its lung resection section.

cards.q: Why does previous bleomycin or cisplatin therapy matter in thoracic anesthesia?
cards.a:
**Bleomycin** predisposes to **oxygen-induced pulmonary toxicity**; **cisplatin** predisposes to renal injury with NSAIDs.
- Bleomycin is used for germ-cell tumours, so these patients often present for resection of lung metastases
- The safe FiO2 and safe interval after exposure are **unknown**
- Use the **lowest FiO2** compatible with safety and monitor oximetry closely; TIVA may help limit FiO2 during OLV; CPAP can be given with an air/oxygen blender
- After recent cisplatin, the authors **avoid routine NSAIDs** (creatinine rises)
cards.e: Bleomycin patients are the classic exception to the first step of hypoxemia treatment ("raise FiO2 to 1.0"). Plan prophylactic CPAP or PEEP early in these patients so that high FiO2 is less needed.

cards.q: What should be arranged about postoperative analgesia at the initial preoperative visit, including neuraxial timing with thromboprophylaxis?
cards.a:
The analgesic plan should be discussed and contraindications identified (coagulopathy, sepsis, neurological disease).
- Only **epidural techniques** have consistently reduced respiratory complications in high-risk patients
- US-guided **ESP or paravertebral** blocks may give similar analgesia with fewer failures and side effects
- ASRA: **4–6 h** after prophylactic UFH before catheter placement (no delay needed after)
- LMWH: **12 h** after low-dose and **24 h** after higher-dose before placement
cards.e: The interval rules are about the timing of needle and catheter placement relative to anticoagulant doses, so they must be planned with the surgeons in advance. Septic patients (e.g., empyema) should not receive a thoracic epidural.

cards.q: What premedication is appropriate for pulmonary resection patients?
cards.a:
Routine sedative or analgesic premedication is **not** needed.
- Light IV short-acting **benzodiazepine** just before invasive lines is common
- **Antisialagogue** (e.g., glycopyrrolate) for patients with **copious secretions**, to help fiberoptic positioning of DLT or blocker; give orally or IV rather than IM
- Short-term IV **antibiotic prophylaxis** (e.g., cephalosporin); plan alternatives for allergy
cards.e: A dry airway matters because the DLT lumens are narrow and the bronchoscope view is easily lost in secretions. Oxford notes the scope for checking a DLT must usually be under 4 mm.

cards.q: What two specific assessments are added at the final (day-of-surgery) preoperative evaluation for thoracic surgery?
cards.a:
After reviewing the initial assessment and test results, assess:
- **Difficulty of lung isolation**: the anesthesiologist should personally review the **chest X-ray** (best predictor of difficult endobronchial intubation) and **CT**
- **Risk of desaturation during OLV**
- CT may show a **"saber-sheath" trachea** (side-to-side distal tracheal compression) that can obstruct the tracheal lumen of a left DLT, or bronchial compression/intraluminal tumour
cards.e: Radiology and surgical reports are not written with lung isolation in mind, so you must look yourself. The anesthesiologist often meets the patient only 10–15 minutes before induction, which is why the assessment is split into two phases.

cards.q: List the factors that predict desaturation during one-lung ventilation.
cards.a:
Box 49.7 factors:
- High fraction of **ventilation or perfusion to the operative lung** on V/Q scan
- Poor **PaO2 during two-lung ventilation**, especially in the **lateral** position (the most important predictor)
- **Right-sided** thoracotomy
- **Normal** preoperative spirometry (FEV1/FVC) or **restrictive** disease
- **Supine** position during OLV
cards.e: The left lung is about 10% smaller, so collapsing it creates less shunt; mean PaO2 was about 70–100 mm Hg higher for left than right thoracotomy. Long-standing unilateral disease reduces perfusion to the operative lung, so those patients rarely desaturate. High-risk patients should get prophylactic CPAP and/or dependent-lung PEEP.

cards.q: Why is arterial PaO2 more useful than SpO2 during thoracic surgery?
cards.a:
PaO2 shows the **margin of safety** above desaturation, which SpO2 cannot.
- Significant desaturation (SpO2 <90%) during OLV still occurs in **1–10%** despite FiO2 1.0
- TLV PaO2 **>400 mm Hg** on FiO2 1.0: unlikely to desaturate on OLV
- TLV PaO2 **200 mm Hg**: prone to desaturate, although both show SpO2 99–100%
cards.e: On the flat part of the dissociation curve SpO2 hides large differences in PaO2. This is one reason most thoracotomies get an arterial line, together with transient hypotension from surgical compression of the heart and great vessels.

cards.q: How does end-tidal CO2 behave during positioning and one-lung ventilation?
cards.a:
PETCO2 is a **less reliable** guide to PaCO2 during OLV, and the **PaCO2–PETCO2 gradient widens**.
- Turning lateral: PETCO2 of the nondependent lung falls (more dead space, less perfusion) though it still excretes a larger fraction of CO2
- Start of OLV: dependent-lung PETCO2 falls briefly, then rises as perfusion shifts to it
- Without minute ventilation change, PaCO2 and PETCO2 both rise with a larger gradient
- Lateral position usually needs about **20% more minute ventilation**
- A severe (**>5 mm Hg**) or prolonged fall in PETCO2 suggests maldistribution of perfusion and may herald **desaturation**
cards.e: Because PETCO2 also reflects perfusion, it gives information about how blood flow is distributing between the lungs. Check an arterial gas to set ventilation during prolonged OLV.

cards.q: What is the role of CVP and pulmonary artery catheters in thoracic surgery?
cards.a:
Both are less reliable in the lateral position with the chest open.
- **CVP**: useful postoperatively when fluids are critical (e.g., pneumonectomy), for vasopressors or access; routine for pneumonectomy, complex or redo cases
- Right IJ for right-sided surgery; some use left IJ for left-sided surgery for easier access; **IJ CVP is unreliable with SVC obstruction**
- **PAC**: unknown whether the tip is in the dependent or nondependent lung; thermodilution may be unreliable with unequal lung perfusion during OLV
- PAC remains the basis of monitoring in significant **pulmonary hypertension**
cards.e: In esophagectomy avoid the left IJ because the anastomosis may be in the left neck. Because adding invasive monitors mid-case is hard, the balance often favours more invasive monitoring at the start.

cards.q: What monitoring confirms the position of lung-isolation devices, and what does continuous spirometry add?
cards.a:
**Fiberoptic bronchoscopy** is the standard; auscultation misses many malpositions, and devices often move when the patient is turned, so recheck after positioning.
- **Lung ultrasound**: alternative if no bronchoscope; better than auscultation; lung sliding and **seashore** sign = ventilated, absent sliding and **barcode** sign = not ventilated; less useful with effusions, adhesions or BPF and for repositioning during surgery
- **Continuous side-stream spirometry**: sudden fall in expired Vt warns of DLT displacement (normal inspired–expired difference 20–30 mL/breath); persistent end-expiratory flow indicates auto-PEEP; quantifies air leaks
cards.e: Lippincott quotes malposition rates of 20–48% when DLT placement is checked by auscultation alone, and identifies a low exhaled tidal volume alarm as the earliest sign of DLT displacement after positioning.

cards.q: What are the indications for TEE and cerebral oximetry in thoracic surgery?
cards.a:
**TEE** gives continuous real-time information on myocardial function and preload, hard to judge in the lateral position.
- Indications: hemodynamic instability, pericardial effusion, cardiac tumour involvement, air embolism, PTE, chest trauma, lung transplantation, pleuropulmonary disease
- Detects **right-to-left shunt through a PFO**: PEEP to 15 cmH2O caused intracardiac R→L shunt in **9%** of noncardiac patients
- **Cerebral oximetry**: falls in SctO2 during OLV are commoner in elderly, debilitated patients and are linked to falls in SpO2 and postoperative cognitive dysfunction; no proof treating them improves outcome
cards.e: An unexplained refractory hypoxemia during OLV with high PEEP should prompt a search for a PFO shunt. Indirect cardiac output monitors are of uncertain validity with an open chest.

cards.q: What are the indications for lung isolation, and what are the three ways to achieve it?
cards.a:
Indications:
- **Surgical exposure** (OLV) for thoracic, cardiac, mediastinal, vascular, esophageal and spinal surgery
- **Protection** from contralateral soiling: bronchopleural fistula, pulmonary hemorrhage, whole-lung lavage, infection
- **Differential ventilation**: unilateral reperfusion injury (after lung transplant or PTE), unilateral trauma
Methods:
- **DLT** (commonest)
- **Bronchial blocker** through or alongside an SLT, or within a Univent tube
- **Single-lumen endobronchial tube** advanced into the contralateral bronchus: rare in adults (difficult airway, carinal resection, post-pneumonectomy); still used in infants
cards.e: Oxford lists the absolute indications (contamination, control of ventilation distribution) separately from relative surgical ones, and notes that DLTs and blockers are clinically equivalent for OLV. Oxford also reminds that OLV always creates a shunt and causes acute lung injury in 2–5%.

cards.q: Trace the development of the double-lumen tube and describe newer DLT designs.
cards.a:
**Carlens (1950)**: left DLT with a **carinal hook**; high resistance, hook hard to pass through the glottis.
- **Robertshaw (1960s)**: separate left and right tubes, no hook, larger lumens; basis of modern disposable **PVC** tubes with blue low-pressure bronchial cuffs and radiopaque markers
- **VivaSight**: integrated **camera** at the tracheal lumen tip for continuous carinal view and lens flushing; may avoid bronchoscopy; use defogger; light source can melt the tube
- **ECOM DLT**: cuff electrodes measure aortic **bioimpedance** for cardiac output (with an arterial line)
- **Silbroncho**: silicone, **wire-reinforced flexible bronchial tip**, shorter bronchial cuff; useful for tube exchange
cards.e: Oxford adds White's right-sided tube with a hook and RUL slit. The VivaSight is also suggested in COVID-19 to reduce bronchoscopy-related aerosol exposure.

cards.q: How is a DLT size selected?
cards.a:
A left DLT's **bronchial tip should be 1–2 mm smaller** than the left main bronchus, to allow room for the deflated cuff.
- Review **chest X-ray and CT** (tracheal and bronchial widths; 3D CT reconstruction can predict size)
- Simplified rule by sex and height (Lippincott): women **<160 cm 35 Fr**, ≥160 cm **37 Fr**; men **<170 cm 39 Fr**, ≥170 cm **41 Fr**
- DLTs have a **large outer diameter**; never push against significant resistance
- The mean **cricoid** diameter is about the same as the **left main bronchus**
cards.e: Lippincott notes bronchial diameter is about 0.68 times tracheal width, so a PA film tracheal measurement does help sizing. Oxford: use the largest tube that passes easily, and remember a 35 Fr Broncho-Cath has lumens of only about 4.5 mm.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 49 · Lippincott Ch 12 · Oxford Handbook Ch 15

cards.q: Describe the methods of inserting a left-sided DLT and how insertion depth is estimated.
cards.a:
**Blind technique**: direct laryngoscopy, then rotate **90° counterclockwise** once the bronchial cuff passes the cords and advance.
- **Fiberoptic-guided technique**: scope guides the bronchial tip into the bronchus after passing the cords; one study showed similar eventual success but longer time (**181 vs 88 s**)
- Depth at the teeth ≈ **12 + (height in cm/10) cm**; unreliable in shorter patients (e.g., <155 cm)
- Too deep insertion risks **left main bronchus rupture**
- **Videolaryngoscopes**: views similar to a Miller blade; GlideScope not recommended routinely in normal airways; benefit depends on operator and anatomy
cards.e: Oxford gives the equivalent: 29 cm at the mouth corner for a 170 cm patient, changing 1 cm per 10 cm of height. Whatever the insertion method, final position must be confirmed by bronchoscopy.

cards.q: Why is a right-sided DLT designed differently, and when is it indicated?
cards.a:
The **right main bronchus is short**, and the **RUL bronchus arises 1.5–2 cm** from the carina, so a right DLT has a modified cuff and a **ventilation slot** for the RUL.
Indications (normal RUL anatomy assumed):
- Distorted entry to the left main bronchus: external or intraluminal tumour, **descending thoracic aortic aneurysm**
- Surgery involving the left main bronchus: **left lung transplant**, left tracheobronchial disruption, **left pneumonectomy**, **left sleeve resection**
cards.e: A left pneumonectomy can be done with a left DLT or blocker, but it must be withdrawn before the bronchus is stapled. Lippincott stresses that uniform ventilation of all lobes is easier with a left DLT, because the RUL slot is easily misaligned.

cards.q: Describe the fiberoptic confirmation of a left-sided DLT.
cards.a:
Scope the **tracheal lumen first**, then the bronchial lumen.
- Tracheal view: bronchial lumen enters the **left** bronchus; the blue bronchial cuff sits about **5–10 mm below the carina** with no herniation over it
- Identify the **RUL**: the only structure with **three orifices** (apical, anterior, posterior), usually at **3–4 o'clock** on the lateral right main bronchus when supine
- Broncho-Cath radiopaque line is **4 cm** from the bronchial tip; seen just above the carina it gives a safety margin
- Bronchial view: lumen patent, and both **left upper and left lower lobe** orifices visible (avoid LLL impaction and LUL occlusion)
- Recheck after turning the patient
cards.e: Recognising the RUL is the anatomical landmark that tells you which side you are on. Auscultation is still done but cannot replace this check; repeat bronchoscopy whenever the patient is repositioned.

cards.q: What are the main problems related to DLTs and how do you deal with them?
cards.a:
The main problems are **malposition** and **airway trauma**.
- Malposition: failure of lung collapse, gas trapping, or partial collapse of the ventilated lung with **hypoxemia**; causes include cuff overinflation, surgical traction, head/neck extension; diagnose and fix with **bronchoscopy**
- If position is correct but collapse incomplete: pass a **suction catheter** down the operative lumen, then remove it so it is not stapled
- Airway trauma: oversized tube, or an undersized tube migrating distally so the main body enters the bronchus; presents as unexpected air leak, **subcutaneous emphysema**, bleeding into the lumen, or a cuff visible in the surgical field; needs bronchoscopy and surgical repair
- **Tension pneumothorax** in the dependent ventilated lung can occur during OLV
cards.e: Lippincott's high-resistance scenario (tracheal lumen cannot be ventilated once both cuffs are up) is usually a tube in the wrong bronchus or a herniated bronchial cuff. Deflating the bronchial cuff is the quick rescue.

cards.q: When might a bronchial blocker be preferred to a DLT?
cards.a:
When a DLT is difficult or disadvantageous:
- **Difficult airway** (previous oral/neck surgery, radiation): secure with an SLT (awake oral or nasal, or tracheostomy), then add a blocker
- **Previous contralateral resection**: selective **lobar** blockade improves oxygenation and access
- Planned **postoperative ventilation** after long thoracic/esophageal surgery: no tube change in an edematous airway
- Tracheostomy patients; children (some blockers can go outside a smaller SLT)
- Tube size: standard 9-Fr blocker needs an **ETT ≥7.0 mm ID** with a bronchoscope <4.0 mm; larger scopes need **>7.5 mm**
cards.e: Lippincott lists blocker drawbacks: high-pressure small cuff, slow collapse through a tiny lumen, and limited suction. Oxford speeds collapse by ventilating with 100% O2 and inflating the blocker at end-expiration. Lippincott's distractor is that blockers do not give better collapse than a DLT.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 49 · Lippincott Ch 12 · Oxford Handbook Ch 15

cards.q: Compare the Arndt, Cohen, Fuji Uniblocker and EZ-Blocker bronchial blockers.
cards.a:
All are used with a standard SLT under bronchoscopic guidance and need good lubrication.
- **Arndt**: wire **loop** snared over the bronchoscope to guide it; enters the right main bronchus easily even without the loop
- **Cohen**: proximal **wheel deflects the pre-angled tip**; an arrow on the shaft shows the deflection direction
- **Fuji Uniblocker**: silicone with a fixed **hockey-stick** tip; simply rotated into the chosen bronchus
- **EZ-Blocker**: 7-Fr, four-lumen, **Y-shaped** with a balloon on each limb; Y sits on the carina; used through a 7.5 SLT
- **Univent**: blocker built into a channel of a modified SLT
cards.e: Cohen and Fuji blockers can also be passed outside the SLT, through the glottis or a tracheostomy, allowing a smaller tube. The choice usually depends on familiarity; the bronchoscope is mandatory for all.

cards.q: What complications are associated with bronchial blockers?
cards.a:
- **Failed isolation** from abnormal anatomy or poor seal
- **Stapling** the blocker or Arndt wire loop into the bronchial stump: withdraw the blocker a few cm before stapling and tell the surgeon it is there
- **Balloon migrates above the carina** or is inflated in the trachea: inability to ventilate, hypoxia, possible arrest; deflate at once
- More malpositions than with DLTs in some reports
- **Failure to deflate** (Fuji): test inflation and full deflation before use
- **Bronchial perforation** (EZ-Blocker advanced blindly in irradiated tissue; Fuji in a 78-year-old): always advance under bronchoscopic view
cards.e: A blocker that suddenly makes ventilation impossible has almost certainly slipped back into the trachea, so deflating it is the first move. Unexplained air leak or mediastinal air should raise suspicion of airway rupture.

cards.q: How do you achieve lung isolation in a patient with a difficult airway?
cards.a:
First secure the airway with an **SLT**, then isolate.
- Fiberoptic oral intubation after airway topicalisation (or asleep with bronchoscope/videolaryngoscope in easy-to-ventilate patients), then an **independent bronchial blocker**
- If oral route impossible: **awake nasal** SLT plus blocker
- Alternative: SLT, then exchange for a **DLT over an exchange catheter**
- Exchange catheter ≥**83 cm**; **14 Fr** for 41/39 Fr DLTs, **11 Fr** for 37/35 Fr; soft-tipped versions reduce trauma
- Test the combination in vitro; sniffing position; do not insert the catheter deeper than **24 cm** at the lips; use a **videolaryngoscope** during exchange
- Bronchoscopy first to assess any distorted lower airway (e.g., aortic aneurysm, tumour at the carina)
cards.e: Between 5% and 8% of lung cancer patients also have a pharyngeal cancer, often irradiated or previously operated, so difficult airways are common in this population. The Silbroncho tube's flexible tip makes exchange easier.

cards.q: How should lung isolation be managed in a COVID-19-positive patient?
cards.a:
Use full **PPE** and reduce aerosol generation.
- Asymptomatic PCR-negative patients are managed as before the pandemic
- Either DLT or SLT plus blocker; blocker use rose about fourfold in an Italian survey
- **Videolaryngoscopy** to keep distance from the airway
- **Disposable** bronchoscope where possible
- **HEPA filter** on the nondependent lumen of the DLT
- **VivaSight** DLT allows positioning without repeated bronchoscopy
cards.e: Every bronchoscopy and lumen opening is an aerosol event, so equipment that minimises them is preferred. Teams should be ready to perform emergency thoracic procedures in infected patients.

cards.q: What are the options for lung isolation in a patient with a tracheostomy?
cards.a:
A conventional DLT is often too long, too wide or too rigid for the stoma, and the shortened airway encourages malposition. Check whether the stoma is **fresh** (airway may be lost on decannulation) or mature.
- SLT through the stoma plus an **independent blocker** (coaxial or alongside)
- **Cuffed tracheostomy cannula** plus independent blocker
- Short purpose-made DLT (**Naruke** tube)
- Small DLT through the stoma
- Oral DLT or blocker if the upper airway is usable
- **Bronchial blockers are optimal** for most
cards.e: The "ABCs" apply: know the Anatomy, use the Bronchoscope, look at the Chest imaging. An online virtual bronchoscopy simulator exists to train these skills.

cards.q: What are the "ABCs" of lung isolation?
cards.a:
- **Anatomy**: know the tracheobronchial tree; lack of familiarity with distal airway anatomy is a major cause of failed isolation
- **Bronchoscopy**: use a fiberoptic bronchoscope to place and confirm tubes and blockers whenever possible; a core skill for thoracic anesthesiologists
- **Chest imaging**: always look at the X-ray and CT before choosing and placing a device
cards.e: The best method in an individual case depends on airway anatomy, the indication for isolation, the equipment available and the anesthesiologist's training. These three principles apply regardless of device.

cards.q: What are the anesthetic concerns when turning a patient to the lateral position?
cards.a:
Induction is usually supine, then the patient is turned.
- **Hypotension** is common because of loss of venous tone under anesthesia
- The anesthesiologist directs the turn and controls head, neck and airway; turn head, neck and tube **en bloc** with the spine
- Some DLT or blocker movement is almost inevitable; carina and mediastinum may shift independently, causing **proximal displacement**
- Do a **head-to-toe survey** after induction and repeat after positioning; recheck tube by auscultation and **bronchoscopy**
- Robotic surgery: airway access mid-case is very hard, so confirm position before docking
cards.e: Lateral induction is occasionally used for unilateral bleeding or bronchiectasis until isolation is secured, but the diseased lung must still end up nondependent. Lippincott notes that a low exhaled volume alarm is often the first sign that the tube moved.

cards.q: Describe brachial plexus injuries in the lateral position and how to avoid them.
cards.a:
The brachial plexus is the commonest site of position-related nerve injury; it is fixed at the **cervical transverse processes** and **axillary fascia**, so it is easily compressed or stretched.
- **Dependent arm (compression)**: arm under the thorax, clavicle pressed into the retroclavicular space, cervical rib, chest padding slipping **into the axilla**
- **Nondependent arm (stretch)**: lateral neck flexion, abduction **>90°**, repositioning semi-prone/supine after the arm is fixed to a rest
- Arms: no abduction >90°, no extension behind neutral, no forward flexion >90°
- Padding goes **under the thorax, never in the axilla** (the "axillary roll" is a misnomer)
- Most injuries recover over months
cards.e: Excess lateral neck flexion adds plexus traction and a "whiplash" injury, and is hard to see once drapes are up, so view the spine alignment from the side after turning. Suprascapular nerve traction (arm circumducted across the chest) may explain some post-thoracotomy shoulder pain.

cards.q: List the elements of the head-to-toe survey for neurovascular injury in the lateral position.
cards.a:
- **Dependent eye** and **dependent ear pinna**
- **Cervical spine** in line with thoracic spine
- **Dependent arm**: brachial plexus and circulation
- **Nondependent arm**: brachial plexus and circulation (worse if suspended on an independent arm rest)
- **Suprascapular nerves** on both sides
- **Nondependent leg**: **sciatic** nerve (tight hip strapping)
- **Dependent leg**: **peroneal** nerve (pad below the knee, leg slightly flexed) and circulation
cards.e: A routine checklist is used because these injuries are silent under anesthesia. Repeat the survey after every position change, not only at the start.

cards.q: How does ventilation change between the lungs in the lateral position?
cards.a:
The two lungs sit on different compliance curves (different sizes, plus chest wall and lung recoil), and anesthesia magnifies the difference.
- Awake, spontaneous: dependent-lung ventilation **rises ~10%**
- Anesthetised and paralysed: dependent-lung ventilation **falls ~15%**
- Opening the nondependent chest: ventilation little changed, but its FRC rises ~10%; total respiratory compliance rises
- With the chest open, lung volume at end-expiration depends on expiratory time
- **Selective PEEP to the dependent lung** (DLT, separate circuits) improves gas exchange; nonselective PEEP mostly overinflates the nondependent lung
- Atelectasis: ~6% of lung after supine induction (both bases); ~5% after turning, all in the **dependent** lung
cards.e: Lippincott explains that awake V/Q matching is preserved because the dependent hemidiaphragm is stretched higher and contracts better, while gravity also sends it more blood. Paralysis and PPV remove that advantage, so ventilation goes to the upper lung while perfusion stays below.

cards.q: How does perfusion and shunt change in the lateral position under anesthesia?
cards.a:
Dependent-lung blood flow increases by about **10%** compared with the same lung supine.
- Distribution may depend more on intrinsic vascular anatomy than on gravity
- V/Q matching is usually **worse** lateral than supine under anesthesia
- Shunt rises from about **5% supine to 10–15% lateral** during GA
cards.e: With paralysis the upper lung gets more ventilation and the lower lung more blood, so mismatch increases even before OLV starts. This is why two-lung PaO2 in the lateral position is the best predictor of OLV oxygenation.

cards.q: What is the "pneumothorax syndrome", and why did it delay thoracic surgery?
cards.a:
An open hemithorax in a **spontaneously breathing** patient causes two problems:
- **Paradoxical respiration (pendelluft)**: gas moves from the intact lung into the open-chest lung on expiration and back on inspiration, causing **hypoxemia and hypercapnia**
- **Mediastinal shift/swing** with each breath, which impairs **venous return** and causes hemodynamic instability
- The solution was **positive-pressure** and endotracheal ventilation, advocated by pioneers such as **Matas**
cards.e: Lippincott emphasises that the main effect of mediastinal shift in an open pneumothorax is to reduce the dependent lung's contribution to tidal volume. Thoracic surgery lagged more than 50 years behind ether until this was solved.

cards.q: State the fluid management principles for pulmonary resection surgery.
cards.a:
Be **restrictive**, because the dependent lung must carry gas exchange and fluid excess causes dependent-lung edema and shunt.
- Positive balance in the first 24 h **≤20 mL/kg**
- Crystalloid **<3 L** in the first 24 h for an average adult
- **No third-space** replacement
- Urine output **>0.5 mL/kg/h is unnecessary**
- If perfusion needs support, use **invasive monitoring and inotropes** rather than fluid overload
cards.e: Lippincott calls the gravitational transudation into the dependent lung the "lower lung syndrome"; it is worsened by crystalloid excess and is not a volutrauma injury. Excess fluid is also an independent risk factor for postpneumonectomy lung injury.

cards.q: Why is temperature control important in thoracic surgery, and how is bronchospasm prevented?
cards.a:
**Temperature**: heat is lost from the open hemithorax, especially at age extremes; hypothermia **inhibits HPV** and most physiological functions. Use warm room, fluid warmers and upper/lower-body forced air.
**Bronchospasm** (common reactive airways plus DLT/blocker manipulation):
- Avoid instrumenting a lightly anesthetised airway
- Induction with **propofol or ketamine** reduces bronchospasm; barbiturates, opioids, benzodiazepines and etomidate do not
- Maintain with propofol and/or a volatile; **sevoflurane** may be the most potent bronchodilator
- Avoid histamine-releasing drugs
cards.e: The DLT is a powerful bronchospastic stimulus because it sits on the carina. Lippincott notes volatile agents dilate bronchi through mechanisms independent of catecholamines.

cards.q: How can collapse of the operative lung be speeded at the start of OLV, and how is the dependent lung prepared?
cards.a:
**Denitrogenate** the operative lung by ventilating with **oxygen** just before isolating it; nitrogen (air) is poorly soluble and delays collapse.
- Slow collapse is a particular problem at the start of **VATS** and in **emphysema** (low elastic recoil)
- **Nitrous oxide** collapses lung even faster but is avoided because of bullae and blebs
- Atelectasis forms in the **dependent lung** during the TLV period: perform a **recruitment manoeuvre** at the start of OLV, e.g. **20 cmH2O for 15–20 s**
cards.e: The aim during OLV is the conflicting one of maximising collapse of the operative lung while avoiding any atelectasis in the ventilated lung. With a blocker, Oxford advises inflating it at end-expiration after 100% O2 to speed collapse.

cards.q: What is an acceptable oxygen saturation during OLV, and why has hypoxemia become less common?
cards.a:
**SpO2 ≥90% (PaO2 >60 mm Hg)** is commonly accepted; brief high-80s may be tolerated in fit patients.
- Accept a **higher** floor with coronary or cerebrovascular disease, anemia, or poor cardiopulmonary reserve
- COPD patients desaturate faster with isovolemic hemodilution
- Incidence of SaO2 <90% fell from **20–25%** (1950–1980) to **<5%**
- Reasons: **fiberoptic** confirmation of tubes (no lobar obstruction), anesthetics with **less HPV inhibition**, better understanding of OLV physiology
cards.e: Older studies used 2–3 MAC halothane, a strong HPV inhibitor, which explains much of the historical hypoxemia. The anesthesiologist aims to maximise PVR in the collapsed lung and minimise it in the ventilated lung.

cards.q: Explain the relationship between lung volume and pulmonary vascular resistance and its relevance to OLV.
cards.a:
PVR has a **U-shaped (hyperbolic) relationship** with lung volume and is **lowest at FRC**.
- Below FRC: extra-alveolar vessels narrow (and atelectasis triggers HPV), so PVR rises
- Above FRC: alveolar vessels are stretched and compressed, so PVR rises
- Goal in OLV: keep the **ventilated lung near FRC** (low PVR) and let the operative lung **collapse** (high PVR), so blood moves to the ventilated lung
cards.e: This explains why both atelectasis and overdistension of the dependent lung worsen oxygenation, and why PEEP helps only if it moves the lung toward FRC. Lippincott notes the effect of PEEP depends on where the lung sits on the PEEP–PVR curve.

cards.q: Why is OLV better tolerated in the lateral than the supine position?
cards.a:
In the lateral position **gravity adds to HPV**, diverting blood away from the uppermost collapsed lung.
- PaO2 during OLV is significantly better lateral than supine
- This holds for normal lungs and for COPD
- **Supine OLV** is listed as a risk factor for desaturation
cards.e: Supine OLV is common in some VATS procedures, bilateral procedures and anterior approaches, so expect more hypoxemia and consider prophylactic measures. In supine bronchopulmonary lavage, oxygenation follows the blood flow shifts as the lavaged lung fills and empties.

cards.q: Describe hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: its stimulus, time course and modifiers.
cards.a:
HPV can cut blood flow to the nonventilated lung by about **50%**.
- Main stimulus: **alveolar PO2**; mixed venous PO2 is a weaker stimulus
- Mechanism: **precapillary** vasoconstriction via pathways involving **NO and/or cyclooxygenase** inhibition
- **Biphasic onset**: rapid phase plateaus at **20–30 min**; delayed phase starts after **40 min**, plateaus at **~2 h**
- **Biphasic offset**: PVR may stay raised for hours, worsening oxygenation when the **second lung** is collapsed in bilateral surgery
- **Preconditioning**: a second hypoxic challenge produces a stronger response
- Inhibited by **vasodilators** (nitroglycerin, nitroprusside), hypothermia, hypocapnia/alkalosis, infection; surgery can release vasoactive substances or mechanically reduce flow
- TEA has little direct effect but can worsen oxygenation if it lowers cardiac output
cards.e: Lippincott lists infection, pulmonary hypotension or hypertension, low PaCO2, altered SvO2, β-agonists, calcium blockers, nitrates and volatile agents as HPV inhibitors; hypercapnia is the exception. Preconditioning explains why oxygenation is often better after a brief reinflation and second collapse.

cards.q: How do anesthetic agents affect HPV and oxygenation during OLV?
cards.a:
All volatile agents inhibit HPV dose-dependently, but modern agents at **≤1 MAC** are **weak and equipotent** inhibitors.
- Older order of inhibition: halothane > enflurane > isoflurane
- 1 MAC isoflurane reduces the HPV response by about **20%**, adding only about **4%** to total shunt
- **TIVA** may still matter in critical cases, e.g. bleomycin patients needing low FiO2
- **Dexmedetomidine** to reduce volatile dose improves OLV oxygenation
- **Nitrous oxide**: more dependent-lung atelectasis (51% vs 24% with air/O2), raises PA pressure in PH, inhibits HPV; avoid
- Volatile techniques may release fewer **proinflammatory cytokines**
cards.e: Lippincott's MCQ asks which agent at a given end-tidal value has least effect on HPV; the answer is whichever is below 1 MAC (e.g., desflurane 5.5%). If oxygenation is poor, reducing volatile to ≤1 MAC is one of the listed steps.

cards.q: How does cardiac output affect oxygenation during OLV?
cards.a:
The effect is **biphasic** because cardiac output changes both shunt and SvO2.
- **Higher output**: raises PA pressure, passively dilates vessels, opposes HPV, so **shunt increases**; but SvO2 rises (fixed VO2)
- These effects oppose each other; SvO2 has a ceiling, so **supranormal** output with inotropes (e.g., dopamine) tends to **lower PaO2**
- **Low output**: shunt falls but SvO2 falls more, so **PaO2 falls**
- With a 20–30% shunt even at best, **maintaining normal cardiac output** is essential
cards.e: A common intraoperative cause of sudden desaturation is the surgeon compressing the IVC or heart, which drops output. Treat epidural-induced hypotension with vasopressors or inotropes rather than accepting a low output.

cards.q: How do respiratory acid–base changes affect HPV and gas exchange during OLV?
cards.a:
**Respiratory acidosis increases** HPV in hypoxic lung and **alkalosis inhibits** it.
- But deliberate **hypoventilation does not help**, because acidosis also constricts vessels in the well-oxygenated ventilated lung, opposing redistribution
- **Hyperventilation** tends to lower pulmonary vascular pressures overall
cards.e: Lippincott's MCQ lists hypocapnia as an HPV inhibitor and hypercapnia as the exception. In practice, aim for normocapnia rather than trying to manipulate HPV with CO2.

cards.q: Why has practice moved from large to small tidal volumes during OLV?
cards.a:
Large Vt (e.g., **10 mL/kg** IBW) may give higher PaO2 by repeatedly recruiting dependent-lung atelectasis, but:
- Hypoxemia is now much less common
- Prolonged large Vt risks **acute injury to the ventilated lung**
- Cyclic **atelectasis and re-recruitment** is itself injurious
- So use smaller Vt with **PEEP**, individualised to the patient's lung mechanics
cards.e: Oxford notes OLV causes acute lung injury in 2–5% of cases, reduced by a protective strategy with lower airway pressures and PEEP. Pneumonectomy and esophagectomy data support 5–6 mL/kg.

cards.q: Give the suggested starting ventilator settings for one-lung ventilation.
cards.a:
A simplified, protective starting point:
- **Vt 5–6 mL/kg IBW** plus **PEEP 5 cmH2O** (except in COPD, where auto-PEEP may suffice)
- **Peak pressure <35 cmH2O**, roughly **plateau <25 cmH2O**; peaks >40 may cause hyperinflation injury
- About **20% more minute ventilation** after turning lateral to keep PaCO2 constant
- **Recruitment manoeuvre** at the start of OLV
- Titrate PEEP (5–10) to the lowest **driving pressure** (plateau minus PEEP), ideally **≤15 cmH2O**
- Follow PaCO2 by blood gas, as PETCO2 is unreliable
cards.e: The optimal combination of Vt, rate, I:E and mode differs between patients, and the response to Vt changes is unpredictable partly because of auto-PEEP. Driving pressure titration is currently the most rational way to individualise PEEP.

cards.q: How do external PEEP and auto-PEEP interact during one-lung ventilation?
cards.a:
Several factors push the ventilated lung below FRC (lateral position, paralysis, mediastinal weight once the chest is open), while **auto-PEEP** (avg **4–6 cmH2O** in COPD) pushes it up.
- Auto-PEEP is most likely with low elastic recoil (elderly, emphysema) and rises with a **higher I:E ratio** (shorter expiration)
- Low auto-PEEP (**<2**): 5 cmH2O external PEEP raises total PEEP considerably
- High auto-PEEP (**>10**): the same external PEEP adds little
- PEEP helps if it moves end-expiratory volume **toward the lower inflection point** (FRC); it harms if it moves the lung further above it
- Auto-PEEP is hard to measure with anesthesia ventilators
cards.e: This is why PEEP improves oxygenation in patients with normal or restrictive lungs but may not in emphysema. Titrating PEEP to the lowest driving pressure is a practical way round the uncertainty.

cards.q: Compare pressure-controlled and volume-controlled ventilation during OLV.
cards.a:
**PCV does not improve oxygenation** for most patients, although measured peak pressures are lower.
- Much of the peak pressure fall may be in the **circuit**, not at the alveolus
- PCV prevents sudden pressure spikes from surgical manipulation: useful with a **bronchial blocker**, after **lung transplantation**, and during **pneumonectomy**
- With PCV the delivered **Vt can change suddenly** as compliance changes, so monitor it closely
cards.e: Oxford suggests switching to PCV to limit peak airway pressure in difficult OLV. Whichever mode is used, the protective targets (Vt, plateau, driving pressure) are what matter.

cards.q: Why do patients with normal spirometry desaturate more on OLV than those with obstructive disease, and how big is the effect of side?
cards.a:
Better preoperative spirometry was linked to **lower PaO2** during OLV; emphysematous LVRS patients tolerate OLV very well.
- Likely explanation: **auto-PEEP** keeps the obstructed dependent lung nearer FRC
- With routine **PEEP**, this difference may no longer matter much
- **Side**: right lung is larger and gets about 10% more blood, so right thoracotomy has more shunt; mean PaO2 difference about **100 mm Hg** in stable OLV
- **Two-lung lateral PaO2** remains the best predictor (relevant in trauma with a contused dependent lung)
cards.e: This is a classic exam paradox. The V/Q scan adds information: chronic unilateral disease on the operated side means low perfusion there and good OLV tolerance.

cards.q: Outline the stepwise management of hypoxemia during one-lung ventilation.
cards.a:
**Severe or sudden** desaturation: **resume two-lung ventilation** (reinflate, deflate bronchial cuff/blocker), then diagnose.
**Gradual** desaturation:
- **FiO2 1.0** (unless bleomycin-type risk)
- **Bronchoscopy** to check DLT/blocker; exclude lobar obstruction
- Check **cardiac output** (IVC compression, epidural hypotension); stop vasodilators; volatile **≤1 MAC**
- **Recruit** the ventilated lung (transiently worsens PaO2 and BP)
- **PEEP** to the ventilated lung (not in emphysema)
- **Apneic O2 insufflation** to the operative lung
- **CPAP 1–2 cmH2O** to a just-recruited operative lung
- **Partial ventilation** of the operative lung; pharmacological measures; surgical **clamping of PA** flow; **VV-ECMO**
cards.e: Most desaturation occurs within the first 10 minutes; SaO2 nadirs at 20–30 minutes and may then rise as HPV develops. Note: Oxford orders the steps differently and uses CPAP 5–10 cmH2O; follow Miller.

cards.q: How should PEEP be used to treat hypoxemia during OLV?
cards.a:
Apply PEEP to the **ventilated lung after a recruitment manoeuvre** to get its full benefit.
- It raises end-expiratory volume toward FRC in normal and restrictive lungs
- Optimal level is unpredictable; titrate **5–10 cmH2O** for best compliance with **driving pressure ≤15**
- As effective as CPAP for raising PaO2 in patients with normal lung function
- Unlike CPAP, it **does not need the operative lung reinflated** or surgery interrupted
- Routine recruitment plus PEEP from the start of OLV is logical in normal lungs
- Less useful in **emphysema** with high auto-PEEP
cards.e: Early PEEP is favoured because it avoids interrupting surgery. Note: Lippincott puts CPAP before PEEP; follow Miller.

cards.q: How should CPAP to the nonventilated lung be applied, and when does it fail?
cards.a:
CPAP with oxygen is a **reliable** way to raise PaO2, but the lung must first be **recruited**.
- Atelectatic units need **>20 cmH2O** to open; CPAP of 5–10 alone will not recruit them
- After recruitment, as little as **1–2 cmH2O** works; 5–10 cmH2O on an open lung produces a large lung that impedes surgery (normal transpulmonary pressure at FRC ~5 cmH2O)
- Circuit: CPAP/PEEP valve, oxygen source, ideally reservoir bag and manometer; FiO2 can be lowered with a blender in bleomycin patients
- **Fails** when the operative bronchus is **blocked or open to atmosphere** (BPF, endobronchial or sleeve surgery) and can interfere with **VATS**
cards.e: A recruited lung needs far less CPAP. Note: Lippincott and Oxford quote 5–10 cmH2O; follow Miller. Lippincott lists BPF, sleeve resection, massive hemorrhage and thoracoscopy as situations where CPAP is unsuitable.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 49 · Lippincott Ch 12 · Oxford Handbook Ch 15

cards.q: Describe partial ventilation techniques and other methods to improve oxygenation during OLV.
cards.a:
Useful when desaturation risk is high (e.g., previous contralateral resection).
- **Intermittent insufflation** (Russell): 2 L/min O2 into a filter on the operative lumen; occluding for 2 s gives ~**66 mL**, repeated every 10 s
- **Fiberoptic segmental insufflation**: 5 L/min O2 via the scope's suction port into a segment remote from surgery
- **Selective lobar collapse** with a blocker in the operative lobe only
- **Small-Vt ventilation** of the operative lung (e.g., **70 mL at 6/min**)
- **Intermittent reinflation** (HPV becomes stronger with repeat hypoxia)
- **Pharmacological**: stop vasodilators; inhaled NO plus phenylephrine; **inhaled epoprostenol or iloprost** (glycine diluent clogs the HME: change hourly)
- **Mechanical restriction**: surgeon clamps the PA, or PA catheter balloon in the operative PA
cards.e: The common thread is giving a little oxygen to the operative lung or less blood to it. Prophylaxis (e.g., 3 L/min O2 via a non-occluding catheter at the start of OLV) reduces later hypoxemia and avoids emergency reinflation at a bad surgical moment.

cards.q: In bilateral pulmonary surgery, which side should be operated on first and why?
cards.a:
Operate first on the lung with **better gas exchange**, usually the **right side first**.
- The second OLV period ventilates a lung already traumatised by surgery, so gas exchange is worse
- **HPV offset** after reinflation of the first collapsed lung is delayed
- Desaturation is mainly a problem in the **second** OLV period
cards.e: Doing the right side first means the more vulnerable second period involves collapsing the smaller left lung while the operated right lung is ventilated, which creates less shunt. Plan prophylactic CPAP or partial ventilation for the second side.

cards.q: What are the anesthetic options for flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy?
cards.a:
Awake or general anesthesia, oral or nasal.
- Local: nebulised or sprayed topical LA, soaked pledgets, laryngeal/glossopharyngeal nerve blocks, **spray-as-you-go**, ± sedation, ± antisialagogue
- GA: spontaneous or controlled ventilation, via **ETT or LMA**; a swivel connector with a self-sealing valve lets ventilation and scoping proceed together
- **LMA** advantages: view of cords and subglottis, **lower airway resistance** with the scope inside than an ETT; good for difficult airways with spontaneous breathing
- Flexometallic self-expanding stents can go via flexible or rigid scope; **silastic stents need rigid bronchoscopy**
cards.e: Anticholinergic premedication helps if secretions are copious. A scope inside an ETT takes up a large proportion of the lumen, which is why the LMA's lower resistance is helpful.

cards.q: What are the four ventilation techniques for rigid bronchoscopy?
cards.a:
- **Spontaneous ventilation**: topical LA or nerve blocks reduce coughing and breath-holding with volatiles; common in children
- **Apneic oxygenation** (± insufflation): needs thorough preoxygenation; surgeon works in intervals of about **3 min or more** and stops for ventilation
- **Ventilating bronchoscope**: standard circuit through the side port; leaks if the scope is small for the airway (throat packs may help)
- **Jet ventilation**: Sanders injector or high-frequency ventilator; best with **TIVA** because entrained gas makes volatile delivery uncertain
cards.e: Lippincott notes PaCO2 rises about 6 mm Hg in the first minute of apnea and 3–4 mm Hg each minute after, so respiratory acidosis limits apneic oxygenation to roughly 10–20 minutes. TIVA with propofol and remifentanil suits all methods and avoids polluting the room.

cards.q: What are the key anesthetic considerations for rigid bronchoscopy?
cards.a:
The airway is **shared and never secure**.
- Review imaging; stabilise severe **stridor** (cool mist, nebulised racemic epinephrine, steroids)
- Surgeon present at induction ready to place the scope; glycopyrrolate 0.2 mg reduces secretions; mouthguard
- **Succinylcholine** for intubation, nondepolarisers for long cases; TIVA with propofol/remifentanil
- Monitoring: **pulse oximetry** is vital; ETCO2 and agent levels cannot be measured, so use ABGs or interrupt to check
- **Aspiration** risk cannot be eliminated: defer in full-stomach patients if possible
- **Nd:YAG laser**: FiO2 **<30%** if possible; avoid combustible material; it penetrates deeper (good for vascular tumours) and travels by fibre, but reflected strikes and delayed edema are commoner than with CO2 laser
- Complications: perforation, mucosal injury, bleeding, edema, loss of airway at the end; may need a small (6.0) SLT, steroids, racemic epinephrine or heliox
cards.e: Desaturation is managed by stopping the procedure and ventilating, via the scope or by removing it and using a mask, LMA or ETT. Oxford advises having atropine available but not giving it routinely, as it worsens tachycardia.

cards.q: What anesthetic considerations apply to robotic navigational bronchoscopy?
cards.a:
It lets the operator reach small peripheral nodules (to about the **9th airway generation**) with higher diagnostic yield than conventional bronchoscopy.
- Use a **large SLT (7.5–8.5 mm ID)** so the scope moves freely
- Robotic arms are near the face: use circuit extensions and secure the tube well
- Can be combined with **indocyanine green** dye marking, cone-beam CT and immediate **VATS** resection in a hybrid room
- Uncommon complications: **pneumothorax**, bleeding
cards.e: When navigation and VATS are combined, the plan may need conversion to lung isolation after the bronchoscopic stage. Airway access is limited once the robot is positioned.

cards.q: What is cervical mediastinoscopy, and what are its complications?
cards.a:
A 2–3 cm suprasternal incision, blunt pretracheal dissection, and a scope advanced toward the carina for **mediastinal node staging** or biopsy of anterior masses (largely replaced by PET plus EBUS for staging). Anterior (Chamberlain) mediastinoscopy is through the 2nd interspace.
- Morbidity **2–8%**
- **Major hemorrhage** (most serious; may need emergency sternotomy/thoracotomy)
- **Innominate artery compression**, airway obstruction, pneumothorax
- **Recurrent laryngeal** (permanent in ~50%) and **phrenic** nerve injury
- Esophageal injury, **chylothorax**, **air embolism**, autonomic (vagal) reflexes
cards.e: Lippincott includes reflex bradycardia, cerebral ischemia and pneumothorax as complications. Uncomplicated cases can be extubated in theatre and go home the same day.

cards.q: Why must the right arm pulse be monitored during mediastinoscopy?
cards.a:
The scope can compress the **innominate artery**, which supplies the **right arm and right common carotid**.
- The surgeon usually does not know it is happening
- Monitor the **right hand** (pulse oximeter, arterial line or a finger on the pulse)
- Put the **NIBP cuff on the left** arm to confirm true systemic pressure
- Patients with poor cerebral collateral flow (unpredictable) risk **cerebral ischemia**
cards.e: A dampened right radial trace with a normal left arm pressure means compression, not hypotension, so tell the surgeon to reposition the scope rather than giving vasopressors. Lippincott calls this a "false" fall in blood pressure.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 49 · Lippincott Ch 12 · Oxford Handbook Ch 15

cards.q: Outline the management of major hemorrhage during mediastinoscopy.
cards.a:
Box 49.13 steps:
- **Stop surgery and pack** the wound; admit early that there is a problem
- Resuscitate and **call for help** (anesthetic and surgical)
- **Large-bore IV access in the lower limbs** (blood given in the arms may leak out of an SVC tear)
- Arterial line if not present
- Blood warmers, rapid infusers, **cross-matched blood in the room**
- **DLT or blocker** if thoracotomy is possible (a blocker through the existing tube is easier than changing tubes while the wound is packed)
- Once ready, re-explore the neck; convert to **sternotomy or thoracotomy** if needed
cards.e: Minor bleeding may settle with head-up tilt, systolic pressure in the 90s and packing. Oxford notes the risk is higher in SVC obstruction, which is why a leg cannula is advised.

cards.q: What other complications must be considered after mediastinoscopy (pneumothorax, RLN injury, air embolism)?
cards.a:
- **Pneumothorax**: uncommon; intraoperatively shows as rising peak pressure, tracheal shift, distant breath sounds, hypotension, cyanosis; needs immediate **chest drain**; every patient needs a **postoperative chest X-ray**
- **RLN injury**: permanent in about half; if suspected, look at the cords during spontaneous breathing; bilateral midline cords risk **laryngeal obstruction**
- **Venous air embolism**: the scope tip lies in the chest exposed to pleural pressure, so a **spontaneously breathing** patient can entrain air through a bleeding vein
- **Autonomic reflexes** from compression of trachea, vagus or great vessels
cards.e: Controlled ventilation reduces the air embolism risk. Lippincott notes a spontaneously breathing patient with the head up may develop a pneumothorax that shows only after surgery.

cards.q: How is anesthesia provided for endobronchial ultrasound-guided biopsy?
cards.a:
EBUS uses an ultrasound bronchoscope to sample mediastinal and hilar nodes, often outside the OR.
- Commonly **topical lidocaine** with **conscious sedation** (fentanyl ± midazolam)
- For GA: the EBUS scope is wide, so use an **LMA or a large ETT (≥8.5 mm ID)**
cards.e: The LMA again gives low resistance with the scope inside and allows a view of the cords. Together with PET, EBUS has largely replaced mediastinoscopy for staging NSCLC.

cards.q: What are the advantages of VATS over open thoracotomy?
cards.a:
VATS spares rib spreading.
- Shorter **length of stay**
- Less **blood loss** (if uncomplicated)
- Less **pain**
- Better postoperative **pulmonary function**
- Earlier mobilisation and return to work
- Smaller **inflammatory (cytokine) response**
- Better outcomes for lobectomy in patients with limited reserve; safe for early NSCLC
- Ports plus a ~5 cm access incision; **uniportal** VATS may reduce pain and stay further
cards.e: VATS is now first choice for pleural disease, undiagnosed peripheral nodules, ILD biopsy, pleurectomy and sympathectomy. Be ready for conversion to thoracotomy for bleeding or failure to find the nodule.

cards.q: What anesthetic techniques are used for VATS?
cards.a:
Local, regional or general, with two-lung or one-lung ventilation.
- Minor diagnostic VATS can be **awake**: intercostal blocks at the incision level and two spaces above and below; the open pleura causes partial lung collapse; give high-FiO2 by mask; **never insufflate gas under pressure** in an awake patient
- Most cases: GA with **DLT or blocker** for OLV
- Arterial line and ABGs for long procedures (lobectomy) or marginal patients
- Postoperative analgesia: US-guided blocks, of which **ESP** may be most useful
- A working **chest drain with underwater seal** is needed before extubation
cards.e: Under local anesthesia with spontaneous breathing, changes in PaO2, PaCO2 and rhythm are surprisingly small. Bilateral VATS (wedges, LVRS) can be done supine.

cards.q: What are the anesthetic considerations for robotic thoracic surgery?
cards.a:
Box 49.14:
- A practised protocol for **emergency undocking in <60 s**
- **Limited access** to the patient: confirm the lung-isolation device **before docking**
- Extension lines for monitors and circuit
- **Intrathoracic CO2 insufflation** may impair venous return
- The **table must not move** while docked
- Long procedures: positional neuropathy risk; restrict fluids
cards.e: Position changes for robotic surgery can move airway devices, and fixing them mid-case is very difficult. Robotic surgery offers the surgeon 3D vision and greater instrument range.

cards.q: Describe the anesthetic management of an open lobectomy, including intraoperative tests by the surgeon.
cards.a:
Lobectomy is the standard cancer operation because local recurrence is lower than with lesser resections.
- Arterial line, two IVs (one large bore), TEA or US block, lower-body warming (hypothermia inhibits HPV)
- Keep **normothermic, normotensive**, adequately oxygenated
- **Bronchus test clamp**: before division the surgeon clamps the lobar bronchus and the operative lung is reinflated (unclamp the DLT limb or deflate the blocker) to confirm the right lobe; in VATS the anesthesiologist may check patency of remaining bronchi by bronchoscopy
- **Stump leak test** at about **20 cmH2O**
- Extubate in the OR if function is adequate and **AWaC**
cards.e: Lobectomy can become bilobectomy or pneumonectomy if staging is worse than expected, so the anesthesiologist must know whether the patient could tolerate a larger resection. Pancoast tumours (superior sulcus) can invade the lower plexus, subclavian vessels, stellate ganglion (Horner syndrome) and spine; they may need staged spinal surgery, massive transfusion, and lines in the contralateral arm.

cards.q: What is a sleeve lobectomy, and what are its anesthetic requirements?
cards.a:
A lobectomy that also removes a segment of **main bronchus** (± pulmonary artery) and reanastomoses it, avoiding pneumonectomy in patients with limited reserve.
- Indications: bronchogenic carcinoma (commonest), carcinoid, endobronchial metastases, airway tumours, adenomas
- Lung isolation with a **contralateral** DLT or endobronchial tube (right DLT for a left sleeve)
- HFJV for resections close to the carina
- Vascular sleeve needs **heparin**: do not manipulate an epidural catheter for **24 h**
- Large-bore access: arterioplasty can bleed uncontrollably
- Usually extubated in the OR
cards.e: Survival is better after sleeve lobectomy than after right pneumonectomy for comparable right upper lobe tumours. A DLT in the operative bronchus would be in the anastomosis, hence the contralateral tube.

cards.q: What are the major risks and anesthetic requirements of pneumonectomy?
cards.a:
Pneumonectomy is high risk: 30-day mortality **5–13%** (inverse to surgical volume); complications rise fivefold at **≥65 years**.
- Deaths come from **cardiac complications** and **acute lung injury** rather than atelectasis/pneumonia
- Large-bore IVs, **arterial line**, **CVP** (fluids and postoperative vasopressors)
- Lung isolation that avoids the operative bronchus (e.g., **left DLT for right pneumonectomy**); a left-sided device used for left pneumonectomy must be **withdrawn before stapling**
- **RV dysfunction**: afterload rises from higher PAP/PVR
- Bronchial stump kept short to avoid a secretion pocket
cards.e: Lippincott quotes mortality of 5–7% for pneumonectomy versus 2–3% for lobectomy, higher for **right**-sided pneumonectomy because more lung is removed. Oxford quotes about 5%.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 49 · Lippincott Ch 12 · Oxford Handbook Ch 15

cards.q: How is the postpneumonectomy space managed, and why does it matter to the anesthesiologist?
cards.a:
There is **no consensus**.
- **Suction** on an empty hemithorax, or a standard underwater-seal drain, can cause **mediastinal shift** and **hemodynamic collapse**
- Options: no drain; a temporary catheter to add or remove air (typically removing **0.75–1.5 L** to centre the mediastinum and trachea); or a special balanced drainage system with high- and low-pressure relief valves
- A **chest X-ray** on arrival in PACU/ICU is mandatory to assess mediastinal position
cards.e: Sudden hypotension after pneumonectomy has a short differential: hemorrhage, cardiac herniation, mediastinal shift from drain mismanagement, and pulmonary embolism. Never put routine suction on a pneumonectomy drain.

cards.q: What is postpneumonectomy pulmonary edema (acute lung injury), and how can it be prevented?
cards.a:
A high-permeability lung injury of the remaining lung: incidence only about **4%** but mortality **30–50%**.
- Risk factors: **pneumonectomy** (right > left, linked to higher PA pressures), **excess IV fluid** (>3 L in 24 h independently), high intraoperative **ventilatory pressure index**, **alcohol** abuse
- Tidal volumes **>8 mL/kg** linked to respiratory failure; **<6 mL/kg** to less; 5 mL/kg reduces cytokines
- Prevention: restrict fluids (use vasopressors/inotropes), **Vt 5–6 mL/kg IBW**, peak <35 and plateau <25 cmH2O
- Treatment is supportive: fluid restriction, diuretics, protective ventilation, lower PA pressure; **ECMO** possible
cards.e: Oxford cites ALI in 2–5% of resections, three times commoner after pneumonectomy, and adds chronic alcohol use, genetic predisposition and more than 4 L of intraoperative fluid as risk factors. Lymphatic disruption and endothelial injury probably both contribute.

cards.q: What are the anesthetic challenges of extrapleural pneumonectomy?
cards.a:
EPP removes lung, parietal pleura and often **pericardium, diaphragm**, nodes and chest wall, for selected **mesothelioma**.
- **Major blood loss** from denuded chest wall: large-bore access, CVP, keep hematocrit and coagulation normal
- **Venous return** may fall from bleeding, tumour compressing the SVC or surgical compression
- **Cardiac herniation** or instability when turned supine, especially after right-sided pericardial resection
- High **arrhythmia** risk
- Often short postoperative ventilation: change DLT to SLT
cards.e: EPP combines all the risks of pneumonectomy with those of diaphragm and pericardial resection. Its survival benefit remains uncertain.

cards.q: What is a sleeve pneumonectomy, and how is ventilation maintained during the anastomosis?
cards.a:
Resection of a lung with the **carina** for tumours of the proximal main bronchus/carina, usually **right-sided** via right thoracotomy without ECMO.
- A long **SLT advanced into the left main bronchus** during the tracheobronchial anastomosis
- Or **high-frequency positive-pressure ventilation**, alone or with a DLT
- Left-sided disease is often done in **two stages** (left pneumonectomy, then right thoracotomy for carinal excision)
- Higher complications and mortality; 5-year survival about **20%**
- Postpneumonectomy edema is especially a problem after **right sleeve pneumonectomy**
cards.e: The carina is more accessible from the right because the aortic arch lies over it on the left. Coordinate tube advancement and withdrawal closely with the surgeon.

cards.q: Compare segmentectomy and wedge resection and list the anesthetic considerations for limited resections.
cards.a:
**Segmentectomy**: anatomic removal of a segment's artery, vein, bronchus and parenchyma, for cancer in patients with limited reserve. **Wedge**: nonanatomic removal with a **1.5–2 cm** margin, for diagnosis or metastases.
- Suitable cancers: usually **<3 cm**, peripheral, node-negative
- Preoperative CT-guided **marker/coil** can cause **pneumothorax or BPF**: minimise PPV before isolation to avoid tension pneumothorax
- After previous contralateral lobectomy/pneumonectomy: **selective lobar collapse** with a blocker (± DLT)
- Selective lobar ventilation: **3–4 mL/kg** to avoid overinflating remaining lobes
- Redo surgery bleeds more; early extubation may not be possible; air leak common
cards.e: Many of these are second primaries after earlier resection; the annual incidence of a second lung primary is about 2%, and these patients should be assessed with the same three-legged framework.

cards.q: What are the general anesthetic principles for esophagectomy?
cards.a:
A major operation with **10–15% morbidity/mortality** (inverse to volume).
- Respiratory complications **18–26%**; ARDS 14.5%, ALI 24% in one study
- Anastomotic **leak 5–26%** (intrathoracic leak mortality **4–30%**), stricture 12–40%
- Outcome improved by **fluid restriction, early extubation, TEA** and **vasopressor/inotrope** support of blood pressure
- **Hypotension reduces anastomotic flow**; vasopressors in normovolemic patients restore it
- Aspiration risk (reflux, obstruction) and malnutrition
cards.e: Lippincott notes the aspiration risk persists after surgery and that vagal stimulation near the esophagus can cause bradycardia, while hand or retractor compression of the heart during transhiatal dissection reduces output. A pulmonary artery catheter is needed only for significant cardiac disease.

cards.q: Compare the anesthetic management of transthoracic, transhiatal and minimally invasive esophagectomy.
cards.a:
**Transthoracic (Ivor Lewis)**: supine laparotomy then **right thoracotomy** in left lateral; RSI; arterial line and CVP (**right IJ**, as a left neck anastomosis may be needed); TEA with **hydrophilic opioid** (hydromorphone) for wide dermatomal spread; **left DLT or right blocker**; protective OLV (Vt 5 mL/kg, PEEP 5) reduces inflammation; esophageal handling can cause hypotension.
**Transhiatal**: SLT; blind blunt dissection causes **cardiac compression** and sudden hypotension and may injure vessels or airway; **do not cut the ETT** so it can be advanced into a bronchus if the airway is torn.
**Minimally invasive**: laparoscopic CO2 (adjust ventilation), thoracoscopic part needs DLT or blocker; often **prone** VATS with a blocker via SLT; less blood loss and pain but longer surgery.
cards.e: If the patient cannot be extubated, replace the DLT with an SLT. Secure the nasogastric tube carefully at the end; it protects the anastomosis.

cards.q: Compare type I and type II hiatus hernia and their anesthetic significance.
cards.a:
**Type I (sliding)**: about **90%**; the gastroesophageal junction and fundus slide axially into the chest within a peritoneal sac; the LES lies above the diaphragm and fails with rises in abdominal pressure, so **reflux/regurgitation** occurs.
**Type II (paraesophageal)**: stomach herniates beside the esophagus; GEJ remains **in the abdomen**; complications are **bleeding, anemia and gastric volvulus**.
- Most reflux patients have a hiatus hernia, but most hiatus hernias do **not** cause significant reflux
- Repair (e.g., **Nissen fundoplication**) via thoracotomy, laparotomy or minimally invasive
cards.e: Patients with heartburn have reduced barrier pressure and need aspiration precautions. Benign strictures from chronic reflux may need gastroplasty or resection with vagotomy, antrectomy and Roux-en-Y drainage.

cards.q: Compare esophageal perforation and rupture.
cards.a:
**Perforation**: commonest cause is **iatrogenic** (upper GI endoscopy), also bougies, gastric tubes, traumatic intubation, foreign bodies.
**Rupture (Boerhaave type)**: a burst from sudden abdominal pressure (vomiting, lifting, childbirth, straining) against a relaxed LES and closed upper esophagus; usually within **2 cm of the GEJ on the left**; contents enter the mediastinum under pressure so symptoms are **abrupt**.
- Features: chest/back pain, hypotension, sweating, tachypnea, cyanosis, emphysema, hydropneumothorax; imaging shows pneumomediastinum, effusion, wide mediastinum
- Minor perforations may be treated conservatively; major ones need **emergency repair and drainage** to prevent mediastinitis and sepsis
cards.e: These patients are septic, hypovolemic and at aspiration risk, often needing lung isolation through a left or right thoracotomy. Delay in diagnosis greatly worsens outcome.

cards.q: What are the anesthetic considerations in achalasia and POEM?
cards.a:
Achalasia: **absent peristalsis** and **failure of LES relaxation**, so the esophagus dilates and holds food, with **regurgitation and aspiration** risk.
- Treatment: dilation (perforation risk) or **Heller myotomy** (often with an antireflux repair)
- **POEM** (peroral endoscopic myotomy) needs GA with **intubation**
- CO2 insufflation can cause **pneumoperitoneum** needing needle decompression (17% in one series) or **pneumothorax** (5%; <2% need drains)
cards.e: Treat these patients as having a full stomach regardless of fasting. Rising airway pressure or abdominal distension during POEM should prompt a check for capnoperitoneum or capnothorax.

cards.q: What are the anesthetic concerns in Zenker's diverticulum?
cards.a:
A pharyngeal pouch arising between **thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus**, with dysphagia, noisy swallowing, regurgitation, nocturnal cough and aspiration.
- **Fasting does not empty** the pouch; best to have the patient **express the contents** just before induction
- The pouch opening is usually **above the cricoid**, so **cricoid pressure does not protect** and may squeeze contents into the pharynx
- Options: **awake fiberoptic intubation**, or modified RSI **without cricoid pressure**, supine **20–30° head-up**
- Risk of perforation when passing orogastric/nasogastric tubes or bougies
cards.e: This is a common trap: applying cricoid pressure in Zenker's can cause rather than prevent aspiration. Surgery is usually through a left neck incision.

cards.q: What are the options for oxygenation during tracheal resection?
cards.a:
Indications include tumours, **post-intubation stenosis** (commonest trauma), congenital lesions, vascular lesions and tracheomalacia.
- LMA; standard oral ETT; **cross-field ventilation** with a sterile tube placed into the opened distal trachea/bronchus; **HFJV** across the stenosis; **ECMO**
- Common sequence: LMA with bronchoscopic examination, then cross-field ventilation during resection; or rigid bronchoscopy and dilation, then an SLT through the stenosis, withdrawn when the distal trachea is opened
- Low tracheal/carinal lesions: right thoracotomy, single-lumen or endobronchial tube, cross-field ventilation; advance the tube past the anastomosis after the posterior wall is sewn
- Surgeon present at induction; **rigid bronchoscope** ready; arterial line in all
cards.e: Fixed stenoses rarely collapse on induction, but intraluminal masses behave like anterior mediastinal masses. Lippincott prefers a left radial line for lower tracheal surgery (innominate compression), and keeps FiO2 below 0.3 if laser is used.

cards.q: Describe postoperative management after tracheal resection, including T-tubes.
cards.a:
- Keep the **neck flexed** (chin-to-sternum suture or splint) to reduce suture-line tension; head-up to reduce swelling
- **Early extubation**; swap SLT for LMA at emergence to allow bronchoscopy
- Reintubation: SLT railroaded over a **fiberoptic scope**; steroids for edema
- Rare **tetraplegia** from neck hyperflexion: cut the chin stitch
- **Vocal cord paralysis** reported in 26%
- **Montgomery T-tube** (uncuffed, for spontaneous breathing): upper limb 0.5–1 cm above the cords; PPV is difficult, so use an **LMA** short term or replace with a cuffed tube/tracheostomy for longer ventilation
cards.e: Lippincott notes tracheal stenosis dyspnea is typically worse lying flat and eased by sitting forward, and that flow–volume loops help localise and grade the lesion. Nonintubated robotic tracheal resection with propofol–remifentanil and an LMA has been reported.

cards.q: What are the anesthetic considerations for surgery for bronchiectasis, lung abscess and empyema?
cards.a:
- **Lung isolation** (preferably a **DLT**, which allows suction) to protect healthy lung from pus, ideally achieved **before** turning the patient
- Inflamed tissue: more difficult surgery and **massive bleeding** risk, especially decortication
- **Sepsis**: avoid thoracic epidural
- Chronically collapsed lung: re-expand gradually to avoid **re-expansion edema**
- Extubate in the OR if criteria met
- Empyema after resection occurs in **2–16%** and raises mortality by about 40%, more with a BPF
cards.e: Stoelting states re-expansion edema risk rises when more than 1 L of air or fluid has been present, when collapse lasted over 24 hours and when re-expansion is rapid. Decortication is chosen when the lung cannot expand under a thick peel; open window thoracostomy drains post-resection empyema.

cards.q: How is a bronchopleural fistula diagnosed, and what are its causes?
cards.a:
Causes: rupture of abscess, bronchus, bulla or cyst; erosion by tumour or inflammation; **stump dehiscence** after resection (pneumonectomy incidence **2–11%**, mortality **5–70%**).
- After **pneumonectomy**: sudden dyspnea, **subcutaneous emphysema**, **contralateral tracheal shift**, and a **falling fluid level** on serial films
- After **lobectomy**: persistent air leak, purulent drainage or sputum
- After drain removal: fever, purulent sputum, new air–fluid level
- Confirm by **bronchoscopy**; also methylene blue into the pleura recovered in sputum, or inhaled xenon/N2O tracers
cards.e: Lippincott dates them: inadequate stump closure presents in the first 24–72 h, whereas ischemic or infective necrosis of the suture line appears after 72 h. Early postpneumonectomy dehiscence may be resutured; late disease needs drainage or a Clagett procedure.

cards.q: What are the anesthetic principles for repair of a bronchopleural fistula?
cards.a:
Core rule: **secure lung isolation before positive-pressure ventilation or repositioning**.
- Challenges: soiling of healthy lung, **tension pneumothorax** with PPV, loss of tidal volume through the leak
- Estimate leak: continuous vs intermittent bubbling in the drain; **inspired minus expired Vt**
- **Chest drain before induction**
- **DLT** is best; for a post-pneumonectomy fistula put the bronchial lumen in the **opposite** lung
- Options: awake fiberoptic DLT; spontaneous ventilation until isolated; or modified RSI with bronchoscopic DLT placement
- Alternatives: HFOV, TEA with sedation for VATS, VV-ECMO; extubate early to protect the stump
cards.e: CPAP to the operative lung will not work because the bronchus is open to the pleura. One-way endobronchial valves have closed fistulae in patients unfit for surgery.

cards.q: What are blebs and when are they resected?
cards.a:
