- **Hypofibrinolysis** (thrombosis): low **plasminogen**
- Standard tests miss hyperfibrinolysis; **viscoelastic tests** detect it during LT
cards.e: The liver also clears activated clotting factors, so loss of hepatic function affects both production and clearance. Oxford notes acute liver disease is characterised by severe coagulopathy with active fibrinolysis.

cards.q: Why do malnutrition, sarcopenia and obesity matter in liver transplant candidates?
cards.a:
Malnutrition worsens with liver disease severity and **sarcopenia independently predicts post-LT mortality**.
- Causes: malabsorption, microbiome change, inflammation, hormonal change, **hypermetabolism**, vitamin and electrolyte deficiencies
- **Sarcopenic obesity** (low muscle, high fat) is increasingly common with NAFLD
- **Extremes of BMI** (severe malnutrition and morbid obesity) increase post-LT morbidity and mortality; some centres exclude
- Assessment: dietitian review, BMI, **radiological muscle mass**, **frailty** and physical performance tests
- Early nutrition, including enteral or parenteral feeding
cards.e: BMI can be misleading in cirrhosis because ascites and oedema add weight while muscle is lost, so imaging of skeletal muscle is useful. Oxford lists poor nutritional state and reduced muscle mass among the preoperative problems to address.

cards.q: Define acute liver failure and describe its causes and prognosis.
cards.a:
**Encephalopathy plus coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5)** in a patient **without prior liver disease**, illness **<26 weeks** (Miller).
- Rare: ~1 per million per year (2000–3000/year in USA)
- **Paracetamol (acetaminophen)** commonest in USA/Europe; **viral** in Asia and developing countries
- **Better prognosis**: paracetamol, ischaemic, hepatitis A; **poor**: non-paracetamol drug injury, acute hepatitis B, **Wilson disease**, autoimmune
- No cirrhosis or portal hypertension; **cerebral oedema with intracranial hypertension** is the most lethal feature; also circulatory failure, AKI, metabolic derangement
- >70% now survive; ALF is only ~1% of LT
cards.e: Note: Stoelting uses 4 weeks (fulminant within 8 days); follow Miller's 26 weeks. Acute-on-chronic liver failure is a separate entity with different causes and prognosis.

cards.q: How is raised intracranial pressure managed in acute liver failure, and how are transplant candidates selected?
cards.a:
General ICP measures plus osmotherapy and controlled ventilation:
- **30° head-up**, **neutral head** position; normovolaemia, **vasopressors**, sepsis prevention
- **Intubate**, sedate, consider **paralysis** to avoid coughing, dyssynchrony and shivering
- **Mannitol** (limited if renal failure); **hypertonic saline** to Na **145–155 mEq/L**
- **Normocapnia**; **hyperventilation only for acute ICP surges**
- Early **plasma exchange or RRT** for ammonia/toxins and acid–base
- Invasive ICP monitoring is controversial and declining
- Selection: **King's College Criteria** (good for paracetamol ALF); the **ALF Study Group index** (2016) may better predict 21-day transplant-free survival
cards.e: Oxford lists the King's paracetamol criteria (pH <7.3, or grade 3–4 encephalopathy with creatinine >300 and INR >6.5) and advises avoiding volatile agents in favour of propofol TCI during LT for fulminant failure. It notes raised ICP in 70% when encephalopathy follows jaundice within 7 days.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Oxford Handbook Ch 7 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22

cards.q: What should the liver transplant anaesthetist review shortly before surgery?
cards.a:
An **organ-system review** focused on changes since listing.
- **New infection** if new encephalopathy, variceal bleed, ascites or haemodynamic deterioration
- Results of **cardiopulmonary work-up** (CAD, heart failure, POPH, arrhythmia)
- **Renal function** (new HRS); dialysis patients may need **preop dialysis**, and oliguria, hyperkalaemia or acidaemia may justify **intraoperative RRT** (risks: circuit thrombosis, hypothermia)
- High-risk: high MELD on ventilator/vasopressors/RRT, **retransplants**, cardiopulmonary disease
- **Blood bank** notified; RBC, FFP, platelets ready
cards.e: Blood loss ranges from under 500 mL to over 10 L. Fewer than 10% of recipients have red cell antibodies; then about 10 antigen-negative units are reserved for the start and 10 for the end, with antigen-unknown units used in between during massive transfusion because antibodies are washed out.

cards.q: Describe the three surgical stages of liver transplantation and the events that define them.
cards.a:
**Dissection (preanhepatic) → anhepatic → neohepatic**.
- **Preanhepatic**: incision to vascular exclusion; liver mobilised; IVC, portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct identified; **hepatic artery usually clamped first**
- **Anhepatic**: begins with **portal vein clamping**, then IVC (complete or partial) clamping and **hepatectomy**; ends at reperfusion
- **Neohepatic**: begins with **caval unclamping and graft reperfusion (usually via portal vein)**; then **hepatic artery anastomosis**, donor cholecystectomy, **biliary anastomosis**, haemostasis, closure
cards.e: Stoelting summarises the problems by phase: dissection brings ascites loss, haemorrhage and reduced venous return; anhepatic brings caval clamp hypotension, lactic acidosis, citrate hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypothermia and hypoglycaemia; reperfusion brings instability, arrhythmia, hyperkalaemia, acidosis and possible arrest.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Stoelting 7e Ch 17 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22

cards.q: Describe induction and vascular access for liver transplantation.
cards.a:
**RSI** and access sufficient for **massive, rapid transfusion**.
- Aspiration risk: **delayed gastric emptying**, **ascites**, oral immunosuppressants or gut decontamination antibiotics
- **Arterial line** before or just after induction; some add **femoral arterial** monitoring because radial pressure may underread during intense vasodilation (no proof of benefit)
- Central **large-bore introducers** (single- or double-lumen) or **dialysis catheters**; two introducers if retransplant/major adhesions; **avoid sites needed for VVB**
- Large-bore **peripheral rapid infusion catheter** (watch for infiltration)
- **Rapid infusion system** (~500 mL/min) with reservoir, filters, warmer, air detection
cards.e: Oxford describes the Level-1 type system delivering about 600 mL/min at body temperature and recommends establishing peripheral venous and arterial access before induction because vasopressors may be needed immediately.

cards.q: Compare the PA catheter and TEE for monitoring during liver transplantation.
cards.a:
PAC use is **declining** (less than half of US centres use it routinely) while **TEE use is increasing**.
- **PAC indicated**: known **POPH** or echo evidence of raised PA pressure; measures mPAP/PVR **before incision** (may cancel surgery) and guides pulmonary vasodilator therapy
- **TEE**: continuous imaging; rapid diagnosis of **ventricular failure, ischaemia, tamponade, intracardiac thrombus/air**
- TEE carries **low bleeding risk even with oesophageal varices**; some centres omit the PAC when TEE is used
- **Pulse contour analysis and 3D echo** do not agree with thermodilution and are not advocated routinely
cards.e: TEE is particularly valuable at reperfusion, when thromboembolism and RV failure can cause sudden collapse. Oxford also suggests a PA catheter where pulmonary hypertension is suspected and notes TOE is used in some centres.

cards.q: Is intraoperative cell salvage acceptable during liver transplantation for hepatocellular carcinoma? What is the role of intraoperative RRT?
cards.a:
**Cell salvage**: reduces allogeneic red cell transfusion; despite theoretical tumour dissemination, there is **no evidence of increased HCC recurrence**.
**Intraoperative RRT**:
- Prevents or treats **hyperkalaemia, acidosis and volume overload** in acute or end-stage renal failure
- **Safe**, but **benefit over medical management is unproven**
- Needs logistics; risks **thrombosis** and **hypothermia**
cards.e: Oxford regards cell salvage as mandatory for LT, typically reinfusing about 2000 mL. In multivisceral transplant salvage is used only while the bowel is intact, and the cell saver can wash stored blood to reduce its potassium load.

cards.q: Which anaesthetic agents are used for maintenance during liver transplantation?
cards.a:
**No regimen is proven superior** for graft function; a balanced technique is typical.
- Volatile at **0.5–1.0 MAC** plus a synthetic opioid (often **fentanyl**)
- **Isoflurane** traditionally favoured: hepatic vasodilation, possibly good for the graft
- **Sevoflurane/desflurane** preserve hepatocyte function (transient fall in splanchnic perfusion); sevoflurane metabolites unlikely to harm the liver
- **Propofol** gave higher hepatic blood flow than desflurane
- **ALF with cerebral oedema**: avoid volatiles or use low concentrations
cards.e: Oxford recommends ventilation to normocapnia with oxygen-enriched air and an opioid infusion (alfentanil, remifentanil or fentanyl), and TCI propofol for fulminant failure because of the ICP risk. Stoelting notes cirrhotic patients may need smaller induction doses.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22 · Stoelting 7e Ch 17

cards.q: How does liver failure and the transplant procedure affect neuromuscular blocker choice in LT?
cards.a:
Rocuronium or succinylcholine for RSI; **cisatracurium or rocuronium** for maintenance, titrated to TOF.
- RSI: **rocuronium 1 mg/kg** or **succinylcholine**; slower clearance (hepatic for roc, low plasma cholinesterase for sux) is irrelevant in a long case
- **Avoid succinylcholine with renal failure and raised K⁺**
- **Cisatracurium**: organ-independent elimination, little histamine release; **larger Vd** but **higher hepatic clearance** → **similar duration**
- **Rocuronium**: metabolism falls in the **anhepatic phase** and **recovers with graft function**
- **Sugammadex** allows rapid reversal for **early extubation**
cards.e: Recovery of rocuronium clearance after reperfusion is itself a marker of graft function. Lippincott notes cirrhosis enlarges the volume of distribution of hydrophilic relaxants, so a larger initial dose may be needed with prolonged action. Stoelting regards cisatracurium and succinylcholine as the safest relaxants in liver disease because neither depends on hepatic metabolism.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Lippincott Ch 14 · Stoelting 7e Ch 17

cards.q: What are the specific technical and anaesthetic considerations in living donor liver transplantation (LDLT)?
cards.a:
The partial graft has **no donor IVC**, so the **recipient cava must be preserved** (piggyback).
- Hepatic vein (right or left) **end-to-side to recipient IVC**; **middle hepatic vein tributaries** must also drain to avoid congestion
- Portal vein and hepatic artery anastomoses, then **duct-to-duct** or **Roux-en-Y** biliary reconstruction
- **Portal hyperperfusion** of a small graft impairs function → **octreotide** to reduce portal flow
- Portal pressure **>20 mm Hg** or high portal–CVP gradient → **splenectomy, splenic artery ligation or partial portocaval shunt**
- US 2020: 425 adult LDLTs (~**5%**); dominant in Asia; outcomes comparable to deceased donors
cards.e: Live liver donors had an 11% readmission rate at 12 months in US data, mostly for biliary and vascular problems. Measuring portal pressure after reperfusion is the key intraoperative step for detecting hyperperfusion.

cards.q: Describe the haemodynamic management of the preanhepatic (dissection) phase of liver transplantation.
cards.a:
Expect **hypovolaemia** and **bleeding**.
- Draining **ascites** drops preload → anticipatory **colloid (5% albumin or FFP)**
- Aim for **euvolaemia**, with a trend to **restrictive** fluid (limited by comorbidity)
- **Bleeding** depends on pre-existing **coagulopathy**, severity of **portal hypertension**, and surgical complexity (previous surgery, adhesions); massive transfusion may be needed
- **Vasopressor infusions** common, especially with cirrhotic cardiomyopathy
- Hostile anatomy or intractable instability → discuss **aborting** to avoid futile care
cards.e: Severe bleeding with haemodynamic compromise is most frequent in this phase. Oxford notes the dissection includes ligation of varices and that hypotension may also arise from cardiac disease, pericardial effusion or vasodilatation. Stoelting likewise lists haemodynamic compromise from ascites loss, haemorrhage and reduced venous return in this phase.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22 · Stoelting 7e Ch 17

cards.q: How should hyponatraemia be managed during liver transplantation?
cards.a:
**Avoid rapid correction**: limit the rise to **≤8 mEq/L in 24 h**.
- Rapid perioperative rises cause **osmotic demyelination syndrome** (central pontine myelinolysis)
- Older data: rises of **21–32 mEq/L** were associated with ODS, **<16 mEq/L** were not; current advice is more conservative
- Large volumes of sodium-containing products (blood, FFP, albumin, bicarbonate) can raise sodium quickly, so monitor frequently
cards.e: The literature is not fully consistent, which is why the current conservative limit is preferred. Oxford lists hyponatraemia among the problems to investigate and correct before transplantation.

cards.q: Describe the electrolyte, glucose and temperature management during the preanhepatic and anhepatic phases.
cards.a:
Frequent **point-of-care** testing (hourly or more often with massive transfusion) guides therapy:
- **Citrate toxicity** → **ionised hypocalcaemia** (no hepatic citrate metabolism) → **calcium chloride**; **ionised hypomagnesaemia** also occurs and recovers after reperfusion
- **Do not aggressively correct hypokalaemia** before reperfusion
- **Hyperkalaemia**: diuretics, **insulin with glucose**, or intraoperative dialysis
- Glucose supplements rarely needed unless insulin given, children, or **fulminant failure**; avoid **>180 mg/dL** (surgical site infection)
- **Low-dose dopamine** for urine output is unproven
- Prevent **hypothermia**: warm fluids, forced-air/liquid warmers above and below, heated circuits on VVB/dialysis
- Coagulation tests: at start, after corrections, after reperfusion, with microvascular bleeding
cards.e: Oxford stresses that hypocalcaemia from citrate depresses the heart and impairs clotting, that patients with acute liver failure may become profoundly hypoglycaemic in the anhepatic phase, and that electrolytes must be rechecked immediately before reperfusion. Stoelting's phase table lists lactic acidosis, citrate hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypothermia and hypoglycaemia as the anhepatic problems.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22 · Stoelting 7e Ch 17

cards.q: What are the haemodynamic effects of complete IVC clamping, and how are they managed?
cards.a:
Caval cross-clamping (caval interposition) cuts **venous return by up to 50%** → severe hypotension.
- **Test clamp**: if poorly tolerated, release and give volume (5% albumin/FFP), repeat until tolerated
- **Venovenous bypass** returns IVC and portal blood to the **SVC via the axillary vein**: maintains preload, improves **renal perfusion pressure**, reduces **splanchnic congestion**, delays **acidosis**
- VVB risks: **air embolism, thromboembolism, decannulation** (can be fatal)
- Meta-analysis (3 trials): **no difference in renal failure or transfusion** with VVB; routine use has declined
cards.e: Lippincott's answer is that VVB's main effect is to support cardiac output; it does not reliably prevent metabolic acidosis. Oxford notes VVB uses heparin-bonded circuits so systemic heparin is unnecessary, and it is used in about 10–20% of cases.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Lippincott Ch 14 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22

cards.q: Compare the piggyback technique with conventional caval interposition.
cards.a:
**Piggyback preserves the recipient retrohepatic IVC**, keeping venous return.
- Conventional: suprahepatic and infrahepatic IVC both clamped, recipient cava removed; **three anastomoses** (two caval + portal) before reperfusion
- Piggyback: right hepatic vein stapled, **side-biting clamp** on the left/middle hepatic veins; donor suprahepatic IVC sewn **end-to-side** to recipient IVC, donor infrahepatic IVC stapled; **two anastomoses** before reperfusion
- Benefits: better anhepatic haemodynamics, **less need for VVB**; retrospective data show shorter **warm ischaemia** and less **AKI**
- Requires careful retrohepatic dissection; **no RCT** versus caval interposition without VVB
cards.e: Piggyback is mandatory for living donor grafts, which lack a donor cava. Oxford adds that some surgeons create a temporary portocaval shunt to preserve gut venous return during the anhepatic phase.

cards.q: Why may fibrinolysis begin during the anhepatic phase?
cards.a:
With no liver, **plasminogen activator inhibitor is not produced**, so **t-PA acts unopposed**.
- Blood loss is usually limited because inflow is clamped, despite no factor synthesis
- Fibrinolysis is **most severe after reperfusion**, when graft endothelium releases t-PA
- Antifibrinolytics are **not given routinely**; reserve them for significant bleeding with hyperfibrinolysis
cards.e: Note: Oxford gives routine tranexamic acid in the anhepatic phase; follow Miller (no routine prophylaxis).

cards.q: What physiological changes occur at liver graft reperfusion and how are they anticipated?
cards.a:
Almost universal: **↑K⁺**, **↑H⁺ (acidosis)**, **↑preload**, **↓SVR and BP**, and a drop in core temperature.
- A fall in **central temperature** (cold graft effluent) marks outflow into the circulation
- **Prophylaxis** before unclamping: catecholamines, anticholinergics, **calcium chloride**
- **Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes**: **calcium chloride, sodium bicarbonate, insulin**
- Early **intraoperative dialysis** for oliguric, hyperkalaemic, high-MELD or massively transfused patients
cards.e: Oxford notes K⁺ can reach 8–9 mmol/L with poor grafts, adenosine in preservation fluid can cause bradycardia and hypotension, and many give 10 mmol calcium at reperfusion with small adrenaline boluses (50 µg) to keep MAP above about 70 mm Hg. Lippincott: bicarbonate and calcium chloride given before unclamping counteract reduced cardiac output. Stoelting explains the hyperkalaemia treatment: calcium stabilises cell membranes, while insulin, bicarbonate and hyperventilation shift potassium into cells.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22 · Lippincott Ch 14 · Stoelting 7e Ch 21

cards.q: Define postreperfusion syndrome (PRS) and list its causes and risk factors.
cards.a:
**Significant haemodynamic instability within 1–5 minutes of reperfusion** with systemic hypotension and sometimes acute **pulmonary hypertension**.
- Very common: **>50%**, unchanged over decades
- Causes: **hyperkalaemia, acidosis, hypothermia, emboli (air/thrombus)**, vasoactive mediators from the ischaemic graft
- **Graft risk factors**: **donor age**, **long cold ischaemia time**, **macrosteatosis**
- Associated with **graft dysfunction and renal failure** (small studies, variable definitions)
cards.e: Lippincott describes PRS as mainly bradycardia, low MAP and low SVR, with hypotension largely from visceral vasodilation; atropine prevents bradycardia but not hypotension. Oxford notes myocardial depression settles in 2–3 minutes while vasodilatation can persist for hours, and that potassium may then fall as graft cells take it back up.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Lippincott Ch 14 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22

cards.q: What causes sudden cardiovascular collapse during liver transplantation, and how is intracardiac thrombosis treated?
cards.a:
Causes include massive bleeding, **reperfusion arrhythmias** (metabolic/electrolyte), **PRS** and **intracardiac thromboembolism** (most likely just after reperfusion).
- TEE-detected thromboemboli at reperfusion in **20%** in one series, linked to **isolated RV dysfunction**
- Clinically significant intracardiac thrombus **0.7–6.25%**; **left-sided** thrombus has **high mortality**
- Treatment: **stop procoagulants (antifibrinolytics)**, **heparin 2000–5000 units**; with collapse, **low-dose t-PA 0.5–4 mg** as rescue
- **Extracorporeal life support** has been used
cards.e: Rapid TEE diagnosis is the key, because the treatment (anticoagulation or lysis) is the opposite of what is done for bleeding. Arrest is more frequent during LT than other surgery and can occur at any stage.

cards.q: What intraoperative signs suggest that the new liver graft is working, and what suggests primary nonfunction?
cards.a:
**Good function**: falling **calcium requirement**, **improving acidosis**, increasing **urine output**, **rising core temperature**, **bile production**.
- **Primary nonfunction** (neohepatic or early postop): no bile, haemodynamic instability, **coagulopathy**, **hypothermia**; usually needs **urgent retransplantation**
cards.e: Each sign reflects restored hepatic metabolism of citrate and lactate, heat production and synthetic activity. Oxford warns that persisting acidosis or hypocalcaemia after reperfusion suggest primary nonfunction, which occurs in up to 5% of cases.

cards.q: When might biliary reconstruction be delayed with abdominal packing after liver transplantation?
cards.a:
In cases with **massive bleeding, coagulopathy, haemodynamic instability or early graft dysfunction**.
- Abdomen packed and temporarily closed; **re-operation within 2–3 days** for biliary reconstruction and closure
- Used in **8%** of LTs over 10 years at one centre; more often in **critically ill** recipients and **retransplants**
cards.e: Packing allows correction of coagulopathy, hypothermia and acidosis in ICU before completing surgery. Normally the hepatic artery and biliary anastomoses are done after venous reperfusion.

cards.q: What mechanisms cause coagulopathy during liver transplantation, and what are the principles of correcting it?
cards.a:
Three mechanisms on top of fragile rebalanced haemostasis, plus dilution:
- **Impaired thrombin generation** (low factors)
- **Weak clot** (low **fibrinogen**, **thrombocytopenia**)
- **Increased clot breakdown** (**hyperfibrinolysis**)
- After reperfusion: loss of synthesis plus a **heparin-like effect**
Principles:
- Treat **clinically significant bleeding only**; **no prophylactic** products
- Guide therapy with **microvascular bleeding** and tests: **ROTEM/TEG** at point of care or PT/INR, fibrinogen, platelets
cards.e: Intraoperative transfusion predicts post-transplant survival in single-centre studies, so avoidable transfusion is harmful. Lippincott's massive transfusion question shows how low platelets, very low fibrinogen, prolonged PT/APTT and high D-dimer point to a consumptive picture rather than isolated dilution.

cards.q: How are viscoelastic tests used to guide haemostatic therapy in liver transplantation, and what is the evidence?
cards.a:
Each abnormality points to a specific product:
- **Prolonged CT (ROTEM) / R time (TEG)** → coagulation factors: **FFP or PCC**
- **Low MCF / MA** (clot firmness) → **fibrinogen** (and platelets)
- **Lysis** → **antifibrinolytic**
- Evidence: one centre using a ROTEM algorithm with PCC and fibrinogen concentrate had a median of **2 RBC units**, platelets in **29%**, plasma in **15%**; another found **no reduction** versus standard protocol; most studies are retrospective
cards.e: Viscoelastic-guided management clearly reduces transfusion in cardiac surgery but the LT evidence is weaker. Point-of-care testing shortens the time to results, and protocols depend on local availability of cryoprecipitate, PCC and fibrinogen concentrate. Oxford describes TEG being used to fine-tune clotting and to guide antifibrinolytic and platelet doses at reperfusion.

cards.q: Compare FFP, prothrombin complex concentrate and recombinant factor VIIa for replacing coagulation factors in liver transplantation.
cards.a:
**FFP**: all pro- and anticoagulant factors at **low concentration**; large volumes risk **TACO** and **hepatic venous congestion**.
- **PCC (4-factor)**: factors **II, VII, IX, X plus protein C and S**; small volume, avoids **TRALI and TACO**; thrombosis risk theoretical, not shown clinically
- **rFVIIa**: **no clinical benefit** in LT, **increases thrombotic events** → **not recommended**
cards.e: Volume matters because many LT recipients also have renal failure, and excess fluid raises CVP and congests the new graft. Oxford's older practice transfuses about 2 units FFP per unit of blood with TEG fine-tuning and advises CVP no higher than 12 mm Hg postoperatively to avoid hepatic congestion.

cards.q: Compare FFP, cryoprecipitate and fibrinogen concentrate for treating hypofibrinogenaemia in liver transplantation.
cards.a:
Target fibrinogen up to **150–200 mg/dL** in a bleeding patient.
- **FFP**: only **100–150 mg/dL** fibrinogen; needs **10–15 mL/kg or more** → volume overload
- **Cryoprecipitate**: rich in **fibrinogen, FVIII, vWF, FXIII**; **150–200 mg/unit**, pool of **5 units = 750–1000 mg**; heavy use linked to **thromboembolism**
- **Fibrinogen concentrate**: ~**1 g per vial**, rapid rise without volume; **pre-emptive dosing did not reduce transfusion**; **off-label** in the USA
cards.e: Fibrinogen levels fall during LT from bleeding, dilution and consumption on top of low baseline levels. Guide replacement with plasma fibrinogen or viscoelastic clot firmness (MCF/MA), not by formula.

cards.q: What is the role of platelet transfusion and antifibrinolytics during liver transplantation?
cards.a:
Both are reserved for **demonstrated need**.
**Platelets**:
- Prophylactic transfusion **barely improves** coagulation
- Linked to **acute lung injury**, higher **1-year graft failure and mortality**
**Antifibrinolytics**:
- Hyperfibrinolysis is **worst after reperfusion** (t-PA from graft endothelium)
- **Aprotinin withdrawn in 2008**; **tranexamic acid** and **ε-aminocaproic acid** available
- Prophylaxis lowered transfusion in three studies but one found more **DVT**
- Use only with **significant bleeding plus suspected/documented hyperfibrinolysis**; no routine prophylaxis
cards.e: Note: Oxford gives routine tranexamic acid in the anhepatic phase; follow Miller. Antifibrinolytics are avoided in multivisceral candidates with thrombosis or hypercoagulability.

cards.q: Define cold and warm ischaemia time for a liver graft and explain static cold storage and machine perfusion.
cards.a:
**Static cold storage**: graft flushed with **high-potassium** preservation solution, bagged and kept on ice at **4–8°C** to slow metabolism.
- **Cold ischaemia time**: from **donor aortic cross-clamp** with cold flush to **removal from cold storage**; **>8 h** reduces graft survival
- **Warm ischaemia time**: from removal from ice (anhepatic phase) to **reperfusion**; usually **30–50 min**; longer → graft dysfunction and loss
- **Machine perfusion**: **hypothermic (0–12°C)** or **normothermic**; normothermic allows testing of **lactate clearance, enzymes and bile** before implantation
- Used for **DCD**, **extended criteria** grafts and long anticipated cold ischaemia
cards.e: The potassium-rich preservation fluid is one source of the potassium surge at reperfusion. Normothermic perfusion runs near body temperature (Miller's printed range, 35–28°C, is garbled).

cards.q: Outline early postoperative care and analgesia after liver transplantation.
cards.a:
ICU care focused on **haemodynamics, metabolic stability and graft function**.
- Serial **liver function tests** for early allograft dysfunction; urine output; coagulation (may need transfusion)
- **Hyperglycaemia** after reperfusion often needs **insulin infusion**
- Analgesia: opioids/PCA (**morphine with caution in renal dysfunction**); needs are lower than other major laparotomies
- **Epidural generally contraindicated** (coagulopathy), though one centre used thoracic epidurals in lower-MELD patients
- Multimodal regimens (ketamine, gabapentin, paracetamol, wound ropivacaine) and **subcostal TAP** reported
- **Early extubation** (even in theatre) feasible in selected patients with good graft function; ERAS/fast-track reduces ICU stay and cost
cards.e: Oxford reports ICU stays as short as about 6 hours with early extubation, recommends avoiding NSAIDs because of calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity, and notes that epidurals are only possible in a minority. Stoelting describes several hours of ventilation while acidosis clears in many cases.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22 · Stoelting 7e Ch 17

cards.q: What are the early surgical and graft complications after liver transplantation?
cards.a:
**Bleeding, wound infection, biliary complications, vascular thrombosis, early allograft dysfunction and primary nonfunction**.
- **Primary nonfunction**: no bile, instability, coagulopathy, hypothermia → **urgent retransplantation**
- **Hepatic artery or portal vein thrombosis** → graft ischaemia and necrosis
- Transaminases and bilirubin that **fail to fall** suggest **hepatic artery thrombosis** → urgent **Doppler ultrasound** ± re-exploration
cards.e: Some enzyme rise is expected from cold ischaemia; it is the trend that matters. Oxford gives incidences of postoperative bleeding 5–10%, primary nonfunction up to 5%, hepatic artery thrombosis 0.5–5% (thrombectomy or super-urgent retransplant), sepsis 10–20% and acute rejection up to 40%. Stoelting notes right upper quadrant ultrasound is performed routinely after LT to confirm vascular patency.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22 · Stoelting 7e Ch 17

cards.q: What cardiopulmonary and renal complications follow liver transplantation, and how can AKI be limited?
cards.a:
Cardiopulmonary complications are **more frequent than after kidney transplant**.
- **Pulmonary oedema** up to 47%, **pleural effusion** 47%, **pneumonia** 38%
- **Systolic heart failure** ~7%, **AF** ~7% (both raise mortality); ~**13% 5-year cardiac events**, about half ACS
- **AKI** is common and multifactorial (pre-existing **HRS**); post-LT renal failure raises early and late mortality
- Consensus measures to limit AKI: **haemodynamic stability**, **short caval clamp time**, **intraoperative dialysis** in selected patients
cards.e: Long-term deaths are driven by renal dysfunction, metabolic syndrome with CAD, and malignancy, all linked to immunosuppression. Oxford adds that no strategy reliably prevents renal failure beyond fluid optimisation and avoiding nephrotoxins, sometimes delaying calcineurin inhibitors.

cards.q: What are the indications for simultaneous liver–kidney (SLK) and combined thoracic–liver transplantation?
cards.a:
**SLK** for LT candidates with **irreversible renal failure**:
- CKD: **GFR <30 mL/min** and on **chronic dialysis**
- AKI: **6 weeks** of GFR **<25 mL/min** or **6 consecutive weeks of dialysis**
- **9%** of US LTs in 2020; justified because chronic renal failure after LT shortens survival; same-donor organs may have **fewer rejections**
**Heart–liver**: end-stage heart disease with advanced liver failure (often **congestive hepatopathy**, incl. adult congenital disease); 5-year survival >90% (USA), 71–82% (Europe)
**Liver–lung**: mainly **cystic fibrosis**; 1-year survival similar to lung alone
cards.e: Allocation follows the thoracic organ for heart–liver and lung–liver transplants but the liver for SLK. Combined procedures bring longer operations, more coagulopathy and higher transfusion needs.

cards.q: How should a patient with a previous liver transplant be managed for nontransplant surgery?
cards.a:
With a good graft, **drug metabolism is normal**; focus on graft function, immunosuppression and renal function.
- Graft function: **PT/INR and bilirubin**; correct coagulopathy with **vitamin K, FFP or PCC** if needed
- Optimise ascites (diuretics, albumin, paracentesis); prevent encephalopathy (lactulose, careful sedation)
- Continue daily **steroids**; routine **stress dosing** has little evidence
- **Chronic renal dysfunction** and **CNI-related hypertension** are common
- **Neuraxial** blocks acceptable if INR normal (e.g. **<1.4**) and no thrombocytopenia; avoid catheters if postoperative hepatic dysfunction is likely
cards.e: Lippincott's question on a patient two years after LT expects a raised creatinine as the most likely abnormality, reflecting chronic renal dysfunction. Strict asepsis is essential in all immunosuppressed patients.

cards.q: Classify intestinal and multivisceral transplant procedures.
cards.a:
Four commonly used categories:
- **Isolated small intestine** (no liver or stomach)
- **Liver–intestine** (no stomach)
- **Modified multivisceral**: stomach + intestine, **no liver**
- **Full multivisceral**: intestine + **liver + stomach**
- The **pancreas** is often included (technical simplicity or pancreatic insufficiency), sometimes a segment of **colon**; a **kidney** may be added for renal failure
cards.e: Only recipients of liver-containing grafts have the physiology of end-stage liver disease, so the anaesthetic challenges vary by graft type. The international registry (2699 patients, 1985–2013) reported pooled patient survival of 76% at one year, falling to 56% at five and 43% at ten.

cards.q: What are the indications for intestinal transplantation?
cards.a:
**Intestinal failure** with life-threatening complications of **parenteral nutrition** or a high-risk underlying disease.
- **Children**: short bowel from **gastroschisis**, **necrotising enterocolitis**, **volvulus**; **microvillous inclusion disease**
- **Adults**: thrombotic or traumatic **intestinal infarction**, **desmoid tumour**, **Crohn's** short bowel, **motility disorders**
- **PN complications**: progressive **cholestasis/liver failure**, **loss of central venous access** from thrombosis, **recurrent line sepsis**
- Others: frequent admissions for **dehydration from stoma losses**; emerging: portomesenteric thrombosis with ESLD, chronic fistula/sepsis, refusal of lifelong PN
cards.e: Better PN lipid emulsions have reduced PN-associated liver disease, shifting indications. Survival and cost-effectiveness still lag behind other organs, so care is concentrated in specialist regional or national units.

cards.q: Describe the surgical procedure for intestinal and liver–intestine transplantation.
cards.a:
Arterial inflow and venous outflow depend on whether a liver is included.
- **Isolated intestine**: donor **SMA** anastomosed to recipient; donor **portal vein to recipient IVC or portal vein**
- **Liver–intestine (± stomach, duodenum, pancreas)**: inflow via **aorta-to-SMA** anastomosis or conduit; outflow via hepatic veins to **IVC** or **piggyback**
- Including the **pancreas** avoids hilar injury, vessel kinking and a Roux biliary limb, and helps diabetics
- After reperfusion: upper GI anastomosis, colon-to-ileum anastomosis, **temporary ileostomy** (decompression and **endoscopic biopsy for rejection**)
- Abdominal closure can be difficult: mesh, muscle flap or **donor abdominal wall** graft
cards.e: The stoma is the window for surveillance endoscopy, which is the main way to diagnose rejection. Keeping the colon improves fluid and electrolyte absorption.

cards.q: What specific issues arise in the preoperative assessment of intestinal and multivisceral transplant candidates?
cards.a:
Assessment mirrors LT, with extra emphasis on **vascular access, coagulation and pain**.
- **Central veins** often thrombosed from PN catheters; SVC/innominate obstruction may present as **facial swelling** and may **contraindicate a liver-containing graft**
- **Supradiaphragmatic access is essential** when a liver is included (IVC occluded intraoperatively); **femoral vein patency** needed for intestine-only
- Map veins by **ultrasound ± MR venography**; plan with interventional radiology **before listing**
- **Viscoelastic testing and thrombophilia screen**: most candidates are **prothrombotic**
- **Chronic opioid use** → involve pain specialists
- Exclude **POPH and HPS**; sarcopenia, ischaemic heart disease and diabetes (especially >60 years) may be prohibitive
cards.e: Vascular access is often the limiting factor in preparing these patients. A prothrombotic baseline explains why antifibrinolytics are used cautiously and why thromboembolism is more frequent than in LT.

cards.q: Describe the key intraoperative considerations for liver–intestine and multivisceral transplantation.
cards.a:
Very long (up to **24 h or more**), bloody operations needing **two experienced anaesthetists** and a massive transfusion protocol.
- Previous surgery (**peritoneal sclerosis**) and portal hypertension → **loss of multiple blood volumes**; pre-op **SMA/coeliac embolisation** may reduce bleeding
- Start the recipient anaesthetic early to minimise ischaemia time
- **Large-bore central lines** with ultrasound; plan alternative supradiaphragmatic sites
- **VVB** from early dissection in some centres (with heat exchanger); **pre-emptive haemofiltration** for acidosis and hyperkalaemia
- **TEE** detects air and thrombus (thromboembolism risk higher than in LT)
- **Cell salvage only while bowel intact**; cell saver can **wash banked blood** to lower K⁺
- Antifibrinolytics avoided with thrombosis history; used only for bleeding with fibrinolysis
cards.e: Reperfusion of an intestine-only graft is usually uneventful, but a composite graft containing liver produces hyperkalaemia, hypotension and a large temperature drop because a big tissue mass is reperfused via both arterial and portal routes. Continuing haemodiafiltration after reperfusion may prolong hypothermia.

cards.q: What are the postoperative issues and outcomes after intestinal and multivisceral transplantation?
cards.a:
Prolonged ventilation, large fluid shifts, intense immunosuppression and frequent complications.
- **Intravascular depletion** from fluid translocation for several days
- Prophylactic antimicrobials, **intensive multi-agent induction**; graft surveillance by **Doppler** and **stoma endoscopy**
- Analgesia: **PCA opioids** routine; rectus sheath/subcostal TAP infusions; **long-term opioid use** common
- **Rejection in one-half to two-thirds** (high antigenicity); liver inclusion gives some tolerance but is reserved for ESLD
- **PTLD ~30%**, **graft-versus-host disease ~10%**; infection, bleeding, thrombosis, leaks
- Survival: 1-year **50–92%**, 5-year **33–83%**; better for isolated intestine, intestine–liver and children
cards.e: The gut is rich in lymphoid tissue, which explains both its high rejection rate and the risk of graft-versus-host disease. Graft loss is now rare thanks to better immunosuppression.

cards.q: A 58-year-old diabetic man on haemodialysis is called in for a deceased-donor kidney transplant. His last dialysis was 2 days ago. He weighs 3 kg above his dry weight, K⁺ is 6.6 mmol/L and the ECG shows peaked T waves. The surgeon wants to start within the hour. What do you do?
cards.a:
**Postpone induction and dialyse first**; hyperkalaemia with ECG changes plus fluid overload is a clear indication.
- Explain to the team: cold ischaemia allows some time (ideal kidney CIT **<24 h**), whereas inducing now risks arrhythmic arrest, especially with succinylcholine and at graft reperfusion (K⁺ washout)
- Immediate temporising therapy while dialysis is arranged: **IV calcium** (membrane stabilisation), **insulin with glucose**, consider bicarbonate; avoid hypoventilation/acidosis
- **Urgent haemodialysis** to correct K⁺ and remove excess volume; recheck K⁺, glucose and volume afterwards
- Then: RSI (rocuronium if K⁺ still raised), arterial line opposite the fistula, plan for reperfusion potassium load
cards.e: Miller states that raised potassium, particularly with ECG changes, mandates delaying surgery for immediate dialysis, and that significant volume overload is also an indication. Oxford sets 6.0 mmol/L as the threshold requiring dialysis and advises allowing 4–6 hours after dialysis for equilibration and heparin clearance; Stoelting describes calcium, insulin, bicarbonate and hyperventilation for acute hyperkalaemia.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Oxford Handbook Ch 6 · Stoelting 7e Ch 21 · Stoelting 7e Ch 22

cards.q: A 45-year-old woman with ESRD from type 1 diabetes is having a living-donor kidney transplant. She has gastroparesis and orthostatic hypotension. K⁺ is 4.6 mmol/L. Plan your induction, neuromuscular management and reversal.
cards.a:
**RSI with attention to autonomic instability**, then an organ-independent relaxant and full reversal.
- Aspiration prophylaxis (nonparticulate antacid, H2 blocker); **arterial line** considered before induction given autonomic neuropathy
- Cautious induction dose, vasopressor ready; anticipate post-induction hypotension (especially if on ACE inhibitor/ARB) and exaggerated laryngoscopy response
- **Succinylcholine is acceptable** (K⁺ normal; expected rise 0.5–1.0 mEq/L for 10–15 min); alternative **rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg**
- Maintenance relaxant: **cisatracurium** (Hofmann), monitored; keep block until **fascia closed**
- Reversal: neostigmine for cisatracurium, or **sugammadex** if rocuronium used (safe in ESRD; label caution)
- Avoid pancuronium; extubate awake with airway reflexes intact
cards.e: Diabetic and uraemic gastropathy together make RSI the standard, and autonomic neuropathy (up to 50% of ESRD patients) causes wide blood pressure swings. A newly functioning living-donor kidney will accelerate drug clearance, but residual blockade still carries pulmonary risk. Stoelting notes symptomatic diabetic gastroparesis may be clinically silent.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Stoelting 7e Ch 23 · Oxford Handbook Ch 6

cards.q: During a deceased-donor kidney transplant under sevoflurane, the clamps are released. MAP falls from 85 to 62 mm Hg, HR 95, and the graft looks soft and pale. CVP is 6 mm Hg. What is your management?
cards.a:
Restore **graft perfusion pressure quickly** without vasoconstricting the graft.
- Check surgical field for **bleeding** at the anastomoses; check ECG/K⁺ (preservative washout)
- **Reduce volatile** concentration
- **Fluid bolus** (crystalloid/colloid; blood if bleeding)
- **Inotrope** to raise cardiac output if fluid insufficient; **avoid α-agonist vasopressors** where possible (denervated graft vasculature)
- Target **MAP ≥70 mm Hg** (lower values after reperfusion linked to delayed graft function)
- Ensure **mannitol and furosemide** were given before reperfusion; consider TEE/cardiac output monitoring if refractory
cards.e: Reperfusion hypotension reflects added vascular capacity (Stoelting: up to about 300 mL), vasodilators from ischaemic tissue and sometimes bleeding. Hypotension aggravates ischaemia–reperfusion injury, so speed matters; Stoelting also advises high-normal pressure with euvolaemia.

cards.q: Two hours after an uneventful kidney transplant, a 50-year-old recipient's urine output falls from 200 mL/h to 15 mL/h. BP is 100/60 mm Hg, HR 110. What is your approach?
cards.a:
Treat as an **emergency evaluation of graft perfusion and drainage**.
- **Catheter**: flush/check for clot obstruction (three-way catheter)
- **Prerenal** (most likely with tachycardia and soft BP): **aggressive volume** resuscitation; check Hb for **bleeding/haematoma**
- Consider invasive monitoring if unstable or oliguria persists
- **Doppler ultrasound** for **arterial/venous thrombosis**, haematoma compressing graft, **ureteric** obstruction or leak
- Inform surgeons early: **ureteric anastomotic problems or vascular thrombosis need re-exploration**
- Also consider hyperacute rejection and delayed graft function (ATN)
cards.e: Miller stresses that a sudden fall in urine output must prompt rapid evaluation, with prerenal causes treated by volume and ureteric problems by surgery. Stoelting notes hyperacute rejection may require graft removal and that delayed graft function from ATN is relatively common in deceased-donor grafts.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Stoelting 7e Ch 22 · Oxford Handbook Ch 6

cards.q: A 38-year-old woman undergoes simultaneous pancreas–kidney transplant. Glucose was 230 mg/dL before reperfusion on an insulin infusion. Thirty minutes after pancreas reperfusion glucose is 70 mg/dL. On postoperative day 2 her glucose suddenly rises to 320 mg/dL. Explain both events and your management.
cards.a:
**Intraoperative fall**: expected **insulin release from the functioning graft** within minutes.
- **Stop/reduce insulin**, give **dextrose**, check glucose about **every 30 min**
- A failure to normalise would have suggested early graft dysfunction
**Postoperative rise**: suspect **graft thrombosis**, the commonest cause of early non-immune graft loss (5–10%)
- Urgent **ultrasound/Doppler**, inform surgeons; **emergency re-exploration** if confirmed
- Check anticoagulation status (thromboprophylaxis protocols reduce thrombosis but increase bleeding)
- Also consider rejection or pancreatitis
cards.e: The glucose trend is the anaesthetist's best real-time graft monitor. Pre-reperfusion targets are under 200 mg/dL to avoid ketoacidosis; after reperfusion the danger switches to hypoglycaemia.

cards.q: A 55-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis (MELD 24) has exertional dyspnoea. SpO₂ is 89% sitting and 94% supine. PaO₂ on air is 56 mm Hg with an A–a gradient of 48 mm Hg. Contrast echo shows bubbles in the left atrium after 4 cardiac cycles. Interpret and discuss implications for transplantation and anaesthesia.
cards.a:
**Severe hepatopulmonary syndrome** (PaO₂ 50–59 mm Hg) with orthodeoxia and **intrapulmonary shunting**.
- Delayed left-sided bubbles (3–4 beats) = **intrapulmonary vascular dilatation**, not an intracardiac shunt
- Exclude other causes (effusion, ascites, COPD)
- **LT is the only cure**, usually correcting hypoxaemia within a year; PaO₂ **<60 mm Hg** qualifies for **MELD exception points**, so list promptly
- Anaesthesia: high FiO₂, expect a limited response to oxygen and PEEP, and slow recovery of oxygenation after LT
cards.e: Stoelting describes platypnoea–orthodeoxia and the timing of bubbles that confirms intrapulmonary shunting, and notes hypoxaemia may be refractory to oxygen and PEEP. Older teaching considered PaO₂ ≤50 mm Hg a predictor of post-LT death, but timely transplantation now gives good results.

cards.q: A 52-year-old woman listed for liver transplant has TTE estimated PASP 58 mm Hg. Right heart catheterisation shows mPAP 42 mm Hg, PAWP 10 mm Hg, cardiac output 7 L/min. Interpret and plan.
cards.a:
**Moderate portopulmonary hypertension**.
- PVR = (42 − 10) × 80 / 7 ≈ **366 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵** (>240) and PAWP <15 → true POPH, not just high flow
- mPAP **35–45 mm Hg** = moderate; >35 mm Hg historically linked to high LT mortality
- Refer to **pulmonary hypertension team** for **vasodilator therapy**; reassess haemodynamics
- Proceed only if pressures respond; on the day, **PA catheter** before incision (may cancel), TEE for RV function
- Intraop: avoid fluid overload, have inotropes ready, anticipate RV failure at reperfusion and graft congestion from high right-sided pressures
cards.e: The PAWP and PVR criteria distinguish POPH from the raised PA pressure of hyperdynamic flow, in which PVR is normal. Effectively treated moderate–severe POPH can do well. Note: Stoelting treats mPAP >45 mm Hg as an absolute contraindication; follow Miller.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Stoelting 7e Ch 17 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22

cards.q: During liver transplantation, the portal vein is unclamped. Within 2 minutes MAP falls from 75 to 40 mm Hg, HR falls to 45/min, the ECG shows peaked T waves and K⁺ is 7.2 mmol/L. Core temperature dropped 1°C. What is happening and how do you treat it?
cards.a:
**Postreperfusion syndrome with hyperkalaemia**.
- **Calcium chloride** IV immediately; **sodium bicarbonate**; **insulin** (with glucose); hyperventilate
- **Adrenaline** in small boluses (and atropine for bradycardia), then **noradrenaline** infusion if needed; aim MAP ~70 mm Hg
- Look with **TEE**: RV dilatation/thrombus/air, LV function, filling
- Check ABG, ionised Ca²⁺, glucose; warm patient
- Watch for later **hypokalaemia** as the graft takes up potassium
- Prevention next time: optimise K⁺, Ca²⁺ and acid–base before unclamping; prophylactic calcium/catecholamine; intraoperative dialysis in oliguric hyperkalaemic patients
cards.e: PRS occurs in over half of LTs and is driven by potassium, acid and cold preservation effluent plus vasoactive mediators. Oxford notes K⁺ can reach 8–9 mmol/L with poor grafts and recommends calcium and incremental 50 µg adrenaline; Lippincott says atropine treats bradycardia but not the vasodilatory hypotension.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22 · Lippincott Ch 14

cards.q: Five minutes after liver graft reperfusion, after tranexamic acid and cryoprecipitate were given for bleeding, a 60-year-old recipient suddenly becomes profoundly hypotensive with ETCO₂ falling from 34 to 15 mm Hg. TEE shows a dilated, hypokinetic RV and a mobile echodensity in the right atrium. Management?
cards.a:
**Intracardiac thromboembolism with acute RV failure**.
- Call for help; **CPR** if output lost; adrenaline/vasopressors and inotropes for RV support
- **Stop procoagulant therapy** (antifibrinolytics, further cryo/factor concentrates)
- **Heparin 2000–5000 units**
- If collapse persists: **low-dose t-PA 0.5–4 mg** as rescue
- Consider **ECLS** if available
- Discuss with surgeon (bleeding risk vs survival); use TEE to monitor clot and RV response
cards.e: Thrombi are most likely just after reperfusion; one series found TEE-detected emboli in 20% of patients, associated with isolated RV dysfunction, and left-sided thrombus carries high mortality. Heavy cryoprecipitate and antifibrinolytic use are both linked to thrombotic complications, a reason Miller advises targeted rather than prophylactic use.

cards.q: After liver graft reperfusion there is diffuse oozing. ROTEM shows a prolonged clotting time (CT), low maximum clot firmness (MCF) and 40% clot lysis. Fibrinogen is 90 mg/dL, platelets 55 × 10⁹/L. How do you treat?
cards.a:
Combined **hyperfibrinolysis**, **hypofibrinogenaemia** and **factor deficiency**; treat in order of impact.
- **Antifibrinolytic** (tranexamic acid or ε-aminocaproic acid): clinically significant bleeding with documented lysis
- **Fibrinogen** to ~150–200 mg/dL: **fibrinogen concentrate** (~1 g/vial) or **cryoprecipitate** (5-unit pool ≈ 750–1000 mg) rather than large FFP volumes
- **Factors** for prolonged CT: **PCC** or FFP (watch volume, TACO, hepatic congestion)
- Platelets only if bleeding persists with low clot firmness after fibrinogen (risks ALI, graft loss)
- Correct **calcium, temperature, acidosis**; repeat ROTEM after treatment
cards.e: Fibrinolysis peaks after reperfusion because graft endothelium releases t-PA. Products are given for bleeding plus test evidence, never prophylactically; FFP contains only 100–150 mg/dL fibrinogen and would need 10–15 mL/kg or more to make a difference.

cards.q: A 24-year-old woman with paracetamol-induced acute liver failure (arterial pH 7.25, grade 4 encephalopathy, INR 7.0) arrives for super-urgent liver transplantation. She is intubated with a serum sodium of 138 mmol/L. Outline your anaesthetic priorities.
cards.a:
**Protect the brain** while managing coagulopathy, circulation and metabolism.
- Meets **King's College** criteria (pH <7.3); transplant justified
- **ICP control**: 30° head-up, neutral head, deep sedation and **paralysis** (no coughing/shivering), **normocapnia** (hyperventilate only for surges), **hypertonic saline** to Na⁺ **145–155**, mannitol if renal function allows; ICP monitoring controversial
- **Avoid volatiles** (or very low concentrations): use **propofol TIVA**
- Maintain MAP/CPP with **noradrenaline** and normovolaemia
- **Glucose** monitoring and dextrose (profound anhepatic hypoglycaemia in ALF)
- Early **RRT/plasma exchange** for ammonia, acidosis, K⁺; treat coagulopathy only for bleeding
cards.e: Cerebral oedema with intracranial hypertension is the most lethal complication of ALF. Oxford advises avoiding volatile agents, using propofol TCI and considering ICP monitoring, and notes raised ICP in 70% of hyperacute cases; paracetamol ALF has a relatively favourable prognosis.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Oxford Handbook Ch 7 · Oxford Handbook Ch 22

cards.q: A cirrhotic patient with Na⁺ 116 mmol/L presents for liver transplantation. During massive transfusion over 3 hours, Na⁺ rises to 126 mmol/L. What is your concern and what should you do?
cards.a:
Risk of **osmotic demyelination syndrome** from **too-rapid correction**.
- Current advice: rise **≤8 mEq/L in 24 h** (already exceeded)
- Minimise sodium loads: choose products and fluids carefully, avoid unnecessary **sodium bicarbonate** and hypertonic fluids
- Check Na⁺ frequently (point-of-care) and anticipate the sodium load of each product
- Inform ICU to continue controlled correction postoperatively and monitor neurologically
cards.e: Older series linked ODS to perioperative rises of 21–32 mEq/L, but current recommendations are more conservative. Massive transfusion of plasma, albumin and bicarbonate can raise sodium rapidly, so anticipation is needed from the start of the case.

cards.q: A 62-year-old man who had a kidney transplant 4 years ago (on tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisolone 5 mg) needs a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. His creatinine has risen from 115 to 170 µmol/L over 2 months and BP is 165/95. How do you proceed?
cards.a:
**Defer elective surgery** and get nephrology review: a new creatinine rise may indicate **rejection** (or CNI toxicity).
When cleared for surgery:
- Assume **reduced GFR** even with near-normal creatinine; avoid **NSAIDs** and other nephrotoxins; adjust renally cleared drugs
- **Continue immunosuppression** and usual steroid dose (routine stress dosing not supported); check drug interactions
- Cardiac risk per **ACC/AHA** (high CVD prevalence)
- Maintain **renal perfusion**: avoid hypovolaemia and hypotension
- Strict **asepsis**; **CMV-negative** blood if CMV-negative and transfusion needed
- GA, regional or combined techniques are all acceptable
cards.e: Stoelting adds that azotaemia, proteinuria and hypertension may indicate chronic rejection, and that immunosuppressants cause hypertension, lowered seizure threshold, anaemia and thrombocytopenia. Oxford emphasises the graft has only half the normal nephron mass and that creatinine underestimates the reduced clearance.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 56 · Stoelting 7e Ch 22 · Oxford Handbook Ch 6

cards.q: A 34-year-old woman with short bowel syndrome and PN-associated liver failure is being assessed for liver–intestine transplantation. She has had multiple line infections; ultrasound shows occluded right and left internal jugular and subclavian veins. What are the anaesthetic implications?
cards.a:
**Vascular access is potentially prohibitive** and must be solved **before listing**.
- A liver-containing graft requires **supradiaphragmatic access** because the IVC is partly or fully occluded intraoperatively; femoral access alone is inadequate
- Full mapping with **ultrasound and MR venography**; check for SVC/innominate obstruction (facial swelling may contraindicate a liver graft)
- Involve **interventional radiology** (recanalisation) or plan surgical access at other supradiaphragmatic sites
- Also: **thrombophilia screen and viscoelastic testing** (usually prothrombotic), exclude **POPH/HPS**, chronic opioid use (pain team)
- Plan for massive transfusion, VVB, haemofiltration and two experienced anaesthetists
cards.e: Miller describes access planning as an essential and sometimes limiting step for these candidates. Intestine-only recipients can manage with confirmed femoral venous patency, but liver-containing grafts cannot.

cards.q: What are the three sources of transplantable organs, and how does each source differ in the physiological insult the graft has suffered before retrieval?
cards.a:
In the USA most organs come from **donation after brain death (DBD)**. **Donation after circulatory death (DCD)** and **living donation** supply the rest.
- **DBD**: the graft is exposed to the **haemodynamic instability and neurohormonal derangement** of brain death, which needs active treatment
- **DCD**: an unavoidable spell of **hypotension and hypoxaemia** comes before cardiac arrest, so there is **warm ischaemia**
- **Living donor**: an elective, planned operation with the **shortest cold ischaemia** and no brain death or DCD physiology. The cost is that a **healthy person** is put at risk
cards.e: Each source therefore brings its own management problem: in DBD you treat the derangements, in DCD you keep warm ischaemia short, and with living donors you protect a healthy volunteer. If these insults are left uncorrected the graft deteriorates, is declined, or has early dysfunction after transplant.

cards.q: How large is the gap between organ supply and demand, and what strategies are used to narrow it?
cards.a:
Organ shortage is the **single biggest obstacle** to transplantation worldwide.
- USA: more than **105,000** candidates are waiting. In 2020 the kidney list was about **6 times** the number of transplants done, the liver list about **3 times**, and the heart and lung lists about **twice**
- Donation rates are highest for **kidney**, then liver, heart, lung and pancreas
- Strategies: public awareness, changes to allocation, **extended criteria donors (ECDs)**, living related and unrelated donation, **paired/chain exchange**, more referrals to procurement agencies, using organs that were retrieved but then discarded, and **machine perfusion**
cards.e: The number of organs transplanted per donor depends on the donor category (standard criteria, ECD or DCD). Countries with moral or legal objections to brain death depend mainly on living donors. COVID-19 increased waiting-list deaths in early 2020 and hit living donation hardest; activity later returned to about pre-pandemic levels.

cards.q: What ASA physical status is given to a brain-dead organ donor, and why is the anaesthetist's role important even though the patient is dead?
cards.a:
A declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donation is **ASA VI**.
- The aim of care moves from protecting the brain to **optimising perfusion and oxygenation of the organs**
- Decisions are made with the **recipients'** needs in mind, not the donor's
- One multiorgan donor may affect the outcome of **more than 6 recipients**
cards.e: Lippincott uses this classification as a quick MCQ (kidney retrieval from a brain-dead donor = ASA VI; a moribund patient not expected to survive without surgery = ASA V). Miller notes that the anaesthetist is involved from identifying the donor through to transplantation, and must understand the physiology of brain death, ischaemia–reperfusion injury and the legal and ethical framework.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 57 · Lippincott Ch 1 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13

cards.q: Outline the historical and legal basis for declaring death by neurological criteria, and how acceptance varies between countries.
cards.a:
The idea of brain death appeared in the **1950s** and was formalised by the **Harvard Ad Hoc Committee on Irreversible Coma (1968)**.
- USA: the **Uniform Determination of Death Act (1981)** was drafted with the AMA, the American Bar Association and a President's Commission
- The ethical principles are decades old but are still considered valid
- Western countries differ slightly in definition and procedure, but the clinical criteria are similar
- Bigger differences exist **between cultures**. In some **Asian countries** brain death has **no legal status**, so DCD and **living donation** dominate there
cards.e: Organs can be retrieved from a DBD donor only **after** death has been declared, so the anaesthetist must know the local criteria and protocol for wherever they work. Stoelting defines brain death as permanent loss of all brain function, and its criteria are an adaptation of the Harvard criteria.

cards.q: What preconditions must be met before brainstem death testing can start?
cards.a:
Testing is valid only when the coma has a known, irreversible cause and every confounder has been excluded.
- **Deep coma, apnoea, and dependence on mechanical ventilation**
- A known cause of **irreversible brain injury** (commonly head injury, intracranial haemorrhage, tumour, hypoxic brain injury)
- Reversible causes excluded: **sedatives, neuromuscular blockers, alcohol, hypothermia, metabolic or endocrine disturbance**
- Timing (UK): usually **at least 6 h** after the onset of apnoeic coma, or **24 h** after return of circulation if the cause was cardiac arrest. If therapeutic hypothermia was used, wait **24 h after normothermia** is restored
cards.e: A classic exam trap is a patient still under the effect of sedatives, neuromuscular blockers or cooling. Testing is invalid until these are excluded. Miller itself says only that declaration must follow national guidelines and local protocol, so the operational detail comes from Oxford and Stoelting.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 57 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13

cards.q: List the clinical tests of brainstem function used to diagnose brainstem death and the conduct rules (who, how many times, time of death).
cards.a:
All brainstem reflexes must be absent:
- **Pupils fixed** with no direct or consensual light response (dilation is not required)
- **Corneal reflex** absent
- **No motor response in the cranial nerve distribution** to central or peripheral pain
- **Oculovestibular reflex** absent: no eye movement during and for at least 1 min after 50 mL of ice-cold water into each ear, once the tympanic membrane has been seen with an auroscope
- **No gag or cough** when a suction catheter is passed into the pharynx or down the tube
- **Apnoea test** (done last)
- UK: **two doctors**, one a consultant and the other with at least 5 years' registration, **neither from the transplant team**. Tests are done **twice**. Death is confirmed by the second set, but the **legal time of death is completion of the first set**
cards.e: The apnoea test is left until last so the patient is not exposed to hypercapnia when another reflex is still present. The UK needs no extra tests. Other countries may require EEG, angiography or evoked potentials. The coroner usually has to be informed.

cards.q: Describe how the apnoea test is performed and compare the UK and US end points.
cards.a:
The test shows that the medullary respiratory centre does not respond to a strong CO2 stimulus.
- **UK (Oxford)**: preoxygenate with 100% O2, adjust ventilation to a starting PaCO2 of **6 kPa (45 mm Hg)**, disconnect and watch for **5 min**. The final PaCO2 must exceed **6.7 kPa (50 mm Hg)**. Give O2 at **5–10 L/min via a catheter** down the ETT
- **US (Stoelting)**: start with PaCO2 **40 ± 5 mm Hg** and pH **7.35–7.45**, preoxygenate for at least **10 min**, disconnect for **10 min** with tracheal O2 insufflation, and take ABGs at 5 and 10 min. The test is **positive** if there is no breathing effort with PaCO2 **> 60 mm Hg**
cards.e: Oxford and Stoelting differ in duration and PaCO2 threshold, so quote the protocol of the country you are being examined in. Lippincott gives the US threshold as PaCO2 > 60 mm Hg. Patients who retain CO2 need a higher end point than the 6.7 kPa used for previously normal people. Apnoeic oxygenation through a catheter prevents hypoxia, which could otherwise cause arrhythmias or force the test to stop.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 57 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Lippincott Ch 13

cards.q: Which findings are compatible with brain death and which exclude it? Include the atropine test and the role of ancillary tests.
cards.a:
**Spinal reflexes may persist**. Any **brainstem-mediated** response, such as **decerebrate posturing**, excludes brain death.
- **Atropine test** (Stoelting): heart rate rises by **≤ 5 beats/min** after **0.04 mg/kg IV atropine**. This shows loss of the vagal nuclei
- Ancillary or confirmatory tests: **isoelectric EEG** and **absent cerebral blood flow** on transcranial Doppler, cerebral angiography or MR angiography
- An EEG may be hard to interpret in electrically noisy ICUs and operating theatres
cards.e: Lippincott's MCQ asks which finding is NOT consistent with brain death. The answer is decerebrate posturing, because posturing needs an intact brainstem, whereas spinal reflexes can remain. In the theatre these spinal reflexes are why the brain-dead donor may move and is given neuromuscular blockade during retrieval.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 57 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13 · Lippincott Ch 13 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16

cards.q: Describe the two-phase cardiovascular response to brain death and the mechanism of each phase.
cards.a:
Brain death produces a **hyperdynamic phase** first, then a **hypotensive phase**.
- **Phase 1, catecholamine storm**: caused by brain ischaemia as **ICP rises**. Massive sympathetic discharge produces **intense vasoconstriction (raised SVR), hypertensive crisis, tachycardia**, shift of blood volume and **visceral ischaemia**. Myocardial injury can occur even with normal coronaries. Parasympathetic activation sometimes causes bradycardia
- **Phase 2, autonomic collapse**: follows **herniation and spinal cord ischaemia**. **Loss of sympathetic tone, vasoplegia, low cardiac output** and blunted homeostatic reflexes
- Phase 1 is **transient**. Phase 2 is **profound and sustained**
cards.e: Hypotension in phase 2 is made worse by blood loss, capillary leak, osmotic therapy given earlier for raised ICP, and diabetes insipidus. About **40%** of brain-dead potential heart donors have myocardial dysfunction on echocardiography. Oxford describes the bradycardia of autonomic collapse as **atropine-resistant**.

cards.q: List the common pathophysiological changes of brain death with their approximate incidence (Miller Table 57.1).
cards.a:
Haemodynamic changes are almost universal and endocrine and coagulation changes are frequent:
- **Hypertension** (catecholamine storm): **80–90%**
- **Hypotension** (vasoplegia, hypovolaemia, reduced coronary flow, myocardial dysfunction): **80–90%**
- **Bradycardia and other arrhythmias**: **25–30%**
- **Pulmonary oedema** (acute volume shift, capillary damage): **10–20%**
- **Diabetes insipidus** (posterior pituitary damage): **45–80%** (the text says up to 90%)
- **DIC** (tissue factor release): **30–55%**
- **Hypothermia**: variable. **Hyperglycaemia**: common
cards.e: Note that Miller's own figures for diabetes insipidus differ (45–80% in the table, up to 90% in the text), so either range is defensible. The clinical point is that most donors will need vasoactive support, fluid and electrolyte correction and some hormone replacement.

cards.q: Why do brain-dead donors develop pulmonary oedema and lung injury?
cards.a:
Both **hydrostatic** and **inflammatory** mechanisms are involved.
- The rise in SVR shifts blood from the systemic circulation into the more compliant **pulmonary circulation**. The higher pulmonary capillary pressure causes leak and **oedema**
- The sympathetic surge sets off a **sterile systemic inflammatory response**: neutrophils infiltrate the lung and **endothelial permeability rises**
- **Proinflammatory cytokines** released in the alveoli are linked to **early graft failure and death after lung transplant**
- Hormonal instability reduces **alveolar fluid clearance**, so extravascular lung water accumulates
- Without ventilatory support, apnoea leads to cardiac arrest
cards.e: The inflammatory state also worsens cardiac function and pushes metabolism towards anaerobic pathways. Oxford adds aspiration, contusion and pre-existing disease. These mechanisms explain why lungs are the hardest organs to preserve and why steroids and fluid restriction increase lung yield.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 57 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13

cards.q: Describe the endocrine and metabolic consequences of brain death.
cards.a:
Failure of the pituitary and hypothalamus is common.
- **Posterior pituitary**: loss of ADH, so **central diabetes insipidus** (up to **90%**) with severe fluid and electrolyte disturbance
- **Anterior pituitary**: low **T3, T4, ACTH, TSH and growth hormone**. The thyroid picture looks like **euthyroid sick syndrome**
- **Hyperglycaemia**: low insulin and **insulin resistance**
- **Temperature**: hypothalamic control is lost, so there is brief hyperpyrexia and then **hypothermia**
cards.e: Oxford explains why low T3 matters: more T4 is converted peripherally to reverse T3, myocardial energy stores are depleted, contractility falls, and metabolism shifts to anaerobic. Oxford lists the electrolyte effects of diabetes insipidus as hypernatraemia, hypermagnesaemia, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia and hypocalcaemia. This is the basis for hormonal resuscitation.

cards.q: Why do brain-dead donors develop coagulopathy and hypothermia?
cards.a:
**Coagulopathy**: necrotic brain releases **tissue thromboplastin (tissue factor)**, which triggers **DIC**. DIC occurs in up to about **one-third** of patients with isolated head injury and in **30–55%** of brain-dead donors.
- **Hypothermia**: the hypothalamus no longer regulates temperature, **metabolic rate and muscle activity fall**, and **peripheral vasodilation** increases heat loss
- Early **hyperpyrexia** can occur before hypothermia sets in
cards.e: Oxford also blames fibrinolytic agents and plasminogen activators from necrotic brain, and advises correction with clotting factors and platelets. Stoelting calls these patients poikilothermic. Hypothermia worsens arrhythmias, coagulopathy and tissue oxygen delivery, which is why most guidance aims to keep the temperature up (Oxford: core above 35°C).
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 57 · Oxford Handbook Ch 16 · Stoelting 7e Ch 13

cards.q: State the Maastricht classification of DCD donors and distinguish controlled from uncontrolled DCD.
cards.a:
There are four original Maastricht categories:
- **I**: dead on arrival at hospital (uncontrolled)
- **II**: resuscitation unsuccessful (uncontrolled)
- **III**: cardiac arrest **expected** after planned withdrawal of life support (controlled)
- **IV**: cardiac arrest in a **brain-dead** donor (controlled)
- **Controlled**: withdrawal is planned and the retrieval team is ready, so **warm ischaemia is short**
- **Uncontrolled**: the arrest is unexpected and donation is considered only after resuscitation fails, so **warm ischaemia is much longer**
cards.e: Most DCD donors used today are **controlled (category III)**, typically patients with devastating brain or spinal cord injury who do not meet brain death criteria. Uncontrolled DCD grafts have been used successfully in some series. In the USA, DCD made up **30.2%** of deceased donors in 2021.

cards.q: What ethical safeguards govern withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment in a potential DCD donor?
cards.a:
The decision to withdraw must be **completely independent of donation**.
- Withdrawal is based on a clinical judgement of **futility** and on the wishes of the patient and family
- The **transplant team takes no part** in the withdrawal decision, in patient care before death, or in declaring death
- Drugs for **comfort** (pain, anxiety) are allowed
- Treatments that help the graft but **not the patient** are controversial. Low-impact measures are allowed in some protocols, usually with **specific consent**
- Drugs that could **hasten death** are not acceptable for donation purposes
cards.e: The guiding tension is between protecting the dying patient's best interests and honouring their wish to donate. Keeping the retrieval team out of end-of-life care avoids any conflict of interest and supports public trust in the donation system.

cards.q: How is circulatory death declared in a controlled DCD donor, and why is there a waiting period?
cards.a:
After extubation and withdrawal of support, a **physician not involved in transplantation** confirms that circulation has stopped.
- Confirmation is clinical: **pulselessness** or **loss of the arterial waveform**
- A **2–5 min** observation period follows to make sure the arrest is **irreversible** (no autoresuscitation)
- Retrieval starts only **after** death is declared
- Follow national policy (in the USA, OPTN minimum requirements and the UNOS DCD pathway) and the local protocol
cards.e: Declaring circulatory death is no different from ordinary clinical practice. The waiting period is a key ethical safeguard. The time from extubation to death decides whether organs can be used: a long agonal phase can make them unsuitable, especially in donors with comorbidity.

cards.q: Describe the University of Wisconsin DCD evaluation tool and how to interpret it.
cards.a:
It is a **six-variable score (range 8–24)** that predicts how likely the patient is to **keep breathing after extubation**.
- **Spontaneous breathing after 10 min off the ventilator**: RR >12 = 1, <12 = 3. VT >200 mL = 1, <200 = 3. NIF >20 cm H2O = 1, <20 = 3. **No breathing = 9**
- **BMI**: <25 = 1, 25–29 = 2, ≥30 = 3
- **Vasopressors**: none = 1, one = 2, two or more = 3
- **Age**: 0–30 = 1, 31–50 = 2, >50 = 3
- **Airway**: ETT = 3, tracheostomy = 1
- **SpO2 after 10 min**: >90% = 1, 80–90% = 2, <80% = 3
- **8–12**: high probability of continuing to breathe. **13–18**: moderate. **19–24**: low (death likely soon)
cards.e: A higher score means the donor is more dependent on support, so apnoea and cardiac arrest are more likely to follow quickly. This makes successful DCD more likely. The score helps teams decide whether to proceed when long survival after withdrawal could make the organs unusable.

cards.q: Why are DCD grafts at greater risk of injury than DBD grafts, and how do outcomes differ by organ?
cards.a:
DCD grafts avoid brain-death physiology but suffer **warm hypoxic ischaemia** during the agonal phase, so **ischaemia–reperfusion injury** is worse.
- **Kidney**: more **delayed graft function (DGF)**, but **short- and long-term graft survival are similar** to DBD kidneys
- **Liver**: more **biliary complications**, especially **diffuse ischaemic cholangiopathy** with intrahepatic strictures. Possibly more primary non-function and DGF
- Risk factors for ischaemic cholangiopathy: **older donor, overweight donor, long ischaemic time**
- **Heart and lung**: very sensitive to ischaemia. Only a few successful DCD cases are reported in Miller
cards.e: So kidneys are the most widely used DCD organ. Lippincott explains that the heart, with its high oxygen demand, is the least tolerant of ischaemia. Miller frames impending cardiac arrest donors as an ideal source, provided warm ischaemia can be kept short.

cards.q: What is the emerging "uniform" concept of death that links brain death and circulatory death?
cards.a:
Having two sets of criteria (DBD and DCD) has led to a proposed **single definition of death**.
- Every criterion for death depends on showing **irreversible loss of the capacity for consciousness** together with **irreversible loss of the capacity to breathe**
- Losing both of these functions is equated with death of the person, whichever route (neurological or circulatory) is used to show it
cards.e: The debate arose because DBD and DCD use separate definitions and procedures. The unified view treats the neurological and circulatory routes as two ways of showing the same end point: permanent loss of consciousness and of the ability to breathe.

cards.q: How is a controlled DCD donor managed around withdrawal of support, and which premortem interventions are used?
cards.a:
Withdrawal usually happens **in or next to the operating theatre** to keep warm ischaemia short. Some units use a nearby room so the family can be present.
- The **retrieval team takes no part** in care until death is declared
- **Opioids and benzodiazepines** are usually continued and titrated for comfort, which also blunts the sympathetic response
- **Premortem heparin** helps retrieval but carries a bleeding risk, so some policies do not allow it
- Most protocols need **specific consent** for any premortem donor treatment
- **Invasive option**: cannulation of the **femoral artery and vein before withdrawal**, allowing **cold preservation solution** to be infused quickly after death, or later ECMO
cards.e: Postmortem ECMO to restore flow to the organs (regional reperfusion) is fiercely debated, because restoring circulation after death has been declared raises questions about whether death was really irreversible. Any drug given mainly to benefit the graft, especially one that could hasten death, is controversial.

cards.q: Which preservation strategies does Miller describe for DCD and high-risk grafts, including regional reperfusion?
cards.a:
The aim is to **shorten or reverse warm ischaemia** before or instead of static cold storage.
- **Premortem femoral cannulation** allows a cold flush straight after death
- **Postmortem ECMO / regional reperfusion** restores warm, oxygenated blood flow to the abdominal organs in the body, but is **ethically contentious**
- **Machine perfusion** after retrieval: hypothermic, subnormothermic or normothermic
- **Combined approaches** (Miller Fig 57.3): regional reperfusion followed by machine perfusion, aiming for an **ischaemia-free** pathway
cards.e: Miller discusses these mainly as ways to protect DCD and extended criteria grafts. The key exam point is the ethical objection to postmortem circulatory support: the dying patient's interests must be protected while their wish to donate is respected. Specific institutional consent and protocols are required.

cards.q: What is an extended criteria donor (ECD), and why is donor risk better expressed as a continuum?
cards.a:
An ECD is a donor whose organs would once have been declined: also called **marginal, suboptimal, non-standard or high-risk**.
- The standard criteria donor (SCD) is young and previously healthy, with an isolated head injury or cerebral event
- ECD features vary by organ but typically include **older age, long cold ischaemia, impaired organ function and comorbidity**
- Risk runs along a **continuum**, not a yes/no split between SCD and ECD, so a **donor risk index (DRI)** was developed
cards.e: ECD use cuts waiting-list deaths and time to transplant, often for the sickest recipients. Oxford notes that the typical UK DBD donor is now older, heavier, has more comorbidity, and more often died of intracranial haemorrhage than head injury. The only absolute contraindications Oxford lists are CJD, HIV, active TB and recent malignancy.

cards.q: Which donor variables make up the kidney donor profile index (KDPI), and how is it interpreted?
cards.a:
The kidney DRI uses **10 donor characteristics** and is converted to the **KDPI (1%–100%)**:
- **Age, height, weight, ethnicity**
- **History of hypertension, history of diabetes**
- **Cause of death**
- **Serum creatinine**
- **Hepatitis C status**
- **DCD status**
- A **higher KDPI** predicts a **higher graft failure rate**
cards.e: Note that all 10 variables describe the donor, not the recipient. KDPI is an allocation and decision aid. A high-KDPI kidney can still benefit a recipient who would otherwise wait a long time on dialysis.

cards.q: Which variables make up the liver donor risk index (DRI), and what does a high-DRI graft mean for recipients?
cards.a:
The liver DRI is a quantitative estimate of graft-failure risk from **8 donor factors**:
- **Age** bands: >40, >50, >60, >70 years
- **Cause of death**: cerebrovascular accident carries the lower risk
- **Race**: African-American carries the higher risk
- **DCD** (yes/no)
- **Partial or split graft** (yes/no)
- **Height**: risk increases below **170 cm**
- **Regional or national share** (yes/no)
- **Cold ischaemia time**
