- Indications: **cleft palate repair**; bilateral blocks for **adenotonsillectomy** analgesia
- Ultrasound: out-of-plane, probe in the infrazygomatic area angled 45° cephalad; it is really a **fossa injection**, not a perineural block
cards.e: For tonsillectomy the aim is the palatine branches of V2 while sparing the glossopharyngeal nerve, preserving airway protective reflexes. It is the safest and most reproducible approach to V2 in children.

cards.q: Describe the mandibular, nasociliary and external nasal nerve blocks in children.
cards.a:
**Mandibular nerve (V3)**: exits the **foramen ovale**; anterior trunk mainly motor (+ buccal), posterior trunk auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar.
- Entry in the **sigmoid notch** below the zygomatic arch, as high as possible to avoid arteries; to the lateral pterygoid plate (**2–4 cm**), then posterior-inferior guided by **jaw elevation twitch** at about **0.5 mA**
- Dose **0.1 mL/kg, max 5 mL**
- **Nasociliary**: 25–27 G needle **1 cm above the medial canthus**, along the orbital roof to about **1.5 cm** (anterior ethmoidal foramen), **max 2 mL**
- **External nasal**: infiltration at the **nasal bone-cartilage junction**; with infraorbital block it is very effective for **cleft lip** repair
cards.e: The nose has mixed V1 and V2 innervation, so complete nasal block is difficult. The mandibular block carries a high-risk rating in Miller's comparison table because of deep vascular structures.

cards.q: Describe the innervation of the external ear and the corresponding blocks in children.
cards.a:
**Auriculotemporal (V3)**: upper two-thirds of the anterior pinna; blocked above the posterior zygoma in front of the ear, **behind the superficial temporal artery**.
- **Great auricular (C2–C3)**: lower posterior auricle, lobule, angle of jaw; **lesser occipital (C2–C3)**: upper ear and lateral occiput; blocked over the **mastoid** behind the ear
- **Auricular branch of vagus (Arnold)**: concha, posterior external canal, lower tympanic membrane; block by **0.2 mL** via a **30 G needle into the tragus** for **myringotomy/tubes**, tympanoplasty
- A ring/field block covers everything **except the Arnold (Ramsay Hunt) area**
- **Great auricular block** for tympanomastoid surgery reduces **opioids and PONV**; superficial cervical plexus block covers both cervical branches (otoplasty, cochlear implant, "bat ears")
cards.e: Knowing which nerve supplies each part explains why a ring block alone often fails for canal and tympanic procedures. Oxford lists the occipital nerves among the neck blocks from the cervical plexus.

cards.q: Describe the greater occipital nerve block and scalp block in children.
cards.a:
**Greater occipital nerve (C2)**: pierces semispinalis capitis and trapezius just below the **superior nuchal line**, **medial to the occipital artery**; supplies posterior scalp to vertex.
- Landmark: about **two-thirds** of the way from mastoid to external occipital protuberance along the nuchal line; 25–27 G needle at 90°, **1–3 mL**; press afterward; success = numb vertex
- Ultrasound: nerve between **obliquus capitis inferior and semispinalis capitis**, artery nearby (preferred)
- **Scalp block**: seven nerves (greater and lesser occipital, great auricular, supraorbital, supratrochlear, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal)
- Ring infiltration above a line from occipital protuberance to eyebrows over the upper ear, about **30 mL with 1:200,000 epinephrine**
- Uses: lacerations, wound exploration, abscess or subdural drainage, **awake craniotomy**, headache
cards.e: Main complications are hematoma and intravascular injection. In children the total volume must be checked against weight-based maximum doses.

cards.q: What are the indications and techniques for superficial cervical plexus, laryngeal and stellate ganglion blocks in children?
cards.a:
**Superficial cervical plexus**: lymph node biopsy, thyroid nodule excision, vocal cord surgery; ultrasound in-plane deep to SCM, superficial to prevertebral fascia at thyroid cartilage level; **2–3 mL 0.2% ropivacaine**.
- **Laryngeal (superior laryngeal) block**: awake laryngoscopy/intubation, prevention or treatment of **laryngospasm**; 27 G needle to the **greater horn of hyoid**, withdraw slightly, **0.1–0.2 mL/kg 1% lidocaine (max 8 mL)** each side
- **Stellate ganglion block** (dangerous, few indications): **congenital long QT** ventricular arrhythmias (**left-sided block**), severe upper limb circulatory disorders, herpes zoster ophthalmicus, sympathetically maintained pain
- Stellate technique: inject over (superficial to) **longus colli** under ultrasound; **Horner syndrome** confirms success
cards.e: Miller rates airway blocks as high risk in its comparison table, and the stellate ganglion block is described as rather dangerous, so these are specialist techniques with narrow indications. The hyoid horn may be hard to see on ultrasound in young children.

cards.q: What is the key anatomical difference in the brachial plexus region between infants and adults, and which upper limb approaches are preferred in children?
cards.a:
In infants the **lung apex and apical pleura rise above the clavicle-first rib plane**, close to the subclavian vessels and lower plexus, so any **perisubclavian approach risks pneumothorax**.
- **Supraclavicular** (ultrasound-guided): now the **commonest upper limb block** in children (PRAN); shoulder, arm, elbow
- **Axillary**: traditional favorite for forearm/hand; easy, high success, few complications
- **Infraclavicular (paracoracoid)**: complete upper limb block; best site for **catheters** (easy fixation)
- **Distal blocks**: hand/finger surgery or rescue of incomplete proximal block
- Begin with simple blocks (axillary, forearm); interscalene and periclavicular need trained operators
cards.e: The perineurovascular sheath concept has been supported radiologically (adult axillary tunnel 5.1–9.5 mL). Ultrasound with continuous needle-tip visualization is what made periclavicular approaches safe in children.

cards.q: Describe the interscalene block in children and why it is rarely used.
cards.a:
Used mainly for **shoulder surgery**, which is uncommon in children.
- Landmarks: cricoid, **C6 transverse process (Chassaignac tubercle)**, interscalene groove behind the SCM
- Needle at about 80° toward the **midpoint of the clavicle** (Borgeat modification) to stimulate trunks; any biceps, triceps or deltoid twitch is acceptable
- **Diaphragm twitch** = phrenic nerve, needle too **anterior**; **trapezius** twitch = too **posterior**
- Ultrasound: transverse oblique at cricoid level; roots/trunks as hypoechoic ovals between anterior and middle scalenes; in-plane lateral to medial
- Drawbacks: **ipsilateral phrenic block**, **vertebral artery** injury/injection, **epidural or intrathecal** spread, pneumothorax
cards.e: Oxford quotes phrenic block in up to 100% of adult interscalene blocks. The parascalene approach (Dalens) enters the groove further from pleura and vessels with near-zero morbidity, but may miss the lower cord (ulnar).

cards.q: Describe the ultrasound-guided supraclavicular block in children.
cards.a:
The plexus is most **compact** here (trunks/divisions), but **pneumothorax** risk is highest, so **in-plane ultrasound** is strongly advised.
- Probe in **coronal oblique plane** behind the clavicle: plexus as **hypoechoic cluster lateral, posterior and superior to the subclavian artery**, above the **first rib**
- Use **color Doppler** to avoid the **suprascapular** and **dorsal scapular** arteries
- In-plane lateral to medial toward the **angle between first rib and subclavian artery**
- Volume about **0.2 mL/kg**
- Check nerve function first if possible: **thumbs-up (radial)**, **"O" sign (median)**, **finger scissoring (ulnar)**
cards.e: Pre-block testing identifies preexisting nerve injury that would otherwise be blamed on the block. Oxford stresses including the "corner pocket" between artery and first rib to improve success.

cards.q: Compare infraclavicular approaches to the brachial plexus in children.
cards.a:
**Vertical midclavicular**: needle straight down below the midclavicle; threatens pleura/lung, so **contraindicated in children**.
- **Anterolateral midclavicular**: 1 cm below midclavicle, angled toward the axilla along the deltopectoral groove; usable supine
- **Medial paracoracoid**: most popular, lowest morbidity; entry **1–2 cm caudal and medial to the coracoid**; arm **abducted 90°** brings the plexus nearer the skin
- **Lateral paracoracoid**: unsafe without ultrasound (pleura)
- Ultrasound: parasagittal view medial/inferior to coracoid; lateral cord easiest to see, medial cord between artery and vein, posterior cord deep; inject **posterior to the axillary artery**
- Advantages: complete arm block, **secure catheter fixation**
cards.e: In coagulopathy, infraclavicular blocks are best avoided because the vessels are not compressible. Oxford notes the needle should not be angled medially below the clavicle as this increases pneumothorax risk.

cards.q: Describe the pediatric axillary block, including how it differs from adult practice.
cards.a:
Indicated for **elbow, forearm and hand** surgery; easy and safe.
- **Transarterial technique is not used** in children (vessel **spasm**, ischemia risk)
- A single injection blocks forearm/hand nerves but **misses the musculocutaneous nerve in about 50%**
- **Transcoracobrachialis** approach: arm supinated, abducted 90°; musculocutaneous nerve met first in coracobrachialis, then deeper to the sheath (median usually first); **0.1 mL/kg (max 5 mL)** for musculocutaneous on withdrawal
- **Intercostobrachial** (tourniquet pain): subcutaneous axillary injection
- Ultrasound: **multi-injection**; median lateral to artery, ulnar superficial-medial, radial deep; musculocutaneous between coracobrachialis and biceps
- Catheters are hard to secure here; periclavicular sites preferred
cards.e: Oxford notes the axillary block cannot cover upper arm and shoulder surgery. With ultrasound, the aim is a "donut" of LA around each nerve, allowing significant volume reduction.

cards.q: What is known about intraneural injection, and what ultrasound signs should prompt you to stop?
cards.a:
Intraneural injection is the **most feared** complication and is usually blamed for permanent nerve injury, especially under GA.
- **Bigeleisen**: deliberate intraneural (extrafascicular) axillary injections caused **no deficits at 6 months**
- Harm is likely from **intrafascicular** injection, which produces **high resistance** and severe pain
- Ultrasound warning signs: needle tip **within the nerve outline** and **nerve swelling** on test injection
- Still avoid intraneural injection
cards.e: Monitoring injection pressure (below 15 psi) and avoiding very low stimulation thresholds add protection in anesthetized children who cannot report pain. Oxford lists difficulty of injection and failure of twitch to disappear on injection as warning signs of intraneural placement.

cards.q: Describe distal upper limb nerve blocks and digital blocks in children.
cards.a:
Previously used mainly to rescue partial brachial plexus blocks; ultrasound has broadened their use; only **0.05 mL/kg (up to 1–2 mL)** per nerve is needed.
- **Median**: medial to the brachial artery at the elbow; best blocked in the **forearm** (at the wrist it looks like tendons)
- **Ulnar**: hyperechoic triangle medial to the ulnar artery at the wrist; block at **mid-forearm**; **never in the cubital tunnel** (compression)
- **Radial**: block in the **antecubital intermuscular compartment** rather than the tight humeral groove
- **Digital**: ring blocks rarely used; **single subcutaneous palmar injection** at the finger base avoids the flexor sheath but may only anesthetize the distal two phalanges and palmar proximal phalanx
cards.e: Avoiding confined spaces such as the cubital tunnel and spiral groove reduces compression injury from injected volume. Metacarpal blocks and infiltration are safer alternatives to ring blocks.

cards.q: What are interfascial plane blocks, and what are their advantages and limitations in children?
cards.a:
Ultrasound-guided injections of LA into a **fascial plane** through which several nerves run, capturing multiple branches at once.
- Chest wall: **ESP, PECS, serratus anterior**; abdominal wall: **TAP, QL**, rectus sheath
- **Advantages**: superficial, clear sonoanatomy, lower risk of **nerve injury, serious hematoma and pneumothorax**; suitable with anticoagulation
- **Limitations**: reduce **somatic** pain and analgesic needs but give **no reliable surgical or sympathetic block**
- Depend on **large volumes**, so **LAST risk** (especially bilateral catheters in neonates); pharmacokinetic data on intermittent boluses are scant
- Comparative efficacy versus neuraxial and perineural blocks still needs study
cards.e: Because absorption occurs over a large fascial surface, dosing must be individualized and closely monitored. This volume-versus-dose tension is the reason for regimens such as ASPIRe.

cards.q: Describe the PECS 1 (interpectoral) and PECS 2 (pectoserratus) plane blocks in children.
cards.a:
Anterior chest wall plane blocks done supine; ribs act as a **bony backstop** against pleural puncture.
- **PECS 1** (between **pectoralis major and minor**): **medial and lateral pectoral nerves**; the thoracoacromial artery lies in this plane
- **PECS 2** (between **pectoralis minor and serratus anterior**): **long thoracic, intercostobrachial and intercostal nerves III–VI**
- Probe below the clavicle, identify 2nd rib, slide to **3rd–4th ribs** laterally; single cephalad-to-caudad pass with a 22 G short-bevel needle
- Do the **deeper (PECS 2) injection first** so air does not obscure the view
- Dose: **0.2% ropivacaine 0.5 mL/kg per side (max 3 mg/kg)**
- Uses: pacemaker/ICD, **minimally invasive pectus repair**, ports; complications: infection, pneumothorax, hematoma, **scapular winging**, LAST
cards.e: Winging occurs because the long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior is blocked. Randomized comparisons with neuraxial and other chest wall blocks are lacking.

cards.q: Describe the thoracic paravertebral block in children.
cards.a:
Injection into the paravertebral space blocks several **unilateral dermatomes** and the **sympathetic chain** with one injection.
- Dose **0.5 mL/kg** long-acting LA, then **0.2–0.25 mL/kg/h**
- Landmark formulas: lateral distance from spinous process **10.2 mm + 0.12 x weight (kg)**; depth **18.7 mm + 0.48 x weight (kg)**
- Level: **T5–T6** for thoracotomy, **T9–T10** for subcostal incisions; Tuohy **LOR through the costotransverse ligament**, or ultrasound
- Indications: thoracotomy (including **coarctation** in infants), unilateral upper abdominal surgery (renal, cholecystectomy, splenectomy), unilateral inguinal hernia
- Contraindications: **previous ipsilateral thoracotomy**, spinal deformity, poor gas exchange (pneumothorax risk)
cards.e: It requires good technical skill; thoracic epidural is an alternative with less risk of direct cord injury. Oxford lists the paravertebral space as a popular catheter site.

cards.q: Describe the erector spinae plane (ESP) and retrolaminar blocks in children.
cards.a:
**ESP** (first described 2016): ultrasound-guided injection deep to the **erector spinae** onto the **transverse process**, spreading cranially and caudally.
- Proposed mechanism: block of **dorsal and ventral rami** and **sympathetic fibers**, giving **somatic and visceral** analgesia
- Used for thoracotomy, pyeloplasty, hernia, hip surgery; single shot, programmed intermittent bolus or catheter
- Advantages: avoids **dural puncture, pneumothorax, spinal hematoma** and bladder catheterization, so attractive in **anticoagulated cardiac** patients and preterm/term infants
- **Retrolaminar block**: probe slid medially from transverse processes to the **laminae** (sawtooth appearance); needle to lamina; **0.5 mL/kg 0.2% ropivacaine (max 20 mL)**; for sternotomy and hernia
cards.e: Evidence is mainly case reports and series. ESP plus parasternal catheters are increasingly used after congenital heart surgery because they avoid neuraxial bleeding risk.

cards.q: What are the indications and dangers of intercostal nerve blocks in children?
cards.a:
Intercostal nerves run below each rib in a space bounded by the innermost intercostal/endothoracic fascia/pleura medially and internal/external intercostals laterally.
- Uses: **thoracotomy**, liver transplant, chest drains, **rib fractures** (several adjacent spaces)
- Safest at the **midaxillary line**, child semi-prone, short **22 or 20 G Tuohy** in-plane under ultrasound (not intradermal needles)
- Dangers: **delayed pneumothorax**, very **high systemic uptake** (catheter safety questionable), spread to **paravertebral/epidural** and contralateral spaces
- Avoid in impaired gas exchange; **not for day cases**; observe in **ICU**
cards.e: The high systemic absorption from intercostal injections is why continuous intercostal infusions are discouraged in children. A surgeon can also place a catheter under direct vision.

cards.q: Describe the serratus anterior plane block in children.
cards.a:
Ultrasound plane block for the **axilla and anterolateral chest wall**.
- **Superficial SAP**: between **serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi** (thoracodorsal artery in this plane)
- **Deep SAP**: between serratus anterior and the **5th–6th rib**; efficacy similar
- Blocks **intercostobrachial, lateral cutaneous branches, long thoracic and thoracodorsal** nerves; **no autonomic block**
- Linear probe in **midaxillary line** at ribs 5–6, rib as backstop
- **0.5 mL/kg 0.2% ropivacaine per injection, up to 3 mg/kg**; if both done, perform **deep first**
- Uses: thoracotomy, sternotomy; catheters may interfere with surgery and dislodge
cards.e: In small infants PECS 1, PECS 2 and SAP can be performed in one needle pass. Interpleural blocks never became established and parasternal blocks reduce morphine and extubation time but need larger trials.

cards.q: Describe the rectus sheath block in children, including the evidence for ultrasound guidance.
cards.a:
Blocks terminal branches of the **lower intercostal nerves (10th at the umbilicus)** within the rectus sheath for **midline/umbilical** incisions.
- Uses: umbilical and epigastric hernia, laparoscopy, **pyloromyotomy**
- Inject **between rectus abdominis and the posterior rectus sheath** (bilateral)
- Dose **0.1–0.5 mL/kg per side** of long-acting LA, often 0.1 mL/kg with ultrasound
- Ultrasound versus fascial click: correct position **88% vs 44%**; fewer **intraperitoneal** (0% vs 20.9%) and too-superficial (11.5% vs 34.5%) injections
- LA spreads as a **biconvex** shadow along the posterior sheath
cards.e: Blind fascial clicks frequently place the needle wrongly, including into the peritoneum, which is the main argument for ultrasound. Oxford gives a total of 1 mL/kg 0.25% bupivacaine for bilateral blocks and favors ultrasound in younger children.

cards.q: Describe the TAP block in children and compare it with the ilioinguinal-iliohypogastric block for inguinal surgery.
cards.a:
LA in the plane between **internal oblique and transversus abdominis** blocks **T9–T12** and the **ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric** nerves.
- Landmark: **triangle of Petit** (iliac crest, latissimus dorsi, external oblique) with a **double pop** (external then internal oblique fascia)
- **Ultrasound recommended** in children: probe between costal margin and iliac crest; spread pushes transversus away
- **Ilioinguinal-iliohypogastric block gives better analgesia** for hernia repair than TAP, probably because TAP misses the **genital branch of genitofemoral**
- Large database: safe with few complications; pharmacokinetics safe in neonates
cards.e: Oxford gives a landmark TAP dose of 1 mL/kg 0.25% bupivacaine and lists intraperitoneal injection, bowel perforation and LA toxicity as risks.

cards.q: Describe the quadratus lumborum (QL) block approaches and their mechanism.
cards.a:
Ultrasound-only block targeting the **thoracolumbar fascia** around quadratus lumborum.
- **QL1 (lateral)**: between QL and **transversus abdominis aponeurosis**
- **QL2 (posterior)**: between QL and **erector spinae**
- **QL3 (anterior/transmuscular)**: between QL and **psoas**
- Spread **T8–L1**, regularly including iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves
- **Visceral analgesia** is attributed to spread to the **paravertebral space** and the TLF's sympathetic fibers
- Dose **0.5 mL/kg 0.2% ropivacaine per side** (max 3 mg/kg, <20 mL); linear probe in small children, curved in teenagers
- Cautions: coagulopathy (**4th lumbar artery** hematoma), kidney puncture, **quadriceps weakness** from fascia iliaca spread
cards.e: The "shamrock" view (transverse process as stem, psoas, QL and erector spinae as leaves) helps identify the targets. Do not inject into muscle.

cards.q: Describe the ilioinguinal-iliohypogastric block in children: anatomy, landmarks, dose and complications.
cards.a:
Inguinal canal innervation: ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and **genitofemoral**; in **50%** the canal depends solely on the **genital branch of genitofemoral**.
- Landmark: divide the **ASIS-umbilicus line into quarters**; puncture at the junction of lateral quarter and medial three-quarters; short-bevel needle, fascial click
- Dose **2.5 mg/kg** long-acting LA; bilateral if needed
- **Orchidopexy** needs extra genitofemoral block or scrotal infiltration
- Complications: **femoral nerve block (up to 10%)**, bowel/peritoneal puncture, intravascular injection (rare)
- Ultrasound (between internal oblique and transversus near ASIS): less volume (**0.19 vs 0.3 mL/kg**); minimum effective **0.075 mL/kg 0.25% levobupivacaine**
- Fascial click: needle misplaced in **85%**, failure **45%**
cards.e: Oxford adds that it does not block visceral pain from cord or peritoneal traction, is useful mainly above 20 kg, and is best avoided for neonatal herniotomy. Transient femoral block can delay ambulation, so warn parents.

cards.q: Describe the penile block in children and its contraindications.
cards.a:
The penis is supplied mainly by the **dorsal nerve of the penis** (branch of the **pudendal** nerve).
- **Subpubic approach**: inject into both compartments of the subpubic space **deep to Scarpa fascia** (gentle traction on penis to feel the click); **0.1 mL/kg (max 5 mL) each side**
- Add **ventral (perineal nerve) infiltration** for circumcision to reduce failure
- Ultrasound confirms crossing of Scarpa fascia and improves early analgesia
- **Contraindications**: **epinephrine-containing solutions** and skin infection
- Serious complications: **dorsal artery** injury with midline puncture; injection into the **corpora cavernosa** (equivalent to IV injection); problems reported with injection **beneath Buck's fascia**
- Uses: circumcision, phimosis, paraphimosis, zipper entrapment
cards.e: The penile arteries are end arteries, so epinephrine risks ischemia. Oxford's alternatives are subcutaneous dorsal wheals or a ring block with 4–10 mL 0.25% bupivacaine, avoiding adrenaline.

cards.q: Describe the pudendal nerve block in children and why some prefer it to penile block.
cards.a:
The pudendal nerve supplies the perineum and external genitalia; its terminal branches include the **dorsal nerve of the penis** and **perineal nerves**.
- Landmarks: **ischial tuberosities and anus**; nerve stimulation gives **external anal sphincter** contraction at **0.5–0.8 mA** (start 1.5–2.0 mA)
- **0.1 mL/kg (max 5 mL)**: mainly perineal nerve (posterior scrotum), to complement inguinal blocks
- **0.3–0.4 mL/kg per side (max 15 mL)**: full pudendal block including dorsal penile nerve
- Ultrasound: frog-leg position, target between **sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments**, out-of-plane, combine with stimulation
- **Naja**: pudendal beat dorsal penile block for **circumcision** (lower pain, less analgesia, higher satisfaction)
- Avoid **epinephrine** (pudendal artery is an end artery)
cards.e: One pudendal injection reaches both dorsal and perineal nerves, explaining its superiority for circumcision. Miller misprint: "ephedrine" (correct: avoid epinephrine).

cards.q: Describe the anatomy of the lumbar plexus and the psoas compartment block in children.
cards.a:
Lumbar plexus: anterior rami **L1–L4** (± T12, L5) in the **psoas compartment** (psoas anteriorly, quadratus lumborum posteriorly); gives **femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, genitofemoral and obturator** nerves.
- Lateral position, operated side up; landmarks: iliac crests, PSIS, L5 spinous process (e.g. modified Chayen: midpoint PSIS-L5)
- Needle perpendicular until **quadriceps twitch**
- Ultrasound "**shamrock**" view at L4 transverse process; plexus hyperechoic in posterior psoas; combine with stimulation
- Indications: **hip and femoral surgery** (needs femoral, LFCN and obturator); good analgesia for 48 h; continuous block equals epidural with **fewer adverse events and less ropivacaine**
- Complications: **intravascular injection/cardiac arrest**, psoas hematoma, **epidural spread**, retroperitoneal injection
cards.e: Plexus depth correlates with **weight rather than age**. Because of its deep, non-compressible location it should be avoided in coagulopathy and performed only by trained operators.

cards.q: Compare the femoral nerve block and the fascia iliaca compartment block in children.
cards.a:
**Femoral**: supine, puncture **0.5–1 cm below the inguinal ligament** (not the crease) lateral to the artery; quadriceps twitch; ultrasound probe just above and parallel to the ligament; for **femoral shaft and knee** surgery.
- **Fascia iliaca**: LA under the fascia iliaca spreads to **femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous** and often **obturator** and genitofemoral nerves
- Fascia iliaca blocks the LFCN, obturator and genitofemoral **more reliably**
- It needs **no nerve stimulator or limb movement** (useful in **femur fracture**) and has **less vascular puncture risk**
- The two have **never been formally compared** for efficacy in children
- **Supra-inguinal approach**: parasagittal probe medial to ASIS, "bowtie" of sartorius/internal oblique; more proximal spread, better for **hip** surgery
cards.e: Oxford describes the landmark fascia iliaca technique with two pops (fascia lata then fascia iliaca). Ultrasound prolongs analgesia, lowers volume and raises success compared with stimulation.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 74 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42 · Oxford Handbook Ch 34

cards.q: State the dosing for fascia iliaca and femoral blocks in children, including continuous techniques.
cards.a:
Single shot or loading bolus **0.2–0.5 mL/kg** long-acting LA; infusion **0.1–0.2 mL/kg/h**.
- **PCRA**: bolus **0.1 mL/kg (max 5 mL)**, up to **3 boluses per hour**
- **Epinephrine** lowers plasma levels (preferred when possible); **clonidine 1–2 mcg/kg** prolongs analgesia
- Continuous fascia iliaca vs IV morphine after pelvic osteotomy: better analgesia, **less sedation**, earlier appetite
- Paut: bupivacaine levels with continuous fascia iliaca (0.25% with epinephrine bolus then 0.1% for 48 h) stayed within safety limits (about **0.7–0.8 mcg/mL**)
- Ultrasound lengthened analgesia (about 508 vs 335 min) versus stimulation
cards.e: Miller misprint: Paut levels printed as g/mL (correct: mcg/mL). Oxford's landmark femoral dose is 0.5 mL/kg 0.25% bupivacaine.

cards.q: Describe the PENG and lateral femoral cutaneous nerve blocks.
cards.a:
**PENG (pericapsular nerve group)**: hip analgesia with **minimal motor block**, targeting articular branches of **femoral, accessory obturator and obturator** nerves.
- Linear probe along the inguinal crease: AIIS, iliopubic eminence, psoas tendon, femoral artery
- In-plane lateral to medial onto the **pubic ramus lateral to the psoas tendon**; **ropivacaine 3 mg/kg (0.2% or 0.5%), up to 20 mL**
- **LFCN block**: mostly a **complement to femoral block** (fascia lata grafts, femoral pinning, muscle biopsy)
- Nerve lies between **fascia lata and fascia iliaca** around **sartorius**, below the ASIS near tensor fasciae latae; do not inject into sartorius
- In young children one in-plane pass can block femoral then LFCN on withdrawal; large volumes can cause **motor block** via femoral spread
cards.e: Miller misprint: "auxiliary" (correct: accessory) obturator nerve. Oxford describes hydrodissection to find the small LFCN between fascia lata and fascia iliaca, with femoral block as its main complication. The old landmark "pop" technique for LFCN has been replaced by ultrasound.

cards.q: Describe the obturator nerve block and adductor canal (saphenous) block in children.
cards.a:
**Obturator**: thigh slightly abducted/externally rotated; groove between adductor longus tendon and pectineus at the level of the greater trochanter.
- Stimulation: **anterior branch** (adductor longus/brevis twitch), then 1–2 cm deeper the **posterior branch** (adductor magnus); half the dose at each; total **0.1 mL/kg (max 5 mL) per nerve**
- Ultrasound: anterior branch between **longus and brevis**, posterior between **brevis and magnus**
- **Saphenous nerve** is **purely sensory**, so it cannot be found with stimulation; blind distal block at the knee has high failure (**30% or more**)
- **Adductor canal block** exploits the nearby **nerve to vastus medialis** (mixed nerve): stimulate it 0.5 cm lateral to the femoral artery at the sartorius border; **0.1–0.2 mL/kg**
- Ultrasound: inject in the subsartorial plane **lateral to the superficial femoral artery**; motor-sparing knee analgesia
cards.e: The saphenous nerve covers the medial leg and foot, so it is often needed to complete a sciatic block for leg or ankle surgery.

cards.q: Describe sciatic nerve anatomy and the proximal sciatic approaches in children.
cards.a:
Sacral plexus: **L4–S3** (± S4) anterior to piriformis; gives the **sciatic** and **posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh**, which exit together through the greater sciatic foramen.
- Divides near the popliteal apex into **common peroneal** and **tibial** nerves
- Indications: **foot and leg** surgery (add **saphenous** block for the medial leg); no specific contraindications, but monitor compartment syndrome risk and use dilute LA
- **Subgluteal**: midpoint of the line from **ischial tuberosity to greater trochanter**; supine with hip and knee flexed 90° in small children, lateral/prone in older ones; foot twitch; catheters work well
- **Lateral approach**: supine, needle horizontal below the femur, then slightly posterior; catheter dislodgement on mobilization
cards.e: When choosing a proximal approach weigh its morbidity, patient positioning, localization method, need for a catheter and operator experience. With ultrasound, tracing the nerve from popliteal to subgluteal level is now common. Oxford places the proximal nerve deep to biceps femoris at the trochanter-tuberosity midpoint.

cards.q: Describe the popliteal sciatic block in children and the evidence for continuous popliteal catheters.
cards.a:
First choice for **major foot and ankle surgery**: simple, safe, effective with small volumes.
- **Lateral approach** (supine): groove between **vastus lateralis and biceps femoris** tendon at the upper patellar border
- **Posterior approach**: prone or semi-prone (Singelyn landmarks adapted to children)
- Stimulation at **0.6 mA**: a tibial or common peroneal (**foot eversion**) motor response
- Ultrasound: nerve **lateral and superficial to the popliteal artery**; ideally inject just **after its division**
- **Continuous popliteal vs epidural**: equal analgesia but **less urinary retention, fewer infusion stops, less PONV**
- **Popliteal catheters** are the most frequent home catheters
cards.e: Tibial stimulation gives plantar flexion and common peroneal gives eversion (Oxford); Miller misprints the tibial response as dorsiflexion. Oxford also notes the nerve lies superficial to the vessels in the popliteal fossa.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 74 · Oxford Handbook Ch 34 · Oxford Handbook Ch 42

cards.q: What is the iPACK block and what are its limitations?
cards.a:
**Infiltration between the Popliteal Artery and Capsule of the Knee**: posterior knee analgesia from articular branches of **tibial, common peroneal and obturator** nerves.
- Probe a few cm above the patella posteriorly: find the femoral condyles, slide cephalad to the flat femoral shaft; artery superficial to femur
- In-plane 22 G needle **between artery and femur**, ideally lifting the artery; **ropivacaine 3 mg/kg (0.2% or 0.5%) up to 20 mL**
- **Motor-sparing** alternative to sciatic block
- Injecting superficial to or beside the vessels risks **sciatic/common peroneal** spread
- No consensus on level, dose or volume; **not shown superior to surgical infiltration**
cards.e: Its advantage over capsular infiltration by the surgeon is visualized needle path avoiding the artery and sciatic nerve.

cards.q: Describe the metatarsal block.
cards.a:
Easy technique for **toe surgery**.
- Child supine; palpate the metatarsal head on the sole
- Insert a needle from the **dorsum** along the **medial border** of the metatarsal base until its tip is felt under the plantar skin
- Inject **1–3 mL** while withdrawing; repeat on the **lateral border**
cards.e: Two injections, one on each side of the relevant metatarsal, block the digital nerves to that toe. It is an alternative to a ring block, which is rarely used by anesthesiologists in children.

cards.q: Describe the anatomy of the sacral hiatus in children and how it changes with age.
cards.a:
The hiatus is a **U- or V-shaped** gap from failed dorsal fusion of the **S5 (often S4) arches**, bounded by the **sacral cornua** and covered by the **sacrococcygeal membrane** (continuation of ligamentum flavum).
- Sacral vertebrae look like lumbar ones until about 1 year; their ossification centers fuse at **2–6 years** (with weight bearing)
- Hiatus apex to **dural sac**: about **30 mm (SD 10; range 13.6–54.7 mm)** from 10 months to 18 years
- Skin to **anterior sacral wall**: about **21 mm (10–39 mm)** from 2 months to 7 years
- Skin to sacral epidural space is little affected by age/weight: a **25 mm needle** is long enough yet short enough to avoid dural puncture
- With growth the hiatus becomes harder to find or closes and epidural fat densifies, so caudal blocks are **less suitable after 6–7 years**
cards.e: The wide range in hiatus-to-dura distance (as little as about 1.4 cm) is why needles should not be advanced far beyond the membrane. Oxford notes the hiatus lies at the apex of a triangle whose base joins the posterior superior iliac spines, though Miller says this is unhelpful when palpation fails.

cards.q: What are the indications, contraindications, failure rate and complications of caudal block in children?
cards.a:
The **commonest pediatric neuraxial block**, for surgery **below the umbilicus** (hernia, urological, perineal, lower limb and pelvic orthopedic).
- Usually under light GA; can be the **sole anesthetic** in awake ex-preterm infants (<50–60 weeks PCA), single shot or via catheter
- Reduces the **stress hormone response**
- **Failure 3–11%**, mostly in children **over 7 years**
- Contraindications: major **sacral malformation** (myelomeningocele, open spina bifida), meningitis, intracranial hypertension
- Complications rare and minor; **dural puncture with injection** can cause **cardiovascular collapse or apnea**
- Database of **18,650 caudals**: complications **1.9%**, no sequelae
cards.e: Its popularity is falling as ultrasound-guided peripheral blocks take over in many countries. Oxford lists motor block, paresthesia, hypotension, urinary retention, dural puncture and intravascular injection, all rare with a single shot, and quotes success around 95%.

cards.q: Describe the technique of caudal block in children.
cards.a:
**Lateral decubitus**, or **prone** (rolled towel or frog position) in awake preterm infants.
- Palpate the **two sacral cornua** at the sacrococcygeal junction; the PSIS-hiatus equilateral triangle is of limited help
- Use a **22 G IV cannula** or short-bevel stylet needle; feel the give through the **sacrococcygeal membrane**, then advance only minimally
- Aspirate gently; give a **test dose** and inject slowly
- **Ultrasound**: transverse view between the cornua (membrane above, sacral base below), then **longitudinal** view to watch the needle/cannula and the injectate distending the space
- Do not use the swoosh test
cards.e: Oxford adds a skin nick to prevent a dermoid, advancing a cannula rather than a needle to reduce dural or vascular puncture, and notes the commonest cause of failure is a needle placed too caudally. Repeated aspiration is needed because small veins can collapse.

cards.q: State the Armitage caudal volume scheme and Miller's recommended limit. How do volume and concentration affect spread?
cards.a:
**Armitage** (still the most dependable):
- **0.5 mL/kg**: all **sacral** dermatomes
- **1 mL/kg**: **sacral and lumbar** dermatomes
- **1.25 mL/kg**: upper level at least **mid-thoracic**
- 1.25 mL/kg can spread **above T4**, so preferably **do not exceed 1 mL/kg**
- **Hong**: same ropivacaine dose (2.25 mg/kg); **high volume/low concentration** (0.15%, 1.5 mL/kg) spread higher (**T6 vs T11**) and lasted longer (**554 vs 363 min**) than low volume/high concentration (0.225%, 1 mL/kg)
cards.e: Lippincott labels the levels lumbosacral, thoracolumbar and mid-thoracic with a 20 mL maximum. Oxford dilutes bupivacaine to 0.19% when volume exceeds 1 mL/kg, keeping the mg/kg dose safe. Note: Lippincott and Oxford use 1.25 mL/kg for thoracolumbar blocks; follow Miller's advice not to exceed 1 mL/kg.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 74 · Lippincott Ch 18 · Oxford Handbook Ch 34

cards.q: How are caudal catheters advanced to lumbar or thoracic levels in infants, and how is the tip position confirmed?
cards.a:
A normal epidural catheter insertion is **2–3 cm**, but the **fluid epidural fat** of infants lets a caudal catheter be threaded to **lumbar or thoracic** levels (experts only).
- Tip is **misplaced in about 28–30%** even in experienced hands
- Risks: cord or vessel trauma, **bacterial contamination** (perineum), breakage, **knotting around a root** on removal
- Confirmation: **contrast radiograph** (usual), **epidural stimulation test** (within 2 segments), **ECG recorded via the catheter wire** matching a surface electrode at the target level, or **ultrasound**
- **Tunnel** the catheter to reduce contamination
- Repeat doses: **half** the initial dose after **60 min** (short-acting) or **90 min** (long-acting), then one-sixth
cards.e: Oxford says caudal threading works because the infant spine has a single curve, notes higher failure over 2 years, and advises removing caudal catheters within 36 hours. For catheters, Miller generally prefers a direct lumbar approach to reduce contamination risk.

cards.q: What does ultrasound add to caudal block?
cards.a:
Pre-scan: sacral anatomy, **hiatus-to-dural sac** distance, occult **spinal dysraphism**.
- Real-time: anterior **displacement of the dura** with saline/LA injection indicates success
- Roberts: sensitivity **96.5%**, specificity **100%**, PPV **100%**
- **Better than the swoosh test** for confirming needle position
- Images degrade as the sacrum ossifies in older children
cards.e: Oxford also mentions using ultrasound to confirm injectate spread in the caudal space.

cards.q: Describe the epidural space and the age-related landmarks relevant to pediatric epidurals.
cards.a:
Extends from **foramen magnum to sacral hiatus**; communicates with paravertebral spaces; contains vessels, lymphatics and **loose fat up to 6–8 years**.
- **Tuffier line** crosses at **L5–S1 in infants under 1 year** (L4–L5 later); flexion shifts it in 58% of patients
- **Lateral decubitus with flexion** moves the cord forward, away from the ligamentum flavum and widens the space (preferred); sitting moves the cord back
- Infant pressures (Vas): entry **1 ± 10 mm Hg**; peak **27.8 mm Hg** at 1 mL/min vs **15.2 mm Hg** at 0.5 mL/min injection
- Single (kyphotic) curve: needle perpendicular to the back; poorly ossified vertebrae
cards.e: Oxford notes the ligamentum flavum is less developed and interspaces narrower in children, and the infant epidural space is rarely deeper than 15 mm. Slower injection halves the peak epidural pressure.

cards.q: What are the indications and contraindications for epidural anesthesia in children, and how is the level of approach chosen?
cards.a:
**Indications**: major abdominal, retroperitoneal, pelvic and thoracic surgery, **pectus excavatum**, **scoliosis** (often two catheters); cardiac surgery is controversial (anticoagulation).
- Single shot below the umbilicus: **caudal** in infants/young children, **lumbar** in older ones
- **Catheters**: lumbar route preferred to avoid **perineal contamination**
- High thoracic dermatomes: **thoracic epidural** most reliable but needs expertise
- **Contraindications**: severe spine/cord malformation (not spina bifida occulta), intraspinal tumor, **tethered cord**
- Usually avoid: hydrocephalus, raised ICP, **unstable epilepsy**, reduced intracranial compliance (not absolute)
- Previous spinal surgery: technically difficult, not a contraindication unless cord lesions exist
cards.e: Young children tolerate epidurals without significant hemodynamic change. Oxford notes UK NAP3 found pediatric epidurals had fewer complications than adult ones.

cards.q: Describe lumbar epidural technique in children: depth, loss-of-resistance medium, catheter length and volumes.
cards.a:
Usually **under GA**, midline **below L2–L3**, semi-prone with operated side down.
- **Skin-to-epidural depth about 1 mm/kg** (6 months to 10 years)
- LOR: saline more popular; **air or CO2 more sensitive in neonates/infants**; use **saline** if ultrasound is used
- Ultrasound shows depth to ligamentum flavum and dura; dura displacement on injection under 2 years
- Insert catheter **no more than 3 cm** (buckling, knotting, lateralization); **tunnel** it
- Volume about **0.1 mL per year of age per segment**; usually **0.5–1 mL/kg (max 20 mL)**; upper level T9–T6 in over 80%
- Single shot with **clonidine 1–2 mcg/kg**, **morphine 30 mcg/kg** or **hydromorphone 10 mcg/kg**
cards.e: Note: Oxford warns that severe neurological complications, including deaths, have followed air LOR in neonates and suggests the caudal route there; follow Miller, which accepts air as more sensitive.

cards.q: State the pediatric epidural initial doses and infusions for bupivacaine/levobupivacaine and ropivacaine.
cards.a:
**Initial**: **0.25% bupivacaine/levobupivacaine with 1:200,000 epinephrine**, or **0.2% ropivacaine** in the same mL/kg:
- Children below 20 kg receive **0.75 mL/kg**; those of 20–40 kg receive **8–10 mL** (alternatively 0.1 mL per year per segment); above 40 kg, adult doses
- **Infusions** (max): **<4 months 0.2 mg/kg/h**; **4–18 months 0.25 mg/kg/h**; **>18 months 0.3–0.375 mg/kg/h**
- e.g. under 4 months: 0.15 mL/kg/h of 0.125% or 0.3 mL/kg/h of 0.0625%
- Ropivacaine (0.1–0.2%) uses the same mg/kg/h; **not beyond 36 h under 3 months**
- **Top-ups**: 0.1–0.3 mL/kg of 0.25% or 0.125% every 6–12 h per pain scores
cards.e: Oxford's practice is similar: lumbar intraoperative 0.75 mL/kg 0.25% bupivacaine and an infusion of 0.1% bupivacaine with fentanyl 2 mcg/mL at 0.1–0.4 mL/kg/h.

cards.q: What is the evidence for patient-controlled epidural analgesia (PCEA) in children?
cards.a:
Suitable for **mature children** who understand and want it.
- 128 children over 5 years: **90.1% success**; stopped for side effects in 6.1% and inadequate analgesia in 3.8%
- Regimen: 0.0625–0.125% bupivacaine with **fentanyl 2–10 mcg/mL**, background **≤0.2 mL/kg/h**, boluses **1–3 mL every 15–30 min**, bupivacaine max **0.4 mg/kg/h**
- 58 children (7–12 years) after lower limb surgery: PCEA with 0.2% ropivacaine (1.6 mL/h + 2 mL, 10 min lockout) gave the **same pain scores** with **half the hourly ropivacaine** of a 0.2 mL/kg/h infusion
cards.e: Lower drug consumption is the key advantage because it reduces accumulation risk. For PCA in general, Oxford stresses that parents must never press the bolus button.

cards.q: When are thoracic and cervical epidurals used in children, and how does technique change with age?
cards.a:
**Thoracic**: thoracic and upper abdominal surgery needing prolonged analgesia via catheter; uncommon because of **spinal cord injury** risk.
- **Under 1 year**: needle **perpendicular** to the spine (single flexure), as for lumbar
- Older children: needle angled cephalad **up to 45°** as in adults; paramedian rarely needed
- In infants ultrasound can show the dura, Tuohy advance and often the catheter tip
- **Cervical**: no surgical indication; rarely for chronic pain or to prevent **phantom pain** before forequarter amputation (adolescent humeral **osteosarcoma**)
cards.e: Where operators lack thoracic epidural experience in infants, threading a caudal catheter is an alternative but misplacement is frequent.

cards.q: How does CSF volume vary with age, and what are the implications for spinal anesthesia in infants?
cards.a:
CSF volume: **>10 mL/kg in neonates**, **4 mL/kg in infants <15 kg**, **3 mL/kg in children**, **1.5–2 mL/kg** in adolescents/adults.
- In infants **50%** of CSF is in the **spinal** subarachnoid space (25% in adults)
- Hence **higher mg/kg doses** and **shorter block** in infants
- **Low CSF pressure** supine and under GA: advance the needle slowly and wait for CSF reflux
- Under **5 years**: hemodynamically stable even with cardiac defects; infants 1.5–5 months may show a brief fall in MAP (bupivacaine 0.8 mg/kg) reversed by fluids; ex-preterm infants may show reduced cerebral blood flow
cards.e: The large spinal CSF volume dilutes the drug, explaining the dose and duration differences. Lippincott notes that apnea rather than hypotension may herald a high spinal in infants.

cards.q: What are the indications and limitations of spinal anesthesia in infants?
cards.a:
Main indication: **inguinal hernia repair in former preterm infants <60 weeks PCA**, who are prone to **postoperative apnea** after GA or even light sedation.
- Apnea can still occur after pure spinal (and occurs preoperatively), so **keep at-risk infants in hospital** with monitoring
- Other uses (lower abdominal/limb, cardiac surgery or catheterization) are controversial
- Interest rising because of concerns about GA neurotoxicity
- **Failure 10–25%**; **short duration** and **no residual analgesia** (supplement with awake caudal or ilioinguinal-iliohypogastric block)
- Ultrasound can image the infant spine but has not been compared with landmark technique
cards.e: Oxford adds that if sedation is given during the spinal, apnea risk equals that after GA, and that ex-preterm infants up to 60 weeks PCA need overnight apnea monitoring. Note: Lippincott sets the threshold for deferring elective surgery at 50 weeks; follow Miller's 60 weeks for this indication.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 74 · Oxford Handbook Ch 34 · Lippincott Ch 18

cards.q: State the drugs and doses for spinal anesthesia in neonates and children.
cards.a:
Commonly **hyperbaric tetracaine 0.5%** or **bupivacaine 0.5%** (isobaric bupivacaine also used); duration about **60–75 min**.
- General: **0.5–0.8 mg/kg** for low-mid blocks, **1 mg/kg** for high (T2–T4) blocks
- **Neonates**: tetracaine **0.6–1 mg/kg**; bupivacaine **0.5–1 mg/kg**; ropivacaine 1.08 mg/kg; levobupivacaine 1 mg/kg (75–90 min)
- The mg/kg requirement **falls as the child grows** (roughly 0.4 mg/kg at 5–15 kg in Miller's table, lower in bigger children)
- Reported: hyperbaric bupivacaine **0.2 mg/kg** (6 months–14 years, 98% success); **ropivacaine 0.5 mg/kg** (1–17 years); **levobupivacaine 0.3 mg/kg** (1–14 years)
- Adjuvants: **clonidine 1 mcg/kg**, **fentanyl 1 mcg/kg**, **morphine 4–5 mcg/kg**
- Ropivacaine and levobupivacaine not yet approved for pediatric spinal use
- **PDPH uncommon under 8 years**; all lumbar epidural complications can occur
cards.e: Neonates are at higher risk of amide toxicity, especially with jaundice. Note: Oxford gives 0.1 mL/kg of 0.5% heavy bupivacaine plus dead space (about 0.5 mg/kg); this is within Miller's range.

cards.q: A 3-year-old boy (15 kg) is anesthetized with sevoflurane for orchidopexy. After placing a caudal cannula you inject a test dose of 0.25% bupivacaine with 1:200,000 epinephrine. Within 30 seconds the T waves become markedly taller and BP rises from 90/50 to 115/70; heart rate is unchanged at 110/min. Interpret and manage.
cards.a:
This is a **positive test dose**: probable **intravascular injection**.
- Test dose used: **0.1 mL/kg = 1.5 mL**, giving about **0.5 mcg/kg epinephrine** (within 0.5–1 mcg/kg)
- Positive criteria: **T-wave amplitude rise or ST elevation**, then **BP rise**; tachycardia appears only occasionally
- **Stop injecting** immediately; aspirate, withdraw and reassess the cannula; observe ECG for arrhythmia or QRS widening
- Prepare LAST treatment (lipid, epinephrine) though a test dose rarely causes toxicity
- Options: reposition with **ultrasound** and repeat a test dose, or switch to an **ilioinguinal-iliohypogastric plus genitofemoral/scrotal** block or surgical infiltration
cards.e: Heart rate is unreliable in anesthetized children, so the ECG T wave is watched for 30–60 s. Lippincott identifies ST-segment change as the most consistent sign of intravascular bupivacaine with epinephrine. Ultrasound can also confirm epidural spread by showing dural displacement.

cards.q: A 6-month-old (7 kg) receives a caudal block with 0.25% bupivacaine 7 mL under GA. Two minutes later the ECG shows wide QRS complexes, then ventricular fibrillation. There were no warning signs. What is happening and how do you treat it?
cards.a:
**LAST** (cardiac toxicity from intravascular bupivacaine); in infants there is **no neurological prodrome** under GA and cardiac and CNS toxicity appear together.
- Call for help, **stop injection**, **100% oxygen**, ventilate, start **CPR**
- **Defibrillate 2–4 J/kg (14–28 J)** for persistent VF
- **Epinephrine** in small increments from **1–2 mcg/kg (7–14 mcg)**
- **20% Intralipid 2–5 mL/kg (14–35 mL) IV bolus**, repeat if no recovery, **up to 10 mL/kg (70 mL)**
- Continue resuscitation until circulation returns; monitor in ICU
cards.e: Contributors in a 6-month-old: low AGP raising free fraction, fast heart rate and rapid absorption; the dose given (17.5 mg, 2.5 mg/kg) also exceeds the 2 mg/kg plain bupivacaine maximum. PRAN found LAST at 0.76 per 10,000 blocks, mainly in infants. Note: Oxford gives a 1.5 mL/kg lipid bolus with infusion; follow Miller.

cards.q: A 2-month-old (5 kg) had a laparotomy with a lumbar epidural catheter. The ward is infusing 0.25% bupivacaine at 1 mL/h, now at 40 hours, and the infant is irritable with a few twitches. What is wrong and how would you change the regimen?
cards.a:
Likely **bupivacaine accumulation/toxicity**: the rate is **2.5 mg/h = 0.5 mg/kg/h**, over twice the **0.2 mg/kg/h** maximum under 4 months.
- Stop the infusion, assess airway, ECG, seizures; treat as **LAST** (oxygen, benzodiazepine for seizures, lipid if cardiovascular signs)
- Under 4 months **racemic bupivacaine never reaches steady state, even at 48 h**, so toxicity can occur even at "safe" rates
- If restarting: max **1 mg/h** (e.g. **0.75 mL/h of 0.125%** = 0.15 mL/kg/h, or 1.5 mL/h of 0.0625%)
- Prefer **ropivacaine or levobupivacaine** (plateau from 24 h); ropivacaine **not beyond 36 h** under 3 months
- **Reduce doses after 48 h**; add multimodal analgesia
cards.e: Irritability and twitching may be the only signs of CNS toxicity in an infant, and cardiac toxicity can follow without warning. The UK epidural audit found neonatal incidents were mostly drug errors, so prescription and pump checks matter.

cards.q: A former 29-week preterm infant, now 45 weeks postconceptional age and 3 kg, needs bilateral inguinal hernia repair. He has mild chronic lung disease. The parents ask about avoiding general anesthesia. Outline your plan.
cards.a:
He is at high risk of **postoperative apnea** (<60 weeks PCA, lung disease): **awake spinal anesthesia** is a good option.
- Position: sitting or lateral, held firmly; puncture **below L3** (cord ends L3 in neonates; Tuffier line L5–S1)
- Needle: **22 G neonatal LP needle** or short spinal needle; advance slowly as **CSF pressure is low**
- Drug: **0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5–1 mg/kg** (1.5–3 mg, 0.3–0.6 mL) or tetracaine 0.6–1 mg/kg; secure **IV access before injecting** any LA
- Duration only about **60–75 min**: for bilateral repair add **ilioinguinal-iliohypogastric** block or plan an awake caudal
- **Avoid sedation**; admit overnight with **apnea monitoring** (apnea can still occur)
cards.e: Failure rates are 10–25% in infants, so a backup plan is needed. Oxford notes supplementary sedation gives the same apnea risk as GA. Lippincott adds anemia (Hct <30%), hypothermia and neurological disease as further apnea risk factors.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 74 · Oxford Handbook Ch 34 · Lippincott Ch 18

cards.q: A 2-year-old (13 kg) is booked for distal hypospadias repair as a day case. You plan a caudal block with 0.25% bupivacaine. What volume would you give, what dose ceiling applies, and what would change if a higher (lower thoracic) block were needed?
cards.a:
Hypospadias needs **sacral** dermatomes: Armitage **0.5 mL/kg = 6.5 mL** of 0.25% (16 mg, about 1.25 mg/kg).
- Maximum bupivacaine **2 mg/kg plain (26 mg)** or **3 mg/kg with epinephrine**
- For lumbar/lower thoracic cover, **1 mL/kg = 13 mL** of 0.25% = **32.5 mg (2.5 mg/kg)**: exceeds the plain limit, so use **epinephrine-containing** solution or a **more dilute** solution
- Miller advises **not exceeding 1 mL/kg** because 1.25 mL/kg can spread above T4
- Prolong analgesia with **clonidine 1–2 mcg/kg** (child is over 6 months; mild sedation, still discharge-compatible); avoid neuraxial morphine for a day case
- Prescribe regular oral analgesia for home
cards.e: Calculating both volume and mg/kg is the core safety step. Oxford dilutes to 0.19% bupivacaine above 1 mL/kg for the same reason, and Lippincott caps caudal 0.25% bupivacaine at 20 mL.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 74 · Oxford Handbook Ch 34 · Lippincott Ch 18

cards.q: A 9-year-old boy has a displaced supracondylar humeral fracture requiring closed reduction and pinning. The surgeon objects to a nerve block because it may mask compartment syndrome. How do you respond and what would you do?
cards.a:
Refusing analgesia on these grounds is **not medically or ethically acceptable**; regional analgesia **does not mask** compartment syndrome if the limb is **properly monitored** (pain is a late sign).
- He is **high risk** (displaced humeral fracture, closed reduction): agree a monitoring plan; consider **invasive compartment pressure monitoring** near the fracture
- Before the block, document nerve function: **thumbs-up (radial), "O" sign (median), finger scissoring (ulnar)**
- Block: **ultrasound-guided supraclavicular** (or axillary) with **dilute LA** to avoid dense motor block, about 0.2 mL/kg
- Postoperatively: no closed cast, elbow **not flexed beyond 90°**, regular checks of perfusion and tissue oxygenation, escalating analgesic need flagged
cards.e: The UK epidural audit recorded four compartment syndromes, none hidden by the epidural. ESRA/ASRA guidance supports regional anesthesia with appropriate monitoring.

cards.q: A 14-year-old girl with sickle cell disease has acute chest syndrome with severe localized right-sided chest wall pain despite IV opioids. Her SpO2 is 93% on 2 L/min oxygen and she is febrile (38.4 °C); blood cultures are pending. Would you offer epidural analgesia?
cards.a:
**Epidural analgesia can help** in sickle cell vaso-occlusive crises and chest syndrome if: pain is **localized**, and fever is **not due to bacteremia**.
- First exclude contraindications: **septicemia**, coagulopathy, **hypovolemia**, skin infection at site
- Fever with pending cultures: treat infection and delay neuraxial block until sepsis is excluded or effectively treated
- If proceeding: **thoracic epidural** at the appropriate level, dilute LA, careful **oxygenation** and **hydration**, avoid hypotension
- Alternatives: **ESP or paravertebral catheter** for unilateral chest pain
cards.e: In sickle cell disease desaturation provokes hemolysis and low flow promotes microthrombosis, so neuraxial blocks are avoided when hypoxemia or hemodynamic instability are likely. Miller notes that regional anesthesia has been shown to reduce pain and improve symptoms in these children.

cards.q: A 4-year-old boy scheduled for circumcision has a tuft of hair and a small dimple over the lower lumbar spine. His mother mentions occasional daytime wetting. Your registrar plans a caudal block. What is your advice?
cards.a:
Suspect **tethered cord syndrome**, which is often missed.
- Clues: **hair tuft or dystrophic skin** over the lower spine, minor **sphincter** symptoms, perineal sensory changes
- Can be screened with **ultrasound**; arrange neurological/surgical assessment
- Tethered cord is a contraindication to epidural blocks; Miller prefers an **alternative technique**
- For circumcision: **pudendal block** (0.3–0.4 mL/kg per side, nerve stimulation or ultrasound; superior analgesia) or **dorsal penile block** (0.1 mL/kg, max 5 mL per side)
- **No epinephrine** in penile or pudendal blocks
cards.e: A low-lying cord tethered to the sacrum could be injured by a caudal needle, and later neurological deterioration would be attributed to the block. Oxford notes circumcision can be managed with caudal, penile or ring block, warning parents it is very painful.

cards.q: A 12-year-old (40 kg) is having a triple arthrodesis for a rigid flatfoot. The family lives 30 minutes away and would like early discharge. Plan the regional analgesia.
cards.a:
**Continuous popliteal sciatic catheter** (first choice for major foot and ankle surgery) plus **saphenous/adductor canal** block for the medial ankle.
- Ultrasound: catheter near the sciatic bifurcation, lateral-superficial to the popliteal artery
- Infusion: **0.1–0.2% ropivacaine or levobupivacaine, 2–5 mL/h** or 2–5 mL boluses; PCRA reduces total dose
- Compared with epidural: equal analgesia with **less urinary retention, PONV and infusion failure**
- **Home management** with elastomeric or electronic pump is feasible in teenagers; popliteal is the commonest home catheter site
- Teach care of the insensate limb, LAST and infection signs; daily contact; rescue analgesia plan
cards.e: Assess compartment syndrome risk and use dilute solutions. Oxford lists popliteal sciatic among popular catheter sites and stresses carer education and a backup plan.

cards.q: A 3.2 kg neonate needs a right thoracotomy for tracheoesophageal fistula repair. Your colleague suggests threading a caudal epidural catheter to the thoracic level. Discuss the options and how you would ensure safety.
cards.a:
Options: **caudal-to-thoracic catheter**, direct thoracic epidural (expert only), **ESP** or **paravertebral** catheter.
- Caudal threading is possible because neonatal **epidural fat is fluid** and the spine has a single curve, but the tip is **misplaced in about 28–30%**
- Confirm tip position: **contrast X-ray**, **epidural stimulation test** (motor response at **1–15 mA** at the target segment), **ECG via catheter**, or **ultrasound**
- **Tunnel** the catheter away from the perineum
- Infusion: max **0.2 mg/kg/h bupivacaine equivalent** (about 0.6 mg/h); prefer **ropivacaine** (≤36 h under 3 months) or levobupivacaine
- Paravertebral: 0.5 mL/kg then 0.2–0.25 mL/kg/h; ESP avoids neuraxial risks
cards.e: A stimulation response below 1 mA would suggest subarachnoid, subdural or root contact. Oxford also suggests the caudal route as easier and possibly safer under 6 months, and to remove caudal catheters within 36 h.

cards.q: A 5 kg infant has bilateral erector spinae plane catheters after median sternotomy for congenital heart surgery. The team wants 0.5 mL/kg boluses on each side every hour. What is your concern and what regimen would you use?
cards.a:
Hourly bilateral boluses double the drug load, risking **LAST**, particularly in an infant with low AGP and possible **conduction abnormalities** after heart surgery.
- Use the **ASPIRe** regimen: **0.5 mL/kg (2.5 mL) to each catheter every 2 hours**, the sides **staggered by 1 hour**
- Overall the patient gets one bolus per hour, keeping the large volume needed for plane spread
- Use the **lowest effective concentration** (ropivacaine 0.1–0.2%); stay within max doses
- Monitor ECG (QRS width, arrhythmia) and neurology; lipid emulsion available
cards.e: ESP catheters suit anticoagulated cardiac patients because they avoid neuraxial hematoma risk. Regional analgesia after congenital heart surgery reduces pain for about 24 h but has not reduced major morbidity.

cards.q: An anesthetized 8-year-old is having a femoral nerve block using combined nerve stimulation and ultrasound. Quadriceps twitches persist at 0.3 mA and the first 1 mL is hard to inject. What do you do?
cards.a:
Both findings suggest a possible **intraneural** (even intrafascicular) needle tip.
- **Stop injecting**; high resistance suggests pressure above **15 psi (775 mm Hg)**
- **Withdraw** the needle until twitches are lost **below 0.5 mA** but present at **0.5–0.8 mA**
- Check ultrasound for needle tip within the nerve or **nerve swelling**
- Resume with low-pressure injection and look for a perineural spread ("donut")
- If using hydrodissection with ongoing stimulation, **D5W** preserves the twitch
cards.e: In children Miller advises withdrawing if a twitch is present below 0.5 mA, and responses below 0.2 mA may indicate intrafascicular placement. Oxford adds that persistent twitch after the first 1 mL also suggests intraneural placement.

cards.q: A 7-year-old (25 kg) has a midshaft femoral fracture and will be in traction before surgery. Plan regional analgesia and calculate doses using 0.2% ropivacaine.
cards.a:
**Fascia iliaca compartment block** with catheter: needs **no nerve stimulation or limb movement** and has **less vascular puncture risk**; covers femoral, LFCN and often obturator.
- Bolus **0.2–0.5 mL/kg = 5–12.5 mL** of 0.2% ropivacaine (10–25 mg); ropivacaine max **3 mg/kg = 75 mg**
- Infusion **0.1–0.2 mL/kg/h = 2.5–5 mL/h**; or **PCRA** bolus 0.1 mL/kg (2.5 mL), max 3 per hour
- Ultrasound guidance prolongs analgesia and lowers volume
- Monitor the limb for compartment syndrome; regular pain scores
cards.e: An epinephrine-containing solution lowers plasma levels for bupivacaine, but epinephrine is not recommended with ropivacaine. Compared with IV morphine, continuous fascia iliaca gives better analgesia with less sedation. Oxford stresses that the block works by placing a large volume beneath the fascia iliaca.

cards.q: A 4-year-old (16 kg) had a caudal with 0.2% ropivacaine and clonidine 1 mcg/kg for inguinal hernia repair. Thirty minutes after arrival in recovery he is drowsy but rousable, cannot stand, and his parents want to go home. What are your discharge considerations?
cards.a:
Discharge after a single-shot block uses standard post-GA criteria plus block-specific checks.
- **Partial motor recovery is mandatory**; a lively child should have **full** motor recovery before going home
- Mild **clonidine sedation** (1–3 h) does **not prevent discharge**
- Ropivacaine plasma levels may peak **up to 2 h** after caudal injection in young children, so observe in PACU for about **2 hours**
- Persisting sensory block only matters if home supervision is inadequate
- Prescribe **regular analgesics** before the block wears off; explain numbness and weakness to parents
- Had **neuraxial morphine** been given, he would need **overnight admission**
cards.e: Most children without motor block can leave within 30 minutes, but this child still has motor block. Persistent motor block can also frighten 3–5-year-olds, so reassurance helps.

cards.q: What should a complete anesthesia-to-PICU handoff contain, and why does Miller insist on a verbal, attending-level exchange?
cards.a:
A structured **attending-to-attending verbal handoff** both before and after the anesthetic, covering:
- **History**: relevant past history, **allergies**
- **Airway**: ease of **mask ventilation**, induction drugs, ease of **intubation**, plan for **extubation**
- **Access**: venous and **arterial lines**
- **Fluids**: blood products given, **fluid totals**
- **Drugs**: **inotropes**, other drugs given and the **timing of antibiotics**
- **Events**: complications, latest **laboratory values** and most recent **blood gas**
cards.e: Most of these data sit in the anesthetic record, but a brief spoken summary carries far more practical detail (for example how hard the airway really was). The flow works both ways: knowing how the child has responded to ICU therapy can simplify a difficult anesthetic, and the intraoperative course shapes the next several days of ICU care.

cards.q: How common is post-traumatic stress in parents of PICU patients, and what does Miller recommend about parental presence during CPR and invasive procedures?
cards.a:
**PTSD occurs in 10–21% of PICU parents**, and some PTSD symptoms are seen in **up to 84% of families**.
- Families should be offered the **choice to stay** during CPR and procedures; parents report benefit
- Presence **cannot be forced on staff**; both clinicians and parents need a way to **decline**
- A named person (e.g. **social worker or chaplain**) must stay with and support the family
- For procedures, someone **other than the operator** looks after the family; **junior trainees may opt out**
cards.e: Family-partnered care (part of the ICU Liberation ABCDEF bundle) includes parents on rounds, which does not lengthen rounds or harm teaching; dedicated interpreters improve engagement. More autonomy can increase parental distress, so psychologists, social workers and family therapists are part of the team. Staff resistance to family presence is falling over time.

cards.q: How should a medical error be disclosed to the family of a PICU patient, and when should palliative care be involved?
cards.a:
**Disclosure** is ethically required and is led by the **most senior clinician** (usually the ICU attending, or the medical director for complex events).
- Explain in **plain language** what happened and how, the **consequences and changes to care**, and what will be done to **prevent recurrence**
- Have the **social worker present**; stay until all questions are answered; perform a **root cause analysis** where indicated
- **Palliative care** should be consulted **early**, not only at end of life: high mortality risk, complex chronic disease, or expected major change in function
- Many PICUs use **automatic triggers**: length of PICU stay, **episodes of CPR**, **prolonged ventilation**, certain operations
cards.e: In a survey of 1018 people, 27% said they would sue after an error, but 38% would recommend the hospital if disclosure and remediation were handled well; patients who trust that errors will be disclosed are not more litigious. Futility is hard to define, but pain relief and support for the child and family are never futile.

cards.q: Why is the neonatal cardiac output so heart-rate dependent? Give the structural basis and the numbers.
cards.a:
The neonatal myocardium is **stiff and contracts inefficiently**, so stroke volume is relatively fixed.
- Shape is complete by **6 weeks' gestation**, but myofibrillar density keeps maturing through the **first year**
- Myocytes are packed with **nuclei, mitochondria and ER** for growth, i.e. more **noncontractile, nonelastic** tissue
- Low ventricular compliance: a **small rise in end-diastolic volume causes a large rise in end-diastolic pressure**
- **Frank–Starling** reserve is limited: volume loading raises output by only about **15%**; raising **heart rate** raises it much more
cards.e: This is why bradycardia is so dangerous in infants and why tachycardia is usually beneficial rather than harmful in sick neonates. Stoelting makes the same point: heart rate is the main determinant of cardiac output and blood pressure in neonates and young infants because stroke volume is relatively fixed.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 75 · Stoelting 7e Ch 30 · Oxford Handbook Ch 34

cards.q: List the four features of the fetal circulation and the five changes that convert it to the adult series circulation at birth.
cards.a:
**Fetal**: (1) **placenta** is the gas-exchange organ, (2) **high PVR**, (3) **low SVR**, (4) ventricles work **in parallel** with **right ventricular dominance**; shunts are the **ductus arteriosus, ductus venosus and foramen ovale**.
**Transition**:
- **First breath**: lung expansion, higher alveolar O2, rising pH, NO and other mediators **drop PVR**
- **Placental separation**: placental vessels constrict, so **SVR and LV afterload rise**
- LA pressure exceeds RA pressure, **functionally closing the foramen ovale** (flap valve)
- Falling PVR **reverses ductal flow**; oxygenated blood plus a rapid fall in **PGE2** closes the **ductus**
- **Ductus venosus** closes passively; PVR then falls further over months to years as the **muscular arterial layer thins** and extends peripherally
cards.e: Fetal blood O2 content is about 20 mL/dL, similar to an adult, because of a high concentration of high-affinity hemoglobin. The foramen ovale may stay anatomically open for months to years and is patent in at least 15% of adults; anatomic ductal closure takes several weeks (Stoelting: functional closure at 10–15 h, anatomic at 4–6 weeks). Hypoxia, acidosis and hypercarbia can reopen these channels and restore right-to-left shunting.
cards.s: Miller 10e Ch 75 · Stoelting 7e Ch 30 · Lippincott Ch 18

cards.q: Describe the maturity of autonomic cardiovascular control in the newborn.
cards.a:
**Parasympathetic dominance** with an immature sympathetic system.
- Adrenergic innervation of the heart is complete at **18–28 weeks' gestation**, but newborns have **low myocardial norepinephrine stores** and fewer sympathetic nerves
- Fetal heart is **more sensitive to exogenous norepinephrine**; adrenergic responses are present but **blunted**
- **Cholinergic system fully developed** at birth: the heart is vagally sensitive, so **bradycardia** is the typical response to increased autonomic tone
- **Baroreflex present but incompletely developed** at term; preterm infants show no HR change with posture
- **Chemoreceptor** response is mature in utero: hypoxia produces **fetal bradycardia** (an O2-conserving, diving-type reflex)
cards.e: Clinically, hypoxia in a neonate presents as bradycardia rather than tachycardia, and the treatment is oxygenation rather than atropine (Oxford makes the same point). Note: Oxford describes autonomic and baroreceptor control as fully functional at term; follow Miller.

cards.q: Why is the newborn heart relatively resistant to hypoxia, and how does neonatal oxygen consumption change after birth?
cards.a:
High **myocardial glycogen** and efficient **anaerobic metabolism** make the fetal/newborn heart tolerant of hypoxia and **easier to resuscitate** if oxygenation and perfusion are restored quickly.
- O2 consumption rises steeply after birth because the baby must now **thermoregulate**
- Term infant in a neutral thermal environment: about **6 mL/kg/min**, rising to **7 mL/kg/min at 10 days** and **8 mL/kg/min at 4 weeks**
cards.e: The high oxygen consumption, together with a small FRC, explains rapid desaturation during apnea in infants (Oxford gives roughly 7 vs 3 mL/kg/min for neonate vs adult and notes children become cyanosed faster). The hypoxic tolerance of the myocardium is not a licence for delay; it simply means prompt reoxygenation often succeeds.

cards.q: Classify the common congenital heart lesions that present in the newborn (Box 75.1).
cards.a:
Two presentations: **cyanosis** or **congestive heart failure**.
- **Cyanotic**: **tetralogy of Fallot**, **TGA**, **HLHS**, **pulmonary atresia (intact septum)**, **single ventricle**, **TAPVR**, **tricuspid atresia**
- **CHF**: **VSD**, **PDA**, **critical aortic stenosis**, **coarctation of the aorta**
cards.e: Miller also frames CHD physiologically as hypoxic lesions (right-sided obstructions such as tricuspid or pulmonary stenosis/atresia and tetralogy) versus normoxic lesions (left-sided obstructions and left-to-right shunts). Diagnosis relies on fetal echo, then examination, ECG, chest radiograph and echocardiography; MRI defines anatomy before surgery and catheterization is mainly interventional.

cards.q: Why do symptoms of a large VSD often appear only after several weeks, and what are the signs of CHF in a newborn?
cards.a:
Left-to-right shunt grows as **PVR falls toward adult levels** over the first weeks to months.
- Many neonates with a big VSD have **little shunt for several weeks**; intraoperative **alkalosis** (lowering PVR) can unmask it
- **Signs of CHF**: **poor feeding**, irritability, **sweating**, **tachycardia**, **tachypnea** (often without retractions), weak peripheral pulses, poor skin perfusion, **hepatomegaly**
- Cyanosis is not always cardiac: consider **lung disease**, **persistent pulmonary hypertension** and **methemoglobinemia**
cards.e: The anesthetic trap is hyperventilation and high FiO2: both lower PVR and can flood the lungs in a child with a large unrestrictive shunt. Initial treatment of CHD aims to relieve CHF, improve systemic perfusion and maintain pulmonary blood flow.

cards.q: Which neonatal lesions are duct-dependent, and how is prostaglandin E1 used?
cards.a:
**PGE1 infusion at about 0.1 mcg/kg/min** keeps the ductus open and can **reopen** a recently closed duct.
- **Duct-dependent systemic flow**: **hypoplastic left heart**, **critical aortic stenosis/atresia**, **interrupted aortic arch**, symptomatic **neonatal coarctation**
- **Duct-dependent pulmonary flow**: **pulmonary atresia**, **critical pulmonary stenosis**
- Common side effects: **apnea, fever, hypotension**
cards.e: PGE1 acts directly on vascular smooth muscle and keeps these babies alive until surgical or catheter palliation. Apnea is the anesthetic concern: a neonate on PGE1 may need airway support before transfer or surgery.

cards.q: Write the equations for arterial oxygen content, oxygen delivery and oxygen extraction, and explain the concept of critical oxygen delivery.
cards.a:
**CaO2 = (1.34 × Hb × SaO2) + (0.003 × PaO2)**, normally about **20 mL/dL**.
- **DO2 = CaO2 × CO × 0.01** (CaO2 in mL/dL, CO in mL/min, giving DO2 in mL/min)
- **VO2 = DO2 × O2 extraction**; **O2EX = (CaO2 − CvO2)/CaO2**
- Normal arteriovenous content difference **4–6 mL/dL**; infant/young child **VO2 about 175 mL/min/m2**
- Above a **critical DO2**, VO2 is **independent** of delivery (extraction rises); **below it VO2 becomes supply-dependent** and anaerobic metabolism begins
cards.e: Shock is defined as failure to deliver enough oxygen to meet tissue demand. When delivery falls, the body sheds nonessential metabolism (growth, thermoregulation, neurotransmitter synthesis) and uses sympathetic vasoconstriction to divert flow from kidney, gut, skin and muscle (high flow relative to need) toward the brain and heart.

cards.q: Classify shock in children with examples of each category.
cards.a:
Four categories (one condition may fit more than one):
- **Hypovolemic**: hemorrhage; nonhemorrhagic losses (vomiting, diarrhea, polyuria, poor intake); redistribution in **burns, trauma, anaphylaxis**
- **Cardiogenic** (pump failure): absolute (**myocarditis, cardiomyopathy**) or relative (valve regurgitation); by convention **intracardiac obstruction** (valve stenosis) and significant **arrhythmias** belong here
- **Extracardiac obstructive**: tension **pneumothorax**, **tamponade**, constrictive pericarditis, mediastinal mass (preload); **pulmonary hypertension, PE, coarctation, aortic dissection** (ejection)
- **Distributive**: low SVR with maldistributed flow: **sepsis**, toxic shock, **anaphylaxis**, SIRS, **spinal (neurogenic) shock**, **adrenal insufficiency**
cards.e: In distributive shock the cardiac output may be high yet blood pressure low because SVR is so reduced. Oxford uses the same broad categories (cardiogenic, distributive, obstructive, hypovolemic).

cards.q: Why is hypotension an unreliable early sign of shock in children, and what should the bedside assessment include?
cards.a:
Children **maintain blood pressure until shock is advanced**; **hypotension marks late, decompensated shock**.
- Early signs: **reduced activity**, **tachycardia**, **cold peripheries**, **slow capillary refill**; in distributive (warm) shock there may be **only tachycardia** with warm skin
- Examine: alertness, peripheral perfusion, mucous membranes, pulse rate and volume, respiratory effort, **urine output**, BP
- **Metabolic acidosis may be absent** on the first tests; cardiogenic shock may present only as vague lethargy
cards.e: A high index of suspicion is essential. History often reveals volume losses, and fever, rash and irritability suggest infection. Compensated shock can look deceptively normal, so trends matter more than a single value.

cards.q: What compensatory mechanisms maintain tissue perfusion in early shock?
cards.a:
Neurohumoral and tissue-level responses:
- Fluid shifts from **intracellular and interstitial spaces into the vasculature**
- **GFR falls**; **aldosterone and vasopressin** limit renal losses
- **Sympathetic activation and epinephrine release**: reduced **venous capacitance**, **tachycardia**, **increased contractility**, diversion of flow from nonvital organs
- Tissue O2 unloading increases with higher **RBC 2,3-DPG**, **fever** and **tissue acidosis** (right shift of the dissociation curve)
cards.e: These mechanisms explain why BP is preserved for so long in children. Treatment aims to correct the cause, restore oxygen delivery and clear the products of anaerobic metabolism; the faster perfusion is restored, the better the outcome.

cards.q: Summarize the 2020 Surviving Sepsis Campaign pediatric recommendations most relevant to anesthesiologists.
cards.a:
Key themes: **early recognition, early antimicrobials, source control**, judicious fluids, vasoactives, lung support and avoiding fluid overload.
- Fluid of choice: **buffered/balanced crystalloid** rather than **albumin, 0.9% saline, starches or gelatins**
- In **resource-limited settings without ICU**, use a **more restrictive** fluid plan in normotensive children
- No single first-line vasoactive, but **epinephrine or norepinephrine preferred over dopamine**
- **Avoid etomidate** for induction in sepsis
- **Hydrocortisone** for **fluid- and vasopressor-refractory** shock
- Sepsis-related PARDS: **high PEEP**, trial of **prone positioning**, **neuromuscular blockade** in severe disease
cards.e: Pediatric sepsis incidence is estimated at about 22 per 100,000 person-years, and systematic screening drives early treatment. Note: Oxford advises 20 mL/kg crystalloid or colloid boluses; follow Miller and use buffered crystalloid.

cards.q: What are the end points of resuscitation in pediatric septic shock, and can vasoactive drugs be started peripherally?
cards.a:
Clinical end points: **urine output >1 mL/kg/h**, **improved mental status**, **age-appropriate vital signs**, **better peripheral perfusion**.
- Because bedside signs are limited, add **serial lactate**, **arteriovenous O2 gradients**, **ScvO2 trends** and **point-of-care ultrasound**
